Name: counterfactual_biophysics_probe
Title: Do Protein Language Models Represent Causal Biophysical Mechanisms or Just Evolutionary Correlations? A Counterfactual Mutational Test
Short Hypothesis: If a protein language model's internal features encode genuine biophysical mechanisms (e.g., hydrophobicity-driven core packing, charge complementarity at salt bridges, disulfide bonding geometry), then targeted point mutations that physically break a mechanism will causally deactivate the corresponding internal feature in a manner predicted by the physics, whereas mutations that only alter evolutionary conservation but preserve the mechanism will not. Distinguishing mechanistic from merely correlational representations is the key open question left by existing annotation-matching interpretability work.
Related Work: A rapidly growing body of work (InterPLM, ProtSAE, Matryoshka SAEs on ESM2-3B, Automated Neuron Labelling, ProtoMech circuit tracing, and the 2026 review 'What Do Biological Foundation Models Compute?') applies sparse autoencoders and probes to protein language models and finds features matching known annotations (binding sites, secondary structure, GO terms). Crucially, that review explicitly identifies a 'critical gap': validation relies almost exclusively on matching features against existing annotations, risking circularity because those annotations derive from the same evolutionary sequences the model was trained on. Zhang et al. (categorical Jacobian) showed ESM-2 stores coevolutionary statistics like a Markov Random Field, hinting that some 'structural' knowledge is actually correlational. No prior work causally tests whether recovered features track the underlying *physical mechanism* versus evolutionary co-occurrence. Our proposal directly closes this gap with a counterfactual, physics-grounded intervention protocol rather than more annotation matching.
Abstract: Foundation models of protein sequence encode features that correlate with known biological concepts, but a fundamental ambiguity remains: do these features represent the causal biophysical mechanisms underlying structure and function, or merely the evolutionary statistics that happen to accompany them? Because the annotations used to validate interpretability are themselves derived from evolutionary data, existing evidence cannot separate the two. We propose a counterfactual mutational framework to resolve this. We first identify interpretable features (via sparse autoencoders and linear probes on ESM-2) that align with three physically well-understood mechanisms: hydrophobic core packing, salt-bridge electrostatics, and disulfide bonding. We then design paired in-silico mutations: (1) mechanism-breaking mutations that physically abolish the interaction (e.g., mutating a buried hydrophobic residue to a charged one, neutralizing a salt-bridge partner, or removing one cysteine of a disulfide pair), and (2) mechanism-preserving control mutations that change conservation/evolutionary signal by comparable amounts but keep the physical mechanism intact (e.g., conservative hydrophobic-to-hydrophobic substitutions, or charge-swapping both partners of a salt bridge to preserve complementarity). If features are mechanistic, feature activation should drop specifically for mechanism-breaking mutations and follow quantitative physical predictions (e.g., magnitude scaling with hydrophobicity change or Coulombic energy). We quantify mechanism-selectivity, dose-response to physical parameters, and agreement with molecular-mechanics energy estimates. This yields the first causal, physics-grounded test of whether biological foundation models learn mechanisms or correlations, with direct implications for their trustworthiness in variant-effect prediction and design.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Mechanism-feature identification and baseline correspondence): Tests the H1 sub-claim that ESM-2 residue activations carry identifiable features corresponding to three biophysical mechanisms (buried hydrophobic core packing, salt-bridge charge complementarity, disulfide geometry). Data: high-resolution X-ray structures from the PDB (~200k structures with resolution <2.0 Å exist); we use a PISCES-culled non-redundant set of 1,000 chains (≤25% pairwise sequence identity, resolution <2.0 Å, R-free <0.25), split 600 train / 200 validation / 200 test by chain — 1,000 is chosen because it yields ~250k labeled residues, enough to fit probes/SAEs, while the identity cull prevents homolog leakage; more chains add compute without new mechanism types. Ground-truth per-residue labels from DSSP + Reduce: buried hydrophobic (relative solvent accessibility <0.1 AND residue in {Leu,Ile,Val,Phe,Met}), salt bridge (oppositely-charged side-chain N/O atoms within 4.0 Å), disulfide (S–S <2.5 Å). Model: ESM-2 150M and 650M, backbone frozen; trainable = per-layer sparse autoencoders (dictionary size 8,192, L1 penalty 1e-3, Adam lr 1e-3, 100 epochs) and L2-logistic linear probes, fit on activations from every 6th layer; 3 seeds. Systems compared: SAE top-feature vs supervised linear probe vs matched-norm random-direction control. Decisive metric first: held-out test AUROC of the best probe and F1 of the best-matching SAE feature, per mechanism. Convincing result: AUROC ≥ 0.90 with one identifiable feature/direction per mechanism at some layer. Undecidable band: AUROC in [0.70, 0.80] — a mechanism whose best readout lands here is too weakly localized for a clean causal test, so it is reported as inconclusive and dropped from Experiments 2–4; this band call is fixed before running. Negative result: all three mechanisms below 0.70 AUROC means ESM-2 carries no identifiable mechanism feature, H1 fails, and H2/H3 are moot.

Experiment 2 (H2 — Counterfactual mechanism-breaking vs conservation-matched-preserving causal test): Tests the H2 sub-claim that mutations physically breaking a mechanism deactivate its feature while mutations that shift only evolutionary conservation but preserve the mechanism do not. Data: from the 200 test chains of Experiment 1, curate 300 proteins carrying at least one clean instance of each mechanism (300 chosen to give ~100 paired sites per mechanism at 3 seeds, feasible on one GPU; fewer would underpower the paired test). For each site build three in-silico single/double point mutations: (i) mechanism-breaking (buried Leu/Ile/Val/Phe→Asp/Lys; charge removal of one salt-bridge partner; Cys→Ser removing one disulfide partner), (ii) mechanism-preserving physical control (hydrophobic→similar-volume hydrophobic; simultaneous Asp–Lys→Lys–Asp swap keeping complementarity), (iii) conservation-matched control whose BLOSUM62/PSSM conservation change equals the breaking mutation's but leaves the physical mechanism intact. Model: same frozen ESM-2 150M/650M and the fixed Experiment-1 feature directions; no new training; 3 seeds over mutation sampling. Systems compared: Δ feature activation at the mutated residue and its partner for breaking vs physical-preserving vs conservation-matched. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity index S = |Δ_break| / |Δ_preserve| (paired across sites, Wilcoxon signed-rank). Convincing result: S significantly > 1 for all tested mechanisms AND breaking > conservation-matched (showing the effect is physical, not conservation-driven). Undecidable band: S in [0.9, 1.3] — a mechanism landing here shows no reliable break-vs-preserve separation, read as "feature is correlational for that mechanism" (H2 not supported there); band fixed before data. Negative result: S ≈ 1 across mechanisms, or breaking indistinguishable from conservation-matched, means the features are correlational rather than mechanistic and H2 fails.

Experiment 3 (H3 — Physics dose-response and molecular-mechanics agreement): Tests the H3 sub-claim that feature deactivation is quantitatively predicted by the physics, not merely present. Data: the same 300 proteins / paired mutations from Experiment 2, plus per-mutation physical quantities computed once: Kyte–Doolittle hydrophobicity change and buried-surface-area change (hydrophobic), Coulombic interaction energy from geometry (salt bridge), and a geometric bonding indicator (disulfide); plus FoldX ΔΔG (single point-mutation ΔΔG, 5 FoldX runs averaged) for every mutation. Model: frozen ESM-2 650M with fixed Experiment-1 directions; no training. Systems compared: correlation of Δ feature activation with the physical quantity for mechanism-breaking mutations vs conservation-matched controls. Decisive metric first: Spearman ρ between Δ activation and the physical driver (per mechanism), and ΔR² of feature change in predicting FoldX ΔΔG for breaking vs conservation-matched mutations. Convincing result: monotone dose-response ρ ≥ 0.5 for breaking mutations AND feature change predicts ΔΔG significantly better for breaking than conservation-matched (ΔR² > 0). Undecidable band: |ρ| in [0.2, 0.35] — weak, physics-consistent-but-not-decisive coupling; a mechanism here is reported as "partially mechanistic" and not counted as H3 support; band fixed in advance. Negative result: ρ near 0 or no monotonicity, and no ΔΔG-prediction advantage over conservation-matched controls, means the representation tracks category not physics, so H3 fails even if H2's binary selectivity held.

Experiment 4 (H1/H2 — Coevolution and PSSM baselines rule out statistics-only explanation): Tests that any observed mechanism-selectivity (H1 features, H2 causal drops) is not explained by coevolutionary statistics alone. Data: for the 300-protein set, compute categorical-Jacobian coevolution couplings from ESM-2 and PSSM/MSA statistics (MSAs from ColabFold's UniRef30 search; existing, no new data). Model: frozen ESM-2; baselines are statistical readouts, not trained networks. Systems compared: mechanism-selectivity index S (Experiment 2) and dose-response ρ (Experiment 3) computed from model features vs from coevolution-coupling features vs PSSM features. Decisive metric first: gap ΔS = S(model feature) − S(coevolution feature). Convincing result: ΔS significantly > 0 — the model's causal selectivity exceeds what couplings/PSSM reproduce. Undecidable band: ΔS in [−0.1, 0.2] — model and coevolution indistinguishable, meaning the apparent mechanism signal is attributable to statistics; band fixed before data and read as failing to isolate a model-specific mechanism. Negative result: coevolution matches or exceeds the model's selectivity, so the earlier positive H1/H2 signals do not demonstrate a representation beyond evolutionary statistics.

Experiment 5 (H1/H2 — Layer and scale trajectory of mechanism-selectivity): Tests where the mechanism representation lives and whether scaling makes ESM-2 more mechanistic or more correlational, sharpening rather than enlarging H1/H2. Data: reuse Experiment 1–2 sites; no new data. Model: frozen ESM-2 150M and 650M as main study, with 3B as a compute-permitting extension (SAE on 3B activations is the expensive step; probes on 3B are cheap and always run); every layer's probe AUROC and Experiment-2 selectivity S recorded; 3 seeds. Systems compared: per-layer and per-scale S and AUROC. Decisive metric first: layer of peak S and the sign of the 150M→650M(→3B) trend in peak S. Convincing result: a consistent, reproducible layer band where S peaks, with a monotone scale trend interpretable as more-mechanistic (S rising) or more-correlational (S falling). Undecidable band: |scale slope of peak S| within its 3-seed standard error — reported as "no scale effect", not evidence either way. Negative result: no reproducible peak layer (S within noise across depth) means the earlier selectivity is not stably localized and weakens confidence in H1/H2 rather than adding scope.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Confound: buried-charged mutations also disrupt evolutionary statistics, so mechanism-preserving controls must be carefully matched on conservation change; if matching is imperfect, causal attribution weakens. We mitigate with explicit conservation-matched control mutations.
Features may be distributed/superposed such that no single feature cleanly maps to one mechanism; we address this using both SAE features and probe directions and reporting aggregate directions.
Molecular-mechanics ddG estimates (FoldX) are approximate and may be noisy, limiting the strength of the physics-agreement comparison.

Results may reveal that models are largely correlational; while scientifically valuable, this could be seen as a negative result — we frame it as a definitive answer either way with implications for variant-effect trust.
Access to ESM-2 3B and structure datasets is feasible for an academic lab, but running SAEs on 3B activations is compute-heavy; we scope the main study to 150M/650M with 3B as an extension.

The main novelty is in the mechanism/test, not the setting or dataset. Relative to SAE/probe work on ESM-2, the delta is a counterfactual, physics-grounded intervention protocol with explicit controls against evolutionary-statistics explanations. Name: periodic_law_probe
Title: Do Foundation-Model Interatomic Potentials Internally Reconstruct the Periodic Law? A Causal Test of Chemical-Trend Representations and Their Link to Out-of-Distribution Failure
Short Hypothesis: Universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) trained on broad materials/molecular data internally organize element embeddings and per-atom feature spaces along the same low-dimensional axes as the periodic law (period, group, electronegativity, atomic radius, valence). We hypothesize that (a) these axes are recoverable and causally load-bearing (perturbing them along a 'chemical trend' direction shifts predictions in the physically-correct direction), and (b) an element's or environment's distance from the model's learned periodic manifold quantitatively predicts where the model extrapolates unreliably. If true, this gives a mechanism-grounded, physics-interpretable failure detector; if false, it shows foundation MLIPs rely on non-transferable memorized statistics.
Related Work: Schutt et al. (2018) showed atomistic NN element embeddings partially recover periodic-table ordering, and 'From Neurons to Neutrons' (2024) found helical embeddings encoding nuclear physics. GNN-LRP work decomposes MLIP energies into physically-consistent n-body terms; 'Beyond Converging Representations' (2025) shows scientific foundation models align and collapse to low-information representations far from training data. These works either (i) match learned features to known chemistry descriptively, or (ii) study alignment/convergence globally. None causally tests whether the periodic-law structure inside modern *universal foundation MLIPs* (MACE-MP-0, Orb, SevenNet, CHGNet, EquiformerV2 trained on Materials Project/OMat) is load-bearing, nor connects the geometry of that internal chemical manifold to concrete out-of-distribution (OOD) failure prediction. Our causal-intervention plus failure-prediction framing is the novel contribution, moving beyond descriptive trend-matching to a predictive, mechanism-grounded diagnostic.
Abstract: The periodic law compresses the chemistry of the elements into a handful of transferable trends. We ask whether modern universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs), now used as chemistry/materials foundation models, internally rediscover these trends and, crucially, whether that internal structure is causally responsible for their predictions and predictive of their failures. Prior interpretability work has descriptively noted periodic-table-like structure in atomistic embeddings, but has not tested whether such structure is load-bearing or whether its geometry governs out-of-distribution reliability. We probe several pretrained foundation MLIPs (e.g., MACE-MP-0, CHGNet, Orb, SevenNet) at both the element-embedding and per-atom-feature level. We first recover, via linear probes and manifold learning, directions encoding period, group, electronegativity, covalent radius, and valence, quantifying how faithfully the learned chemical manifold matches the true periodic table. We then perform causal interventions: steering an atom's internal representation along a recovered 'electronegativity' or 'radius' direction should shift predicted energies, forces, and charges in the physically-correct, quantitatively-scaled direction; scrambling the direction should not. Finally, we test whether an atom's or structure's distance from the learned periodic manifold predicts per-structure error on held-out and deliberately OOD systems (rare elements, unusual oxidation states, exotic coordination), yielding a physics-interpretable, calibration-free failure detector. The result is a causal, mechanism-grounded account of whether foundation MLIPs learn the periodic law or memorize training statistics, with direct implications for their safe deployment in materials discovery.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Recovering the periodic manifold from embeddings and atom features): Tests the H1 claim that universal MLIPs organize element embeddings and per-atom features along periodic-law axes (period, group, Pauling electronegativity, covalent radius, valence-electron count, first ionization energy). Data: 5,000 structures sampled from the Materials Project (~150k materials exist) and QM9 (134k molecules exist), stratified to cover all 89 elements up to Bi plus a rare-element tail; 5,000 is chosen so every element appears ≥30 times for stable per-element statistics while keeping activation extraction to a few GPU-hours — more structures repeat element contexts without adding periodic coverage. Ground-truth periodic descriptors are tabulated constants (Mendeleev/pymatgen). Model: four pretrained foundation MLIPs with public weights — MACE-MP-0, CHGNet, Orb, SevenNet — all frozen, inference only; trainable = ridge linear probes and partial-least-squares maps on the invariant scalar channels of element embeddings and per-atom features, per layer; 5 CV folds, 3 seeds. Systems compared: probe on model features vs probe on a random-permutation of the same features (destroying element identity) as a floor. Decisive metric first: held-out probe R² for each descriptor, averaged over folds. Convincing result: R² ≥ 0.8 for group/period/electronegativity in at least one layer of each model, and a 2-D PCA that visibly reproduces periodic-table row/column topology. Undecidable band: R² in [0.4, 0.6] for a descriptor — present but weak structure; such a descriptor is not used as a steering axis in Experiment 2 and is reported as partially encoded; band fixed before data. Negative result: R² < 0.4 across descriptors and models means the periodic law is not linearly recoverable, H1 fails, and the causal/failure tests targeting recovered directions are moot.

Experiment 2 (H2 — Causal steering along chemical-trend directions): Tests the H2(a) claim that recovered periodic axes are causally load-bearing — perturbing a per-atom representation along an electronegativity or covalent-radius direction shifts energy/force/charge predictions in the physically-correct direction. Data: 500 structures from the Experiment-1 test split spanning diverse coordination environments (500 keeps the α-sweep × seed × structure grid affordable; each structure yields many atoms, so this is ample). Model: the four frozen MLIPs with the fixed Experiment-1 unit directions; steering adds ±α·(unit direction) to a target atom's invariant channels at the best-R² layer, α swept over {0.25,0.5,1,2}× the per-channel activation std; 3 seeds. Systems compared: true-direction steering vs matched-norm random/scrambled-direction control. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity index M = |Δoutput along true direction| / |Δoutput along random direction|, plus sign-consistency (fraction of atoms whose predicted change has the physically-expected sign) and monotonicity of Δoutput in α. Convincing result: M ≥ 3 with sign-consistency ≥ 0.8 and monotone dose-response in at least one model. Undecidable band: M in [1.2, 2.0] or sign-consistency in [0.55, 0.65] — weak causal use, reported as inconclusive for that model/axis; band fixed before data. Negative result: M ≈ 1 or chance sign-consistency means recovered axes are decodable but not causal, so H2(a) fails even where H1 held.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Trend-swap counterfactual by element-embedding substitution): Tests H2(a) with a discrete, interpretable intervention — replacing a target element's embedding with a same-group neighbor's (e.g., Na→K, Cl→Br) should move predictions along the true periodic trend. Data: 40 same-group substitution pairs across groups 1, 2, 13–17 applied to 300 host structures where the substituted site is chemically sensible (300 hosts × 40 pairs is tractable; hosts drawn from the Experiment-1 set). Ground-truth trend deltas from experimental/DFT tables (ionization energy, covalent radius). Model: four frozen MLIPs; embedding table entry swapped, no retraining; 3 seeds over host sampling. Systems compared: predicted property delta under true-neighbor swap vs under a random-element swap of matched embedding-norm. Decisive metric first: Spearman ρ between predicted deltas and true periodic-trend deltas across substitutions. Convincing result: ρ ≥ 0.6 for true-neighbor swaps and near-zero for random swaps. Undecidable band: ρ in [0.3, 0.45] — directionally suggestive but not decisive, reported as partial support; band fixed in advance. Negative result: ρ ≈ 0 means embedding geometry does not carry usable trend structure, reinforcing an H2 failure.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Manifold-distance predicts extrapolation failure): Tests the H3(b) claim that an atom's/structure's distance from the learned periodic manifold predicts where force/energy error is large. Data: (a) held-out in-distribution MP/QM9 structures with existing DFT labels, 2,000 structures; (b) deliberately OOD sets with published DFT references — rare-element compounds, unusual oxidation states, exotic coordination, high-pressure phases — 1,000 structures assembled from existing benchmark subsets (e.g., MPtrj tails, Matbench rare splits); we reuse existing DFT labels only, no new DFT, to stay in academic budget. Model: four frozen MLIPs; manifold distance = reconstruction residual from the Experiment-1 low-dimensional chemical subspace and Mahalanobis distance in probe space; no training beyond the fitted subspace. Systems compared: manifold distance vs generic baselines — embedding norm, deep-ensemble variance, feature-space kNN distance. Decisive metric first: AUROC for flagging the top-decile-error structures, and Spearman ρ between distance and per-structure force MAE. Convincing result: manifold-distance AUROC ≥ 0.75 AND exceeds every baseline's AUROC by ≥ 0.05. Undecidable band: AUROC within 0.03 of the best baseline — no physics-specific advantage, reported as "not distinguishable from generic OOD detection"; band fixed before data. Negative result: manifold distance at chance (AUROC ≤ 0.55) or below baselines means periodic geometry is not a failure detector and H3 fails.

Experiment 5 (H1 — Cross-model convergence of the periodic subspace): Tests whether the recovered periodic structure is a convergent property (strengthening H1's generality, not enlarging it). Data: the Experiment-1 activations for all four models on the shared 5,000 structures. Model: four frozen MLIPs; no training beyond CKA/Procrustes alignment of the fitted chemical subspaces. Systems compared: linear CKA between each model pair's periodic subspace vs CKA between a model's periodic subspace and a random subspace of equal dimension. Decisive metric first: mean pairwise CKA of periodic subspaces. Convincing result: CKA ≥ 0.6 across pairs, well above the random-subspace floor. Undecidable band: CKA in [0.3, 0.45] — partial alignment, reported as weakly convergent; band fixed before data. Negative result: CKA near the random floor means each model encodes an idiosyncratic representation, so convergence is not supported (does not by itself refute per-model H1).

Experiment 6 (H1/H2 — Scale and training-breadth ablation): Tests whether periodic-manifold faithfulness and its causal load-bearing-ness grow with model scale/data breadth. Data: the Experiment-1/2 splits. Model: frozen MLIP variants that differ only in scale or training set where public — MACE-MP-0 size variants and MP-trained vs OMat-trained checkpoints; probes/steering re-run identically; 3 seeds. Systems compared: Experiment-1 probe R² and Experiment-2 selectivity M across the ordered variants. Decisive metric first: sign and magnitude of the R²-vs-scale and M-vs-scale slopes. Convincing result: monotone positive slopes reproducible across seeds, indicating scale/breadth increases periodic faithfulness and causal use. Undecidable band: |slope| within its 3-seed standard error — reported as no scale effect. Negative result: flat or negative slopes mean broader training does not buy more periodic-law structure, an informative bound on H1/H2 rather than a contradiction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Probe recovery of a direction does not guarantee causal use; we mitigate with steering interventions and random-direction controls, but distributed/superposed encodings may weaken clean single-direction effects.
Steering in a nonlinear equivariant network may push representations off-manifold, producing uninterpretable outputs; we bound alpha to stay near the data manifold and report sensitivity to alpha.
Equivariance constraints mean per-atom features are tensorial; probing must respect invariant vs equivariant channels, adding methodological care (we focus probes on invariant scalar channels first).

Manifold-distance may correlate with error simply through data density rather than genuine periodic-law geometry; we control against generic OOD detectors (kNN, ensemble variance) to isolate the physics-grounded signal.

A negative result (models memorize statistics rather than encode transferable periodic trends) is scientifically informative but may be perceived as less exciting; we frame either outcome as a decisive, deployment-relevant finding.
Ground-truth OOD errors require DFT reference labels; we rely on existing labeled benchmark subsets and published DFT to keep costs within an academic budget.

novelty.reasoning: Core novel claims: (1) modern universal MLIPs internally recover periodic-law axes in element embeddings/per-atom features; (2) those axes are causally load-bearing, so steering along learned chemical-trend directions changes outputs in the physically correct direction; (3) distance from the learned periodic manifold predicts OOD failure; (4) this is tested in foundation MLIPs rather than older atomistic NNs. The setting is meaningfully updated, but descriptive recovery of periodic structure is already known, and embedding-geometry-to-reliability also has overlap with recent MLIP OOD work. The real delta is the causal intervention plus the explicit link from chemical-manifold geometry to failure prediction. That is non-trivial, but still an incremental extension of known representation-analysis and OOD-geometry findings rather than a wholly new theory or task.

Who cares: researchers and practitioners using foundation MLIPs for materials discovery, screening, and surrogate DFT. review.reasoning: The hypothesis is testable but currently overpacked. There are multiple claims bundled together: representation recovery, causal use, trend-swap counterfactuals, and OOD prediction. Some are more precise than others; the causal claim risks ambiguity because steering a latent direction may alter outputs without proving the model 'uses' periodic law. Name: conservation_law_manifold_probe
Title: Do Physics Foundation Models Obey the Laws They Encode? Probing Conservation Constraints and Lawful Coupling in Internal Representations
Short Hypothesis: Physics foundation models (neural PDE surrogates trained across many systems) are known to linearly encode individual physical quantities like energy or vorticity. We hypothesize the deeper, untested question is relational: does the model's internal representation over a rollout obey the *constraints* that link these quantities — i.e., conserving conserved quantities (energy, mass, momentum) and coupling non-conserved ones along physically-lawful directions (equation-of-state, advection)? If the internal state lives on a conservation-constrained manifold, causal interventions that respect a conservation law should be tolerated while those that violate it should be resisted or corrected; if the model merely stores independently-decodable features, no such structure will exist.
Related Work: Recent interpretability work shows physics/LLM foundation models linearly encode single physical concepts and that these are causally load-bearing: 'Physics Steering' (2025) extracts steerable directions for vorticity/diffusion/speed that transfer across systems; 'Uncovering Emergent Physics Representations Learned In-Context by LLMs' (2025) finds SAE features correlating with energy whose ablation degrades forecasting; 'From Neurons to Neutrons' (2024) recovers the semi-empirical mass formula; 'Deep learning of thermodynamic laws' (2025) and Siamese-network invariant discovery (2020) show networks can learn entropy/invariants from data. All of these establish that a quantity is *encoded and matters*. None tests whether the model's representation respects the *relationships and conservation constraints* that tie multiple quantities together — i.e., whether physics is stored as a consistent constrained manifold vs. a bag of separable features. Our conservation-consistency and lawful-coupling tests, and the causal 'Noether test' (constraint-respecting vs constraint-violating interventions), are the novel contribution.
Abstract: Neural PDE foundation models trained across many physical systems have recently been shown to linearly encode individual physical quantities such as energy and vorticity, and to allow causal steering of these features. Yet physics is not a list of independent quantities: it is defined by the constraints and functional relationships among them — conservation of energy, mass, and momentum, and lawful couplings like an equation of state. We ask whether physics foundation models internally respect these relationships, or merely store separately-decodable features. We probe pretrained multi-physics surrogates (e.g., Poseidon, Multiple-Physics-Pretraining, DPOT) on standard PDE benchmarks (Navier-Stokes, shallow water, diffusion-reaction, compressible flow). First, we train linear probes for conserved quantities and test conservation-consistency: does the *probed* value stay constant across autoregressive rollout steps for genuinely conserving systems, and drift lawfully when forcing/dissipation is present? Second, we test lawful coupling: steering one quantity (e.g., temperature) should shift a coupled quantity (e.g., pressure) along the correct equation-of-state direction, not arbitrarily. Third, we introduce a causal 'Noether test': interventions along a conservation-preserving direction should be tolerated (small downstream error, conserved quantity intact), while equal-magnitude conservation-violating interventions should incur larger downstream error or be spontaneously corrected by the model. Metrics quantify conservation drift, coupling-direction alignment, and asymmetry between lawful and unlawful interventions. This yields the first test of whether physics foundation models learn constrained, mechanism-consistent manifolds, with direct implications for their reliability as scientific simulators.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Conserved-quantity encoding and internal conservation-drift): Tests the H1 claim that, in genuinely conserving regimes, the model's internal state keeps the conserved quantities (energy, mass, momentum) constant over its own rollout — beyond what its output fields show. Data: evaluation trajectories from standard PDE benchmarks (PDEBench and PDEArena, each providing thousands of trajectories); we use 200 trajectories in a conserving regime (inviscid/undriven Navier–Stokes or a Hamiltonian wave) at 100 timesteps each — 200 gives tight drift statistics per system while inference-only extraction stays at a few GPU-hours; conserved quantities are computed analytically from the field data at every step. Model: 2–3 pretrained physics foundation models with public weights (Poseidon, Multiple-Physics-Pretraining, DPOT), frozen; trainable = per-layer ridge linear probes to energy/mass/momentum fit on a disjoint 150-trajectory split; 3 seeds. Systems compared: drift of the probed (internal) conserved quantity vs drift of the model's actual predicted-field quantity vs the true constant. Decisive metric first: internal-representation conservation drift = coefficient of variation of the probed quantity across the rollout (dimensionless), reported alongside probe R² (must be ≥0.8 to license the drift reading). Convincing result: internal drift significantly below the field-level drift and below 5% CV in conserving systems — the internal state 'knows' the quantity is constant. Undecidable band: internal CV in [5%, 12%] and statistically indistinguishable from field-level drift — reported as "internal state tracks the output, no extra conservation structure"; band fixed before data. Negative result: internal drift ≈ field drift (or worse) means no conservation structure beyond the outputs, H1 unsupported.

Experiment 2 (H1 — Lawful drift in driven-dissipative regimes): Tests the complementary H1 claim that when a quantity should change, the internal representation changes it in the physically-correct direction and magnitude (e.g., monotone energy decay under viscosity). Data: 150 trajectories from a viscous forced-flow regime in PDEBench (existing), 100 steps each; the true monotone energy/enstrophy change is computed from the fields. Model: same frozen Poseidon/MPP/DPOT and the fixed Experiment-1 probes; no new training; 3 seeds. Systems compared: probed-quantity change vs true change; and against a shuffled-probe control. Decisive metric first: Spearman ρ between probed-quantity change and true change across the rollout, plus sign of the monotone trend. Convincing result: ρ ≥ 0.7 with the correct decay sign in all models. Undecidable band: ρ in [0.3, 0.5] — the internal quantity moves but not reliably with physics, reported as partial support; band fixed before data. Negative result: ρ ≈ 0 or wrong sign means the representation does not track lawful non-conservation, H1's dissipative half fails.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Lawful coupling of non-conserved quantities): Tests the H2 claim that non-conserved but linked quantities are coupled along physically-lawful directions — steering one coupled quantity induces the equation-of-state-correct change in the other. Data: 150 compressible-flow / shallow-water trajectories with a known equation of state (PDEBench compressible NS), giving paired temperature–pressure (or height–velocity) fields. Model: frozen models; steering identifies decoded directions for the two coupled quantities at the best-R² layer and adds ±α·(unit direction), α over {0.5,1,2}× activation std; 3 seeds. Systems compared: induced coupled-quantity change under true-direction steering vs matched-norm random direction. Decisive metric first: coupling-alignment = regression slope / cosine between the induced coupled change and the equation-of-state prediction. Convincing result: alignment ≥ 0.6 (cosine) and monotone in α, with the random control near 0. Undecidable band: alignment in [0.3, 0.45] — weak, reported as inconclusive coupling; band fixed before data. Negative result: alignment ≈ 0 means quantities are stored independently with no lawful coupling, H2 fails.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Causal Noether asymmetry between lawful and unlawful interventions): Tests the decisive H3 claim that conservation-preserving activation perturbations are tolerated while conservation-violating ones cause larger error and/or are spontaneously corrected. Data: 200 conserving-regime trajectories from Experiment 1. Model: frozen models; two matched-magnitude interventions per trajectory — (a) preserving: redistributes the conserved quantity within its level set (e.g., moves energy spatially at fixed total), constructed in field space then mapped to activations; (b) violating: changes the total conserved quantity by the same activation norm; both rolled out; 3 seeds. Systems compared: preserving vs violating perturbations, plus a random matched-norm control. Decisive metric first: lawful-vs-unlawful asymmetry ratio A = downstream field error(violating) / downstream field error(preserving), and the self-correction rate (fraction of violating runs where the total conserved quantity relaxes back toward its initial value). Convincing result: A ≥ 1.5 and/or self-correction significantly above the preserving/random baseline. Undecidable band: A in [0.9, 1.3] with no excess self-correction — read as "model does not distinguish lawful from unlawful", H3 unsupported; band fixed before data. Negative result: A ≈ 1 means the internal state is not on a conservation-constrained manifold, the core H3 claim fails even if H1/H2 decodability held.

Experiment 5 (H1/H2/H3 — Cross-system, cross-model convergence and physics-model brackets): Tests whether conservation-consistency and coupling generalize to unseen systems and are convergent, and brackets the effect against reference models. Data: 100 held-out trajectories per unseen system not used above. Model: frozen Poseidon/MPP/DPOT; plus two brackets run identically — a from-scratch single-system surrogate (lower reference) and a conservation-constrained physics-informed model (upper reference). Systems compared: Experiment-1 drift, Experiment-3 coupling, and Experiment-4 asymmetry across models and systems; CKA between the conserved-quantity subspaces of the foundation models. Decisive metric first: for each metric, where the foundation models fall between the from-scratch lower and physics-informed upper brackets, plus mean pairwise CKA of the conserved-quantity subspaces. Convincing result: foundation models sit clearly above the from-scratch bracket on drift/asymmetry and CKA ≥ 0.6, indicating convergent constrained structure. Undecidable band: foundation-model metrics within noise of the from-scratch bracket, or CKA in [0.3,0.45] — reported as no advantage / weak convergence; band fixed before data. Negative result: foundation models indistinguishable from the from-scratch surrogate means multi-system pretraining confers no extra conservation structure, bounding H1–H3.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Linear probes may recover a quantity that the model does not causally use; we mitigate with the causal Noether test and random-direction controls, but distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions.

Conservation-preserving interventions in a nonlinear network can push activations off-manifold, confounding the lawful-vs-unlawful comparison; we bound perturbation norms and report sensitivity, and design perturbations that exactly preserve the target quantity in field space then map to activations.
Ground-truth conserved quantities for some benchmark PDEs are only approximately conserved numerically; we restrict conservation tests to systems with well-controlled numerical conservation.
Available physics foundation models differ in architecture/tokenization, complicating cross-model comparison; we standardize probing on invariant scalar summaries and report per-model results.

A negative result (models store separable features but violate constraints) is scientifically informative and deployment-relevant, though possibly perceived as less flashy; we frame either outcome as a decisive reliability finding.
Compute: rollouts and probing on pretrained models are academic-scale (inference only, small linear probes), avoiding any retraining of large models.

Name: conditional_independence_scfm_probe
Title: Do Single-Cell Foundation Models Represent the Conditional-Independence Structure of Gene Regulation, or Just Marginal Co-Expression? A d-Separation Test
Short Hypothesis: The defining feature of a genuine regulatory mechanism, versus raw co-expression, is its conditional-independence (d-separation) structure: a directly-regulated target should remain associated with its regulator after conditioning on mediators, whereas a purely-mediated (indirect) target should become independent. We hypothesize that if single-cell foundation models (scFMs) internally represent mechanism rather than marginal correlation, then their internal gene representations will encode this conditional-independence structure — direct edges will survive representational conditioning on mediators while indirect edges will vanish — and that this internal structure will causally govern how the model propagates in-silico perturbations. This is a stronger, mechanism-defining test than the marginal edge-recovery (AUROC) studies that dominate the literature and that have found only co-expression-level signal.
Related Work: A 2026 benchmark (Ye et al.) and Qi et al. (2026) evaluate GRN edge recovery from scFMs and find transferable but limited regulatory signal; a 2026 systematic evaluation (paper 1) shows scGPT/Geneformer attention captures co-expression, not causal regulatory signal, and adds no incremental predictive value over gene-level baselines. SAE/transcoder interpretability work (InterPLM-style, transcoder circuits, scFeatureLens) recovers concept features but validates against marginal annotations. Causal single-cell VAEs (sVAE+, SAMS-VAE) learn causal latent structure by construction from perturbation data — but they are bespoke models, not tests of what large pretrained scFMs already encode. Crucially, no prior work tests whether pretrained scFMs internally represent the *conditional-independence / d-separation* structure that formally distinguishes direct from mediated (indirect) regulation. Since marginal co-expression cannot separate these, showing internal conditional-independence structure would be the first mechanism-defining (rather than correlation-consistent) evidence, directly addressing the 'co-expression not causation' verdict of recent work.
Abstract: Recent studies conclude that single-cell foundation models (scFMs) capture gene co-expression rather than causal regulation, based on marginal edge-recovery benchmarks. But marginal correlation is fundamentally incapable of distinguishing a direct regulatory edge from an indirect, mediated one — that distinction requires conditional independence, the formal signature (d-separation) of a causal mechanism. We propose the first test of whether pretrained scFMs internally represent this conditional-independence structure. Using known regulatory cascades (regulator R -> mediator M -> target T) curated from validated pathways and perturbation-derived ground truth, we compare, in the model's internal gene representation space, the association between R and its direct target versus R and a purely-mediated target, before and after representationally conditioning on M. A mechanistic representation should retain R-direct association after conditioning while eliminating R-mediated association; a co-expression representation should show both surviving or both vanishing equally. We further run a causal in-silico perturbation test: perturbing M should block propagation of an R-perturbation to a mediated target but not to a direct target, if the internal structure is load-bearing. We test scGPT, Geneformer, and scFoundation across immune and fibroblast cell types, using Perturb-seq data (K562, RPE1) for ground-truth cascades. Metrics quantify a conditional-independence selectivity index, mediation-blocking asymmetry, and agreement with perturbation-derived causal structure. Either outcome is decisive: it moves the field beyond 'is it correlation?' to 'does the model encode the conditional structure that defines mechanism?'.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Cascade ground truth and marginal-association baseline): Establishes the labeled direct-vs-mediated edges H1 needs and confirms the starting point that both edge types are marginally associated (the co-expression finding). Data: ground-truth regulatory triples (R→M→T_indirect and R→T_direct) from (a) Replogle et al. genome-scale Perturb-seq in K562 and RPE1 (~2,000 perturbations, ~2.5M cells exist), (b) linear cascades from Reactome/KEGG, (c) STRING/ChIP-seq for TF binding; we curate 300 high-confidence triples (each with a designated mediator M and perturbation-established causal ordering) — 300 balances statistical power for the paired index against the scarcity of clean linear cascades; provenance and confidence tier recorded per triple. Model: scGPT, Geneformer, scFoundation, all frozen, inference only; per-gene contextual representations (token embeddings and final hidden states) extracted for each cell. Systems compared: representational R–T association for direct vs mediated pairs. Decisive metric first: marginal association (cosine / co-activation) of R and T representations, per pair type. Convincing (expected) result: both direct and mediated pairs show high marginal association (median cosine > 0.5), replicating co-expression and setting up the conditioning test. Undecidable/If-here note: if even marginal association is absent (< 0.2 for direct pairs), the models do not represent these relationships at all and Experiments 2–3 cannot separate direct from mediated; this floor is fixed before data. Negative interpretation: no marginal signal would make the conditional test uninterpretable and is reported as such.

Experiment 2 (H1 — Conditional-independence selectivity after conditioning on the mediator): Tests the core H1 claim that direct edges survive representational conditioning on the mediator while indirect edges vanish. Data: the 300 triples from Experiment 1 across their native cell types. Model: frozen scGPT/Geneformer/scFoundation representations; conditioning done two ways — (a) linear partialling-out of mediator M's representation, (b) a nonparametric kernel conditional-independence test (KCIT) conditioned on M; no model training, only the CI estimators; 3 seeds over cell subsampling. Systems compared: partial association of direct vs mediated pairs, plus three controls — condition on a random gene R′ of matched marginal correlation, a reverse-cascade control, and a raw-log-expression baseline run through identical CI tests. Decisive metric first: Conditional-Independence Selectivity Index CISI = (partial association of direct pairs) / (partial association of mediated pairs). Convincing result: CISI significantly ≫ 1 (mediated pairs drop toward independence, direct pairs retained) AND the model's CISI exceeds the raw-expression baseline's, with the random-gene control near 1. Undecidable band: CISI in [0.9, 1.4] — no reliable direct-vs-mediated separation, read as pure co-expression (H1 unsupported); band fixed before data. Negative result: CISI ≈ 1 or not above the raw-expression baseline means the representation encodes marginal correlation, not conditional-independence structure, and H1 fails.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Causal mediation-blocking under in-silico perturbation): Tests the H2 claim that the internal conditional-independence structure causally governs perturbation propagation — clamping the mediator cuts the indirect path but not the direct one. Data: the 300 triples; perturbations delivered through each model's masked-prediction / perturbation head. Model: frozen models with their native perturbation heads; simulate perturbation of R, measure induced change at T_direct and T_indirect, then clamp M and re-measure; 3 seeds. Systems compared: effect reduction at T_indirect vs T_direct when M is clamped. Decisive metric first: Mediation-Blocking Asymmetry MBA = (reduction in R→T_indirect effect when M clamped) − (reduction in R→T_direct effect when M clamped). Convincing result: MBA large and positive (indirect path collapses, direct path preserved), significant across models. Undecidable band: MBA within its 3-seed CI of 0 — no differential blocking, reported as no causal mediation structure; band fixed before data. Negative-result caveat stated in advance: scFM perturbation heads are known to be weak predictors, so a null MBA is interpreted conservatively — the representational CISI of Experiment 2 remains the primary H1 evidence, and a null here is reported as head-limited rather than refuting H1.

Experiment 4 (H1 — Layer localization and cross-cell-type invariance): Sharpens H1 by locating where conditional-independence structure lives and whether it is context-invariant. Data: the subset of Experiment-1 cascades active in ≥2 cell types (e.g., immune vs fibroblast), ~100 triples. Model: frozen models; CISI recomputed per layer and per component (token embeddings vs contextual hidden states vs attention); 3 seeds. Systems compared: CISI across layers/components and across cell types. Decisive metric first: layer/component of peak CISI and the cross-cell-type correlation of per-triple CISI. Convincing result: a reproducible layer where CISI peaks and cross-cell-type CISI correlation ≥ 0.5, indicating context-invariant mechanistic structure. Undecidable band: cross-type correlation in [0.2, 0.35] — reported as partially context-specific; band fixed before data. Negative result: CISI present in one cell type but uncorrelated across types means the model encodes cell-state-specific co-expression, bounding H1's generality.

Experiment 5 (H1 — Brackets against purpose-built causal and marginal GRN models): Places the scFMs on a correlation-to-mechanism spectrum without enlarging the claim. Data: the 300 triples, plus the same perturbation data used to train a causal single-cell VAE (sVAE+) as an upper reference. Model: frozen scFMs; brackets are sVAE+ (upper, trained on matched perturbation data) and classical GRN inference GENIE3 and PIDC (marginal lower bounds), each producing a comparable direct-vs-mediated selectivity. Systems compared: scFM CISI vs sVAE+ CISI (upper) vs GENIE3/PIDC selectivity (lower). Decisive metric first: where scFM CISI falls between the marginal lower bracket and the causal upper bracket. Convincing result: scFM CISI clearly above the GENIE3/PIDC lower bracket, indicating structure beyond marginal inference. Undecidable band: scFM CISI within noise of the marginal lower bracket — reported as no advantage over co-expression methods; band fixed before data. Negative result: scFMs at or below the marginal bracket means they add no conditional-independence structure over classical marginal GRN inference, a decisive bound on H1.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Conditioning in a nonlinear representation via linear partialling may be incomplete; we mitigate with nonparametric kernel CI tests, but residual nonlinear dependence could inflate or deflate the selectivity index.

Ground-truth mediator assignment from Perturb-seq epistasis is noisy and some 'direct' edges may themselves be mediated by unmeasured genes; we restrict to well-supported cascades and report sensitivity to cascade confidence thresholds.
Distributed/superposed gene representations may make single-mediator conditioning imprecise; we address this with subspace-level conditioning and report aggregate directions.

The in-silico perturbation heads of scFMs are known to be weak predictors; a null mediation-blocking result may reflect head quality rather than representation structure, so we emphasize the representational CI test as the primary evidence.

A negative result (no conditional-independence structure beyond co-expression) is scientifically decisive and consistent with recent findings, but may be perceived as confirmatory; we frame it as the first mechanism-defining test that closes the 'correlation vs. mechanism' question rather than re-litigating edge AUROC.
All experiments are inference-only on pretrained public models plus small probes and CI tests, keeping compute at academic scale.

Uptake/citation potential is decent because it gives a sharper evaluation standard than existing edge-recovery benchmarks. Direction-shifting potential is moderate: it could shift evaluation from marginal AUROC to causal/conditional criteria, but only if the protocol is robust and adopted. Real-world reach is moderate: relevant to biological discovery and perturbation design, less directly to broad industry. Phenomenon value is high even if the method is simple, because a null or positive result would inform what pretrained biological foundation models actually learn. So what? If the result is negative, serious researchers may stop over-interpreting scFM representations as causal; if positive, it would materially raise confidence in mechanistic use of these models.

Name: dimensional_homogeneity_probe
Title: Does the Model Know Its Units? Probing Dimensional Homogeneity and Buckingham-Pi Structure in Physics Foundation Models
Short Hypothesis: Dimensional analysis is the most universal, theory-independent constraint in physics: physical laws are dimensionally homogeneous, and the Buckingham Pi theorem says a system's behavior depends only on dimensionless groups, invariant under rescaling of base units. We hypothesize that if physics foundation models represent genuine physical mechanism rather than surface numerical statistics, their internal representations will (a) organize variables along axes corresponding to physical dimensions (length, time, mass), (b) be approximately invariant to unit-rescaling transformations that leave the dimensionless Pi groups fixed, and (c) causally use dimensionless-group structure when forecasting. A model that merely fits numbers will lack this scale-covariant, dimensionally-homogeneous internal organization. No prior interpretability work tests unit/dimension structure, only individual quantities like energy.
Related Work: Prior interpretability work shows physics foundation models linearly encode and causally steer individual physical *quantities* (Physics Steering 2025; Uncovering Emergent Physics Representations 2025 on energy; From Neurons to Neutrons 2024 recovering the semi-empirical mass formula; the GraphCast weather-model SAE study 2025; Interpreting Physics in Video World Models 2026). Separately, an entire mathematical literature formalizes dimensional analysis, dimensional homogeneity, and the Buckingham Pi theorem (Formalizing dimensional analysis in Lean 2025; Dimensioned Algebra 2021; Quantities, Dimensions and Dimensional Analysis 2014), and NUMCoT (2024) shows LLMs struggle with unit conversions at the token level. Crucially, no interpretability study asks whether a physics foundation model's *internal representation* respects the dimensional/unit structure and scale-covariance (Buckingham Pi) that underlies all physical law. Existing work tests whether a single quantity is encoded and matters; we test whether the deeper, relational, symmetry-level constraint of dimensional homogeneity is internalized. This scale-covariance / Pi-group test is the novel contribution, complementing (not extending) the quantity-encoding line of work.
Abstract: Dimensional analysis is the closest thing physics has to a universal, theory-agnostic law: every valid physical equation is dimensionally homogeneous, and the Buckingham Pi theorem guarantees that a system's dimensionless behavior is invariant under any consistent rescaling of the base units of length, time, and mass. This makes it an ideal, mechanism-defining probe for whether physics foundation models learn physics or merely fit numbers. We investigate whether pretrained multi-physics surrogates and time-series/PDE foundation models internally represent dimensional and unit structure. We introduce three tests. First, a dimensional-axis probe: we test whether internal representations linearly encode the physical dimension (length/time/mass exponents) of variables and quantities, organizing them along interpretable dimensional axes. Second, a scale-covariance test: we apply unit-rescaling transformations to inputs that leave all dimensionless Pi groups fixed (e.g., simultaneously rescaling length and time so a Reynolds or Froude number is unchanged) and measure whether internal representations and predictions remain invariant, versus rescalings that change the Pi groups, which should change them. Third, a causal dimensional-homogeneity test: we steer representations along dimensionally-inconsistent directions and check that forecasts degrade more than for dimensionally-consistent perturbations of equal magnitude. Metrics quantify dimensional-probe accuracy, a Pi-invariance index (representation change under fixed-Pi vs Pi-changing rescalings), and a homogeneity-selectivity ratio. This yields the first test of whether physics foundation models internalize the scale-covariant, dimensionally-homogeneous structure at the heart of physical law, with direct implications for their extrapolation reliability across scales.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Dimensional-axis probe): Tests the H1(a) claim that physics foundation models organize variables along axes corresponding to base physical dimensions (length L, time T, mass M). Data: evaluation trajectories from PDE/dynamical benchmarks whose governing dimensionless groups are analytically known — pipe/channel flow (Reynolds), shallow-water (Froude), pendulum/oscillators (dimensionless amplitude, damping), reaction-diffusion (Péclet, Damköhler); we draw 150 trajectories per system (600 total) from PDEBench and generated ODE integrations, enough to cover each dimensionless-group range while keeping extraction to a few GPU-hours. Each field variable carries its ground-truth (L,T,M) exponent vector. Model: 2–3 pretrained physics/time-series foundation models with public weights (a multi-physics PDE surrogate — Poseidon or MPP/DPOT — plus a numerical time-series foundation model), frozen; trainable = per-layer linear probes mapping per-variable activations to the (L,T,M) exponent vector, with a dimension-classification head; 5 folds, 3 seeds. Systems compared: probe on model activations vs probe on raw numerical inputs (to show structure is model-contributed). Decisive metric first: probe R² for the exponent vector and dimension-classification accuracy on held-out variables. Convincing result: classification accuracy ≥ 0.85 and a PCA/CCA where variables cluster by dimension, exceeding the raw-input baseline by a clear margin. Undecidable band: accuracy in [0.5, 0.65] (chance depends on class count) — weak dimensional structure, reported as partially encoded and not used as a homogeneity axis in Experiment 4; band fixed before data. Negative result: accuracy near the raw-input baseline means dimensions are not organized as internal axes, H1 fails and the causal test is moot.

Experiment 2 (H2 — Pi-invariance / representation scale-covariance): Tests the H2(b) claim that representations are approximately invariant to unit rescalings that leave the dimensionless Pi groups fixed, yet sensitive to rescalings that change a Pi group. Data: the 600 Experiment-1 trajectories; for each, construct (a) fixed-Pi rescalings (multiply all lengths by λ_L, times by λ_T so every governing dimensionless group is exactly unchanged) and (b) Pi-changing rescalings (shift one variable so e.g. Reynolds changes by a controlled amount), λ swept over a small range around 1. Model: frozen models; no training beyond reusing Experiment-1 readouts; 3 seeds. Systems compared: internal representation change under fixed-Pi vs matched-magnitude Pi-changing rescalings. Decisive metric first: Pi-Invariance Index PII = (representation change under Pi-changing) / (representation change under matched-magnitude fixed-Pi). Convincing result: PII ≥ 3 (nearly invariant to fixed-Pi, sensitive to Pi-changing) in at least one model. Undecidable band: PII in [1.2, 2.0] — partial scale-covariance, reported as inconclusive; band fixed before data. Negative result: PII ≈ 1 (responds to both equally) means the model is a number-fitter lacking scale-covariant structure, H2 fails. Note (matched to Risk): rescalings use small λ and are compared against Pi-changing rescalings of equal input-space magnitude so generic OOD failure cannot masquerade as Pi-sensitivity.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Prediction-level scale-covariance and cross-scale extrapolation): Tests the H2(b) claim at the output level — a fixed-Pi-rescaled input should forecast the correctly rescaled trajectory. Data: the 600 trajectories with their fixed-Pi rescalings across a range of λ. Model: frozen models, forecasting only; 3 seeds. Systems compared: predicted rescaled trajectory vs ground-truth rescaled trajectory, as a function of λ. Decisive metric first: normalized forecast error between the model's rescaled-input prediction and the true rescaled trajectory, versus λ. Convincing result: error stays below the model's own in-distribution forecast error out to a rescaling factor of at least 2× in each direction, showing genuine covariance. Undecidable band: rescaled-input error within [1×, 1.5×] the in-distribution error only for |log λ| < 0.2 — covariance holds only infinitesimally, reported as weak; band fixed before data. Negative result: error grows immediately with any λ ≠ 1 means predictions are not scale-covariant, H2 fails at the output level.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Causal dimensional-homogeneity intervention): Tests the H3(c) claim that the model causally expects dimensional homogeneity — perturbing along dimensionally-consistent directions harms forecasts less than dimensionally-inconsistent perturbations of equal magnitude. Data: the 600 trajectories; using the Experiment-1 dimensional axes, build matched-magnitude activation perturbations that are (a) dimensionally consistent (perturb a variable along its own dimension's directions) vs (b) dimensionally inconsistent (inject a length-typed component into a time-typed quantity). Model: frozen models; both rolled out; controls = matched-norm random directions and shuffled-dimension-label directions; 3 seeds. Systems compared: consistent vs inconsistent perturbations. Decisive metric first: Homogeneity-Selectivity Ratio HSR = downstream forecast error(inconsistent) / downstream forecast error(consistent). Convincing result: HSR ≥ 1.5 with the shuffled-label control near 1. Undecidable band: HSR in [0.9, 1.3] — no differential sensitivity, read as the model not enforcing homogeneity (H3 unsupported); band fixed before data. Negative result: HSR ≈ 1 means dimensional consistency is not causally used, H3 fails even if H1/H2 decodability held.

Experiment 5 (H1/H2 — Cross-system, cross-model universality and construction brackets): Tests whether dimensional structure transfers and is convergent, and brackets it. Data: Experiment-1 activations; a probe trained on flow systems is tested on diffusion systems (transfer). Model: frozen foundation models; brackets run identically — a from-scratch single-system surrogate (expected weak Pi-invariance, lower) and, where feasible, a model trained on nondimensionalized inputs (expected strong Pi-invariance by construction, upper). Systems compared: transfer probe accuracy, CKA between models' dimensional subspaces, and PII across the brackets. Decisive metric first: cross-system transfer accuracy and mean pairwise CKA of dimensional subspaces. Convincing result: transfer accuracy well above chance and CKA ≥ 0.6, with foundation-model PII above the from-scratch bracket, indicating convergent dimensional structure. Undecidable band: CKA in [0.3, 0.45] or transfer within noise of chance — reported as non-transferable/weakly convergent; band fixed before data. Negative result: no transfer and foundation-model PII at the from-scratch bracket means dimensional structure is idiosyncratic and not conferred by broad pretraining, bounding H1/H2.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Fixed-Pi rescalings may push inputs outside the model's training distribution, confounding invariance measurement with generic OOD failure; we mitigate by using small rescaling factors, reporting sensitivity to lambda, and comparing against Pi-changing rescalings of matched input-space magnitude.

Some benchmark models normalize/standardize inputs internally, which may trivially remove or destroy dimensional signal; we document each model's preprocessing and, where possible, probe pre-normalization activations.

Linear probes recovering a dimensional axis do not guarantee causal use; we address this with the causal homogeneity test and random/shuffled-label controls, though distributed encodings may blur single-direction interventions.
Constructing exactly-fixed-Pi transformations requires knowing the full set of governing dimensionless groups; we restrict to well-characterized benchmark systems where these are analytically known.

A negative result (models are number-fitters lacking scale-covariant structure) is scientifically decisive and extrapolation-relevant, though possibly perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-level test of dimensional homogeneity in foundation models.
All experiments are inference-only on pretrained public models plus small linear probes and controlled input transformations, keeping compute at academic scale.

novelty.reasoning: Core novel claims: (1) probing whether pretrained physics foundation models internally encode physical dimension vectors (L,T,M) rather than only individual quantities; novelty lives in the interpretability question/problem definition. (2) testing Pi-group / unit-rescaling invariance inside representations, not just in model outputs; novelty lives in the mechanism/representation-level symmetry claim. (3) causal intervention on dimensionally consistent vs inconsistent directions to test whether the model uses dimensional homogeneity in forecasting; novelty lives in the causal test design. (4) using Buckingham-Pi fixed-Pi rescalings as a benchmark for scale-covariant internal structure across physics/time-series FMs; novelty lives in the setting and test. Relative to prior work, the closest family is interpretability of physics FMs on single quantities (energy/vorticity) plus separate applied work that builds dimensionless models by construction. The actual delta is from 'does the model encode quantity X?' to 'does it spontaneously organize around dimensional structure and invariances?' That is a real and non-obvious step. The main caveat is that parts of the hypothesis are adjacent to existing dimensional-analysis literature and unitless model design, so the result is novel mostly as an interpretability/finding in pretrained FMs, not as a new theorem.

Name: spatial_tme_relational_probe
Title: Does the Foundation Model See the Neighborhood? Testing Whether Pathology Models Encode Spatial-Relational Tumor-Microenvironment Mechanisms, Not Just Local Morphology
Short Hypothesis: The prognostic and biological mechanism of cancer is not local cell identity alone but the spatial-relational organization of the tumor microenvironment (TME): immune infiltration into tumor nests, spatial exclusion of lymphocytes, tumor-stroma boundary geometry. We hypothesize that pathology foundation models trained on large tissue-patch collections internally encode these relational (neighborhood-context) structures, distinct from and beyond their well-documented local cell-type concepts, and that this relational structure (a) is decodable, (b) is causally load-bearing for prognostic prediction, and (c) matches spatial biology as measured by spatial transcriptomics. If instead the models encode only a bag of local morphologies, patch-context ablations and spatial-relation probes will show no structure beyond local cell counts.
Related Work: A wave of pathology interpretability work (PICASSO/Kim et al. 2026; CytoSAE 2025; Mammo-SAE 2025; 'Learning biologically relevant features via SAEs' 2024; ICFL microscopy 2024) uses sparse autoencoders/dictionary learning to recover monosemantic features that match LOCAL morphological annotations — cell types, calcifications, tissue classes. Concept-MIL and ConceptCLIP link patch concepts to diagnosis; representational-similarity and robustness-index papers characterize global embedding geometry and center confounds. Critically, all validate features against MARGINAL, local annotations (what a patch contains), not against the SPATIAL-RELATIONAL organization among cells/regions that constitutes the actual cancer-biology mechanism (immune infiltration, exclusion, boundary structure) known to drive prognosis. No prior work tests whether pathology FMs encode neighborhood-context relational structure, whether that structure is causally used, or whether it aligns with spatial-transcriptomics ground truth. Our relational, causal, spatial-omics-grounded test is the novel contribution, moving beyond 'the model recognizes cell X' to 'the model represents that immune cells are excluded from the tumor nest.'
Abstract: Interpretability studies of pathology foundation models have shown they encode local morphological concepts such as cell types and tissue classes. But the mechanism that actually governs cancer behavior and prognosis is relational and spatial: whether cytotoxic lymphocytes infiltrate a tumor nest or are excluded from it, the geometry of the tumor-stroma boundary, and immune-desert versus inflamed ecologies. We ask whether pathology foundation models internally represent this spatial-relational tumor-microenvironment (TME) structure, beyond a bag of local morphologies, and whether that structure is causally load-bearing and biologically faithful. Using public whole-slide datasets with paired or co-registered spatial transcriptomics (e.g., 10x Xenium/Visium colorectal and lung cohorts) and immunohistochemistry, we extract patch- and neighborhood-level representations from several public pathology FMs (UNI2, Virchow2, Prov-GigaPath, CONCH). First, we build relational probes that predict TME relationships defined from cell segmentation and spatial statistics — infiltration score, immune-tumor colocalization/exclusion, boundary curvature — and test whether these are decodable beyond local cell-count baselines. Second, we run causal context-ablation experiments: we swap or scramble a patch's spatial neighbors and measure whether relational features and prognostic predictions change as predicted by TME biology (e.g., breaking infiltration should shift an immune-inflamed feature toward immune-desert). Third, we validate against spatial transcriptomics by testing whether relational features align with measured immune-signaling gene programs (T-cell cytotoxicity, IFN-gamma) at the same tissue location. Metrics quantify a relational-beyond-local index, context-ablation causal selectivity, and transcriptomic alignment. Either outcome sharpens what these clinically-deployed models actually 'see.'
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Relational structure decodable beyond local cell counts): Tests the H1(a) claim that pathology foundation models encode spatial-relational TME structure distinct from local cell identity. Data: public whole-slide-image cohorts (TCGA colorectal COAD/READ and lung LUAD, ~1,000 slides available) with cell segmentation/classification via HoVer-Net, plus co-located spatial transcriptomics (10x Xenium/Visium colorectal and lung); we use 400 slides tiled into ~20,000 neighborhood windows — 400 slides span centers and phenotypes while keeping SAE/probe fitting tractable. Ground-truth relational descriptors per window: immune-infiltration score (lymphocyte fraction within tumor nests), immune–tumor spatial exclusion (cross-type Ripley's K), tumor–stroma boundary length/curvature, and inflamed/excluded/desert label. Model: UNI2, Virchow2, Prov-GigaPath, CONCH, all frozen; trainable = ridge probes on patch/neighborhood embeddings and per-model SAEs (dictionary 4,096, L1 1e-3) for candidate relational features; 5 folds, 3 seeds. Systems compared: probe on model representations vs a strict LOCAL baseline given only the same window's cell-type counts/densities (no arrangement). Decisive metric first: Relational-Beyond-Local Index RBLI = probe R²(model) − probe R²(local-count baseline), per relational descriptor. Convincing result: RBLI > 0.1 for infiltration/exclusion/boundary in at least one model, significant over folds. Undecidable band: RBLI in [0.0, 0.05] — no reliable structure beyond bag-of-cells, reported as local-only for that descriptor; band fixed before data. Negative result: RBLI ≤ 0 across models means only local morphology is encoded, H1 fails and the causal/biology tests targeting relational features are moot.

Experiment 2 (H1 — Neighborhood-permutation control): Tests that the Experiment-1 relational signal is genuinely spatial by destroying arrangement while preserving composition. Data: the 20,000 windows; for grid/aggregator models, permute neighbor patches within a window (preserving cell-type counts); where pixel re-embedding is cheap, spatially scramble cells and re-render. Model: same frozen models and fixed Experiment-1 features. Systems compared: relational-feature prediction on true vs scrambled windows, and local-morphology-feature prediction on the same. Decisive metric first: relational-feature drop under scrambling = R²(true) − R²(scrambled), contrasted with the (expected near-zero) drop for local features. Convincing result: relational features collapse under scrambling (drop > 0.1) while local features stay stable (drop < 0.03). Undecidable band: relational drop in [0.03, 0.08] — weak spatial dependence, reported as inconclusive; band fixed before data. Negative result: relational features unchanged by scrambling means the Experiment-1 signal was not truly relational (it rode on composition), undercutting H1.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Causal context-ablation on relational feature and prognosis): Tests the H2(b) claim that relational structure is causally load-bearing — swapping a tumor patch's neighborhood context shifts the 'inflamed' feature and the downstream prediction in the biologically-correct direction. Data: 2,000 tumor windows from Experiment 1 with clear phenotype labels. Model: frozen patch-context / neighborhood-attention models; intervention replaces a tumor patch's true immune-rich neighbors with immune-poor neighbors (and vice versa) at the embedding level; control swaps with neighbors matched on stain/center but same TME phenotype (should not shift); 3 seeds. Systems compared: relation-breaking swap vs matched-phenotype control. Decisive metric first: context-ablation causal selectivity = |shift_relation-breaking| / |shift_matched-control| for the inflamed feature and for the subtype/prognostic head. Convincing result: selectivity ≥ 3 with shifts in the biologically-correct direction. Undecidable band: selectivity in [1.2, 2.0] — weak causal use, reported as inconclusive; band fixed before data. Negative result: selectivity ≈ 1 means the relational feature is decodable but not causal for prediction, H2 fails.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Spatial-transcriptomics faithfulness): Tests the H3(c) claim that recovered relational features match spatial biology beyond local composition. Data: co-registered spatial-transcriptomics spots (Xenium/Visium) at Experiment-1 windows, using immune-signaling gene programs (T-cell cytotoxicity, IFN-γ response, exhaustion) as ground truth; restricted to high-quality-registration datasets. Model: frozen models, fixed relational features. Systems compared: relational feature vs measured gene program, controlling for local cell composition. Decisive metric first: partial Spearman ρ between the relational feature and the gene program, partialling out local cell-type composition. Convincing result: partial ρ ≥ 0.3 retained after the composition control, in ≥2 programs. Undecidable band: partial ρ in [0.1, 0.2] — weak residual signal, reported as inconclusive; band fixed before data. Negative result: partial ρ ≈ 0 after control means the feature adds nothing over local composition in explaining spatial biology, H3 fails.

Experiment 5 (H2 — Prognostic load-bearing and center-confound control): Tests the clinically-relevant half of H2(b) — that prognostic signal rides on relational features — while ruling out center/stain artifacts. Data: TCGA cohorts with survival (COAD/READ, LUAD; ~800 slides with outcome). Model: frozen models; feature-group ablation removes relational vs local feature groups from a Cox/discrete-time survival head fit on top of frozen features; center/stain confound controlled via the Robustness-Index approach (hold out centers, report stratified performance); 3 seeds. Systems compared: survival performance with vs without relational features, and across held-out centers. Decisive metric first: drop in concordance index (C-index) when relational features are ablated, and its stability across centers. Convincing result: relational-feature ablation drops C-index by ≥ 0.03 and the drop persists across held-out centers (not a center artifact). Undecidable band: C-index drop in [0.0, 0.015] or a drop that vanishes under center stratification — reported as no robust prognostic contribution; band fixed before data. Negative result: no C-index drop, or drop explained by center confound, means relational structure is not prognostically load-bearing, bounding H2.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Grid-based FMs process patches independently, so 'context' must come from the slide-level aggregator; models with weak or absent spatial context may show no relational structure by construction — we report per-model and use neighborhood-attention aggregators where available.

Re-rendering scrambled tissue for causal ablation is nontrivial; for patch-grid models we operate at the neighbor-patch level (permute/swap embeddings), which is feasible, while pixel-level scrambling is used only where re-embedding is cheap.

Co-registration between H&E and spatial transcriptomics is imperfect, adding noise to the transcriptomic-faithfulness test; we use datasets with high-quality registration and report registration-error sensitivity.

Center/stain confounds strongly organize pathology embeddings (per the Robustness-Index literature); relational signal could be confounded and we explicitly control for it.

A negative result (models encode only local morphology, no relational TME structure) is scientifically decisive and clinically important, though possibly perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as a sharpening of what deployed pathology FMs represent.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes/SAEs and public data, keeping compute at academic scale.
