Name: implicit_electron_flow_probe
Title: Recipes or Mechanisms? Probing Whether Reactant-to-Product Transformers Internally Represent Arrow-Pushing Electron Flow They Were Never Taught
Short Hypothesis: Standard product-prediction transformers (Molecular Transformer / Chemformer trained on USPTO reactant->product SMILES) are widely assumed to learn reactions as 'recipes' rather than mechanisms, which is precisely why an entire line of purpose-built electron-flow models was created. We hypothesize the opposite is partially true at the representational level: even without any mechanistic supervision, these models internally encode the arrow-pushing electron-redistribution structure of a reaction - which atoms are electron donors/acceptors, which bonds form/break, and the direction of electron flow - and that this latent mechanistic structure is causally load-bearing for prediction and predicts where the model generalizes versus hallucinates. If instead they are pure recipe learners, mechanism-defined features (electron source/sink, bond-electron changes) will be no more decodable than shuffled controls, and mechanism-aligned interventions will not selectively affect predictions.
Related Work: Two lines of work bracket this gap. (1) Purpose-built mechanistic models - ELECTRO (2018), non-autoregressive electron redistribution (2021), FlowER (Nature 2025, mass/electron-conserving flow matching), Reactron (2025), DeepMech (2025), PMechRP/ArrowFinder (2025) - are motivated by the explicit premise that standard product-prediction models 'treat reactions as recipes with limited mechanistic insight' and 'hallucinate' because they ignore electron flow. They BUILD mechanism in by construction; they do not ask whether standard models already encode it. (2) Interpretability of chemistry models - 'BERT Learns Chemistry' (attention to reactive functional groups), 'Circuits, Features, and Heuristics in Molecular Transformers' (2025, SAEs/valence circuits on a generative transformer), and the SchNet reaction-analogy paper (2025, constant reaction vectors) - shows chemistry models encode substructures and even reaction-difference directions. But none tests whether a REACTION product-prediction transformer internally represents the ELECTRON-FLOW / bond-electron-matrix mechanism, uses it causally, or whether that structure governs OOD/hallucination behavior. Our contribution is a mechanism-defining, causally-tested probe that uses external mechanistic datasets (mech-USPTO-31k, PMechDB, FlowER's mechanism sequences) - which the product model never saw - as ground truth to arbitrate the 'recipe vs mechanism' debate at the representational level.
Abstract: The dominant machine-learning approach to reaction outcome prediction maps reactant SMILES directly to product SMILES, and a whole research program of electron-flow models has been built on the premise that such models are mere 'recipe' learners that ignore mechanism and therefore hallucinate mass-imbalanced products. Yet whether these product-prediction transformers implicitly encode reaction mechanism internally has never been tested. We ask a simple, mechanism-defining question: does a reactant-to-product transformer, trained without any mechanistic supervision, internally represent the arrow-pushing electron-flow structure of a reaction - the electron sources and sinks, the bonds that form and break, and the direction of electron redistribution? We use pretrained Molecular Transformer and Chemformer as the models under study and treat external mechanism datasets (mech-USPTO-31k, PMechDB, and FlowER's elementary-step sequences) - which these models never saw - as held-out ground truth. First, we train linear probes and sparse autoencoders on internal activations to decode per-atom electron donor/acceptor role, per-bond formation/breaking, and net electron change (from the bond-electron matrix), comparing against strict atom-mapping and reactivity-shuffled controls. Second, we run causal interventions: steering activations along the recovered electron-source or bond-breaking directions should shift predicted products along the mechanistically-correct path, while matched random directions should not. Third, we test whether the strength/consistency of the internal electron-flow representation predicts, per reaction, when the model produces mass-balanced correct products versus hallucinations and how it generalizes out-of-distribution. Either outcome decisively resolves the recipe-versus-mechanism debate at the level of learned representations.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Electron-flow structure decodable from product-model activations): Tests the H1 claim that reactant→product transformers internally encode arrow-pushing structure (per-atom donor/acceptor role, per-bond form/break, reaction-center membership) that was never in their training data. Data: held-out mechanism ground truth from mech-USPTO-31k (~31k reactions), PMechDB, and FlowER elementary-step bond-electron (BE) matrices; we use 8,000 high-confidence, mass-balanced, atom-mapped reactions — 8,000 gives thousands of labeled atoms/bonds per class while excluding low-confidence mappings; per-atom electron role and per-bond change derived from atom-mapping + BE matrix. None of this annotation was in the product models' training data. Model: pretrained Molecular Transformer and Chemformer (public weights), frozen; trainable = linear probes and SAEs (dictionary 8,192, L1 1e-3) on encoder residual-stream (and decoder cross-attention) activations, per layer; 5 folds, 3 seeds. Systems compared: model-activation probe vs baselines — raw one-hot atom/bond features, Morgan fingerprints, and a reactivity-shuffled control (electron roles permuted across same-type atoms). Decisive metric first: probe accuracy/F1 for donor/acceptor role, bond form/break, and reaction-center membership, minus the shuffled-control and fingerprint baselines. Convincing result: F1 ≥ 0.75 for all three targets, exceeding fingerprint and shuffled baselines by a clear margin. Undecidable band: model-minus-baseline F1 gap in [0.0, 0.05] — decodability attributable to substructure identity, not mechanism, reported as unsupported for that target; band fixed before data. Negative result: probes no better than shuffled/fingerprint controls means no decodable electron-flow structure, H1 fails and H2/H3 are moot.

Experiment 2 (H1 — Directional donor-vs-acceptor within the reaction center): Tests the stricter H1 sub-claim that the model encodes electron-flow direction, not merely reactive-site location. Data: the reaction-center atoms of the 8,000 reactions, labeled donor vs acceptor. Model: frozen Molecular Transformer / Chemformer, fixed Experiment-1 activations; probe restricted to atoms already known to be in the reaction center; 3 seeds. Systems compared: donor-vs-acceptor classifier vs chance (both are reactive, so location cannot help) and vs the shuffled-role control. Decisive metric first: donor-vs-acceptor classification accuracy conditioned on reaction-center membership. Convincing result: accuracy ≥ 0.75, well above the 0.5 chance floor and above the shuffled control. Undecidable band: accuracy in [0.55, 0.65] — weak directional signal, reported as inconclusive; band fixed before data. Negative result: accuracy ≈ 0.5 means the model flags where reaction happens but not the electron-flow direction, so H1's directional core fails even if reaction-center localization succeeded.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Causal steering along electron-flow directions): Tests the H2 claim that electron-flow structure is causally load-bearing — steering an atom toward 'donor' shifts predicted products toward mechanisms where it donates electrons. Data: 1,000 reactions from the Experiment-1 test split (1,000 keeps the α-sweep × seed × decode grid affordable). Model: frozen models with fixed Experiment-1 donor/acceptor and bond-breaking directions; add ±α·(unit direction) to the atom's activations at the best-F1 layer, α over {0.5,1,2}× activation std; decode products; 3 seeds. Systems compared: true-direction steering vs matched-norm random-direction control. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity index M = |effect_true direction| / |effect_random direction|, plus the fraction of interventions producing the mechanistically-predicted product change and SMILES validity rate. Convincing result: M ≥ 3 with predicted-change fraction well above the random control and validity ≥ 0.8. Undecidable band: M in [1.2, 2.0] or validity < 0.5 (off-manifold) — reported as inconclusive; band fixed before data. Negative result: M ≈ 1 means directions are decodable but not causal, H2 fails.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Representation strength predicts hallucination and OOD accuracy): Tests the H3 claim that electron-flow representation strength predicts where the model generalizes vs hallucinates, and checks internal electron/mass conservation. Data: the 8,000 reactions plus held-out OOD reaction classes (reaction types withheld from USPTO training splits); model-predicted products labeled correct/mass-balanced vs hallucinated. Model: frozen models; per-reaction 'electron-flow strength' = probe confidence / SAE feature coherence over the reaction center; also probe net-electron conservation (electrons removed at breaking bonds vs added at forming bonds). Systems compared: electron-flow strength vs baselines — output token log-probability and deep-ensemble variance. Decisive metric first: AUROC for flagging hallucinated (mass-imbalanced/incorrect) products from electron-flow strength, and Spearman ρ with per-reaction accuracy on OOD classes. Convincing result: AUROC ≥ 0.75 and above both baselines by ≥ 0.05, with probed conservation-consistency higher on correct than hallucinated reactions. Undecidable band: AUROC within 0.03 of the best baseline — no representation-specific predictive value, reported as not distinguishable from confidence heuristics; band fixed before data. Negative result: electron-flow strength at chance or below baselines means the structure does not predict generalization/hallucination, H3 fails.

Experiment 5 (H1/H2 — Layer/emergence, cross-model convergence, and recipe-to-mechanism brackets): Locates the structure and places the product models on the recipe-to-mechanism spectrum without enlarging the claim. Data: the 8,000-reaction set. Model: frozen Molecular Transformer and Chemformer, per-layer and encoder-vs-decoder analysis; brackets = a mechanism-supervised model's representations (FlowER, upper) and a model trained on shuffled reactant–product pairs (lower), each probed identically; CKA between the two product models' recovered electron-flow subspaces; 3 seeds. Systems compared: per-layer probe F1 and steering M across depth/components; product-model decodability vs FlowER upper and shuffled lower brackets. Decisive metric first: layer/component of peak electron-flow decodability, mean pairwise CKA, and where product-model F1 falls between the shuffled lower and FlowER upper brackets. Convincing result: a reproducible peak layer, CKA ≥ 0.6 (convergent), and product-model F1 clearly above the shuffled lower bracket. Undecidable band: CKA in [0.3, 0.45] or product-model F1 within noise of the shuffled bracket — reported as weakly convergent / no advantage over recipe-learning; band fixed before data. Negative result: product-model decodability at the shuffled-pair bracket means they are genuine recipe learners, bounding H1/H2 and (as noted) justifying the purpose-built mechanistic-model program.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Atom-mapping errors in USPTO-derived mechanism annotations introduce label noise into probes; we restrict to high-confidence atom-mapped and mass-balanced reactions (mech-USPTO-31k, FlowER, PMechDB) and report sensitivity to mapping confidence.

Decodability of electron roles could reflect trivial correlation with atom/functional-group identity rather than genuine mechanistic representation; we control with reactivity-shuffled labels, within-reaction-center donor-vs-acceptor tests, and fingerprint baselines, and rely on causal steering as the primary mechanism evidence.

Steering in a nonlinear seq2seq transformer may push activations off-manifold and produce invalid SMILES; we bound alpha, report validity rates and sensitivity to alpha, and use matched random-direction controls.
Distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions; we use both linear probe directions and SAE features and report aggregate-direction effects.

A negative result (product models are genuinely recipe learners with no decodable, causal electron-flow structure) is scientifically decisive - it would justify the purpose-built mechanistic-model program - though it may be perceived as confirmatory; we frame either outcome as resolving the recipe-vs-mechanism debate at the representational level.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes/SAEs and public datasets, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: reading_frame_degeneracy_probe
Title: Does the Model Read in Frame? Causally Testing Whether Genomic Foundation Models Internally Represent the Triplet Reading Frame and Codon-Degeneracy Structure of the Genetic Code
Short Hypothesis: The genetic code is an exactly-known discrete mechanism: nucleotides are read in non-overlapping triplets anchored by a reading frame, and 61 sense codons map many-to-one onto 20 amino acids (degeneracy). We hypothesize that genomic foundation models trained on raw nucleotides internally represent this mechanism rather than mere k-mer statistics, meaning (a) their internal representations are frame-aware (encode a codon's position modulo 3 relative to the true reading frame), (b) synonymous codons are organized by their shared amino-acid identity (degeneracy geometry), and (c) this frame structure is causally load-bearing: a single-nucleotide frameshift insertion catastrophically and specifically reorganizes downstream codon-level representations and predictions, whereas a length-matched in-frame (3-nucleotide) insertion does not. Frameshift-vs-in-frame is an exact counterfactual matched on length and local composition, making this a rare mechanism-defining rather than correlation-matching test.
Related Work: Interpretability of genomic FMs has surged: Interpreting Evo 2 (2025) and Decode-gLM (2025) use SAEs to recover coding-sequence, tRNA/rRNA, and viral features; SAE studies on small gene LMs and Nucleotide Transformer recover transcription-factor motifs; nucleotide-dependency analysis (2024) reveals functional elements; cdsFM (2024) reports models 'recapitulate the overall structure of the genetic code'; Genomic Tokenizer (2025) builds codon/frame biology into tokenization by construction. Crucially, all of these are descriptive annotation-matching or build codon structure in by design. cdsFM shows the map is learnable when codons are tokenized, but does not test nucleotide-level models, nor whether the reading FRAME (position mod 3, the anchoring mechanism) is internally represented and causally used, nor whether degeneracy (synonymous equivalence) is geometrically encoded independent of local composition. No prior work uses the exact frameshift-vs-in-frame counterfactual to causally arbitrate whether a nucleotide-level FM represents the triplet-reading mechanism versus k-mer statistics. This causal, exact-counterfactual, degeneracy-geometry test is our novel contribution.
Abstract: The genetic code is one of biology's few exactly-known, discrete mechanisms: DNA is read in non-overlapping triplets anchored by a reading frame, and 61 sense codons map many-to-one onto 20 amino acids. This makes it an ideal, unambiguous probe for whether genomic foundation models learn mechanism or merely nucleotide-level statistics. We ask three mechanism-defining questions of nucleotide-level genomic FMs (Nucleotide Transformer, DNABERT-2, and Evo 2). First, are internal representations frame-aware: can we linearly decode a nucleotide's position modulo 3 relative to the true reading frame, beyond what local composition permits, and is a distinct feature dedicated to frame? Second, is codon degeneracy geometrically encoded: do synonymous codons cluster by their shared amino acid while remaining separable at the codon level, controlling for GC-content and dinucleotide statistics? Third, and most decisively, is frame structure causally load-bearing? We construct an exact counterfactual: inserting a single nucleotide (a frameshift) versus inserting a length-matched triplet (in-frame) within a coding sequence. A model that represents the reading mechanism should show catastrophic, specific downstream reorganization of codon-level representations and amino-acid predictions after a frameshift but near-invariance after an in-frame insertion; a k-mer statistical model should respond similarly to both. We further steer the recovered frame feature and test whether it induces frameshift-like downstream effects. Metrics quantify a frame-decodability-beyond-composition index, a degeneracy-clustering score, and a frameshift-vs-in-frame causal asymmetry. Either outcome sharpens what genomic foundation models actually represent, with direct implications for variant-effect and indel interpretation.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Frame-awareness probe beyond local composition): Tests the H1(a) claim that genomic foundation models encode a nucleotide's position modulo 3 relative to the true reading frame. Data: well-annotated coding sequences (CDS) from RefSeq/Ensembl across 5 species with known frames and start/stop codons (millions of CDS exist); we use 5,000 CDS (~5M nucleotides), stratified by species and length — 5,000 gives ample per-frame-class examples while keeping activation extraction feasible; each nucleotide carries its ground-truth position mod 3. Model: Nucleotide Transformer, DNABERT-2, and Evo 2 at a feasible size, all frozen; trainable = per-layer linear probes predicting position mod 3; 5 folds, 3 seeds. Systems compared: model-activation probe vs two strict baselines — a local one-hot/k-mer feature probe (frame must exceed local composition) and a randomly-initialized same-architecture model (confirms the structure is learned during pretraining). Decisive metric first: Frame-Decodability-Beyond-Composition Index = probe accuracy(model) − probe accuracy(local-composition baseline). Convincing result: index ≥ 0.15 with absolute model accuracy ≥ 0.9, and the random-init model near the composition baseline. Undecidable band: index in [0.03, 0.08] — frame decodability barely exceeds composition, reported as inconclusive; band fixed before data. Negative result: index ≈ 0 (or random-init as good as pretrained) means frame is not represented beyond k-mer statistics, H1 fails.

Experiment 2 (H2 — Degeneracy geometry of synonymous codons): Tests the H2(b) claim that synonymous codons are organized by shared amino-acid identity. Data: codon occurrences from the 5,000 CDS; codon-level representation = mean-pool of the triplet or codon-token embedding. Model: frozen NT/DNABERT-2/Evo 2, fixed activations. Systems compared: codon geometry colored by amino acid vs a GC/dinucleotide-regressed-out version (partial geometry), and vs the true codon-table degeneracy pattern (4-/2-/6-fold boxes). Decisive metric first: silhouette/clustering score of codons grouped by amino acid, plus a nested test (amino acid decodable AND codon identity still separable within amino acid). Convincing result: silhouette significantly positive after regressing out GC/dinucleotide content, and the learned degeneracy pattern mirrors the true code's fold structure. Undecidable band: partial silhouette in [0.0, 0.05] — clustering attributable to composition not degeneracy, reported as unsupported; band fixed before data. Negative result: no synonymous clustering beyond composition means degeneracy geometry is absent, H2 fails.

Experiment 3 (H3 — Frameshift-vs-in-frame causal counterfactual, primary test): Tests the decisive H3(c) claim that a single-nucleotide frameshift catastrophically and specifically reorganizes downstream codon representations while a length-matched in-frame (3-nt) insertion does not. Data: within each of 2,000 CDS from the Experiment-1 test split, at matched interior positions, construct paired edits — (a) insert 1 nucleotide (frameshift), (b) insert 3 nucleotides (in-frame) — with insertions matched on local nucleotide composition; this exact counterfactual is matched on length and local composition. Model: frozen models; measure change in downstream codon-level representations and per-position amino-acid/codon (masked-token) predictions after the insertion; 3 seeds. Systems compared: frameshift vs in-frame edits, as a function of distance downstream. Decisive metric first: Frameshift-vs-In-frame Causal Asymmetry = downstream-representation-change(frameshift) / downstream-representation-change(in-frame). Convincing result: asymmetry ≫ 1 (e.g., ≥ 3), rising with downstream distance, for the single-nucleotide models. Undecidable band: asymmetry in [0.9, 1.4] — frameshift and in-frame edits perturb the model equally, read as k-mer behavior (H3 unsupported); band fixed before data. Negative result: asymmetry ≈ 1 means the model does not represent the reading frame causally, H3 fails and (per the hypothesis) the model is a k-mer statistic.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Amino-acid consistency of frameshift effects and frame-feature steering): Tests that the frameshift's downstream effect is the biologically-correct shifted-frame reinterpretation, and that steering an internal frame feature reproduces it. Data: the 2,000 paired-edit CDS from Experiment 3, plus stop/start anchoring stimuli (premature in-frame stop insertion vs a synonymous same-length non-stop change). Model: frozen models; for coding-aware readouts, translate model-preferred codons or use Evo 2's coding-sequence feature; frame-feature steering uses the recovered frame direction / SAE frame feature at a chosen position, controls = matched-norm random and shuffled-frame-label directions; 3 seeds. Systems compared: (i) induced downstream reinterpretation vs the ground-truth +1/+2 shifted reading; (ii) frame-direction steering vs random/shuffled controls; (iii) premature-stop insertion vs synonymous control. Decisive metric first: agreement between induced downstream codon reinterpretation and the true shifted-frame amino-acid sequence, and steering mechanism-selectivity = |effect_frame direction| / |effect_random direction|. Convincing result: downstream agreement well above chance AND selectivity ≥ 3, with premature-stop causing a larger loss-of-coding reorganization than the synonymous control. Undecidable band: agreement near chance or selectivity in [1.2, 2.0] — reported as inconclusive causal frame use; band fixed before data. Negative result: no shifted-frame agreement and null steering means frame is not the causal variable even if Experiment-3 asymmetry appeared, so H3's mechanism reading is unsupported.

Experiment 5 (H1/H2 — Layer/emergence, cross-model convergence, and statistics-to-mechanism brackets): Locates frame/degeneracy structure and brackets it, without enlarging the claim. Data: the Experiment-1 CDS set. Model: frozen NT/DNABERT-2/Evo 2, per-layer analysis; brackets = a codon-tokenized model where frame is built in (cdsFM/EnCodon, upper) and a model trained on frame-scrambled sequences (lower); CKA between the three models' frame subspaces; 3 seeds. Note: BPE-tokenized models (DNABERT-2) are handled by mapping token spans to nucleotide positions, with single-nucleotide Evo 2 prioritized for the cleanest test. Systems compared: per-layer frame accuracy and degeneracy silhouette across depth; nucleotide-model decodability vs the codon-tokenized upper and scrambled lower brackets. Decisive metric first: layer of peak frame-awareness, mean pairwise CKA of frame subspaces, and where nucleotide-model frame accuracy falls between the brackets. Convincing result: a reproducible emergence layer, CKA ≥ 0.6, and frame accuracy clearly above the scrambled lower bracket. Undecidable band: CKA in [0.3, 0.45] or accuracy within noise of the scrambled bracket — reported as weakly convergent / no learned frame advantage; band fixed before data. Negative result: nucleotide-model frame structure at the scrambled bracket means frame is not learned, bounding H1/H2.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Frame position modulo 3 correlates with local codon composition in real CDS, so frame decodability could partly reflect composition; we mitigate with strict local-composition baselines, GC/dinucleotide controls, and the exact frameshift-vs-in-frame counterfactual which is matched on length and local composition.

Some models (e.g., BPE-tokenized DNABERT-2) do not tokenize per-nucleotide or per-codon, complicating position-mod-3 alignment; we handle this by mapping token spans to nucleotide positions and report per-model tokenization caveats, prioritizing single-nucleotide models (Evo 2) for the cleanest test.

Steering the frame feature in a nonlinear model may push activations off-manifold and yield uninterpretable outputs; we bound perturbation magnitude, report sensitivity, and use random/shuffled-label controls, relying primarily on the input-space frameshift counterfactual as causal evidence.
Distributed/superposed encodings may mean no single clean 'frame' feature exists; we use both linear probe directions and SAE features and report aggregate-direction results.

A negative result (models respond similarly to frameshift and in-frame insertions, i.e., k-mer statistics dominate) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting these models for indel/variant-effect prediction, though it may be perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as the first exact-mechanism causal test of the reading frame.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes/SAEs and public genome annotations, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: geostrophic_balance_manifold_probe
Title: Wind Follows Pressure, Inside the Model Too? Probing Whether Weather Foundation Models Internally Encode Geostrophic and Thermal-Wind Balance, Including Its Latitude-Dependent Breakdown
Short Hypothesis: Atmospheric dynamics is governed not by independent fields but by diagnostic balance relationships that couple them: geostrophic balance ties the horizontal wind to the pressure-gradient force via the Coriolis parameter f, thermal wind ties vertical wind shear to horizontal temperature gradients, and hydrostatic balance ties vertical pressure structure to density. We hypothesize that if data-driven weather foundation models represent atmospheric mechanism rather than field-wise pattern matching, their internal representations will (a) encode these balance relationships as coupled directions (wind and pressure-gradient live on a shared balance manifold, not as independently decodable features), (b) causally enforce them (perturbing internal pressure-gradient structure induces the geostrophically-consistent wind change and vice versa), and, most decisively, (c) reproduce the physically-mandated latitude-dependent breakdown of geostrophic balance near the equator where f -> 0. The equatorial breakdown is an exact, physics-predicted signature that a mere pattern matcher would not reproduce internally.
Related Work: Two lines bracket the gap. (1) Interpretability of weather models: SAE studies on GraphCast (2025) recover single physical features (tropical cyclones, atmospheric rivers, sea-ice) and steer them; GraphDOP work (2025) shows unified world-model representations and applies data-assimilation diagnostics (FSOI). These recover and manipulate individual quantities/objects, not the diagnostic BALANCE RELATIONSHIPS that couple fields. (2) Dynamical/physics tests: 'Dynamical Tests of a Deep Learning Weather Prediction Model' (2024) and the Matsuno-Gill/ASL studies subject Pangu-Weather to classical perturbation experiments and find geostrophic adjustment and wave responses AT THE INPUT-OUTPUT LEVEL; the hydrostatic-balance-constraint (2025) and neural background-error-covariance (2026) papers impose or exploit balance in outputs/latents by construction. None tests whether the model's INTERNAL REPRESENTATION encodes the balance constraints as coupled structure, whether that coupling is causally load-bearing, or whether it reproduces the latitude-dependent (f -> 0) breakdown of geostrophy that formally distinguishes mechanism from pattern matching. Our relational, causal, and physics-predicted-breakdown test is the novel contribution.
Abstract: Data-driven weather foundation models now rival physics-based forecasts, and interpretability studies have shown they encode recognizable physical objects such as cyclones and atmospheric rivers. But atmospheric dynamics is defined by diagnostic balances that couple fields: geostrophic balance links horizontal wind to the pressure-gradient force through the Coriolis parameter, thermal wind links vertical wind shear to horizontal temperature gradients, and hydrostatic balance links vertical pressure structure to density. We ask whether weather foundation models internally represent these coupling relationships rather than storing fields as independently decodable features. Using pretrained models (GraphCast and Pangu-Weather) evaluated on ERA5, we first train probes to test whether the wind field and the pressure-gradient force share a common internal balance subspace, quantifying coupling beyond what independent field decoding predicts. Second, we run causal balance-consistency interventions: perturbing internal pressure-gradient structure should induce the geostrophically-correct wind change (parallel to isobars, magnitude scaling as 1/f) while a matched non-balance perturbation should not, and the analogous test for thermal wind. Third, and most decisively, we test the physics-mandated latitude dependence: geostrophic coupling in the representation should be strong in midlatitudes and break down near the equator where the Coriolis parameter vanishes, exactly as theory dictates; a pattern matcher would lack this internal latitude-structured breakdown. Metrics quantify a balance-coupling-beyond-independence index, a causal balance-consistency asymmetry, and the correlation between internal coupling strength and the true Coriolis parameter across latitude. Either outcome sharpens what these operationally deployed models actually represent.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Balance coupling beyond independent field encoding): Tests the H1(a) claim that weather foundation models encode balance relationships as coupled directions — wind and pressure-gradient share a balance subspace rather than being independently decodable. Data: ERA5 reanalysis snapshots (hourly global fields, decades available); we use 500 snapshots stratified across seasons and latitude bands — 500 gives stable per-band statistics while keeping inference-only extraction to a few GPU-hours; from ERA5 we compute ground-truth geostrophic wind v_g = (1/(f·rho)) k×∇p, the ageostrophic residual, thermal-wind shear, and hydrostatic residual per grid point. Model: pretrained GraphCast and Pangu-Weather (public weights), frozen; trainable = per-layer linear probes for wind, pressure-gradient, temperature-gradient; canonical correlation analysis / PLS between the wind and pressure-gradient subspaces; 3 seeds. Systems compared: shared balance-subspace prediction vs independent per-field encoding, with a shuffled-probe control; repeated for thermal-wind and hydrostatic relations. Decisive metric first: Balance-Coupling Index BCI = shared-subspace predictive R² − what independent per-field encoding predicts. Convincing result: BCI > 0.1 for geostrophic (and ideally thermal-wind/hydrostatic), significant over seeds — a single low-dimensional direction predicts both the pressure gradient and the geostrophically-implied wind. Undecidable band: BCI in [0.0, 0.05] — coupling attributable to fields being separately encoded, reported as no shared manifold; band fixed before data. Negative result: BCI ≤ 0 means fields are encoded independently, H1 fails and the latitude/causal tests targeting the balance subspace are moot.

Experiment 2 (H3 — Latitude-dependent breakdown of geostrophic coupling, decisive test): Tests the decisive H3(c) claim that internal coupling strength follows the physics-mandated latitude dependence, vanishing near the equator where f→0. Data: the 500 ERA5 snapshots binned into latitude bands (e.g., 10° bins from equator to pole). Model: frozen GraphCast/Pangu, fixed Experiment-1 subspaces; BCI recomputed per band; 3 seeds. Systems compared: per-band geostrophic BCI vs the true Coriolis parameter f = 2·Omega·sin(latitude); control = temperature/humidity decodability (not geostrophically constrained) which should NOT show latitude structure. Decisive metric first: Spearman/partial correlation between per-band coupling strength and |f|, controlling for data density and field magnitude. Convincing result: coupling strength scales with |f| (correlation ≥ 0.6), strong in midlatitudes and vanishing near the equator, while the humidity control shows no such structure. Undecidable band: correlation in [0.3, 0.45] — a latitude trend too weak to attribute to f, reported as inconclusive; band fixed before data. Negative result: no correlation with |f| (or the humidity control shows the same latitude structure) means the model does not reproduce the physics-predicted equatorial breakdown, the decisive H3 test fails. As pre-specified, the equatorial region is treated as the predicted breakdown zone, not a region where geostrophic coupling is expected.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Causal geostrophic-consistency intervention): Tests the H2(b) claim that the model causally enforces balance — perturbing internal pressure-gradient structure induces the geostrophically-consistent wind change (and the thermal-wind analogue). Data: 200 ERA5 snapshots with target midlatitude regions where f is well away from 0. Model: frozen models; at a chosen layer, perturb the decoded pressure-gradient direction and measure the induced change in decoded wind and next-step wind forecast; run the analogous temperature-gradient→vertical-shear intervention; controls = matched-norm random directions and a non-balance (divergent) perturbation; 3 seeds. Systems compared: balance perturbation vs random / non-balance controls. Decisive metric first: Balance-Consistency Selectivity = |geostrophic-aligned response to balance perturbation| / |response to matched control|, with the induced wind expected parallel to isobars and scaling as 1/f. Convincing result: selectivity ≥ 3 with the induced wind change parallel to isobars and 1/f magnitude scaling. Undecidable band: selectivity in [1.2, 2.0] or no isobar alignment — reported as inconclusive causal enforcement; band fixed before data. Negative result: selectivity ≈ 1 means balance is decodable but not causally enforced, H2 fails.

Experiment 4 (H2 — Geostrophic-adjustment timescale test): Tests the dynamical half of H2(b) — that a deliberately unbalanced internal state relaxes toward balance on the physically-expected latitude-dependent timescale. Data: 150 ERA5 snapshots across latitude bands. Model: frozen models; perturb the internal state into a wind–pressure-inconsistent configuration and roll forward; 3 seeds. Systems compared: restoration rate vs the true inertial timescale 2·pi/f across latitude bands. Decisive metric first: rate and latitude-dependence of balance restoration in representation and outputs, compared to 2·pi/f. Convincing result: the model relaxes toward balance with a restoration timescale that tracks the latitude-dependent inertial period (correlation with 2·pi/f ≥ 0.5). Undecidable band: restoration observed but its latitude dependence correlates with 2·pi/f only in [0.2, 0.35] — reported as weak/inconclusive; band fixed before data. Negative result: no relaxation toward balance, or a timescale unrelated to f, means the model does not implement geostrophic adjustment, bounding H2.

Experiment 5 (H1 — Cross-model convergence and pattern-matching-to-mechanism brackets): Tests whether balance structure is convergent and brackets it, without enlarging the claim. Data: the Experiment-1 ERA5 set. Model: frozen GraphCast and Pangu; brackets = a constraint-imposed model (hydrostatic/geostrophic by construction, e.g. a hydrostatic-constrained DLWP variant, upper) and a randomly-initialized same-architecture model (lower), probed identically; CKA between GraphCast and Pangu balance subspaces; grid/mesh artifacts controlled by latitude-band aggregation and grid-position controls. Systems compared: BCI and latitude-|f| correlation across models and brackets; CKA of balance subspaces. Decisive metric first: mean pairwise CKA of balance subspaces and where the operational models' BCI falls between the random lower and constrained upper brackets. Convincing result: CKA ≥ 0.6 (convergent) and operational-model BCI clearly above the random lower bracket. Undecidable band: CKA in [0.3, 0.45] or BCI within noise of the random bracket — reported as weakly convergent / no learned balance advantage; band fixed before data. Negative result: operational-model balance structure at the random-init bracket means balance is not learned during pretraining, bounding H1.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Wind and pressure-gradient fields are strongly correlated in real data, so shared-subspace coupling could partly reflect data statistics rather than encoded constraint; we mitigate with independent-encoding baselines, the latitude-dependent breakdown test (a signature data correlation alone would not structure by f), and causal interventions.
Linear probes and CCA may miss nonlinear coupling; we report nonlinear (kernel-CCA) variants and rely on causal interventions as primary evidence.

Interventions in a nonlinear GNN/transformer may push activations off-manifold and produce unphysical outputs; we bound perturbation magnitude, report sensitivity, and use matched-norm and non-balance controls.
GraphCast operates on an icosahedral mesh with grid-locked features reported in prior work; we account for mesh artifacts by controlling for grid position and using latitude-band aggregation.

Near the equator, additional balances (e.g., equatorial wave dynamics) replace geostrophy; we treat the equatorial region as the predicted breakdown zone rather than expecting geostrophic coupling, and cross-check with expected equatorial balance signatures.

A negative result (fields encoded independently, no latitude-structured balance coupling) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting these operationally deployed models beyond their training distribution, though it may be perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as the first internal, relational, physics-predicted test of atmospheric balance in weather foundation models.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes/CCA and public ERA5 data, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: saha_boltzmann_abundance_probe
Title: Does the Model Know the Curve of Growth? Testing Whether Stellar Foundation Models Disentangle Abundance from Temperature via Saha-Boltzmann Line Physics
Short Hypothesis: The strength of an absorption line in a stellar spectrum is not a monotone readout of elemental abundance: it is governed by the Saha-Boltzmann excitation/ionization equilibrium (line strength depends on temperature through level populations) and by the nonlinear curve of growth (linear -> saturated -> damping regimes). We hypothesize that if a stellar foundation model represents this mechanism rather than surface line-depth statistics, its internal abundance representation will (a) be invariant to temperature-driven line-strength changes at fixed abundance, (b) follow the curve of growth (saturating with respect to equivalent width) rather than tracking raw line depth, and (c) encode the physically-mandated coupling among multiple lines of the same element that share excitation potential. An exact counterfactual - vary Teff at fixed [Fe/H] versus vary [Fe/H] at fixed Teff - makes this a mechanism-defining rather than correlation-matching test.
Related Work: Astronomy interpretability has grown quickly: SAEs on galaxy morphology (Euclid Q1, 2025; SFNet, 2024), attention analyses showing SpectraFM (2024) attends to chemically-informative wavelengths, disentangled chemical-tagging networks (Price-Jones/Bovy line, 2021), symbolic regression from GNNs for cosmology (2020), and interpretable anomaly/attribution methods for spectra (2021-2025). AstroCLIP (2024) and OJALA (2026) provide cross-modal / SED foundation models that decode stellar parameters. All of these either (i) attribute which wavelengths matter, (ii) recover monosemantic morphology features, or (iii) show a parameter is decodable. None tests whether a stellar foundation model internally represents the Saha-Boltzmann/curve-of-growth mechanism that determines how abundance maps to line strength, whether the model correctly disentangles the well-known abundance-Teff degeneracy at the representational level, or whether its internal abundance direction is causally load-bearing and physics-consistent. Because line strength is jointly set by abundance and temperature via an exactly-known physical law, this is a rare setting where mechanism can be cleanly separated from correlation. Our counterfactual, curve-of-growth, and multi-line-coupling tests are the novel contribution.
Abstract: Stellar spectra are among the most physically constrained data in science: the strength of any absorption line is set jointly by elemental abundance and by the Saha-Boltzmann excitation/ionization equilibrium through temperature-dependent level populations, and it grows with abundance along a nonlinear curve of growth (linear, saturated, and damping regimes). This makes stellar foundation models an ideal testbed for whether scientific foundation models learn mechanism or surface statistics. We ask whether stellar spectral foundation models (e.g., SpectraFM, AstroCLIP's spectrum encoder, and open transformer spectral models) internally represent this line-formation mechanism. First, we test disentanglement of the classic abundance-temperature degeneracy: using synthetic spectra where we can hold [Fe/H] fixed while varying Teff (which strongly changes Fe line strengths) and vice versa, we probe whether the model's internal 'abundance' direction is invariant to Teff-driven line-strength changes at fixed abundance and responds selectively to true abundance changes. Second, we test curve-of-growth structure: does the internal abundance representation saturate (as physics dictates) rather than track raw line depth or equivalent width linearly? Third, we test multi-line coupling: lines of the same element sharing excitation potential must vary together per Saha-Boltzmann; we test whether the model encodes this coupling and whether it correctly separates high- versus low-excitation lines' temperature sensitivity. We validate causally by ablating/steering the recovered abundance direction and by transferring from synthetic to real spectra (APOGEE/GALAH). Metrics quantify a temperature-invariance-of-abundance index, curve-of-growth agreement, and multi-line coupling fidelity. Either outcome sharpens what stellar foundation models actually represent, with implications for trusting them in low-metallicity and parameter-degenerate regimes.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Abundance–temperature disentanglement, primary counterfactual): Tests the H1(a) claim that the model's internal abundance representation is invariant to temperature-driven line-strength changes at fixed abundance. Data: a synthetic grid of stellar spectra generated with a standard radiative-transfer code (Turbospectrum/MOOG with MARCS atmospheres) spanning Teff, log g, [Fe/H], and a few element abundances, where abundance and temperature can be varied exactly independently; we generate ~5,000 spectra covering matched counterfactual pairs — (a) fix [Fe/H], vary Teff over a range producing large Fe line-strength change; (b) fix Teff, vary [Fe/H] by a matched line-strength amount — 5,000 is sufficient to sample the pairs across the grid and is cheap to synthesize. Also assemble real labeled spectra from APOGEE (~650k) and GALAH (~600k) for the later transfer test. Model: public stellar spectral foundation models — SpectraFM and the AstroCLIP spectrum encoder (plus an open transformer spectrum model if available) — frozen; trainable = per-layer linear probes decoding Teff, log g, [Fe/H] (baseline decodability, must reach R² ≥ 0.8 to license the readout); 5 folds, 3 seeds. Systems compared: change in the decoded-abundance direction under the abundance-varying pair (b) vs the temperature-varying pair (a). Decisive metric first: Temperature-Invariance-of-Abundance Index TIA = |Δabundance representation under (b)| / |Δabundance representation under (a)|. Convincing result: TIA ≫ 1 (e.g., ≥ 3) — abundance representation moves with true abundance, not with Teff-driven line strength. Undecidable band: TIA in [0.9, 1.4] — abundance readout responds to temperature-driven line strength as much as to abundance, read as a line-depth statistic (H1 unsupported); band fixed before data. Negative result: TIA ≈ 1 means no disentanglement, H1 fails and the curve-of-growth/coupling structure targeting the abundance direction is compromised.

Experiment 2 (H2 — Curve-of-growth test): Tests the H2(b) claim that the internal abundance readout follows the saturating curve of growth rather than tracking raw line depth. Data: for a fixed Fe line/element, sweep abundance across linear, saturated, and damping regimes, computing the true equivalent-width curve of growth from the synthesis (~50 abundance steps × several lines, from the Experiment-1 synthesizer). Model: frozen SpectraFM/AstroCLIP, fixed Experiment-1 abundance readout. Systems compared: internal abundance readout vs true log-abundance, contrasted with a raw-equivalent-width readout (saturates) and a raw-line-depth readout (does not). Decisive metric first: goodness-of-fit of the internal abundance readout to the true log-abundance across regimes, and whether it reproduces the saturation plateau (curvature parameter). Convincing result: internal readout tracks the saturating curve of growth (fit R² ≥ 0.8 across regimes) with a saturation plateau, unlike the linear raw-line-depth readout. Undecidable band: the internal readout matches raw line depth as well as it matches the curve of growth (ΔR² between the two fits in [−0.05, 0.05]) — cannot distinguish mechanism from line-depth statistic; band fixed before data. Negative result: internal readout linear in line depth with no saturation means it tracks surface statistics, H2 fails.

Experiment 3 (H3 — Multi-line Saha–Boltzmann coupling): Tests the H3(c) claim that the model encodes the physically-mandated coupling among multiple lines of the same element sharing excitation potential — shared abundance dependence but excitation-dependent Teff sensitivity. Data: for an element with multiple lines of differing excitation potential (e.g., clean, well-separated Fe I lines identified from the synthesis), synthesize spectra varying Teff and abundance; restrict to non-blended lines. Model: frozen models; per-line temperature sensitivity measured by masking/occluding each line region; a shared-abundance-subspace coherence score computed across same-element lines vs different-element lines (control); 3 seeds. Systems compared: per-line temperature sensitivity in the representation vs the Saha–Boltzmann-predicted sensitivity; same-element vs different-element subspace coherence. Decisive metric first: alignment (correlation) between representational per-line Teff-sensitivity and the Saha–Boltzmann prediction, plus the shared-abundance coherence gap (same-element − different-element). Convincing result: alignment ≥ 0.6 AND same-element coherence clearly exceeds different-element coherence. Undecidable band: alignment in [0.3, 0.45] or a coherence gap within its 3-seed CI of 0 — reported as inconclusive coupling; band fixed before data. Negative result: no alignment with Saha–Boltzmann sensitivity and no shared-abundance coherence means multi-line coupling is absent, H3 fails.

Experiment 4 (H1 — Causal load-bearing (ablation/steering) and synthetic-to-real transfer): Tests that the disentangled abundance/temperature directions are causally load-bearing and survive on real data. Data: the Experiment-1 synthetic grid plus real APOGEE/GALAH spectra (pipeline labels as ground truth). Model: frozen models; ablate the recovered abundance direction and measure degradation of abundance prediction while Teff prediction is preserved (and vice versa); steer along the abundance direction and check that predicted/reconstructed spectra (where a decoder or masked head exists) move in the curve-of-growth-correct direction; controls = matched-norm random directions; 3 seeds. Systems compared: abundance-direction ablation vs Teff-direction ablation vs random-direction ablation; synthetic vs real. Decisive metric first: selective degradation ratio = (abundance-prediction error increase when abundance direction ablated) / (abundance-prediction error increase when a random direction of equal norm ablated), with Teff prediction expected preserved. Convincing result: ratio ≥ 3 with Teff prediction largely intact, and the disentanglement/curve-of-growth structure reproduces on real APOGEE/GALAH spectra. Undecidable band: ratio in [1.2, 2.0] or structure that holds on synthetic but only weakly on real — reported as inconclusive causal use / limited transfer; band fixed before data. Negative result: ratio ≈ 1 (ablation no more damaging than random) or no transfer to real spectra means the directions are entangled or synthetic-only, bounding H1.

Experiment 5 (H1 — Low-metallicity/degeneracy stress, failure prediction, and cross-model convergence): Tests where disentanglement degrades and whether the invariance index flags unreliable estimates, plus convergence across models — sharpening, not enlarging, H1. Data: metal-poor and strong abundance–Teff-degeneracy regions of the synthetic grid, plus real metal-poor stars from APOGEE/GALAH with pipeline labels. Model: frozen SpectraFM/AstroCLIP; per-layer emergence analysis and CKA between models' abundance subspaces; 3 seeds. Systems compared: TIA and abundance-prediction error across metallicity regimes; TIA as a flag for high-error stars. Decisive metric first: AUROC of the temperature-invariance index for flagging high-error stars, plus mean pairwise CKA of abundance subspaces. Convincing result: TIA-based flagging AUROC ≥ 0.75 and CKA ≥ 0.6 (convergent Saha–Boltzmann-consistent structure). Undecidable band: AUROC in [0.55, 0.65] or CKA in [0.3, 0.45] — reported as weak failure-prediction / weak convergence; band fixed before data. Negative result: TIA at chance for flagging errors and CKA at the random floor means the invariance signal is neither diagnostic nor convergent, bounding H1's practical and universality claims.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Abundance and Teff are correlated in real stellar populations, so disentanglement could be confounded; we mitigate with synthetic spectra where the two are varied exactly independently and use matched-line-strength controls.

Synthetic spectra may differ from real spectra (synthetic gap), so representations learned on real data may not fully engage the synthetic grid; we test synthetic-to-real transfer explicitly and, where possible, use models pre-trained partly on synthetic data (e.g., SpectraFM).

Linear probes recovering an abundance direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with ablation/steering and random-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions.

Some models tokenize/normalize spectra (continuum normalization, resampling) in ways that may alter line-strength information; we document each model's preprocessing and probe pre-normalization activations where feasible.
Occlusion-based per-line sensitivity measurements can be noisy for blended lines; we restrict multi-line coupling tests to clean, well-separated lines identified from the synthesis.

A negative result (models track line-strength statistics and do not disentangle abundance from temperature per Saha-Boltzmann) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting these models in degenerate/metal-poor regimes, though it may be perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of line-formation physics in stellar foundation models.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and standard synthesis tools/public spectral surveys, keeping compute at academic scale.

novelty.reasoning: Core technical claims: (1) a stellar foundation model's internal abundance representation should be invariant to temperature-driven line-strength changes at fixed abundance; (2) it should encode the nonlinear curve-of-growth (linear->saturated->damping) rather than raw line depth; (3) it should capture multi-line coupling predicted by Saha-Boltzmann for lines sharing excitation potential; (4) causal steering/ablation should change abundance but preserve Teff if the representation is mechanistic; (5) exact Teff-vs-[Fe/H] counterfactuals on synthetic spectra provide a mechanism test, not just correlation. This is a genuine novel test/setting, not a new dataset or model. The closest prior family is astronomy interpretability and parameter decodability (SpectraFM attention analyses, AstroCLIP, chemical-tagging networks), which mostly ask what is decodable or salient. The actual delta is shifting from 'can the model read out abundance/Teff?' to 'does the internal abundance direction obey known line-formation physics under controlled counterfactuals?' That is a non-trivial next step and meaningfully different from prior work because the law is known and counterfactuals can be exact. The novelty lives mainly in the mechanism test and the problem framing, with some novelty in the evaluation metric and causal probing rather than in a new task/dataset.

Name: activity_cliff_geometry_probe
Title: Smooth Where It Should Jump: Do Chemistry Foundation Models Internally Represent Activity Cliffs as Pharmacophore-Localized Discontinuities, or Just Smooth Structural Similarity?
Short Hypothesis: Activity cliffs — pairs of near-identical molecules with large potency differences — are exactly where molecular property models fail. We hypothesize this failure has a mechanistic signature: chemistry foundation models embed structurally-similar molecules close together regardless of whether a tiny change flips potency, so their internal representation is locally SMOOTH across cliffs (structure-driven) rather than DISCONTINUOUS at the potency-flipping substructure (mechanism-driven). If instead a model represents the underlying pharmacophore mechanism, then (a) cliff-forming matched transformations should produce a larger, localized representational jump than potency-neutral (non-cliff) matched transformations of comparable structural magnitude, and (b) that jump should causally localize to the pharmacophore-relevant substructure via activation patching. The exact matched-molecular-pair cliff-vs-non-cliff counterfactual makes this a mechanism-defining test of WHY cliffs are hard, not another cliff predictor.
Related Work: A large body of work treats activity cliffs (ACs) as a prediction problem: MoleculeACE (Exposing the Limitations, 2022) shows all ML methods struggle at ACs and descriptor methods beat deep models; ACNet, ACES-GNN, ACANet, ACtriplet, and SCAGE (Nature Comm 2025) build AC-aware predictors or explanation-supervised GNNs. Separately, interpretability of chemistry models (Unveiling Latent Knowledge via SAEs 2025; MoleX 2024; concept-whitening GNNs) recovers concept features aligned with functional groups and pharmacological classes, and roughness/RePRA analyses (ROGI-XD 2023; RePRA 2023) show pretrained representations do NOT produce smoother QSPR surfaces. Crucially, none of these asks the mechanism-defining question: is the AC failure caused by the model's internal representation being locally smooth across cliffs (blind to the discontinuity), and does the representational change at a cliff causally localize to the pharmacophore substructure that actually flips potency? Prior AC work measures output error or trains cliff-aware losses; prior interpretability work matches features to marginal annotations. Our exact cliff-vs-matched-non-cliff counterfactual, representational-smoothness geometry, and causal pharmacophore-localization patching are the novel contribution, explaining WHY cliffs are hard at the representational level rather than engineering around them.
Abstract: Activity cliffs — pairs of molecules differing by a minor structural change yet showing large potency differences — are the single most reliable failure mode of molecular property models, but why they are hard remains a black box. We propose a mechanism-defining test of whether chemistry foundation models represent the pharmacophore mechanism behind cliffs or merely encode structural similarity. Our central hypothesis is that these models embed structurally-similar molecules close together regardless of potency, making their internal representation locally SMOOTH across a cliff — blind to the very discontinuity that defines it — which would mechanistically explain the observed failures. We test this with an exact counterfactual built from matched molecular pairs (MMPs): cliff pairs (same transformation, large potency jump) versus matched non-cliff pairs (comparable structural transformation, negligible potency change) against the same targets, drawn from MoleculeACE and ChEMBL. First, we measure the internal representational distance induced by each transformation across layers in models such as ChemBERTa/MoleculeSTM, SMI-TED (FM4M), and Uni-Mol, testing whether cliff transformations produce larger, sharper representational jumps than matched non-cliff transformations — or whether both are equally smooth (the failure signature). Second, using sparse autoencoders and linear probes we test whether a dedicated feature/direction tracks potency independent of structure. Third, via activation patching we test whether the cliff-induced representational change causally localizes to the pharmacophore-relevant substructure (e.g., the atom whose modification creates a steric clash or breaks a hydrogen bond), versus being diffuse. Metrics quantify a cliff-vs-non-cliff jump ratio, a potency-beyond-structure decoding index, and a pharmacophore-localization score. Either outcome sharpens why deployed chemistry models fail precisely where drug discovery needs them most.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — cliff-vs-non-cliff representational jump): Tests the core claim that a chemistry foundation model's internal geometry is locally smooth across activity cliffs — i.e. a tiny structural edit that flips potency (a cliff) moves the representation no more than a comparable edit that leaves potency unchanged (a non-cliff). Data (existing, adapted): MoleculeACE (public; 30 ChEMBL targets, ~48,000 molecules with curated pIC50). From it we build, per target, cliff pairs (ECFP4 Tanimoto >= 0.9, |dpIC50| >= 2.0) and non-cliff pairs (Tanimoto >= 0.9, |dpIC50| <= 0.5), each a single matched-molecular-pair transformation, and match the two sets on transformation magnitude (heavy atoms changed within +/-1, ECFP4 distance within +/-0.02) so only the potency consequence differs. MoleculeACE yields ~10^3-10^4 candidate cliff pairs; we cap at 200 matched pairs/target (limited by the scarcer cliff side), ~4,000-6,000 pairs total, enough for per-model bootstrap CIs. Models (all frozen, inference only): ChemBERTa-2 (~46M params, MLM checkpoint), Uni-Mol (~48M, 3D graph), plus an ECFP4 2048-bit fingerprint as a purely-structural lower bound; representations taken at every layer, seeds only affect the later probes (0,1,2). Systems compared: each deep model vs ECFP, per layer. Decisive metric first: Cliff-vs-Non-cliff Jump Ratio = median cosine distance over cliff pairs / median over matched non-cliff pairs, with 95% bootstrap CI over pairs, best layer per model. Indecision band, stated up front: a ratio whose CI falls within [1.1, 1.5] cannot decide, and we then report the smoothness question unresolved for that model and defer to the H3 patching test; CI lower bound > 1.5 is a mechanism-aware jump; CI upper bound < 1.1 (expected for ECFP by construction) is the hypothesized smooth-failure signature. Convincing support: deep models sit at <= 1.1 like ECFP. Negative result (deep models >= 1.5) would refute the smoothness claim and show these models already jump at cliffs.

Experiment 2 (H2 — potency encoded beyond structure): Tests whether the representation carries potency information above raw structural similarity, the encoding that a mechanism-aware model must have and a purely smooth one lacks. Data: the same matched cliff pairs from Experiment 1 (MoleculeACE, 30 targets). Model: same frozen ChemBERTa-2 and Uni-Mol; the only trainable part is a ridge linear probe (L2 chosen by 5-fold CV on the training targets), trained on 20 targets and tested on the 10 held-out targets, 3 seeds. Systems compared: model-representation probe vs a fingerprint-distance-only predictor. Decisive metric first: Potency-Beyond-Structure Index = within-pair accuracy of predicting which molecule of a matched cliff pair is more potent from the representation, minus the accuracy from ECFP distance alone. Indecision band up front: an index in [0.03, 0.10] (accuracy points) cannot decide and is reported as weak/ambiguous potency encoding; index >= 0.10 with bootstrap CI lower bound > 0.03 is convincing evidence of potency-beyond-structure; index <= 0.03 means the model adds nothing beyond structure, consistent with the smooth-failure hypothesis. Negative result here strengthens the core claim.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal pharmacophore localization via patching): Tests hypothesis assertion (b): that any cliff-induced representational jump is causally carried by the pharmacophore-relevant substructure, not diffused across the molecule. Data (adapted): single-transformation MMP cliffs from Experiment 1 for which the changed atom/group is unambiguous (we keep only pairs with exactly one MMP transformation; ~30-40% of cliffs qualify, ~1,500-2,000 pairs). Model: Uni-Mol and ChemBERTa-2 (frozen), which expose per-atom/per-token activations. Method: for each cliff pair, patch the low-potency molecule's activations with the high-potency molecule's at (i) the pharmacophore substructure only vs (ii) matched-size off-target substructures, and read the change in a frozen potency-probe output (probe from Experiment 2). Systems compared: pharmacophore patch vs off-target patch. Decisive metric first: Pharmacophore-Localization Score = |delta prediction from pharmacophore patch| / |delta from matched off-target patch|, bootstrap CI over pairs. Indecision band up front: a score whose CI lies in [1.3, 2.0] cannot decide and is reported as partial/uncertain localization; CI lower bound > 2.0 is convincing causal localization to the pharmacophore; CI upper bound < 1.3 means the effect is spatially diffuse (no localized mechanism), consistent with the smoothness hypothesis. A negative result (score ~1) supports the core claim that cliffs are not represented as pharmacophore-localized discontinuities.

Experiment 4 (H4 — smoothness predicts the documented cliff failure): Tests the framing claim that this representational signature explains WHERE the model's potency predictions actually fail. Data: MoleculeACE cliff pairs (30 targets) with the benchmark's reported per-molecule potency errors from a standard fine-tuned regressor head. Model: frozen backbones from Experiment 1; the per-pair jump ratio and localization score are the predictors, no new training beyond a logistic link (3 seeds). Systems compared: internal-signal predictor vs an output-confidence baseline (predicted-variance / ensemble disagreement). Decisive metric first: AUROC for flagging the high-error cliff pairs (top-quartile absolute error) from the internal smoothness signal. Indecision band up front: AUROC in [0.60, 0.70] cannot decide and is reported as a weak link; AUROC >= 0.70 with CI lower bound > 0.60 and beating the confidence baseline is convincing that the representational signature explains the failure; AUROC <= 0.60 (near the 0.50 chance line) means the signature does not track failures, weakening the mechanistic-signature claim even if Experiments 1-3 are positive. This experiment is what ties the internal geometry to the real-world cliff failure the hypothesis is about.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Matching cliff and non-cliff pairs on structural-transformation magnitude is imperfect; residual structural differences could confound the jump ratio. We mitigate with tight fingerprint-distance and atoms-changed matching and report sensitivity to the matching threshold.

Pharmacophore-relevant substructure assignment from MMP transformations may be ambiguous for pairs with multiple simultaneous changes; we restrict causal-patching to single-transformation MMP-cliffs and, where available, use docking/known SAR to confirm the responsible group.

Some FMs pool to a single molecule embedding, limiting token/atom-level patching; we prioritize models with per-atom/per-token activations (Uni-Mol, ChemBERTa) for the localization test and use whole-molecule patching as a coarser fallback.
Potency labels (pIC50) are assay-dependent and noisy across ChEMBL sources; we use MoleculeACE's curated targets and report robustness to potency-difference thresholds defining a cliff.

A finding that models are locally smooth across cliffs (ratio ≈ 1) is a negative result about mechanism, but it is precisely the mechanistic explanation for the well-documented AC failure mode and is decision-relevant for trusting these models in lead optimization; we frame either outcome as explaining WHY cliffs are hard at the representational level.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes/SAEs and public benchmark data (MoleculeACE, ChEMBL), keeping compute at academic scale.

novelty.reasoning: Core novelty is the mechanistic framing: a matched cliff-vs-non-cliff counterfactual plus representational geometry and activation patching to test whether FMs encode activity cliffs as pharmacophore-localized discontinuities or remain smooth. That is more than another cliff predictor, and the exact delta versus prior AC work is meaningful. Still, the underlying hypothesis that models are smooth across cliffs is adjacent to existing roughness/smoothness and cliff-failure findings, so the novelty is stronger in the causal/interpretability setup than in the finding itself.

Name: convergence_vs_ancestry_probe
Title: Similarity Is Not Ancestry: Do Genomic Foundation Models Encode True Common Descent or Just Sequence Resemblance? A Convergent-Evolution Counterfactual
Short Hypothesis: The scientifically-correct mechanism of biological relatedness is common descent (a phylogenetic tree of shared-derived characters), which is NOT the same as raw sequence/phenotypic similarity: convergent evolution, long-branch attraction, and horizontal gene transfer are exactly the cases where similarity misleads about ancestry. Recent work shows genomic foundation models encode a 'tree of life' whose geodesic distances correlate with phylogenetic distance, but correlation cannot separate genuine ancestry-encoding from mere sequence-similarity clustering. We hypothesize that if a genomic FM's internal representation encodes true common descent (mechanism) rather than similarity (correlation), then on discordant cases where similarity and true phylogeny disagree, the model's internal geometry will track the true tree, not the misleading similarity; if it merely clusters by resemblance, it will place convergent/HGT sequences with their look-alikes rather than their true relatives.
Related Work: The Evo 2 blog 'Finding the Tree of Life in Evo 2' (2025) shows phylogeny is encoded as a curved manifold whose geodesic distances correlate with phylogenetic distance, and that embeddings capture codon statistics. 'Investigating Representation Universality: Genealogical Representations' (2024) finds tree-like cone subspaces in LLMs and confirms causal relevance via patching. The geometry-of-hierarchy line (Park et al. 2024) formalizes hierarchical concepts as orthogonality, and vision-model work (SAE ImageNet-hierarchy, DCNN semantic relatedness) shows taxonomic structure emerges from recognition training. Crucially, systematics itself (Hierarchies, classifications, cladograms and phylogeny 2023; Wiley & Lieberman) stresses that nested-set taxonomic similarity and generative phylogeny (common descent via synapomorphy) are conceptually distinct, and that convergent evolution/homoplasy is precisely where they diverge. No interpretability work tests whether a genomic FM encodes the mechanism (common descent) versus the correlate (sequence similarity). Because prior evidence relies on correlation with phylogenetic distance on concordant data — where similarity and ancestry agree — it cannot arbitrate this. Our discordant-case counterfactual (convergence, long-branch attraction, HGT) is the mechanism-defining test that distinguishes ancestry from resemblance, and is the novel contribution.
Abstract: Biological relatedness has a precise scientific mechanism — common descent, a bifurcating tree of shared-derived characters — which is deliberately distinct from raw similarity: convergent evolution, long-branch attraction, and horizontal gene transfer make unrelated lineages resemble each other and true relatives look distant. Genomic foundation models have recently been shown to encode a 'tree of life' whose internal geodesic distances correlate with phylogenetic distance, prompting claims that they represent evolutionary relationships. But correlation on concordant data cannot distinguish encoding true ancestry (mechanism) from encoding sequence resemblance (a mere correlate). We propose the first mechanism-defining test using discordant cases where similarity and true phylogeny disagree. We curate three classes of ground-truth discordance from the systematics literature: (1) molecular convergence / homoplasy (independently evolved identical sequence traits in distant lineages), (2) long-branch-attraction pairs (rapidly-evolving lineages that similarity-based methods erroneously group), and (3) horizontally-transferred genes whose gene tree contradicts the species tree. For each, similarity places a query with its look-alike; true phylogeny places it with its actual relative. We test whether the internal representations of genomic FMs (Evo 2, Nucleotide Transformer, DNABERT-2) place the query with its true relative or its look-alike, using a discordance-resolution index, and whether a recoverable 'ancestry subspace' resists similarity confounds. We validate causally by patching the ancestry subspace into similarity-driven decisions. Either outcome sharpens whether these models learn evolutionary mechanism or resemblance, with direct implications for their use in phylogenomics and variant interpretation.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — discordance resolution: true relative vs look-alike): Tests the core claim that on cases where sequence similarity and true phylogeny disagree, a genomic foundation model's internal geometry follows true common descent rather than resemblance. Data (existing, curated into triples): documented discordant cases from the systematics literature and databases -- convergent molecular evolution (echolocating-mammal Prestin/convergent substitutions, C4 photosynthesis genes, antifreeze glycoproteins), classic long-branch-attraction cases with densely-sampled resolved trees, and horizontal-gene-transfer genes with well-supported donor lineages (HGT databases plus manually validated cases). Each case gives a triple (query Q, true-relative T by common descent, look-alike L by sequence similarity) with similarity(Q,L) > similarity(Q,T). Such well-supported discordant triples number in the low hundreds; we use up to 200 triples and report per-category counts, accepting modest n with paired bootstrap statistics. As a calibration control we first replicate the known result that embedding distance correlates with patristic distance on ~500 non-discordant taxa (Spearman rho) to select best layers. Models (frozen, inference only): Nucleotide Transformer (500M and 2.5B checkpoints), DNABERT-2 (117M), and Evo 2 at a feasible size; mean-pooled per-sequence embeddings per layer; input length standardized, per-model tokenization caveats reported. Systems compared: model embedding vs an explicit k-mer/alignment-identity similarity baseline (scores ~0 by construction) and a maximum-likelihood phylogenetic gold standard (scores ~1). Decisive metric first: Discordance-Resolution Index = fraction of triples with d(Q,T) < d(Q,L), paired-bootstrap CI. Indecision band up front: an index whose CI lies in [0.45, 0.60] cannot decide and is reported as no reliable ancestry preference; index with CI lower bound > 0.60 is convincing ancestry-over-similarity encoding; index with CI upper bound < 0.45 means the model follows the look-alike (similarity representation). A negative result (index <= 0.45) is the decisive finding that these models encode resemblance, not descent.

Experiment 2 (H2 — ancestry signal beyond raw resemblance): Tests whether any descent signal survives removal of the raw sequence-composition similarity that embeddings are known to carry, and whether the failure scales with homoplasy severity as a genuine mechanism (not noise) would. Data: the same up-to-200 discordant triples plus the concordant calibration set. Model: frozen backbones from Experiment 1; the only trainable component is a linear probe predicting patristic distance (ridge, L2 by CV), trained on concordant taxa in one clade and tested on held-out clades (cross-clade transfer) and on discordant triples, 3 seeds. Procedure: (i) regress out a k-mer-frequency similarity component from the representation and recompute the Discordance-Resolution Index on the residual; (ii) rank triples by homoplasy/branch-length asymmetry and fit index vs severity. Systems compared: full-embedding vs residualized-embedding vs k-mer baseline. Decisive metric first: residual Discordance-Resolution Index (same units as H1) and the Spearman slope of resolution-failure vs homoplasy severity. Indecision band up front: residual index CI in [0.45, 0.60] cannot decide (reported as ancestry signal indistinguishable from resemblance once composition is removed); CI lower bound > 0.60 is convincing surviving ancestry encoding; CI upper bound < 0.45 means the apparent signal was resemblance. For the dose-response, a severity slope with CI spanning 0 is indecisive; a clearly negative slope (more homoplasy -> more failure) is the mechanistically-expected pattern. Negative results here reinforce the similarity-only conclusion.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal ancestry-subspace intervention): Tests whether the ancestry structure is causally used: steering the recovered ancestry subspace toward the true relative should flip similarity-driven-wrong decisions, whereas control directions should not. Data: the subset of discordant triples the model gets wrong under H1 (places Q with L). Model: frozen backbones; the ancestry direction is the probe subspace from Experiment 2 (no backbone training). Procedure: patch/steer Q's ancestry-subspace component toward T at matched norm and read whether a nearest-relative ranking flips to T; controls are matched-norm random directions and a k-mer-composition direction. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = fraction of correct flips under ancestry steering / fraction under matched random steering, bootstrap CI. Indecision band up front: selectivity CI in [1.3, 2.0] cannot decide and is reported as no clean causal handle; CI lower bound > 2.0 with an absolute ancestry-flip rate > 0.5 is convincing causal ancestry encoding; CI upper bound < 1.3 (ancestry steering no better than random) means no causal ancestry direction exists. A negative result is consistent with distributed/absent ancestry encoding and, combined with H1-H2 nulls, supports the similarity-representation conclusion.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Ground-truth discordant cases are limited in number and some 'true' phylogenies are themselves debated; we restrict to well-supported, densely-sampled cases and report sensitivity to case-confidence thresholds, accepting modest sample sizes with appropriate statistics.

Molecular convergence at the whole-sequence level is rarer than at single-site level; we include both single-gene convergent cases and site-level convergence aggregated over informative positions, and document which regime each model can access given its context window.

Some FMs tokenize/normalize sequences (BPE tokenization in DNABERT-2, context limits in others) which may prevent access to whole-gene or genome-scale phylogenetic signal; we standardize input lengths, prioritize the model best suited to each case, and report per-model tokenization caveats.

Removing the similarity confound via k-mer residualization is imperfect and may over- or under-correct; we report results both with and without residualization and treat the residual test as a conservative lower bound on ancestry encoding.

The ancestry subspace recovered by a probe may reflect training-data phylogenetic labeling correlated with similarity; cross-clade transfer and the causal patching test mitigate this but distributed encodings may blur single-subspace interventions.

A negative result (models track resemblance and fail on convergence/LBA/HGT) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting FMs for phylogenomics and variant interpretation, though it may be perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test separating common descent from sequence similarity.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes, standard phylogenetic gold-standard tools, and public curated datasets, keeping compute at academic scale.
