Name: convex_hull_competition_probe
Title: Stable Relative to What? Testing Whether Crystal Foundation Models Represent the Relational Convex-Hull Competition of Thermodynamic Stability, Not Just Pointwise Formation Energy
Short Hypothesis: Thermodynamic stability is not a pointwise property of a compound but a relational, competitive one: a phase is stable only if no combination of competing phases at the same composition has lower energy (its energy above the convex hull). We hypothesize that crystal foundation models—now routinely conditioned on 'distance to hull' to generate 'stable' materials—internally encode pointwise formation energy (a correlational proxy) rather than the relational competition that actually defines stability. A mechanistic representation must change a compound's internal stability signal when its competing neighbors in composition space change, even though the compound itself is untouched; a pointwise representation will not. This competitor-context counterfactual is a clean, mechanism-defining test that correlation with hull distance on the standard database cannot provide.
Related Work: Crystal foundation models are explicitly built around convex-hull stability: Matra-Genoa (2026) and UniMat diffusion (2023) condition generation on distance-to-hull; CLOUD (2025) is a physics-informed crystal FM; Matbench Discovery (2025) shows the decision-critical boundary is 0 eV/atom above the hull, where accurate regressors incur high false-positive rates. The 'seven-facet polyhedron' work (2026) shows the formation-energy hull has a compact, interpretable relational structure, and Sun et al. (2016) quantified the thermodynamic scale of metastability. Interpretability of materials models (CGCNN interpretability 2018; 'Comparing latent features of uMLIPs' 2025; 'Beyond Converging Representations' 2025; 'Occupancies vs Embeddings' 2025) recovers site-energy contributions, cross-model feature alignment, and DFT-like internal structure—but all examine POINTWISE energetics or generic latent geometry. None tests whether a crystal FM's internal representation encodes the RELATIONAL, COMPETITIVE convex-hull mechanism that distinguishes formation energy from actual stability, nor whether that internal signal is causally sensitive to the competitor context. Because hull distance and formation energy are highly correlated on the standard database, correlation-based benchmarks cannot separate the two; our competitor-context counterfactual is the novel, mechanism-defining contribution.
Abstract: Machine-learning models of crystals are now used to discover 'stable' inorganic materials, and stability is defined by the convex hull of formation energies: a compound is stable only if no linear combination of competing phases at the same composition has lower energy. Stability is therefore intrinsically relational—a compound's fate depends on its competitors—yet it is nearly perfectly correlated with pointwise formation energy on the standard Materials Project database, so ordinary benchmarks cannot tell whether models learn the relational competition or merely a pointwise energy proxy. We propose the first mechanism-defining test. Using public crystal foundation models (a generative model conditioned on hull distance such as Matra-Genoa/UniMat, a crystal representation FM such as CLOUD, and a universal MLIP such as MACE-MP-0), we ask whether their internal representations encode the convex-hull competition structure. First, a relational-beyond-pointwise probe: can we linearly decode a compound's energy-above-hull from its representation beyond what its own formation energy predicts, and is a distinct direction dedicated to 'competitive margin'? Second, and most decisively, a competitor-context counterfactual: we present the same target compound in two composition-space contexts that differ only in which competing phases exist (constructed from Materials Project phase diagrams), such that the target is on-hull in one context and above-hull in the other. A mechanistic representation must shift its internal stability signal and its generation/classification decision accordingly; a pointwise representation will not. We validate causally by steering the recovered competition direction. Metrics quantify a relational-beyond-pointwise index, a competitor-context sensitivity ratio, and a hull-boundary failure predictor. Either outcome sharpens what deployed materials-discovery models actually represent.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — relational stability beyond pointwise formation energy): Tests whether a crystal foundation model encodes energy-above-hull (the relational, competitive quantity) beyond the compound's own formation energy (the pointwise proxy). Data (existing): Materials Project (public; >150,000 compounds with DFT formation energy, energy-above-hull E_hull, phase diagrams, and decomposition/competing phases). We use a stratified sample of 20,000 compounds spanning E_hull from 0 to 0.2 eV/atom, oversampling the near-hull region, split 70/15/15 train/val/test by chemical system (no system crosses splits). Model (frozen, inference only): a hull-conditioned generative crystal model (public diffusion checkpoint), a crystal representation model (CLOUD), and the universal MLIP MACE-MP-0 (~4-5M params); pooled per-structure activations per layer. Trainable part: ridge linear probes only (L2 by CV, 3 seeds). Systems compared: probe from model representation vs a formation-energy-only regressor. Decisive metric first: Relational-Beyond-Pointwise Index = test R^2 for E_hull from the representation minus R^2 from formation energy alone, after regressing out the formation-energy-predictable component of the representation. Indecision band up front: an index in [0.01, 0.05] (R^2 units) cannot decide and is reported as ambiguous relational encoding; index >= 0.05 with bootstrap CI lower bound > 0.01 is convincing competitive-margin encoding beyond pointwise energy; index <= 0.01 means the model carries only pointwise energetics. Negative result here supports the core hypothesis that these models are pointwise, not relational.

Experiment 2 (H2 — competitor-context counterfactual, decisive): Tests the defining prediction: changing a compound's competing neighbors while leaving the compound itself untouched must change a mechanistic model's internal stability signal, but not a pointwise one; and the change must be local to the compound's hull facet. Data (constructed from existing): for ~300 curated target compositions, build two contexts from real Materials Project phase diagrams -- (a) target ON the hull (stable), and (b) an added real lower-lying competing phase so the SAME target is ABOVE the hull -- plus a control edit that alters distant phases not touching the target's facet (facet-change computed exactly from the phase diagram). Real competing phases are used where available; any synthetic competitor is flagged. Model: the hull-conditioned generative model is the cleanest testbed (it explicitly ingests distance-to-hull); for CLOUD and MACE-MP-0 the competing set is supplied as a co-embedded reference and the internal readout measured relative to the constructed local hull. Frozen weights; readout via the Experiment 1 probe. Systems compared: context-(a) vs context-(b) shift, and true-facet-change edits vs distant-phase control edits. Decisive metric first: Competitor-Context Sensitivity Ratio = |internal-stability shift between (a) and (b)| / |shift under the distant-phase control edit|, with CI over targets. Indecision band up front: a ratio whose CI lies in [1.3, 2.0] cannot decide and is reported as weak relational sensitivity; CI lower bound > 2.0, together with the facet-locality control showing shifts scale with true facet change, is convincing relational encoding; CI upper bound < 1.3 (the model ignores competitor context) is the pointwise signature. This is the decisive test; a null here is the headline negative result.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal competition-direction steering): Tests whether the recovered competitive-margin direction is causally load-bearing -- steering it should flip an on-hull compound to predicted-unstable without changing its formation-energy readout. Data: on-hull test compounds from Experiment 1. Model: frozen; the competition direction is the supervised probe (and, where feasible, a sparse-autoencoder feature) separating high/low E_hull at fixed formation energy. Procedure: add matched-norm perturbations along the competition direction; controls are matched-norm random directions and the formation-energy direction. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |stability-decision change under competition direction| / |change under random direction|, plus the fraction of on-hull compounds flipped to unstable while the formation-energy readout stays within noise. Indecision band up front: selectivity CI in [1.3, 2.0] cannot decide (no clean causal direction); CI lower bound > 2.0 with a flip fraction > 0.5 is convincing causal use of a relational direction; CI upper bound < 1.3 means no separable causal competition direction exists. A negative result, with H1-H2 nulls, supports the pointwise conclusion.

Experiment 4 (H4 — hull-boundary failure prediction): Tests whether the relational-representation strength explains where the model misclassifies stability near E_hull = 0, the regime where crystal models are documented to fail. Data: Materials Project test compounds within 0.05 eV/atom of the hull, labeled stable vs metastable. Model: frozen backbones; predictor is the per-compound competitor-context sensitivity or residual-E_hull probe confidence, logistic link only (3 seeds). Systems compared: internal-signal predictor vs output-confidence and formation-energy-only baselines. Decisive metric first: AUROC for flagging near-boundary misclassifications from the internal relational signal. Indecision band up front: AUROC in [0.60, 0.70] cannot decide and is reported as a weak link; AUROC >= 0.70 with CI lower bound > 0.60 and beating both baselines is convincing that relational encoding governs boundary reliability; AUROC <= 0.60 (near the 0.50 chance line) means it does not, weakening the mechanistic reading even if the counterfactual is positive.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Formation energy and E_hull are strongly correlated on the standard database, making the relational-beyond-pointwise separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with residualization, the competitor-context counterfactual (which holds the target fixed), and facet-locality controls.

Providing 'competitor context' is architecture-dependent: representation FMs and MLIPs do not natively take a phase-diagram context, so context must be injected via co-embedded reference sets or by evaluating the internal readout relative to a constructed local hull; we report per-model how context is supplied and treat the hull-conditioned generative model as the cleanest testbed since it explicitly ingests distance-to-hull.

Constructing counterfactual contexts requires curated phase diagrams and, ideally, hypothetical competing phases; we use Materials Project phase diagrams and real competing phases where possible, and clearly flag any synthetic competitors.

Linear probes recovering a competition direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering and random/formation-energy-direction controls, though distributed encodings may blur single-direction interventions.
Some models pool to a single structure embedding, limiting fine-grained analysis; we prioritize models exposing usable per-structure representations and report pooling caveats.

A negative result (models encode pointwise formation energy but not the relational competition) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting hull-conditioned generative discovery pipelines, though it may be perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether crystal FMs represent the convex-hull competition that defines stability.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes/SAEs and public Materials Project data, keeping compute at academic scale.

novelty.reasoning: Core novel claims: (1) stability should be tested as a relational competitor-sensitive property, not just pointwise formation energy; (2) current crystal FMs/MLIPs may encode only a pointwise proxy; (3) a competitor-context counterfactual plus steering can distinguish internal relational vs pointwise representations; (4) this is a mechanism test on representations, not just an output benchmark. The underlying phenomenon is not new, and prior work already shows output-level stability mistakes near the hull. The novelty is in the mechanistic/interventional framing and internal-representation claim, which is meaningfully different but not a new task or theory. Closest prior family: hull-conditioned crystal generators/benchmarks and papers showing formation-energy models fail on stability; the delta is moving from 'does the model predict E_hull?' to 'does its latent state change when competitors change, holding the target fixed?'

Name: cyp450_bypass_ddi_probe
Title: Same Enzyme, Same Danger? Testing Whether Drug Foundation Models Represent the Shared-CYP450 Metabolic Mechanism of Drug-Drug Interactions, Not Just Structural or Co-Mention Similarity
Short Hypothesis: A large and clinically dominant class of drug-drug interactions (DDIs) has an exactly-known pharmacokinetic mechanism: one drug inhibits/induces a specific cytochrome-P450 (CYP450) enzyme that metabolizes a second drug (the substrate), so the pair interacts because they share a metabolic pathway - not because they look alike or are co-mentioned. We hypothesize that if drug/medical foundation models represent this mechanism rather than surface correlation, then (a) PK-interacting pairs will be organized in the model's internal representation by their SHARED CYP isoform even when structurally dissimilar, (b) a metabolic-bypass counterfactual - replacing the substrate with a therapeutically-equivalent drug metabolized by a DIFFERENT enzyme - will abolish the model's internal interaction signal, whereas a control swap that changes structure but keeps the same enzyme will preserve it, and (c) steering along a recovered 'shared-enzyme' direction causally shifts interaction predictions. The enzyme-swap bypass is an exact, mechanism-defining counterfactual that correlation-based DDI benchmarks cannot provide.
Related Work: Two lines bracket the gap. (1) Interpretable DDI predictors - KnowDDI (2023), MolecBioNet (2025), TRACE (2026), LaGAT (2022), MEN/CYP450 (2025), DeepMetab (2025) - build mechanism in by construction (knowledge-graph subgraphs, attention over substructures, curated CYP rules) and validate via edge AUROC or attention heatmaps; none tests what a general drug/medical FM already encodes. (2) Medical-LLM interpretability - 'Medical Interpretability and Knowledge Maps' (2025) reports the striking descriptive finding that in Llama3.3-70B 'drugs cluster better by medical specialty than by mechanism of action'; 'Elucidating Mechanisms of Demographic Bias' (2025) and medical SAE work (2025-2026) recover and intervene on medical concepts. These are descriptive or bias-focused; none tests whether the representation encodes the PK interaction MECHANISM (shared-enzyme competition) versus structural/co-mention correlation, nor uses a causal metabolic-bypass counterfactual. Because structurally similar drugs, co-prescribed drugs, and shared-enzyme drugs are all correlated in clinical text, correlation-based DDI benchmarks cannot separate mechanism from resemblance; our shared-enzyme grouping test, enzyme-swap bypass counterfactual, and causal steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, and they transfer a correlation-vs-mechanism probe into a safety-critical clinical setting.
Abstract: Drug-drug interactions (DDIs) are a leading, preventable cause of adverse drug events, and machine-learning models are increasingly used to flag them. A clinically dominant class of DDIs has an exactly-known pharmacokinetic mechanism: one drug inhibits or induces a specific cytochrome-P450 (CYP450) enzyme that metabolizes another (the substrate), so the pair interacts because they share a metabolic pathway - independent of how structurally similar they are or how often they co-occur in text. This makes DDIs an ideal, high-stakes testbed for whether drug and medical foundation models learn mechanism or surface correlation. Using public representations from a medical LLM (e.g., MedGemma/Llama medical variants), a chemistry drug FM (e.g., ChemBERTa/SMI-TED on drug SMILES), and a molecule-text model, we ask three mechanism-defining questions. First, a shared-enzyme organization probe: are PK-interacting drug pairs grouped in the internal representation by their shared CYP isoform even when structurally dissimilar, beyond what structural or co-mention similarity predicts? Second, and most decisively, a metabolic-bypass counterfactual: replacing a substrate with a therapeutically-equivalent drug metabolized by a DIFFERENT enzyme should abolish the model's internal interaction signal, whereas a structure-changing control swap that keeps the SAME enzyme should preserve it. Third, causal steering: perturbing a recovered shared-enzyme direction should shift interaction predictions in the enzyme-consistent direction. Metrics quantify a shared-enzyme-beyond-structure index, a bypass-vs-same-enzyme causal asymmetry, and a mechanism-based failure predictor. Either outcome sharpens whether deployed models flag DDIs for the right pharmacological reason - critical before clinical use.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — shared-CYP enzyme organizes interactions beyond structure): Tests assertion (a): pharmacokinetically-interacting drug pairs are organized in the representation by their SHARED cytochrome-P450 isoform even when structurally dissimilar. Data (existing, curated): PK-DDI pairs from DrugBank, the Flockhart CYP450 tables, and the University of Washington Drug Interaction Database, each labeled by responsible isoform (CYP3A4, CYP2D6, CYP2C9, CYP1A2, ...); pharmacodynamic (target-level, no shared enzyme) DDIs collected as a distinct class. These sources yield on the order of 10^3 well-annotated PK pairs; we use up to 1,000 PK pairs and 500 PD pairs, reporting the structurally-dissimilar shared-enzyme subset (ECFP4 Tanimoto < 0.4) separately as the most diagnostic. Models (frozen, inference only): a medical LLM (MedGemma, 4B), ChemBERTa-2 (~46M) on SMILES, and MoleculeSTM (molecule-text); per-drug and per-pair representations. Trainable: linear probes only (3 seeds). Systems compared: model representation vs an ECFP/Tanimoto structural-similarity baseline and a text co-mention-frequency baseline. Decisive metric first: Shared-Enzyme-Beyond-Structure Index = accuracy of decoding 'shared responsible enzyme' from the representation minus what structural + co-mention similarity achieve, after regressing both out. Indecision band up front: an index in [0.03, 0.10] (accuracy points) cannot decide and is reported as ambiguous metabolic-structure encoding; index >= 0.10 with CI lower bound > 0.03, especially on the structurally-dissimilar subset, is convincing enzyme-mechanism encoding; index <= 0.03 means grouping is driven by resemblance, supporting the surface-correlation hypothesis.

Experiment 2 (H2 — metabolic-bypass counterfactual, decisive): Tests assertion (b): replacing the substrate with a therapeutically-equivalent drug metabolized by a DIFFERENT enzyme should abolish the internal interaction signal, whereas a same-enzyme structural swap should preserve it; symmetric on the inhibitor side; and PK-only (a PD interaction should not be abolished by an enzyme bypass). Data (constructed from existing): for each PK-DDI (inhibitor I + substrate S metabolized by enzyme E) restricted to drugs with a single dominant CYP isoform, build (a) a bypass swap S->S_bypass (equivalent indication, different enzyme E') and (b) a same-enzyme control swap S->S_same (structurally different, still enzyme E), matched on structural-change magnitude; repeat on the inhibitor side; include PD pairs as a double-dissociation control. We target ~200 clean single-isoform PK pairs. Model: same three frozen models; interaction signal is a probed interaction score plus, for MedGemma, the interaction likelihood under several prompt templates (representation probe is primary). Systems compared: bypass swap vs same-enzyme swap; PK vs PD. Decisive metric first: Bypass-vs-Same-Enzyme Causal Asymmetry = |signal drop under bypass swap| / |signal change under same-enzyme control|, CI over pairs. Indecision band up front: an asymmetry whose CI lies in [1.3, 2.0] cannot decide and is reported as weak mechanism sensitivity; CI lower bound > 2.0, with the PD control showing NO abolition, is convincing shared-enzyme-mechanism encoding; CI upper bound < 1.3 (both swaps change the signal alike) is the surface-feature signature. This is the decisive, safety-relevant test; a null is the headline negative result.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal shared-enzyme steering): Tests assertion (c): steering a drug's representation along a recovered 'CYP-E substrate/inhibitor' direction causally shifts its predicted interaction with a CYP-E inhibitor in the enzyme-consistent direction. Data: single-isoform drugs from Experiment 2. Model: frozen; the enzyme direction is the Experiment 1 probe direction (no backbone training). Procedure: add matched-norm perturbations moving a drug toward/away from 'CYP-E substrate' and read the pairwise interaction prediction; controls are matched-norm random directions and a structural-feature direction. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |interaction-prediction shift under enzyme direction| / |shift under random direction|, CI over drugs. Indecision band up front: selectivity CI in [1.3, 2.0] cannot decide (no clean causal handle); CI lower bound > 2.0 with an enzyme-consistent shift is convincing causal use of the metabolic mechanism; CI upper bound < 1.3 means no separable causal enzyme direction. A negative result, with H1-H2 nulls, supports the surface-correlation conclusion and warns against FM-based DDI screening for structurally-atypical pairs.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Shared-enzyme drugs, co-prescribed drugs, and structurally similar drugs are correlated in clinical text, making the shared-enzyme-beyond-structure separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with structural/co-mention residualization, the enzyme-swap bypass counterfactual (which holds the interacting partner fixed), and matched structural-change controls.

Constructing 'therapeutically-equivalent but different-enzyme' bypass swaps requires curated pharmacology knowledge and clean CYP annotations; some drugs are metabolized by multiple enzymes, blurring the bypass. We restrict counterfactuals to drugs with a single dominant responsible CYP isoform and report sensitivity to isoform-assignment confidence.

For prompted medical LLMs, the 'internal interaction signal' may depend on prompt phrasing; we use multiple prompt templates and both probed representations and generated interaction judgments, treating the representational probe as primary evidence.

Chemistry FMs that pool to a single molecule embedding limit fine-grained substructure analysis; we prioritize models exposing usable per-molecule representations and report pooling caveats, and treat cross-model agreement as supporting rather than definitive.

Steering directions recovered by probes may not be causally used; we address this with steering plus random/structural-direction controls, though distributed encodings may blur single-direction interventions.

A negative result (models flag DDIs by structural/co-mention resemblance and fail the bypass counterfactual) is scientifically decisive and directly safety-relevant - it would warn against trusting FM-based DDI screening for novel or structurally-atypical drug pairs - though it may be perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether drug FMs represent the shared-CYP450 mechanism of pharmacokinetic interactions.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and public/curated pharmacology databases, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: phase_amplitude_coupling_probe
Title: Coupling, Not Just Power: Do EEG Foundation Models Represent Cross-Frequency Phase-Amplitude Coupling, or Only Marginal Band Power?
Short Hypothesis: A defining, relational mechanism of brain activity is cross-frequency phase-amplitude coupling (PAC): the phase of a slow oscillation (e.g., theta/alpha) modulates the amplitude of a fast oscillation (e.g., gamma), a coupling that carries cognitive and clinical meaning and cannot be captured by marginal band power. We hypothesize that if EEG foundation models represent this neurophysiological mechanism rather than surface spectral statistics, then (a) PAC strength will be decodable from internal representations beyond what per-band power predicts, (b) a phase-scrambling counterfactual that destroys coupling while preserving each band's power spectrum will specifically collapse the internal PAC signal, whereas an amplitude-matched control that changes power but preserves coupling will not, and (c) steering a recovered PAC direction causally shifts downstream predictions. The phase-scramble-vs-power-match counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that marginal-spectral interpretability cannot provide.
Related Work: EEG foundation models (CSBrain 2025, BrainOmni 2025, CodeBrain 2025, MSBraM 2026, LaBraM, CBraMod) achieve strong cross-task decoding, and reviews (Kwon & Shin 2025) call for physiology-aware, interpretable representations. Existing EEG-model interpretability is (i) saliency/attribution over frequency bands (Frequency-band GNN dementia biomarkers 2025; activation-maximization for spectral features 2021), or (ii) descriptive alignment of learned features with spectral rhythms (CodeBrain's tokenizer). Neuroscience establishes PAC and cross-frequency coupling (CFC) as a core relational coding mechanism (Cracking the Code of Oscillatory Activity 2011; oscillatory representational content studies), and Riemannian pipelines have hand-engineered CFC covariance features (SPD-CFC 2023) precisely because standard band-power features miss it. Crucially, no work tests whether pretrained EEG FMs internally represent PAC (a relational, cross-frequency mechanism) beyond marginal band power, whether that representation is causally load-bearing, or uses a phase-scrambling counterfactual that isolates coupling from power. Prior interpretability answers 'which band matters'; PAC asks 'do bands interact as the brain's mechanism dictates'. Our relational-beyond-marginal probe, phase-scramble-vs-power-match counterfactual, and causal PAC steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, transferred into a safety-critical clinical/BCI setting.
Abstract: EEG foundation models now deliver strong, transferable decoding across cognitive, emotional, and clinical tasks, yet what neurophysiology they actually internalize remains unclear. Existing interpretability tells us which frequency bands a model weights, but band power is a marginal, per-band statistic; the brain's information is carried substantially by relational mechanisms, chief among them cross-frequency phase-amplitude coupling (PAC), in which the phase of a slow rhythm modulates the amplitude of a fast one. PAC is diagnostically and cognitively meaningful (working memory, seizure dynamics, Parkinsonian beta-gamma coupling) and is provably invisible to marginal band power, making it an ideal mechanism-defining probe. We ask whether pretrained EEG foundation models (e.g., LaBraM, CBraMod, CodeBrain) internally represent PAC. First, a relational-beyond-marginal probe: we test whether PAC strength (modulation index) is decodable from internal representations beyond what per-band power predicts. Second, and most decisively, a phase-scrambling counterfactual: we surrogate-scramble the slow-oscillation phase to abolish coupling while exactly preserving each band's power spectrum, and compare against an amplitude-matched control that alters power but preserves coupling. A mechanistic representation must collapse its internal PAC signal under phase-scrambling but not under the power-matched control; a spectral-statistics model responds oppositely. Third, causal steering: perturbing a recovered PAC direction should shift downstream clinical/cognitive predictions coupling-consistently. Metrics quantify a PAC-beyond-power index, a scramble-vs-power-match causal asymmetry, and a mechanism-based failure predictor. Either outcome sharpens what deployed brain foundation models represent, with direct implications for their clinical and BCI reliability.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — PAC decodable beyond marginal band power): Tests assertion (a): cross-frequency phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) is decodable from internal representations beyond what per-band power predicts. Data (existing): public EEG with established PAC -- a working-memory/cognitive-load set (theta-gamma PAC), Sleep-EDF (slow-oscillation-spindle coupling), and a clinical cohort where PAC is a biomarker (e.g., an epilepsy corpus); ground-truth PAC per epoch via the Tort modulation index and comodulograms, plus per-band power (delta-gamma). We use >= 5,000 epochs total, split by subject (no subject crosses splits). Models (frozen, inference only): LaBraM, CBraMod, and CodeBrain (public EEG foundation models with per-token representations); preprocessing per model documented, pre-tokenization activations probed where feasible. Trainable: ridge linear probes (L2 by CV, 3 seeds). Systems compared: representation probe vs a probe on the full per-band power vector. Decisive metric first: PAC-Beyond-Power Index = test R^2 for the modulation index from the representation minus R^2 from the full band-power vector, after regressing out the power-predictable component, reported per phase-amplitude band pair. Indecision band up front: an index in [0.01, 0.05] (R^2 units) cannot decide and is reported as ambiguous coupling encoding; index >= 0.05 with CI lower bound > 0.01 is convincing relational-coupling encoding beyond marginal spectra; index <= 0.01 means only marginal power is encoded, supporting the surface-spectral hypothesis.

Experiment 2 (H2 — phase-scramble vs power-match counterfactual, decisive): Tests assertion (b): a phase-scramble that destroys coupling while preserving each band's power spectrum should specifically collapse the internal PAC signal, whereas an amplitude-matched control that changes power but preserves coupling should not; and the internal signal should reproduce the correct comodulogram specificity. Data (constructed from the Experiment 1 epochs): (a) amplitude-adjusted-Fourier-transform surrogates that abolish cross-frequency phase relations while preserving each band's power (verified: power preserved, modulation index abolished, surrogate diagnostics reported); (b) power-matched surrogates that rescale band amplitudes to change power by a comparable amount while keeping coupling intact. Model: same three frozen models; readout is the probed modulation index / recovered PAC feature. Systems compared: phase-scramble vs power-match; also the model-implied coupling map vs the ground-truth comodulogram against a shuffled-band-pair control. Decisive metric first: Scramble-vs-Power-Match Causal Asymmetry = |PAC-signal drop under phase-scramble| / |PAC-signal change under power-match|, CI over epochs. Indecision band up front: an asymmetry whose CI lies in [1.3, 2.0] cannot decide and is reported as weak coupling sensitivity; CI lower bound > 2.0, with the comodulogram-fidelity correlation beating the shuffled control, is convincing coupling encoding; CI upper bound < 1.3 (or a reversed response driven by power) is the marginal-spectral signature. This is the decisive test; a null is the headline negative result.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal PAC steering): Tests assertion (c): steering a recovered PAC direction causally shifts downstream predictions in the coupling-consistent direction. Data: epochs with downstream labels (cognitive-load level, sleep stage, or pathology likelihood). Model: frozen; the PAC direction is the Experiment 1 probe direction (or an SAE feature aligned with coupling); no backbone training. Procedure: add matched-norm perturbations moving representations toward/away from high PAC and read the downstream prediction; controls are matched-norm random directions and a band-power direction. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |downstream shift under PAC direction| / |shift under random direction|, CI over epochs. Indecision band up front: selectivity CI in [1.3, 2.0] cannot decide (no clean causal handle); CI lower bound > 2.0 with a coupling-consistent downstream shift is convincing causal use of PAC; CI upper bound < 1.3 means no separable causal PAC direction. A negative result, with H1-H2 nulls, supports the marginal-power conclusion and warns against trusting EEG FMs for PAC-driven diagnoses.
Risk Factors and Limitations: PAC and band power are correlated in real EEG (high-power epochs can inflate spurious PAC), making the relational-beyond-power separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with power-residualization, the phase-scramble-vs-power-match counterfactual (which holds power fixed), amplitude-adjusted surrogates, and established bias-corrected PAC estimators.

Phase-scrambling surrogates that perfectly preserve power while destroying coupling are nontrivial; we use standard amplitude-adjusted Fourier-transform surrogates and validate that per-band power is preserved and modulation index is abolished before feeding to the model, reporting surrogate-quality diagnostics.

Some EEG FMs tokenize/normalize signals (patching, spectral tokenization, per-channel normalization) that may discard or transform phase information; we document each model's preprocessing, probe pre-tokenization activations where feasible, and prioritize models retaining temporal/phase structure.

PAC ground truth is itself estimator-dependent and noisy for short epochs; we use longer epochs where possible, multiple PAC metrics (Tort modulation index, mean vector length), and report sensitivity to estimator choice.

Linear probes recovering a PAC direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/band-power-direction controls, though distributed encodings may blur single-direction interventions.

A negative result (models encode marginal band power but not cross-frequency coupling) is scientifically decisive and directly clinically relevant, since it would warn against trusting EEG FMs for PAC-driven diagnoses (seizure, Parkinsonian, working-memory biomarkers); we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether brain foundation models represent cross-frequency phase-amplitude coupling.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes/SAEs and public EEG datasets, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: allosteric_propagation_probe
Title: Feeling the Distant Site: Do Protein Language Models Internally Represent Long-Range Allosteric Coupling, or Only Local Context?
Short Hypothesis: Allostery is a relational, long-range mechanism: a mutation at a site far from the active site perturbs function through a physically-propagated coupling path, and recent large-scale data show these effects decay with distance from the active site in a conserved way. We hypothesize that if protein language models (PLMs) internally represent this mechanism rather than only local sequence context, then (a) a mutation's internal representational perturbation will propagate to distant functionally-coupled residues (not just its local neighborhood), (b) the magnitude of this propagated internal signal will reproduce the conserved distance-decay law of allosteric mutational effects, and (c) the internal coupling will causally track true allosteric partners, not merely spatial or sequence proximity. A propagation-vs-locality counterfactual makes this a mechanism-defining test that local-annotation interpretability cannot provide.
Related Work: Existing PLM interpretability matches features to LOCAL structure/function: BERTology (attention to contacts, binding sites), InterPLM and 'Interpreting and Steering PLMs' (SAE features for binding sites, motifs, transmembrane regions), ProtoMech (cross-layer transcoder circuits for local motifs), and XAI-attribution work (active sites, PROSITE patterns). All validate against marginal, spatially-local annotations. Separately, the allostery literature establishes long-range coupling as a real mechanism: 'Allostery is a widespread cause of loss-of-function variant pathogenicity' (2025) shows a CONSERVED distance-dependent decay of allosteric mutational effects outside active sites from large-scale deep mutational scanning; coevolution methods (KeyAlloSite), MD-based GNNs (AlloPool, NRI), and energy-based predictors (ZHMolEReP) model allosteric pathways. Critically, 'When Does Structure Help?' (2026) reports ESM-2 gives below-chance allostery predictions while AF2 barely exceeds chance, hinting sequence-only PLMs may be blind to long-range mechanism. No interpretability work tests whether a PLM's INTERNAL representation propagates a mutation's effect to distant allosterically-coupled residues, reproduces the conserved distance-decay law, or causally distinguishes true allosteric partners from mere spatial/sequence neighbors. Our propagation-distance-decay-and-causal-coupling test is the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, moving beyond 'the model sees the local motif' to 'the model represents that a distant site talks to the active site.'
Abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) are known to encode local structural and functional features such as contacts, binding sites, and motifs. But one of the most important protein mechanisms is inherently long-range and relational: allostery, in which a mutation at a site far from the active site alters function through a physically-propagated coupling path. Recent large-scale deep-mutational-scanning studies establish that allostery is a widespread cause of variant pathogenicity and that allosteric mutational effects decay with distance from the active site in a conserved, quantifiable way. This makes allostery an ideal, physics-grounded probe for whether PLMs represent long-range mechanism or only local context. We ask whether ESM-2 internally represents allosteric coupling. First, a propagation probe: applying an in-silico mutation at a residue, we measure how far its perturbation to the model's internal representation travels along the chain and in 3D, testing whether it reaches distant functionally-coupled residues rather than only its local neighborhood. Second, and most decisively, a distance-decay test: we test whether the magnitude of the internally-propagated signal reproduces the conserved distance-dependent decay of true allosteric mutational effects measured experimentally, versus a local-context model whose perturbation stays local. Third, a coupling-specificity counterfactual: we test whether the internal coupling is stronger for true allosteric partners than for distance-matched, spatially-close-but-non-coupled control residues, and whether steering along a recovered allosteric-coupling direction causally shifts predictions at the distant partner. Metrics quantify a propagation-range index, distance-decay agreement, and coupling-specificity ratio. Either outcome sharpens whether PLMs, increasingly used for variant-effect prediction, represent the long-range mechanism behind a major class of pathogenic variants.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — long-range propagation of a mutation's internal perturbation): Tests assertion (a): a single mutation's representational perturbation propagates to distant functionally-coupled residues, not just its local neighborhood. Data (existing): proteins with resolved allosteric sites and high-resolution PDB structures from ASBench, AlloReverse, and AlloSigDB, giving active-site location, 3D coordinates, and allosteric-residue annotations; we use up to 60 well-characterized proteins (limited by high-quality allosteric annotation + structure). Model (frozen, inference only): ESM-2 at 150M and 650M params, with 3B as compute allows; per-residue representations at every layer. Procedure: apply a single in-silico point mutation at a residue (masked/single-substitution edit, perturbation magnitude bounded, OOD diagnostics reported) and measure the induced per-residue representational delta at all other positions, per layer. Systems compared: propagation profile of allosteric-site mutations vs local/active-site mutations. Decisive metric first: Propagation-Range Index = fraction of the total representational perturbation deposited beyond a local window (> 8 residues in sequence AND > 10 Angstrom in 3D), with CI over mutations. Indecision band up front: an index in [0.10, 0.25] cannot decide and is reported as mostly-local with an ambiguous long-range tail; index >= 0.25 with CI lower bound > 0.10 is convincing long-range propagation; index <= 0.10 means the model deposits perturbation almost entirely locally, supporting the local-context hypothesis.

Experiment 2 (H2 — reproduction of the conserved distance-decay law, decisive): Tests assertion (b): the propagated internal signal reproduces the conserved distance-dependent decay of true allosteric mutational effects. Data (existing): the large-scale allosteric deep-mutational-scanning distance-decay dataset (per-residue allosteric effect vs distance to the active site) paired with the Experiment 1 structures. Model: frozen ESM-2 (150M/650M/3B); no training for the propagation measurement. Procedure: for mutations at allosteric sites, measure the internally-propagated perturbation arriving at active-site residues as a function of distance, fit the same decay form as the experimental law, and compare decay constants. Controls: (a) active-site/local mutations should show a distinct steep short-range profile; (b) shuffled distance labels should destroy the fit. Systems compared: internal propagated signal vs experimental allosteric-effect-vs-distance law. Decisive metric first: Pearson correlation between internal propagated signal and experimental effect across the distance range, and agreement of fitted decay constants (ratio of internal to experimental constant). Indecision band up front: a correlation whose CI lies in [0.2, 0.5] (or decay-constant ratio outside 0.5-2.0 but with the correlation weak) cannot decide and is reported as no faithful decay reproduction; correlation CI lower bound > 0.5 with decay-constant ratio in [0.67, 1.5] is convincing mechanism reproduction; correlation CI upper bound < 0.2 means the model does not reproduce the conserved law. This is the decisive test; a null (expected if ESM-2 is genuinely weak at allostery) is the headline finding.

Experiment 3 (H3 — coupling specificity and causal steering): Tests assertion (c): the internal coupling causally tracks true allosteric partners, not mere spatial/sequence proximity. Data: true allosteric-partner pairs (allosteric residue A coupled to active/effector site F) with distance-matched non-coupled control residues (equally far in sequence and 3D but not coupled per experimental data). Model: frozen ESM-2; an 'allosteric-coupling' direction recovered by a supervised probe (or SAE feature aligned with A->F propagation), no backbone training. Procedure: (i) compare internal coupling A->F against the distance-matched non-coupled control; (ii) steer the coupling direction at A with matched magnitude and read the masked-prediction/variant-effect readout at the distant partner F, with matched-norm random directions and the distance-matched control residue as controls. As a positive-control comparison, run the same propagation/steering on AlphaFold2 single-sequence Evoformer representations. Decisive metric first: Coupling-Specificity Ratio = internal coupling(true partner) / internal coupling(distance-matched control), and mechanism-selectivity = |steering effect at true partner| / |effect at matched control|, CIs over pairs. Indecision band up front: either ratio with CI in [1.3, 2.0] cannot decide and is reported as coupling indistinguishable from distance; CI lower bound > 2.0 is convincing partner-specific causal coupling; CI upper bound < 1.3 means coupling is driven only by proximity. A negative result for ESM-2 alongside a positive AF2 control would localize the mechanism to models with evolutionary-coupling access.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Allosteric coupling correlates with 3D and sequence distance and with coevolution, so the coupling-specificity separation is statistically demanding; we mitigate with distance-matched non-coupled controls, the conserved-distance-decay test (which a distance-only model cannot reproduce in the correct functional form), and the allostery-beyond-locality baseline that regresses out distance.

The 2026 information-bonus result suggests ESM-2 may genuinely be weak at allostery; a null internal signal could reflect true model blindness rather than probing failure. We treat this as a scientifically decisive outcome (sequence-only PLMs do not represent long-range allosteric mechanism) and include AF2 representations as a positive-control comparison.

Ground-truth allosteric coupling and experimental per-mutation allosteric effects are limited and noisy; we restrict to well-characterized proteins with deep-mutational-scanning allostery data and report sensitivity to annotation confidence.

In-silico mutation perturbations in a nonlinear transformer may push representations off-manifold; we bound perturbation magnitude, use masked-position and single-substitution edits, and report sensitivity, relying on the input-space mutation propagation as primary evidence and steering as corroboration.
Distributed/superposed encodings may mean no single clean coupling direction exists; we use both probe directions and SAE features and report aggregate-direction results.

All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models (ESM-2, optionally AF2 single-sequence) plus small probes/SAEs and public allostery datasets and structures, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: spin_state_exchange_probe
Title: Does the Model Know About Spin? Testing Whether Atomistic Foundation Models Represent the Exchange/Hund's-Rule Mechanism of Spin-State Energetics, or Only Nuclear Geometry
Short Hypothesis: A defining, exactly-known quantum-chemical mechanism is that molecular energy and reactivity depend on electronic spin state through exchange interactions (Hund's rule, singlet-triplet gaps, high-/low-spin splitting) — a dependence that is invisible to nuclear geometry alone. We hypothesize that (a) most universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs), which take only nuclei/charge as input, are structurally blind to spin state and therefore collapse distinct spin isomers to a single representation, whereas (b) spin-aware atomistic/quantum-chemistry foundation models that do receive spin information internally encode the exchange-driven spin-state ordering as a recoverable, causally load-bearing direction that reproduces the correct sign and magnitude of singlet-triplet and high-/low-spin gaps. A spin-flip counterfactual at fixed geometry is an exact, mechanism-defining test that geometry-only correlation cannot pass.
Related Work: Prior interpretability of atomistic models shows embeddings encode DFT-derived quantities: 'Occupancies vs Embeddings' (2025) recovers atomic occupancies from GNN embeddings; Schutt et al. (2018) extract atom-wise energies, partial charges, and periodic-table-like element embeddings; GNN-LRP work (2024-2025) decomposes NNP energies into physically-meaningful many-body terms; 'Comparing latent features of uMLIPs' (2025) and 'Beyond Converging Representations' (2025) characterize and align MLIP latent geometry. Separately, an entire ML-DFT literature (differentiable Kohn-Sham XC functionals, DM21, Skala) learns the exchange-correlation functional, whose whole purpose is to capture the exchange energy that governs spin-state ordering. Crucially, all atomistic-interpretability work probes geometry- or density-derived pointwise quantities; none tests whether a foundation model internally represents the SPIN-STATE / EXCHANGE mechanism — the dependence of energy on spin multiplicity at fixed nuclear geometry — nor uses a spin-flip counterfactual to arbitrate whether the model captures this mechanism or is blind to it. Because most MLIPs cannot even ingest spin state, this is a rare setting where a mechanism (exchange-driven spin energetics) is provably separable from the geometry correlate. Our spin-degeneracy counterfactual, exchange-direction probe, and causal spin-state steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution.
Abstract: The energy and reactivity of molecules and materials depend not only on where the nuclei sit but on the electronic spin state: exchange interactions and Hund's rule set singlet-triplet gaps in carbenes and O2, and high-spin/low-spin splittings in transition-metal complexes, all at fixed nuclear geometry. This makes spin-state energetics an ideal, exactly-known mechanism for testing whether atomistic foundation models learn quantum-chemical mechanism or merely a geometry-to-energy correlate. We first show that a large class of universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) is structurally blind to spin state — taking only nuclear positions and total charge as input, they must assign identical energies and representations to distinct spin isomers of the same geometry, a decisive negative result for their use on open-shell chemistry. We then ask, for spin-aware atomistic/quantum-chemistry foundation models that do receive spin multiplicity (or are trained across spin states), whether they internally represent the exchange mechanism. Using curated spin-state pairs (singlet/triplet carbenes and O2, high-/low-spin Fe(II)/Co(III) complexes) with reference CASPT2/DFT energies, we probe whether an 'exchange/spin-state' direction is recoverable and reproduces the correct sign and magnitude of the spin gap beyond what geometry predicts. Most decisively, a spin-flip counterfactual holds geometry fixed and flips only the spin label: a mechanistic representation must shift its energy readout and internal state by the correct spin gap, while a geometry-only model cannot. We validate causally by steering the recovered spin direction. Metrics quantify a spin-blindness index, a spin-gap-beyond-geometry index, and a spin-flip causal asymmetry. Either outcome sharpens whether atomistic foundation models can be trusted on the open-shell, spin-dependent chemistry that dominates catalysis and radical reactions.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — spin-blindness of geometry-only MLIPs): Tests assertion (a): universal MLIPs that ingest only nuclei/charge are structurally blind to spin state and collapse distinct spin isomers to one representation. Data (existing): spin-state pairs at fixed geometry with reliable references -- singlet/triplet methylene and substituted carbenes, singlet/triplet O2, and octahedral transition-metal complexes with high-/low-spin states (Fe(II), Co(III), Mn) from published CASPT2/DMRG/DFT spin-gap benchmarks (TMC/SSE datasets); we use up to 300 spin pairs. Models (frozen, inference only): geometry-only MLIPs MACE-MP-0, CHGNet, SevenNet, and Orb; per-structure energies and representations. Systems compared: energy and representation of spin isomer A vs B at identical geometry. Decisive metric first: Spin-Blindness Index = fraction of spin pairs with |energy(A) - energy(B)| exactly 0 AND representation distance exactly 0. Indecision band up front: for these input-invariant models the outcome is analytic, so any index in (0, 1) would flag an unexpected implicit spin channel to be investigated; an index of 1.0 is the decisive confirmation that this deployed model class cannot represent spin-state energetics at all; an index below 1.0 would mean some spin information leaks in (e.g., via charge), which we would then characterize. This is a definitional negative result, separately reported, that motivates restricting the richer tests to spin-aware models.

Experiment 2 (H2 — spin-gap-beyond-geometry and spin-flip counterfactual, decisive): Tests assertion (b): spin-aware models internally encode the exchange-driven spin-state ordering with the correct sign and magnitude, recoverable beyond geometry, and responsive to a spin-flip at fixed geometry. Data: the Experiment 1 spin pairs plus, for dose-response, ligand-field-strength and carbene-substituent series that tune the gap. Models (frozen, inference only): spin-aware atomistic models that ingest spin multiplicity (SpookyNet, a spin-conditioned MACE/AIMNet2 variant, or any spin-aware foundation MLIP with public weights); trainable part is ridge linear probes only (3 seeds). Procedure: (i) regress out the geometry-predictable component (using a geometry-only MLIP's energy/features) and re-decode the reference spin gap from the residual; (ii) at FIXED geometry flip only the spin multiplicity input and read the energy/representation change against the reference gap; (iii) across the tuning series test the trend. Systems compared: spin-aware model vs geometry-only features; spin-flip edit vs a matched control geometry perturbation of comparable energy scale. Decisive metric first: Spin-Flip Causal Asymmetry = |shift under spin-flip| / |shift under matched geometry-control edit|, plus the correlation between the model's spin-flip energy response and the reference gap (and fraction with correct sign). Indecision band up front: an asymmetry whose CI lies in [1.3, 2.0], or a gap-correlation CI in [0.2, 0.5], cannot decide and is reported as spin-sensitive-but-not-faithful; asymmetry CI lower bound > 2.0 WITH gap-correlation CI lower bound > 0.5, correct sign in > 80% of pairs, and a monotonic dose-response is convincing exchange encoding; asymmetry CI upper bound < 1.3 (~0 response) is the spin-insensitive signature. This decisive test separates genuine exchange encoding from a trivial spin-label lookup (which would fail the transfer/dose-response).

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal spin-state steering): Tests assertion (b)'s causal-load-bearing clause: a recovered spin-state/exchange direction, when steered, shifts the energy prediction in the spin-gap-consistent direction. Data: the spin pairs and tuning series from Experiment 2. Model: frozen spin-aware model; the spin direction is a supervised probe (or SAE feature) separating spin isomers, no backbone training. Procedure: steer along the spin direction at matched magnitude and read the energy prediction; controls are matched-norm random directions. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |energy shift under spin direction| / |shift under random direction|, CI over systems. Indecision band up front: selectivity CI in [1.3, 2.0] cannot decide (no clean causal direction); CI lower bound > 2.0 with a spin-gap-consistent shift is convincing causal exchange encoding; CI upper bound < 1.3 means no separable causal spin direction. A negative result -- spin-aware models gating on the label without a steerable exchange direction, and geometry-only models blind -- is the decisive combined finding about atomistic FMs on open-shell chemistry.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Many public MLIPs are geometry-only and thus spin-blind by construction; the spin-blindness result is definitional for those models, so the richer mechanism tests apply only to spin-aware models, of which fewer public foundation-scale weights exist. We prioritize the strongest available spin-aware model and treat the geometry-only blindness as a decisive, separately-reported finding.

Spin-aware models may simply gate energy on the spin label without internally representing exchange; we mitigate by requiring correct sign AND magnitude AND monotonic ligand-field/substituent trends (dose-response), which a trivial label-lookup would not reproduce across unseen systems, and by cross-system transfer tests.

Reference spin gaps (CASPT2/DMRG) are themselves method-dependent and can disagree, especially for transition metals; we use consensus benchmark subsets, report sensitivity to the reference method, and emphasize sign and trend agreement over exact magnitude.

Spin and geometry can be correlated in equilibrium structures (different spin states relax to different geometries); the spin-flip counterfactual controls this by holding geometry fixed, but off-equilibrium single-point energies may fall outside training distribution — we bound this and report OOD diagnostics.

Linear probes recovering a spin direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random-direction controls, though distributed encodings may blur single-direction interventions.

A negative result (spin-aware models gate on the label but do not reproduce exchange trends, and geometry-only models are blind) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting atomistic foundation models on catalysis, radicals, and magnetism, though it may be perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of spin-state exchange energetics in atomistic foundation models.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes/SAEs and public spin-state benchmark datasets, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: sabatier_volcano_probe
Title: Too Weak or Too Strong? Testing Whether Catalysis Foundation Models Internally Represent the Sabatier Volcano, Not Just Monotone Binding Energy
Short Hypothesis: Catalytic activity follows the Sabatier principle: it is a NON-MONOTONE, relational function of intermediate binding energy — optimal at an intermediate value, with activity limited by poor reactant activation when binding is too weak and by poor product desorption when binding is too strong. Models trained to predict pointwise adsorption energies (e.g., on OC20) are never required to learn this two-sided, rate-determining-step structure. We hypothesize that if a catalysis foundation model internally represents the mechanism, its representation will (a) encode the volcano's two-sided distance-to-peak, (b) distinguish weak-binding-limited from strong-binding-limited catalysts even when their binding-energy deviation magnitudes are equal, and (c) causally track the switch in rate-determining step across the peak; a pointwise/monotone representation collapses the two limiting regimes. The opposite-side-of-the-peak counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that monotone binding-energy prediction cannot pass.
Related Work: Post-hoc XAI on shallow catalysis ML (SHAP/LIME/symbolic regression on adsorption-energy predictors; 'Explainable Data-driven Modeling of Adsorption Energy' 2024; HEA scaling-relation studies 2023; 'Beyond Scaling Relations' 2019; AutoML feature-deletion 2024) recovers descriptors and MONOTONE linear scaling relations, and volcano-plot ML (Meyer et al. 2018; Sharma et al. 2024 'Mapping and Reshaping the Activity Volcano') USES models to construct volcanoes downstream. Interpretability of atomistic foundation models ('Comparing latent features of uMLIPs' 2025; 'Beyond Converging Representations' 2025; CGCNN interpretability 2018) recovers pointwise site energies and characterizes latent geometry. Crucially, all of these either (i) attribute features to a monotone adsorption-energy target, or (ii) apply the model's energy predictions to build a volcano externally. None tests whether the model's INTERNAL representation encodes the Sabatier principle itself — the non-monotone, two-sided, rate-determining-step structure that defines catalytic activity — nor uses an opposite-side-of-the-peak counterfactual to separate weak- from strong-binding limitation. Because these models are trained on pointwise adsorption energies, whether they internalize the relational volcano mechanism is untested; that is our novel, mechanism-defining contribution.
Abstract: The central organizing principle of heterogeneous catalysis is the Sabatier principle: catalytic activity is a non-monotone function of how strongly a surface binds key intermediates, peaking at an intermediate binding strength. Below the peak, activity is limited by weak reactant activation; above it, by poor product desorption. This yields the iconic volcano plot — a relational, two-sided mechanism in which the rate-determining step switches across the summit. Catalysis foundation models are trained to predict pointwise adsorption energies (e.g., on the Open Catalyst dataset), a target that never requires learning this two-sided structure, so whether they internalize the Sabatier mechanism is unknown. We probe pretrained catalysis foundation models (e.g., GemNet-OC, EquiformerV2, and universal MLIPs on OC20/OC22 systems) at the representation level. First, a two-sided volcano probe: we test whether the model's internal representation encodes signed distance-to-peak and, critically, on which SIDE of the peak a catalyst lies, beyond what its scalar binding energy alone predicts. Second, and most decisively, an opposite-side counterfactual: we pair a too-weak-binding catalyst with a too-strong-binding one whose binding-energy deviation from the peak has equal magnitude but opposite sign, so their activities are similar but their limiting mechanisms opposite; a Sabatier-aware representation must separate them into weak- versus strong-limited regimes, while a monotone representation collapses them. Third, causal steering across the peak tests whether the internal rate-determining-step signal flips as predicted. Metrics quantify a volcano-side-beyond-energy index, an opposite-side separation ratio, and a rate-determining-step flip asymmetry. Either outcome sharpens whether deployed catalyst-discovery models represent the mechanism they are used to optimize.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — two-sided volcano side encoded beyond scalar binding energy): Tests assertion (a): the representation encodes the volcano's two-sided distance-to-peak (which SIDE, at fixed magnitude) beyond the scalar binding energy. Data (existing): well-characterized reactions with established descriptors and DFT/experimental volcano data -- hydrogen evolution (H* binding), oxygen reduction (O*/OH* binding), CO oxidation, and ammonia synthesis (N* binding) -- across transition-metal surfaces and alloys from the Open Catalyst dataset (OC20/OC22); for each catalyst-reaction pair we record key-intermediate binding energy, known volcano peak, signed distance-to-peak, limiting-step side, and a proxy activity (thermodynamic limiting potential / microkinetic turnover). We use several thousand catalyst-reaction pairs across the four reactions. Models (frozen, inference only): an OC20 adsorption-energy predictor (GemNet-OC and/or EquiformerV2) and the universal MLIP MACE-MP-0 on the same surfaces; pooled per-structure activations per layer. Trainable: linear probes only (3 seeds). Systems compared: representation probe vs a scalar-binding-energy predictor. Decisive metric first: Volcano-Side-Beyond-Energy Index = signed-distance-to-peak sign-classification accuracy from the representation minus the accuracy from scalar binding energy alone, at matched |deviation| (so magnitude is controlled). Indecision band up front: an index in [0.03, 0.10] (accuracy points) cannot decide and is reported as ambiguous two-sided encoding; index >= 0.10 with CI lower bound > 0.03 is convincing Sabatier-side encoding; index <= 0.03 means the representation is monotone in binding energy (sign collapses), supporting the pointwise hypothesis.

Experiment 2 (H2 — opposite-side counterfactual, decisive): Tests assertion (b): the model internally distinguishes weak-binding-limited from strong-binding-limited catalysts even when their binding-energy deviations are equal in magnitude. Data (constructed from existing): matched catalyst pairs -- one too-weak, one too-strong -- with equal-magnitude, opposite-sign deviations from the peak (similar proxy activity, opposite limiting mechanism), plus same-side control pairs matched on |deviation|, drawn from the OC20 systems above. Model: same frozen models. Systems compared: opposite-side pairs vs same-side control pairs. Decisive metric first: Opposite-Side Separation Ratio = representational distance(opposite-side pair) / representational distance(same-side, same-|deviation| pair), CI over pairs, reported across reactions and as a function of |deviation|. Indecision band up front: a ratio whose CI lies in [1.1, 1.5] cannot decide and is reported as weak two-sided structure; CI lower bound > 1.5 is convincing that opposite limiting regimes are internally distinguished; CI upper bound < 1.1 (only magnitude matters, sign collapses) is the monotone/pointwise signature. This is the decisive test; a null is the headline negative result about volcano representation.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal across-peak steering of the rate-determining step): Tests assertion (c): the model causally tracks the switch in rate-determining step across the peak -- steering a signed distance-to-peak direction should move predicted activity non-monotonically. Data: catalysts at, below, and above the peak from Experiment 1, for models with an activity-relatable head (reported per model). Model: frozen; the signed direction is a supervised probe (or SAE feature) separating the two sides, no backbone training. Procedure: steer at matched magnitude toward the strong- or weak-binding side and read predicted activity -- moving a peak catalyst either way should DECREASE activity, moving a too-strong catalyst toward the peak should INCREASE it. Controls: matched-norm random directions and a pure binding-energy-magnitude direction. Decisive metric first: Rate-Determining-Step Flip Asymmetry = fraction of steers producing the volcano-predicted (non-monotone) activity change, and mechanism-selectivity = |volcano-consistent effect| / |random-direction effect|, CIs over catalysts. Indecision band up front: selectivity CI in [1.3, 2.0], or flip fraction CI spanning 0.5, cannot decide (no clean causal two-sided handle); selectivity CI lower bound > 2.0 with flip fraction > 0.6 is convincing causal two-sided encoding; selectivity CI upper bound < 1.3 means the direction is not causally two-sided. A negative result, with H1-H2 nulls, supports the monotone conclusion and warns against trusting these models to rank near-peak catalysts.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Binding energy and volcano side are correlated across a catalyst set (side is the sign of the deviation), so the beyond-energy separation is statistically demanding; we mitigate with the opposite-side counterfactual that matches |deviation| exactly and controls that regress out binding-energy magnitude.

The 'true' volcano peak and limiting-step side depend on the chosen descriptor and microkinetic assumptions; we restrict to well-established reactions (HER, ORR, CO oxidation, NH3 synthesis) with consensus descriptors and report sensitivity to peak-location and activity-proxy choices.

Adsorption-energy foundation models may not natively output an 'activity' quantity; we derive proxy activity externally (thermodynamic limiting potential / microkinetic turnover) for ground truth and probe whether the internal representation nonetheless organizes by the two-sided structure. This is a strength (mechanism need not be in the training target) but limits the causal-steering readout to models with an activity-relatable head; we report per-model.

Steering in nonlinear equivariant networks can push representations off-manifold; we bound perturbation magnitude, report sensitivity, and use matched-norm and binding-energy-direction controls, relying primarily on the input-space opposite-side counterfactual as causal-adjacent evidence.

Linear probes recovering a volcano-side direction do not guarantee causal use; distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions — we use both probe directions and SAE features and report aggregate-direction results.

A negative result (models encode monotone binding energy but collapse the two limiting regimes) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting catalysis foundation models used to build volcano plots and rank candidates, though it may be perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether catalysis foundation models represent the Sabatier principle.

All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes/SAEs and public catalysis datasets (OC20/OC22) and DFT/experimental volcano references, keeping compute at academic scale.
