Name: reproduction_number_threshold_probe
Title: Above or Below One? Testing Whether Epidemic Time-Series Foundation Models Represent the Reproduction-Number Threshold Mechanism, Not Just Curve Momentum
Short Hypothesis: The defining mechanism of epidemic dynamics is the effective reproduction number R_t and its exact threshold at R_t=1: R_t>1 implies growth, R_t<1 implies decline, and the same recent case curve can be heading up or down depending only on R_t (e.g., a peak plateau vs. an inflection). Time-series foundation models (TSFMs) now used for epidemic forecasting and policy counterfactuals are trained to extrapolate curve shape, which never requires learning this threshold. We hypothesize that if a TSFM represents the epidemic mechanism rather than curve momentum, then (a) R_t and its side relative to 1 are decodable from internal representations beyond what the recent curve shape/slope predicts, (b) an R-holding counterfactual (matched recent curve, opposite R_t side) will be internally distinguished and forecast in opposite directions, and (c) steering a recovered 'R-threshold' direction causally flips growth-vs-decline forecasts. The matched-curve/opposite-R counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that curve-fitting cannot pass.
Related Work: Recent work shows TSFMs (Chronos, TimesFM, TimeGPT, TabPFN-TS, Lag-Llama) forecast epidemics well and even produce policy counterfactuals ('Foundation time series models for forecasting and policy evaluation', 2025), and epidemiology-aware pretrained models exist (CAPE, 2025, with 'compartmental prototypes'). Physics-informed and hybrid mechanistic-neural models (EINNs 2023; PINN-SIR 2025; hybrid neural-ODE 2026) BUILD R/SIR structure in by construction. TSFM interpretability shows encoded, steerable concepts: time2time (2025) causally implants 'crash/regime' semantics and finds severity encoded as a continuous latent; 'Exploring Representations...' (2024) and 'On the Internal Semantics of TSFMs' (2025) recover linear trend/periodicity/level-shift concepts. Crucially, none tests whether a TSFM internally represents the reproduction-number threshold mechanism (R_t vs. 1) that governs whether an epidemic grows or declines, nor uses a matched-curve/opposite-R counterfactual to separate this mechanism from mere growth momentum. Because R_t and recent curve slope are correlated in ordinary data, correlation-based forecasting benchmarks cannot arbitrate this; our threshold probe, R-holding counterfactual, and causal R-steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, transferred into a safety-critical public-health setting.
Abstract: Time-series foundation models (TSFMs) are increasingly used to forecast infectious-disease epidemics and even to evaluate public-health policies through counterfactual scenarios. Yet epidemic dynamics are defined by an exact, threshold-based mechanism: the effective reproduction number R_t, whose value relative to 1 determines whether cases grow or decline. Because TSFMs are trained to extrapolate observed curve shape, they can succeed by learning growth momentum without ever internalizing the R_t=1 threshold. This distinction is decision-critical: the most consequential forecasts are precisely at turning points, where recent curve shape is ambiguous and only R_t settles the direction. We propose the first mechanism-defining test of whether epidemic-forecasting TSFMs represent the reproduction-number mechanism. Using synthetic SIR/SEIR trajectories (where R_t is exactly known and controllable) and real surveillance data with estimated R_t, we probe pretrained TSFMs (Chronos, TimesFM, Lag-Llama, and the epidemiology-aware CAPE). First, a threshold-beyond-momentum probe: can R_t and its side relative to 1 be decoded from internal representations beyond what recent slope/curvature predicts? Second, and most decisively, an R-holding counterfactual: we construct trajectory pairs with near-identical recent curves but opposite R_t sides (one approaching a peak from below, one just past it), so momentum is matched but mechanism is opposite; a mechanistic representation must separate them and forecast opposite directions. Third, causal steering along a recovered R-threshold direction should flip growth-vs-decline forecasts. Metrics quantify a threshold-beyond-momentum index, a matched-curve turning-point asymmetry, and a steering flip rate. Either outcome sharpens whether deployed epidemic TSFMs forecast for the right mechanistic reason.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — R_t and its threshold side decodable beyond curve momentum): Tests assertion (a): the reproduction number R_t and its side relative to 1 are decodable from internal representations beyond what recent curve shape/slope predicts. Data (constructed + existing): synthetic SIR/SEIR/SAIRD trajectories with exactly-known time-varying R_t (varying transmission and recovery rates) spanning growth (R_t>1), decline (R_t<1), and turning-point regimes -- we generate >= 20,000 windows; plus real surveillance series (influenza-like illness, RSV, COVID-19, dengue) with published EpiEstim R_t estimates as a transfer/robustness check. Split by trajectory (no trajectory crosses splits). Models (frozen, inference only): general time-series foundation models Chronos, TimesFM, and Lag-Llama, and the epidemiology-aware CAPE; per-timestep representations, preprocessing documented, pre-normalization activations probed where feasible. Trainable: ridge linear probes (L2 by CV, 3 seeds). Systems compared: representation probe vs momentum features computed from the input window (recent slope, curvature, short-window AR fit). Decisive metric first: Threshold-Beyond-Momentum Index = R_t-side classification accuracy (and continuous-R_t R^2) from the representation minus what momentum features achieve, after regressing out the momentum-predictable component. Indecision band up front: an index in [0.03, 0.10] (accuracy points) cannot decide and is reported as ambiguous threshold encoding; index >= 0.10 with CI lower bound > 0.03 is convincing R_t encoding beyond momentum; index <= 0.03 means the model carries only curve momentum, supporting the curve-fitting hypothesis.

Experiment 2 (H2 — R-holding counterfactual and threshold locality, decisive): Tests assertion (b): matched recent curves with opposite R_t sides are internally distinguished and forecast in opposite directions, and the internal change localizes at R_t=1. Data (constructed): matched trajectory pairs whose recent observed windows are made near-indistinguishable by the synthetic generator (matched level, slope, curvature) but that sit on opposite R_t sides -- e.g., approaching a peak from below (R_t just above 1) vs just past the peak (R_t just below 1); residual window-matching error quantified and swept. Plus a sweep of R_t across a range to test where the internal growth-vs-decline signal changes. Model: same frozen TSFMs. Systems compared: opposite-R pairs vs same-R control pairs matched on recent shape; and the transition location vs the true threshold at 1. Decisive metric first: Matched-Curve Separation Ratio = representational distance(opposite-R pair) / representational distance(same-R control), and Turning-Point Direction Accuracy = fraction of opposite-R pairs where the model forecasts growth for the R>1 member and decline for the R<1 member. Indecision band up front: a separation ratio whose CI lies in [1.1, 1.5], or direction accuracy CI in [0.5, 0.65], cannot decide and is reported as momentum-following; ratio CI lower bound > 1.5 WITH direction accuracy CI lower bound > 0.65 and the internal transition localized near R_t=1 (not at arbitrary R_t) is convincing threshold encoding; ratio CI upper bound < 1.1 with direction accuracy CI upper bound < 0.5 (near the 0.5 chance line, following shared shape) is the momentum signature. This is the decisive test; a null is the headline safety-relevant negative result at turning points.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal R-threshold steering and policy-counterfactual faithfulness): Tests assertion (c): steering a recovered R-threshold direction causally flips growth-vs-decline forecasts, and the model's response to an R-reducing intervention is mechanism-consistent. Data: synthetic trajectories sitting near the threshold, with known SIR counterfactuals for an R-reducing intervention. Model: frozen; the R-threshold direction is a supervised probe or a delta-representation between matched R>1 and R<1 states, no backbone training. Procedure: add matched-magnitude perturbations along the R direction and read whether the forecast flips growth<->decline (controls: matched-norm random directions and a pure recent-slope direction); separately, apply an R-reducing intervention and compare the model's counterfactual turning behavior against the true post-intervention R_t side. Decisive metric first: Steering Flip Rate = fraction of steers producing the R-consistent forecast flip, and mechanism-selectivity = |effect of R direction| / |effect of random direction|; plus correlation between model counterfactual turning and true post-intervention R_t side. Indecision band up front: selectivity CI in [1.3, 2.0], or flip rate CI spanning 0.5, cannot decide (no clean causal handle); selectivity CI lower bound > 2.0 with flip rate > 0.6 and counterfactual correlation CI lower bound > 0.5 is convincing causal threshold encoding; selectivity CI upper bound < 1.3 means no separable causal R direction and unfaithful policy counterfactuals. A negative result, with H1-H2 nulls, warns against TSFM epidemic policy counterfactuals precisely at turning points.
Risk Factors and Limitations: R_t and recent curve slope are correlated in ordinary trajectories, making the threshold-beyond-momentum separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with momentum-residualization, the R-holding counterfactual (which matches the recent curve exactly in the synthetic generator), and the threshold-locality control that a momentum model cannot reproduce.

Real-data R_t is an estimate (method- and delay-dependent), adding label noise; we use synthetic data with exactly-known R_t for the primary decisive tests and treat real surveillance as a robustness/transfer check, reporting sensitivity to the R_t estimator.

Constructing near-identical recent windows with opposite R_t requires careful synthetic generation (matching level, slope, curvature over the input window); residual differences could leak the side. We quantify and report the residual matching error and show results as a function of match tightness.

TSFMs normalize/tokenize input series (scaling, patching), which may discard absolute-level information relevant to R; we document each model's preprocessing, probe pre-normalization activations where feasible, and prioritize models exposing per-timestep representations.

Linear probes recovering an R direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/slope-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions.

A negative result (models forecast from curve momentum and fail the matched-curve/opposite-R counterfactual) is scientifically decisive and directly safety-relevant, warning against trusting TSFM epidemic forecasts and policy counterfactuals precisely at turning points where they matter most; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether epidemic TSFMs represent the reproduction-number threshold.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and standard epidemic simulators / public surveillance data, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: universality_class_collapse_probe
Title: Same Exponents, Different Stuff: Do Physics Foundation Models Represent Universality Classes, or Just Microscopic Detail?
Short Hypothesis: Universality is the defining, exactly-known mechanism of critical phenomena: near a continuous phase transition, microscopically-different systems collapse onto the SAME critical exponents, determined only by symmetry and spatial dimensionality, not microscopic details. We hypothesize that if a physics/scientific foundation model represents this mechanism rather than surface configuration statistics, its internal representation near criticality will (a) organize systems by universality class (collapsing microscopically-distinct systems of the same class together while separating same-looking systems of different classes), (b) encode a recoverable 'reduced temperature / distance-to-criticality' direction that reproduces finite-size scaling collapse, and (c) causally track class membership. A same-class-different-microscopics vs different-class-similar-microscopics counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that correlation with raw configurations cannot pass.
Related Work: A large literature draws an ANALOGY between deep networks and the renormalization group (Scale-invariant feature extraction and RG flow 2018; Towards quantifying information flows 2022; Interpreting Deep Learning via RG 2022; RG for DNNs: Universality of learning 2025), and studies criticality signatures IN networks (Universal Scaling Laws of Absorbing Phase Transitions in DNNs 2023; Critical Phase Transition in LLMs 2024; Internal Representations in SNNs and criticality 2024). These treat the NETWORK itself as a critical/RG system, or map data-derived RG flows. None tests whether a model TRAINED ON PHYSICAL SYSTEM DATA internally represents the physics concept of universality classes — that critical exponents depend only on symmetry and dimensionality, not microscopic details — nor uses a same-class/different-class counterfactual to separate this mechanism from raw-configuration correlation. Statistical-physics work (Potts/percolation hyperuniversality 2025; lower-bound-on-nu conjecture 2025; quantum critical exponent extraction 2026) rigorously defines universality classes and exponents as ground truth. Our contribution is the first mechanism-defining test of whether a scientific foundation model encodes universality-class structure, its causal load-bearingness, and its finite-size-scaling faithfulness — distinct from the network-as-RG analogy line.
Abstract: The single deepest organizing principle of critical phenomena is universality: near a continuous phase transition, systems that differ completely at the microscopic level — different lattices, interactions, and degrees of freedom — exhibit identical critical exponents, determined only by symmetry and spatial dimensionality. Two systems that look nothing alike can belong to the same universality class, while two that look almost identical can belong to different ones. This makes universality an ideal, exactly-known mechanism for testing whether foundation models that ingest physical system data learn the underlying mechanism or merely surface configuration statistics. We probe scientific foundation models applied to spin/lattice systems (either public multi-physics/statistical-mechanics surrogates, or a modest transformer/CNN foundation model pretrained across many statistical-mechanics systems), evaluated on Monte-Carlo configurations from the 2D Ising, 3-state Potts, XY, and site/bond percolation models whose universality classes and critical exponents are exactly known. First, a class-organization probe: near criticality, are microscopically-distinct systems of the same class collapsed together in the representation, and same-looking systems of different classes separated, beyond raw-configuration similarity? Second, a finite-size-scaling test: does a recovered 'reduced-temperature' direction reproduce the data-collapse scaling function with the correct critical exponents? Third, and most decisively, a universality-class counterfactual: pairs matched to be same-class-but-different-microscopics versus different-class-but-similar-microscopics; a mechanistic representation groups by class, a configuration-statistics one groups by appearance. We validate causally by steering the class direction. Metrics quantify a class-beyond-configuration index, scaling-collapse fidelity, and a same-class/different-class separation ratio. Either outcome sharpens what these models represent.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — organization by universality class beyond configuration statistics, decisive): Tests assertion (a): near criticality the representation organizes systems by universality class -- collapsing microscopically-distinct systems of the same class while separating same-looking systems of different classes -- beyond raw-configuration similarity. Data (constructed): Monte-Carlo configuration ensembles (Metropolis/Wolff/Swendsen-Wang) for models with exactly-known classes -- 2D Ising, 2D q=3 Potts, 2D XY (BKT), 2D site and bond percolation, and dilute/next-nearest-neighbor Ising variants (same 2D-Ising class, different microscopics) -- swept through each transition at several lattice sizes L, labeled by class, reduced temperature t, and known exponents (nu, beta, gamma); >= 50,000 configurations, split so held-out systems exist. Model (frozen for analysis): either a public scientific foundation model with per-configuration representations, or, as a documented academic-scale fallback, a modest CNN/transformer pretrained self-supervised (masked reconstruction / temperature regression) across MULTIPLE systems and never told class labels (one pretraining run, seeds 0,1,2); analysis is inference-only plus linear probes. Systems compared: (i) representation probe vs raw-configuration/order-parameter features for class decoding; and (ii) the counterfactual pairs -- same-class/different-microscopics (nearest-neighbor vs dilute/NNN 2D Ising at their critical points) vs different-class/similar-appearance (q=2 vs q=3 Potts at criticality). Decisive metrics first: Class-Beyond-Configuration Index = class-decoding accuracy from the representation minus what raw-configuration/order-parameter features achieve (after residualizing configuration features); and Same-Class/Different-Class Separation Ratio = representational distance(same-class pair) / representational distance(different-class-but-similar-appearance pair). Indecision bands up front: a Class-Beyond-Configuration Index in [0.03, 0.10] cannot decide (ambiguous class encoding); index >= 0.10 with CI lower bound > 0.03 is convincing class-beyond-appearance encoding; index <= 0.03 is the appearance-only signature. For the ratio, mechanism predicts < 1: a ratio whose CI lies in [0.67, 0.90] cannot decide; CI upper bound < 0.67 (same class collapses together despite different microscopics) is convincing universality encoding; CI lower bound > 0.90 (groups by appearance, not class) is the configuration-statistics signature. These together are the decisive test; a null is the headline negative result.

Experiment 2 (H2 — finite-size-scaling faithfulness): Tests assertion (b): a recoverable reduced-temperature / distance-to-criticality direction reproduces finite-size-scaling collapse with the CORRECT class exponents and fails with the wrong ones. Data: the Experiment 1 ensembles across multiple L and t for the clean second-order classes (Ising, Potts, percolation); XY/BKT treated as a separate carefully-analyzed case, not a decisive counterfactual. Model: frozen backbone; a reduced-temperature direction recovered by a linear probe across L and t, no backbone training. Procedure: test whether model-implied observables obey M*L^(beta/nu) = f(t*L^(1/nu)) with the true known exponents, and whether the collapse degrades when wrong-class exponents are imposed. Systems compared: collapse under correct vs wrong-class exponents. Decisive metric first: scaling-collapse quality = ratio of collapse residual with wrong-class exponents to residual with correct-class exponents (larger means the correct exponents collapse the data selectively), CI over bootstrap resamples of configurations. Indecision band up front: a ratio whose CI lies in [1.0, 1.5] cannot decide and is reported as no selective collapse (exponents not faithfully encoded); CI lower bound > 1.5 is convincing that the internal signal collapses only under its true class's exponents; CI upper bound < 1.0 or ~1.0 means the representation does not encode the correct scaling. A negative result here, even with a positive H1, would mean class structure is present but not quantitatively faithful.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal class steering and generalization): Tests assertion (c): a recovered class-membership direction is causally load-bearing, and class structure generalizes to a held-out system, distinguishing an encoded mechanism from per-system memorization. Data: configurations at criticality for two classes, plus a system held out of pretraining but in a known class (a 2D Ising variant, or 3D Ising if feasible). Model: frozen; the class direction is a supervised probe or a delta-representation between two classes at criticality, no backbone training. Procedure: steer a configuration's representation with matched magnitude toward another class and read the class/exponent readout (or masked-reconstruction statistics); controls are matched-norm random directions and a raw-configuration direction; separately, test class decoding on the held-out system. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |class-readout change under class direction| / |change under random direction|, CI over configurations; plus held-out-system class-decoding accuracy above the raw-configuration baseline. Indecision band up front: selectivity CI in [1.3, 2.0] cannot decide (no clean causal class direction); CI lower bound > 2.0 with class-consistent steering, and held-out class-decoding beating the configuration baseline by > 0.10 accuracy, is convincing causal, generalizing class encoding; selectivity CI upper bound < 1.3, or held-out decoding at the configuration baseline, means class membership is memorized per system rather than encoded as a mechanism. A negative result supports the configuration-statistics conclusion.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Universality-class membership correlates with visible configuration features near criticality (e.g., cluster geometry), making the class-beyond-configuration separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with raw-configuration residualization, the matched same-class/different-microscopics counterfactual, and the finite-size-scaling test which a configuration-statistics model cannot pass with correct exponents.

Public scientific foundation models trained on statistical-mechanics configurations may be scarce; we fall back on pretraining a modest multi-system CNN/transformer surrogate ourselves, which is academic-scale (small lattices, standard Monte-Carlo data) but is not a 'large' foundation model — we report this scope clearly and treat cross-system generalization as the foundation-model-relevant test.

Distinguishing BKT (XY) scaling from second-order transitions requires care (essential singularity, no simple power-law nu); we treat XY as a separate, carefully-analyzed case and focus decisive counterfactuals on clean second-order classes (Ising, Potts, percolation).

Finite-size effects and limited lattice sizes blur exponents; we use standard finite-size scaling with multiple L and report exponent-estimation uncertainty, relying on relative collapse quality (correct vs wrong-class exponents) rather than absolute precision.

Linear probes recovering a class direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/configuration-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions.

A negative result (models encode configuration statistics and group by appearance, not universality class) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting such models for cross-system extrapolation and critical-point prediction, though it may be perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether scientific foundation models represent universality classes.
All experiments are inference-only on the model plus small probes and standard Monte-Carlo simulations (or one modest self-supervised pretraining run), keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: ps_traveltime_distance_probe
Title: Timing, Not Loudness: Do Seismic Foundation Models Represent the P–S Travel-Time Distance Mechanism, or Just Waveform Amplitude Statistics?
Short Hypothesis: Earthquake distance is fixed by an exactly-known relational mechanism: the arrival-time difference between the fast P-wave and the slower S-wave grows linearly with hypocentral distance (delta_t ≈ distance × (1/v_S − 1/v_P)), and magnitude follows a saturating log-amplitude-corrected-for-distance law—not raw amplitude. Seismic foundation models are trained on waveforms where distance and amplitude are correlated (nearer, larger). We hypothesize that if these models represent the seismological mechanism rather than amplitude/morphology statistics, then (a) distance is decodable from internal representations beyond what waveform amplitude predicts, (b) a P–S-gap counterfactual that stretches only the inter-arrival time (at fixed amplitude and morphology) will shift the internal distance estimate as physics dictates, while a whole-trace time-shift control (which leaves the gap unchanged) will not, and (c) steering a recovered 'P–S gap' direction causally shifts distance predictions. The gap-vs-shift counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that amplitude-based correlation cannot pass.
Related Work: Interpretability of seismic models is entirely post-hoc XAI attribution confirming LOCAL, descriptive alignment: Grad-CAM/SHAP show PhaseNet attends to P/S arrivals and that vertical vs horizontal components drive P vs S picks (2025); Integrated Gradients traces feature-importance drift in earthquake forecasting (2026) and pre-rupture deformation (2025); RNN hidden-state visualization for volcano-seismic events (2022). Seismic foundation models with public weights now exist (SeisLM 2024, SeisCLIP 2023, Seismic Foundation Model 2023, SeisMoLLM 2025) and decode distance/magnitude as downstream tasks. Crucially, all interpretability work is correlational attribution ('the model looks at the P and S arrivals'); none tests whether the model's INTERNAL representation encodes the RELATIONAL travel-time law—that the P–S time gap, not amplitude, determines distance—nor uses a gap-vs-shift counterfactual to separate this mechanism from amplitude/morphology correlation. Because distance and amplitude are correlated in catalogs, ordinary attribution and benchmark accuracy cannot arbitrate this. Our P–S-gap counterfactual, distance-beyond-amplitude probe, and causal gap-steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, moving beyond 'the model sees the arrivals' to 'the model represents that the arrival SEPARATION sets the distance.'
Abstract: Seismic foundation models now estimate earthquake distance and magnitude from raw waveforms, and interpretability studies confirm they attend to P- and S-wave arrivals. But attending to the arrivals is not the same as representing the mechanism that makes them informative: hypocentral distance is set by the travel-time difference between the fast P-wave and slower S-wave, a relation that grows linearly with distance and is independent of how loud the signal is, while magnitude requires correcting amplitude for that distance. Because nearer earthquakes are also larger and louder, distance and amplitude are correlated in training data, so benchmark accuracy and attribution maps cannot tell whether a model uses the P–S timing mechanism or an amplitude shortcut. We propose the first mechanism-defining test. Using pretrained seismic foundation models (SeisLM, SeisCLIP, Seismic Foundation Model) evaluated on public labeled waveform datasets (STEAD, DiTing) with known source distances, we ask three questions. First, a distance-beyond-amplitude probe: is distance decodable from internal representations beyond what waveform amplitude/energy predicts? Second, and most decisively, a P–S-gap counterfactual: we resample the segment between the P and S arrivals to stretch or compress only the inter-arrival time at fixed amplitude and waveform morphology, which by physics must change the inferred distance, and compare against a whole-trace time-shift control that leaves the gap unchanged; a mechanistic representation must move its distance estimate for the gap edit but not the shift, while an amplitude-statistics model does the opposite. Third, causal gap-direction steering. Metrics quantify a distance-beyond-amplitude index, a gap-vs-shift causal asymmetry, and a magnitude-distance-correction fidelity test. Either outcome sharpens whether deployed seismic models locate earthquakes for the right physical reason.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — distance decodable beyond waveform amplitude): Tests hypothesis clause (a): hypocentral distance is recoverable from internal representations beyond what raw waveform amplitude/energy predicts. Data: STEAD (~1.2M labeled three-component waveforms with P and S picks, hypocentral distance, magnitude) and DiTing (~2.7M); use a 40,000-trace subset (24k train / 4k val / 12k test, split by seismic event so no event crosses splits), keeping only SNR>10 dB traces with analyst-confirmed P and S picks and stratifying uniformly over 0–200 km — fewer than the full catalog because the confident-pick, SNR, and distance-balancing filters (which deliberately weaken the natural distance–amplitude correlation) are essential to the test. Model: SeisLM (transformer waveform encoder, ~30M parameters) and the Seismic Foundation Model (SFM, masked-autoencoder ViT, ~100M parameters); backbone frozen, only a ridge-regression linear probe (L2 chosen by 5-fold CV) trained on the best layer, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: probe R^2 for distance from the frozen representation vs an amplitude baseline (ridge on log peak amplitude, RMS energy, and 8 envelope-shape features), with the representation residualized against those amplitude features before re-decoding. Decisive metric (first): Distance-Beyond-Amplitude Index = test R^2(distance | representation) − R^2(distance | amplitude features). Convincing: Index ≥ 0.15 with 95% CI lower bound above 0.05, and the residual distance direction correlates more with a delta_t (P–S gap) probe than with an amplitude probe. Indecision band: Index in [−0.03, 0.05] — within probe noise of zero; a result here means distance adds nothing beyond amplitude and clause (a) is unsupported (amplitude-shortcut reading). Negative result (Index ≤ −0.03 or inside the band): the representation is an amplitude statistic, not a distance code, which already undercuts the mechanism hypothesis.

Experiment 2 (H2 — P–S-gap vs whole-trace-shift counterfactual): Tests clause (b): stretching only the inter-arrival gap shifts the internal distance estimate, while a whole-trace time-shift (which leaves the gap unchanged) does not. Data: 3,000 high-SNR confident-pick traces drawn from the Experiment-1 test events; each yields a matched pair — (gap edit) resample only the P-to-S segment to change delta_t by a controlled factor with tapered splice joins, preserving amplitude scale and the P and S packet morphology; (shift control) translate the whole trace by an equal number of samples, leaving delta_t fixed. Model/probe as Experiment 1 (frozen backbones, seeds 0–4); read-out is the Experiment-1 distance probe and the model's distance head where present. Systems compared: |change in distance estimate| under gap edit vs under shift control, on the same traces. Decisive metric (first): Gap-vs-Shift Causal Asymmetry = median(|Δdistance gap edit|) / median(|Δdistance shift control|). Convincing: asymmetry ≥ 3 and the gap-edit Δdistance has the correct (positive) sign. Indecision band: asymmetry in [0.7, 2.0] — the timing gap is not privileged over a generic shift; a result here means the model is insensitive to the mechanism-defining inter-arrival timing and clause (b) fails. Negative result: asymmetry ≈ 1, i.e., displacement moves the estimate as much as the physically meaningful gap, indicating a morphology/statistics reading rather than the travel-time mechanism.

Experiment 3 (H2 — physics dose-response of the linear travel-time law): Tests the quantitative content of clause (b): that the induced distance change follows delta_t = distance × (1/v_S − 1/v_P). Data: the same 3,000 test traces; sweep the gap-stretch factor across 7 levels spanning ±30% of delta_t. Model/probe as above, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: model-induced Δdistance vs the physically predicted Δdistance from the regional v_P, v_S; shuffled-stretch-factor labels as a null control. Decisive metric (first): slope agreement = fitted slope(model Δdistance vs predicted Δdistance), plus Spearman rho of the same relation. Convincing: rho ≥ 0.6, correct sign, and fitted slope within ±30% of 1.0 (predicted). Indecision band: rho in [0.2, 0.4] or slope outside ±30% but same sign — a weak, physically-loose response; a result here means the model tracks gap direction but not the law's magnitude, partial support for (b) that should be reported as inconclusive on quantitative fidelity. Negative result: rho < 0.2 or wrong sign, indistinguishable from the shuffled control — no travel-time law is represented.

Experiment 4 (H3 — causal P–S-gap-direction steering): Tests clause (c): steering a recovered 'P–S gap' direction causally shifts distance predictions. Data: the same 3,000-trace test set; the gap direction is recovered two ways — a supervised delta_t probe direction, and the mean delta-representation between short-gap and long-gap traces at matched amplitude. Model/probe as above; add matched-norm perturbations along the gap direction to the frozen best-layer activations and read the distance head, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: gap direction vs matched-norm random directions vs an amplitude-probe direction. Decisive metric (first): Steering Selectivity = |Δdistance from gap-direction steering| / |Δdistance from random-direction steering|. Convincing: selectivity ≥ 3, Δdistance in the gap-consistent sign, and amplitude-direction steering not reproducing it. Indecision band: selectivity in [0.7, 2.0] — the gap direction is no more causal than a random one; a result here means the recovered direction is correlational, not a causal handle, and clause (c) is unsupported. Negative result: selectivity ≈ 1, indicating no dedicated causal distance-via-timing direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Distance and amplitude are strongly correlated in real catalogs, making the distance-beyond-amplitude separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with amplitude-residualization, the gap-vs-shift counterfactual (which holds amplitude and morphology fixed while varying only the timing gap), and the physics dose-response test that an amplitude model cannot reproduce with the correct slope.

The gap-edit counterfactual is a synthetic waveform manipulation; time-stretching the inter-arrival segment may introduce spectral artifacts or push traces off the model's data distribution, confounding the gap-edit response with generic OOD failure. We mitigate with small stretch factors, tapered splice joins, spectral-artifact diagnostics, and by comparing against the whole-trace shift control of matched sample-count perturbation; we report sensitivity to stretch magnitude.

Some foundation models ingest time-frequency spectra (e.g., SeisCLIP) or normalize/tokenize waveforms in ways that may discard absolute timing or amplitude; we document each model's preprocessing, probe pre-normalization activations where feasible, and prioritize models that retain raw temporal structure (SeisLM) for the cleanest timing test.

Arrival picks (P and S) in STEAD/DiTing are pipeline estimates with error, adding noise to the gap edit and to delta_t labels; we restrict counterfactuals to high-SNR traces with confident picks and report sensitivity to pick-quality thresholds.

Linear probes recovering a gap/distance direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/amplitude-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions.

A negative result (models estimate distance from amplitude/morphology statistics and fail the gap-vs-shift counterfactual) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting seismic foundation models for earthquake location and early warning—especially for atypical events where the amplitude–distance correlation breaks—though it may be perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether seismic FMs represent the P–S travel-time distance law.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and public labeled waveform datasets (STEAD, DiTing), keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: protonation_state_ph_probe
Title: Does the Model Know the pH? Testing Whether Chemistry Foundation Models Represent the Protonation-State (Henderson-Hasselbalch) Mechanism, Not Just Neutral Structure
Short Hypothesis: A molecule's charge state - and therefore its solubility, permeability, and binding - is governed by an exactly-known mechanism: the Henderson-Hasselbalch relation, which says the fraction of a molecule that is protonated flips discontinuously as pH crosses its pKa. Chemistry foundation models are typically fed a single (often neutral) structure and no pH, so whether they internally represent this pH-dependent ionization mechanism is untested. We hypothesize that if a chemistry FM represents the mechanism rather than surface neutral-structure statistics, then (a) a molecule's dominant protonation state at a given pH is decodable from internal representations beyond what its neutral structure alone predicts, (b) a pH-crossing counterfactual - moving pH across an ionizable group's pKa while holding the input structure fixed - shifts the internal charge-state/property signal as Henderson-Hasselbalch predicts, whereas an equal pH change that does NOT cross a pKa does not, and (c) the effect localizes to the ionizable site. The pH-cross-vs-no-cross counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that pKa-prediction accuracy and neutral-structure correlation cannot provide.
Related Work: Two lines bracket the gap. (1) pKa/protonation prediction models - Uni-pKa (2023/24), Starling (2025), TripKa (2026), AcepKa/PlayMolecule (2026), BCL-XpKa (2024) - BUILD the protonation ensemble and thermodynamic consistency in by construction and are judged by pKa accuracy; none asks whether a general chemistry FM already encodes the pH-dependent ionization mechanism. (2) Chemistry-model interpretability - MoleX (2024, functional-group linear decomposition), 'Unveiling Latent Knowledge via SAEs' on SMI-TED (2025), 'Circuits, Features, and Heuristics in Molecular Transformers' (2025, valence circuits), 'BERT Learns Chemistry' (2020), and attribution studies for solubility (2024) - recover features aligned with functional groups and physicochemical properties, but all validate against neutral-structure, pH-independent annotations. Crucially, no work tests whether a chemistry FM internally represents the RELATIONAL, pH-dependent Henderson-Hasselbalch mechanism (charge state flips as pH crosses pKa), whether that representation is causally load-bearing, or uses a pH-crossing counterfactual to separate mechanism from neutral-structure correlation. Because pKa and neutral structure are entangled in training data (and pH is usually absent as input), correlation and pKa-benchmark accuracy cannot arbitrate this. Our protonation-state-beyond-structure probe, pH-cross-vs-no-cross counterfactual, and causal ionization-site steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, transferred into a safety-critical drug-property setting where charge state controls bioavailability.
Abstract: The physicochemical behavior of drug-like molecules - solubility, membrane permeability, and protein binding - is dominated by their charge state, which is set by an exactly-known mechanism: the Henderson-Hasselbalch relation, in which the protonated fraction of an ionizable group flips discontinuously as environmental pH crosses the group's pKa. The same molecule can be neutral in the stomach and charged in the blood, radically changing its properties. This makes protonation an ideal, mechanism-defining probe for whether chemistry foundation models learn pH-dependent mechanism or merely encode a static neutral structure - especially since these models are usually given no pH input at all. We probe pretrained chemistry FMs (e.g., SMI-TED/FM4M, ChemBERTa-2, Uni-Mol) plus a pH-aware variant, using molecules with well-characterized ionizable groups and experimental pKa/pH-dependent property data. First, a protonation-state-beyond-structure probe: is a molecule's dominant charge state at a given pH decodable from internal representations beyond what its neutral structure predicts? Second, and most decisively, a pH-crossing counterfactual: we vary pH across an ionizable group's pKa while holding the input structure fixed and measure whether the internal charge-state and pH-dependent-property signal shifts as Henderson-Hasselbalch dictates (sigmoidal titration curve centered at pKa), versus an equal-magnitude pH change that does not cross any pKa, which should not. Third, causal steering along a recovered ionization direction and site-localization. Metrics quantify a protonation-beyond-structure index, a cross-vs-no-cross causal asymmetry, and a titration-curve fidelity score. Either outcome sharpens whether deployed chemistry models represent the ionization mechanism that controls drug behavior.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — protonation state decodable beyond neutral structure): Tests clause (a): the dominant protonation state at a given pH is decodable from internal representations beyond what the neutral structure alone predicts. Data: monoprotic drug-like molecules with a single confident experimental pKa — pooled from ChEMBL/AstraZeneca pKa (~7,900 measurements) and SAMPL6–8 (~110 combined); use 1,200 molecules (700 train / 200 val / 300 test, split by Bemis–Murcko scaffold so no scaffold crosses splits), evaluated on a pH grid of 0.5 units over 0–14 — fewer than all of ChEMBL because we require a single dominant ionizable group and a reliable pKa. pH is supplied to structure-only models by feeding the pH-appropriate protonation microstate SMILES, and to pH-aware models via pH conditioning. Model: ChemBERTa-2 (SMILES transformer, ~46M parameters) and Uni-Mol (3D graph, ~48M parameters), frozen; only a logistic-regression probe is trained, seeds 0–4; Uni-pKa serves as an upper-bracket reference. Systems compared: charge-state decoding from the representation vs a neutral-structure baseline (probe on ionizable-group identity/count from the neutral graph), representation residualized against the neutral-structure features. Decisive metric (first): Protonation-Beyond-Structure Index = balanced accuracy(charge state | representation) − balanced accuracy(charge state | neutral-structure features). Convincing: Index ≥ 0.10 with 95% CI lower bound above 0.03. Indecision band: Index in [−0.02, 0.03] — within probe noise; a result here means pH-conditioned charge adds nothing beyond static structure and clause (a) fails. Negative result (Index ≤ −0.02 or in band): the model carries neutral-structure statistics, not a pH-dependent ionization code.

Experiment 2 (H2 — pH-crossing vs no-crossing counterfactual): Tests clause (b): moving pH across an ionizable group's pKa (holding the input fixed) shifts the internal charge-state/property signal as Henderson–Hasselbalch predicts, whereas an equal pH change that does not cross a pKa does not. Data: 600 monoprotic test molecules from Experiment 1; each yields a matched pair — (cross edit) pH from pKa−2 to pKa+2 (flips dominant charge); (no-cross control) an equal 4-unit pH change entirely on one side of the pKa (charge unchanged). For structure-only models the microstate SMILES is swapped only when the edit crosses the pKa; for pH-aware models only the pH token changes. Model/probe as Experiment 1, seeds 0–4; read-out is the charge-state probe and the logD/solubility head where present. Systems compared: |signal change| under cross edit vs under no-cross control. Decisive metric (first): Cross-vs-No-Cross Causal Asymmetry = median(|Δsignal cross|) / median(|Δsignal no-cross|). Convincing: asymmetry ≥ 3. Indecision band: asymmetry in [0.7, 2.0] — crossing the pKa is not privileged over an equal non-crossing pH change; clause (b) fails here. Negative result: asymmetry ≈ 1, i.e., the model responds to pH magnitude, not to the mechanism-defining pKa crossing.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Henderson–Hasselbalch titration-curve fidelity): Tests the quantitative content of clause (b): the internal charge-state signal traces a sigmoid centred at the true pKa. Data: the same 600 molecules; sweep pH finely (0.25-unit steps) across each pKa. Model/probe as above, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: internal-signal-vs-pH fit to a Henderson–Hasselbalch sigmoid vs shuffled-pKa labels. Decisive metric (first): inflection-point error = |recovered inflection pH − true pKa| (pH units), with sigmoid fit R^2 as secondary. Convincing: median inflection error ≤ 0.5 pH units and fit R^2 ≥ 0.8. Indecision band: inflection error in (0.5, 1.5] pH units — a titration-like but mislocated response; a result here means the shape is present but not quantitatively tied to the true pKa, partial and inconclusive support for (b). Negative result: inflection error > 1.5 pH units or fit R^2 < 0.5, indistinguishable from shuffled labels — no titration mechanism represented.

Experiment 4 (H3 — ionization-site localization): Tests clause (c): the pH-crossing effect localizes to the ionizable site rather than being diffuse. Data: the same 600 molecules, restricted to the subset with per-atom/per-token representations (Uni-Mol; ChemBERTa-2 via token attribution). Model as above, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: representational change at the ionizable atom/group vs matched non-ionizable atoms under the pH-cross edit; occlusion of the ionizable group as an additional control. Decisive metric (first): Localization Fraction = share of the total pH-induced representational-change norm concentrated at the ionizable site. Convincing: Localization Fraction ≥ 0.5 (site occupies a small fraction of atoms yet carries at least half the change), well above the atom-count-proportional null. Indecision band: fraction within ±50% of the atom-count-proportional expectation — no meaningful concentration; clause (c) fails here. Negative result: fraction at or below the atom-count null, i.e., the ionization signal is diffuse and not tied to the titrating group.
Risk Factors and Limitations: pKa and neutral structure are entangled (the ionizable group is part of the structure), making the protonation-beyond-structure separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with neutral-structure residualization, the pH-crossing counterfactual (which holds structure fixed and varies only pH), and the titration-curve fidelity test that a neutral-structure model cannot pass with the correct inflection at pKa.

Most chemistry FMs take no pH input, so 'varying pH' must be operationalized either by supplying the pH-appropriate protonation microstate SMILES (which changes the input, partially confounding the structure-fixed ideal) or via pH conditioning only in pH-aware models. We run both operationalizations, clearly report the caveat, and treat the microstate-swap as changing only the ionization of the target group while matching the rest of the structure; a truly mechanism-aware model should nonetheless respond only when the swap corresponds to a real pKa-crossing.

Providing protonated microstates as input tests whether the model correctly propagates a charge-state change to properties, which is a slightly different (but still mechanism-relevant) claim than 'the model infers pH-dependence from neutral structure'; we distinguish these two claims explicitly and report both.

Experimental pKa and pH-dependent property data are noisy and assay-dependent (SAMPL, ChEMBL, Novartis); we use curated benchmark subsets, focus counterfactuals on molecules with a single dominant ionizable group and confident pKa, and report sensitivity to data confidence thresholds; multiprotic molecules are analyzed separately.

Linear probes recovering an ionization direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random-direction controls and site-localization, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions - we use both probe directions and SAE features.

A negative result (models encode neutral structure but not the pH-dependent ionization mechanism, failing the cross-vs-no-cross counterfactual) is scientifically decisive and directly safety-relevant - it would warn against trusting chemistry FMs for pH-dependent solubility, permeability, and bioavailability predictions, especially for ionizable drugs that change charge between gut and blood pH; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether chemistry FMs represent the Henderson-Hasselbalch protonation mechanism.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes/SAEs and public pKa/property datasets (SAMPL6-8, ChEMBL, Novartis), keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: cascade_flux_irreversibility_probe
Title: Which Way Does Energy Flow? Testing Whether Turbulence Foundation Models Represent the Directional, Time-Irreversible Energy Cascade, Not Just Instantaneous Field Statistics
Short Hypothesis: The defining mechanism of turbulence is the Richardson-Kolmogorov energy cascade: kinetic energy is transferred directionally across scales (net forward, large-to-small) at a rate Pi(k) whose mean is set by the dissipation rate, and this transfer breaks time-reversal symmetry (a time-reversed turbulent flow would carry energy up-scale, which is physically forbidden). A single velocity snapshot is nearly statistically identical under time reversal, so instantaneous field statistics cannot encode cascade direction. We hypothesize that if a turbulence/physics foundation model represents the cascade mechanism rather than instantaneous spatial statistics, then (a) the signed inter-scale energy flux Pi(k) is decodable from internal representations of a short trajectory beyond what single-snapshot statistics predict, (b) feeding the model a time-reversed trajectory (identical instantaneous statistics, inverted cascade direction) flips its internal flux signal and degrades its rollout as physics dictates, while a spatially-scrambled control matched on the spectrum does not, and (c) steering a recovered cascade-flux direction causally shifts small-scale energy generation. The forward-vs-time-reversed counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that field-statistics correlation cannot pass.
Related Work: Interpretability of physics/weather foundation models shows single physical QUANTITIES are encoded and steerable: 'Physics Steering' (2025) extracts steerable vorticity/diffusion/speed directions that transfer across systems; 'Uncovering Emergent Physics Representations Learned In-Context by LLMs' (2025) finds energy features whose ablation degrades forecasting; GraphCast SAE work recovers cyclones/atmospheric rivers. All recover a scalar quantity at a point/instant. Separately, a rich turbulence literature (Kolmogorov -5/3 spectrum; the coherent structure of the energy cascade, 2023; information-flux causality of inter-scale transfer, 2024; hidden scale invariance, 2023-2025) establishes the cascade as a directional, time-irreversible, scale-relational mechanism, and the emerging thermodynamics-of-turbulence view frames the cascade explicitly as an arrow of time. Crucially, no interpretability work tests whether a foundation model's INTERNAL representation encodes the directional, time-irreversible inter-scale energy flux Pi(k) that DEFINES turbulence, whether that flux representation is causally load-bearing, or uses a time-reversal counterfactual to separate cascade mechanism from instantaneous field statistics. Prior physics-interpretability answers 'is a quantity encoded'; the cascade asks 'is the directional flow of energy across scales, and its broken time-symmetry, represented'. Our directional-flux probe, forward-vs-time-reversed counterfactual, and causal flux steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, distinct from conservation-law or single-quantity tests.
Abstract: Turbulence is defined not by any single field value but by a directional, scale-relational mechanism: the Richardson-Kolmogorov energy cascade, in which kinetic energy is transferred on average from large to small scales at a flux Pi(k), a process that breaks time-reversal symmetry and constitutes a physical arrow of time. Foundation models for physics have been shown to encode individual quantities such as energy and vorticity, but whether they represent the cascade itself remains untested. This is decisive because the cascade cannot be read off a single snapshot: a velocity field and its time-reverse are statistically almost identical, yet their cascade directions are opposite. We probe pretrained multi-physics PDE surrogates (e.g., Poseidon, Multiple-Physics-Pretraining, DPOT) on isotropic-turbulence trajectories (JHTDB DNS), where the signed inter-scale flux Pi(k) is computable exactly. First, a flux-beyond-snapshot probe: is Pi(k) decodable from internal representations of a short trajectory beyond what single-frame spectral statistics allow? Second, and most decisively, a time-reversal counterfactual: we feed the model a forward trajectory versus its time-reverse (identical instantaneous statistics, inverted energy flux) and compare against a phase-scrambled control matched on the energy spectrum; a mechanistic representation must flip its internal flux signal and mis-forecast the reversed (unphysical, up-scale-cascading) trajectory, while responding little to the spectrum-matched scramble. Third, causal steering of a recovered cascade-flux direction should shift small-scale energy generation as physics predicts. Metrics quantify a flux-beyond-snapshot index, a forward-vs-reversed asymmetry, and a steering-selectivity ratio. Either outcome sharpens whether turbulence foundation models represent the mechanism that defines turbulence.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — signed inter-scale flux decodable beyond single-snapshot statistics): Tests clause (a): the signed inter-scale energy flux Pi(k) is decodable from internal representations of a short trajectory beyond what single-snapshot statistics predict. Data: Johns Hopkins Turbulence Database (JHTDB) forced isotropic turbulence (1024^3 field, ~5,000 stored time frames); sample 2,000 short trajectories of 10 consecutive frames each (1,200 train / 200 val / 600 test, split by non-overlapping time windows), plus a decaying-isotropic DNS set for cross-check — fewer than all frames because trajectories must be non-overlapping to avoid leakage. Per timestep and scale band compute ground-truth spectral flux Pi(k) via filtered subgrid energy transfer. Model: DPOT (Fourier-transformer physics FM, ~30M-parameter base variant) and Poseidon (~158M), frozen; only a ridge probe on the best layer, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: probe R^2 for signed Pi(k) from the trajectory representation vs a single-frame baseline (ridge on one frame's spectrum and structure-function statistics). Decisive metric (first): Flux-Beyond-Snapshot Index = R^2(signed Pi(k) | trajectory representation) − R^2(signed Pi(k) | single-frame statistics). Convincing: Index ≥ 0.15 with 95% CI lower bound above 0.05, and the recovered flux has the correct net-forward sign across the inertial range. Indecision band: Index in [−0.03, 0.05] — within probe noise; a result here means the model adds no directional information over an (essentially time-symmetric) snapshot and clause (a) fails. Negative result: Index ≤ −0.03 or in band — the representation is an instantaneous field statistic, blind to cascade direction.

Experiment 2 (H2 — forward vs time-reversed counterfactual): Tests clause (b): a time-reversed trajectory (identical instantaneous statistics, inverted cascade) flips the internal flux signal and degrades rollout, while a spectrum-matched scramble does not. Data: 600 test trajectories; for each build (forward), (exact time-reverse: reverse frame order and flip velocity sign), and (phase-scramble control: randomize spatial phases preserving E(k)). Model/probe as Experiment 1, seeds 0–4; read-outs are the Experiment-1 flux probe and one-step rollout error where the model forecasts. Systems compared: internal flux-sign response and rollout error across forward, reversed, and scrambled. Decisive metrics (first): (i) Flux-Sign Flip Rate = fraction of trajectories whose internal flux sign reverses under time reversal; (ii) Reversed/Forward Rollout Ratio. Convincing: Flip Rate ≥ 0.7 and Rollout Ratio ≥ 1.5, while the scramble produces a flip rate below 0.3 and a rollout ratio near 1 (effect is cascade-specific, not generic OOD). Indecision band: Flip Rate in [0.4, 0.6] or Rollout Ratio in [0.9, 1.2] — no clear directional asymmetry; clause (b) fails here. Negative result: symmetric response (Flip Rate ≈ 0.5, Rollout Ratio ≈ 1) — the model treats a physically forbidden reversed cascade like the real one.

Experiment 3 (H2 — flux magnitude dose-response): Tests the quantitative content of clause (b): the internal flux tracks the physically correct mean flux (equal to dissipation rate in the inertial range). Data: trajectories spanning a range of dissipation rates / Reynolds numbers drawn from JHTDB and DNS (300 trajectories across ~5 dissipation levels). Model/probe as above, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: internal flux read-out vs true mean Pi; shuffled labels as null. Decisive metric (first): Spearman rho and slope agreement between internal flux and true Pi. Convincing: rho ≥ 0.6, correct sign, slope within ±30% of 1.0. Indecision band: rho in [0.2, 0.4] — weak magnitude tracking; report as inconclusive on quantitative fidelity. Negative result: rho < 0.2, indistinguishable from shuffled — no dissipation-set flux magnitude represented.

Experiment 4 (H3 — causal cascade-flux steering): Tests clause (c): steering a recovered cascade-flux direction causally shifts small-scale energy generation. Data: 600 test trajectories; direction recovered as a supervised flux-probe direction and as a delta-representation between high-forward-flux and low/backward-flux states. Model/probe as above; add matched-norm perturbations along the flux direction at the best layer and roll out, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: flux direction vs matched-norm random directions vs an energy-magnitude direction. Decisive metric (first): Steering Selectivity = |change in small-scale (high-k) energy generation from flux-direction steering| / |change from random-direction steering|. Convincing: selectivity ≥ 3 with the physically consistent sign (increasing forward flux builds small-scale energy / sharpens the spectrum tail), and the energy-magnitude direction not reproducing the directional effect. Indecision band: selectivity in [0.7, 2.0] — no better than random; clause (c) fails here. Negative result: selectivity ≈ 1, indicating no dedicated causal cascade-flux direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The signed flux Pi(k) correlates with instantaneous spatial structure (strain/enstrophy configurations), making the flux-beyond-snapshot separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with single-snapshot residualization, the time-reversal counterfactual (which holds instantaneous statistics fixed and inverts only direction), and the spectrum-matched phase-scramble control that a cascade-specific effect would not respond to.

Feeding a time-reversed (unphysical) trajectory pushes the model off its training distribution, so the reversed-rollout error could reflect generic OOD failure rather than cascade sensitivity; we control this with the spectrum-matched scramble (also OOD but non-directional) and by testing the internal flux-sign flip on inputs, which is an intra-representation measure less confounded by output-space OOD.

Some physics FMs operate on fixed short input windows or specific resolutions that may limit access to multi-frame temporal information needed to see direction; we document each model's input protocol, use the maximal available window, and prioritize models that ingest trajectories.

Ground-truth Pi(k) depends on the filtering/decomposition choice (spectral vs physical-space filter); we use standard filtered subgrid transfer and report sensitivity to filter width and scale-band definition.

Linear probes recovering a flux direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/energy-magnitude-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions.

A negative result (models encode instantaneous field statistics but not the directional, time-irreversible cascade, responding symmetrically to time reversal) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting turbulence surrogates for long rollouts and extrapolation, though it may be perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether turbulence foundation models represent the energy cascade and its broken time-symmetry.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and public DNS/turbulence datasets (JHTDB), keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: contralateral_symmetry_probe
Title: Compared to the Other Side? Testing Whether Radiology Foundation Models Represent the Bilateral-Symmetry Comparison Mechanism, Not Just Local Texture
Short Hypothesis: A large, clinically dominant class of radiological findings is defined RELATIONALLY by bilateral asymmetry: the body is approximately bilaterally symmetric, so radiologists call a region abnormal when it DIFFERS from its contralateral counterpart (one whiter lung, one denser breast, one effusion-filled hemithorax), and the identical local texture appearing symmetrically on both sides is often a normal variant or systemic. We hypothesize that if radiology foundation models represent this contralateral-comparison mechanism rather than absolute local texture, then (a) a region's abnormality signal is decodable from internal representations beyond what its local patch texture alone predicts, (b) a symmetry counterfactual - implanting the same abnormal-looking texture bilaterally (symmetric, should suppress asymmetry-defined pathology) versus unilaterally (asymmetric, pathology) - shifts the internal finding signal accordingly, whereas a texture-only model responds identically, and (c) the effect causally depends on the contralateral region. The bilateral-vs-unilateral implant is an exact, mechanism-defining counterfactual that texture-based correlation and concept-alignment interpretability cannot provide.
Related Work: Radiology-imaging interpretability is dominated by (i) shortcut/spurious-feature detection and mitigation (Detecting Shortcuts in Chest X-Rays 2023; 'Shortcuts Causing Bias in Radiology AI' 2023; RoentMod counterfactual editing 2025; Reveal2Revise medical-AI-safety 2025; Weight-Space Correlation feature-utilization 2025), (ii) concept dissection and alignment (Mammo-CLIP Dissect 2025; Mammo-SAE 2025; expert-labeled CNN units 2018), and (iii) representation-quality/robustness critiques (ViT semantic-meaningfulness 2025; pathology representational-similarity 2025) and anatomy-aware SSL (AFiRe 2025, RayDINO 2024, EXACT 2026). All of these test whether features are spurious, whether units align with named concepts, or whether representations are robust - i.e. LOCAL, per-region annotation-matching or shortcut auditing. None tests whether the model internally performs the RELATIONAL contralateral (bilateral-symmetry) COMPARISON that formally defines a major class of radiological findings, whether that comparison is causally load-bearing, or uses a bilateral-vs-unilateral implant counterfactual to separate the symmetry mechanism from absolute texture. Because abnormal texture and abnormal asymmetry co-occur in real scans, correlation and concept-alignment cannot arbitrate this. Our relational-beyond-local probe, symmetric-vs-asymmetric implant counterfactual, and causal contralateral-ablation are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, moving beyond 'the model sees the opacity' to 'the model represents that this side differs from the other.'
Abstract: Radiologists diagnose a large fraction of findings not by absolute local appearance but by comparison: the body is approximately bilaterally symmetric, so a whiter lung, a denser breast, or a fluid-filled hemithorax is flagged because it differs from the opposite side, while the same texture appearing on both sides is often a normal variant. This relational bilateral-symmetry mechanism is exactly known and clinically central, making it an ideal probe for whether radiology foundation models learn mechanism or merely local texture. We test whether models such as RayDINO, a multi-anatomy X-ray encoder, and Mammo-CLIP internally represent the contralateral-comparison mechanism, using public chest X-ray (MIMIC-CXR, CheXpert) and mammography data with lateralized finding labels. First, a relational-beyond-local probe: is a region's abnormality decodable from internal representations beyond what its local patch texture alone predicts, and does the recovered signal track left-right difference? Second, and most decisively, a symmetry counterfactual: using anatomically realistic image editing we implant the same abnormal-looking texture either bilaterally (symmetric, which for asymmetry-defined findings should suppress the pathology signal) or unilaterally (asymmetric, pathology), and measure whether the internal finding signal responds to the asymmetry rather than the raw texture; a texture-only model responds identically to both. Third, causal contralateral ablation: masking or replacing the opposite side should shift the finding signal for a mechanism-representing model but not a local one. Metrics quantify a relational-beyond-local index, a bilateral-vs-unilateral causal asymmetry, and a contralateral-dependence ratio. Either outcome sharpens whether deployed radiology models diagnose for the right relational reason.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — abnormality decodable beyond local patch texture): Tests clause (a): a region's abnormality signal is decodable from internal representations beyond what its local patch texture alone predicts. Data: MIMIC-CXR (~377k chest radiographs) and CheXpert (~224k) for asymmetry-defined findings (pleural effusion, pneumothorax, unilateral consolidation, asymmetric opacity), plus CBIS-DDSM (~10k mammograms) for breast asymmetry/density; use 5,000 chest images (3,000 train / 500 val / 1,500 test, split by patient) with laterality-annotatable findings — fewer than the full sets because we require reliable laterality and near-symmetric anatomy. Model: RayDINO (chest X-ray ViT SSL encoder, ~300M parameters, per-patch tokens) and patch-level Mammo-CLIP, frozen; only a logistic probe on the best layer, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: pathology decoding from the region representation vs a strict local-texture baseline (probe seeing only the target patch, no contralateral context), representation residualized against the local-patch features; absolute-texture-defined findings (e.g., calcifications) serve as a built-in double-dissociation control expected to show near-zero relational signal. Decisive metric (first): Relational-Beyond-Local Index = balanced accuracy(pathology | region representation) − balanced accuracy(pathology | local patch). Convincing: Index ≥ 0.10 (95% CI lower bound above 0.03) for asymmetry-defined findings and ≤ 0.03 for texture-defined controls. Indecision band: Index in [−0.02, 0.03] — within probe noise; a result here means no contralateral information beyond local texture and clause (a) fails. Negative result: Index ≤ −0.02 or in band for asymmetry-defined findings — the model reads absolute local texture, not the bilateral comparison.

Experiment 2 (H2 — bilateral vs unilateral implant counterfactual): Tests clause (b): implanting the same abnormal-looking texture bilaterally (symmetric, should suppress asymmetry-defined pathology) versus unilaterally (asymmetric, pathology) shifts the internal finding signal, whereas a texture-only model responds identically. Data: 1,000 near-symmetric test images (lung fields/breast parenchyma) from Experiment 1; using anatomically realistic editing (RoentMod-style insertion for chest X-ray; controlled contralateral copy for symmetric implants) build matched pairs — (unilateral) implant on one side; (bilateral) the same texture on both sides — matched on total implanted texture and edit realism. Model/probe as Experiment 1, seeds 0–4; read-out is the pathology probe and classification head. Systems compared: |finding-signal change| under unilateral vs under bilateral implant, per finding type. Decisive metric (first): Bilateral-vs-Unilateral Causal Asymmetry = median(|Δsignal unilateral|) / median(|Δsignal bilateral|). Convincing: asymmetry ≥ 3 (unilateral raises the finding, bilateral suppresses it). Indecision band: asymmetry in [0.7, 2.0] — both edits raise the signal comparably; clause (b) fails here (texture-counting reading). Negative result: asymmetry ≈ 1, i.e., the model counts implanted texture regardless of symmetry, not the contralateral comparison.

Experiment 3 (H3 — contralateral-region ablation): Tests clause (c): the finding effect causally depends on the contralateral region. Data: 1,000 test images with a genuine unilateral finding; mask/replace the healthy contralateral region with a matched normal patch and measure the change in the finding signal on the untouched pathological side. Model/probe as above, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: contralateral ablation vs a matched-size, matched-distance ipsilateral non-diagnostic ablation (control). Decisive metric (first): Contralateral-Dependence Ratio = |Δfinding signal under contralateral ablation| / |Δfinding signal under ipsilateral-control ablation|. Convincing: ratio ≥ 3 — removing the reference side materially changes the judgment while an equal ipsilateral removal does not. Indecision band: ratio in [0.7, 2.0] — the contralateral side is no more load-bearing than an ipsilateral region; clause (c) fails here. Negative result: ratio ≈ 1, i.e., the judgment is unaffected by removing the reference side — a local-texture model.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Abnormal texture and abnormal asymmetry co-occur in real scans, making the relational-beyond-local separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with local-patch residualization, the bilateral-vs-unilateral implant counterfactual (which holds implanted texture fixed and varies only symmetry), the absolute-texture-defined-finding double-dissociation control, and matched ipsilateral-ablation controls.

The implant and ablation counterfactuals are synthetic edits; anatomically unrealistic implants (especially bilateral copies) could push images off the model's data distribution, confounding the effect with generic OOD failure. We mitigate with validated realistic editing (RoentMod-style for chest X-ray, careful contralateral mirroring/copy for controlled texture), report realism/artifact diagnostics, and compare unilateral vs bilateral edits of matched realism so any OOD effect is shared.

Bilateral symmetry is only approximate (cardiac silhouette, gastric bubble, handedness), so a truly symmetric implant is not perfectly normal; we restrict primary tests to anatomically near-symmetric regions (lung fields, breast parenchyma) and report sensitivity, and we use radiologist-adjudicated laterality labels where available.

Some findings ARE defined by absolute texture (calcifications, specific nodules) rather than asymmetry; we explicitly separate asymmetry-defined from texture-defined findings and use the latter as a negative control rather than expecting a relational signal.

Foundation models that pool to a single global embedding limit per-region/contralateral analysis; we prioritize models exposing per-patch spatial representations (RayDINO, ViT patch tokens, patch-level Mammo-CLIP) and report pooling caveats.

Linear probes recovering an asymmetry direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering, contralateral ablation, and random/texture-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions.

A negative result (models diagnose from absolute local texture and respond identically to symmetric vs asymmetric implants, failing the contralateral-ablation test) is scientifically decisive and directly safety-relevant - it would warn that deployed radiology models miss the relational comparison radiologists rely on, risking false positives on symmetric normal variants and false negatives when contralateral context matters; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether radiology foundation models represent the bilateral-symmetry comparison mechanism.

All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and public radiology datasets (MIMIC-CXR, CheXpert, CBIS-DDSM/VinDr-Mammo) with validated counterfactual editing tools, keeping compute at academic scale.
