Name: hill_cooperativity_shape_probe
Title: Steepness Is Not Potency: Testing Whether Drug-Response Foundation Models Represent the Cooperative Hill Dose-Response Mechanism, Not Just Where the Curve Sits
Short Hypothesis: The dose-response of a drug is governed by an exactly-known relational mechanism, the Hill equation: response is a sigmoidal function of dose whose LOCATION is set by potency (IC50/EC50) but whose STEEPNESS is set by the Hill coefficient nH, which encodes cooperativity/multi-site binding (nH=1 is non-cooperative Michaelis-Menten-like; nH>1 is positively cooperative, ultrasensitive; nH<1 is negatively cooperative). Potency and cooperativity are physically independent axes: two drugs with identical IC50 can have completely different curve shapes and therefore different therapeutic windows and safety margins. We hypothesize that if drug-response foundation models represent this mechanism rather than a scalar potency proxy, then (a) the Hill coefficient (curve shape/cooperativity) is decodable from internal representations along an axis distinct from potency, (b) a shape-vs-potency counterfactual - changing nH at fixed IC50 versus changing IC50 at fixed nH - moves the two internal signals separately, and (c) steering a recovered 'cooperativity' direction causally reshapes predicted dose-response steepness without shifting its location. The shape-holding counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that dose-response prediction accuracy and potency correlation cannot provide.
Related Work: The Hill equation is the century-old, exactly-known model of dose-response and cooperativity (A hundred years of the Hill equation 2013; Hill coefficients, dose-response curves and allosteric mechanisms 2009; multiphasic dose-response fitting 2015 shows ~28% of curves need beyond-Hill shape), and it explicitly separates potency (IC50) from cooperativity (nH). Drug-response and pharmacology ML - DrugCell, cell-viability foundation models, and molecular-property FMs - predict dose-response or IC50 from drug/cell features, and interpretability of chemistry/toxicity models (Interpreting NN Toxicity Prediction by Extracting Learned Chemical Features 2024; SAE studies on chemistry FMs; MoleX) recovers substructure/functional-group features validated against POINTWISE, potency-like annotations. Physics/scientific-model interpretability (From Neurons to Neutrons 2024; Physics Steering 2025) recovers and steers single scalar quantities, and 'What Has a Foundation Model Found?' (2025) shows models often learn task-specific heuristics rather than the underlying world model. Crucially, no interpretability work tests whether a drug-response FM internally represents the RELATIONAL Hill mechanism - specifically that curve STEEPNESS/cooperativity (nH) is a distinct axis from potency (IC50) - whether that shape representation is causally load-bearing, or uses a shape-holding counterfactual to separate cooperativity from potency. Because nH and IC50 are entangled and both correlate with overall efficacy in screening data, correlation-based benchmarks and pointwise-feature interpretability cannot arbitrate this. Our cooperativity-beyond-potency probe, shape-vs-potency counterfactual, and causal steepness steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, and they land in a safety-critical setting because curve steepness (Hill coefficient) directly governs therapeutic window and toxicity margins.
Abstract: A drug's dose-response curve is described by an exactly-known relational mechanism, the Hill equation: response rises sigmoidally with dose, its location fixed by potency (IC50) and its steepness fixed by the Hill coefficient, which encodes cooperativity and multi-site binding. These are physically independent axes - two drugs with identical potency can have radically different curve shapes, and the shape (steepness) determines the therapeutic window and safety margin. This makes the Hill equation an ideal, mechanism-defining probe for whether drug-response foundation models learn the underlying pharmacological mechanism or merely a scalar potency proxy. We probe pretrained drug-response and molecular-property foundation models on large cell-viability screens (GDSC, PRISM, NCI-60) whose curves are fitted to Hill parameters. First, a cooperativity-beyond-potency probe: is the Hill coefficient (curve steepness) decodable from internal representations along an axis distinct from potency? Second, and most decisively, a shape-vs-potency counterfactual: using controlled synthetic and matched real curves we change the Hill coefficient at fixed IC50 (reshape without relocating) versus change IC50 at fixed Hill (relocate without reshaping), and test whether the two internal signals move independently - a mechanistic representation separates them, a potency-proxy representation collapses shape onto location. Third, causal steepness steering: perturbing a recovered cooperativity direction should reshape the predicted curve's steepness without shifting its midpoint. Metrics quantify a cooperativity-beyond-potency index, a shape-potency disentanglement ratio, and a Hill-fidelity dose-response test. Either outcome sharpens whether deployed drug-response models represent the curve-shape mechanism that governs drug safety.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Hill coefficient decodable along an axis distinct from potency): Tests clause (a): the Hill coefficient nH (curve shape/cooperativity) is decodable from internal representations along an axis distinct from potency. Data: fitted dose-response curves from GDSC1/2, PRISM Repurposing, and NCI-60 (together several hundred thousand drug–cell curves with fitted IC50, nH, Emax and raw points); use 30,000 well-sampled high-confidence curves (18k train / 3k val / 9k test, split by drug so no drug crosses splits) plus synthetic Hill curves for exact control — fewer than the full screens because we require ≥6 dose points and a confident single-Hill fit. Model: a transformer dose-response predictor trained on GDSC (DrugCell-style) and ChemBERTa-2 (~46M parameters) on the drug SMILES, frozen; only ridge probes on the best layer, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: probe R^2 for nH from the representation vs a baseline predicting nH from IC50 and Emax and simple raw-curve features, representation residualized against potency; also the angle between the recovered potency and cooperativity probe directions. Decisive metric (first): Cooperativity-Beyond-Potency Index = R^2(nH | representation) − R^2(nH | potency+Emax features). Convincing: Index ≥ 0.15 (95% CI lower bound above 0.05) and potency–cooperativity axis angle ≥ 60 degrees (near-orthogonal). Indecision band: Index in [−0.03, 0.05] or axis angle in [30, 45] degrees — shape barely separable from potency; clause (a) fails or is inconclusive here. Negative result: Index ≤ −0.03 or angle < 30 degrees — shape collapses onto potency, a scalar-potency-proxy representation.

Experiment 2 (H2 — shape-vs-potency double-dissociation counterfactual): Tests clause (b): changing nH at fixed IC50 versus changing IC50 at fixed nH moves the two internal signals separately. Data: matched curve pairs — (reshape) change nH holding IC50 fixed; (relocate) change IC50 holding nH fixed — built from 4,000 synthetic Hill curves (exact control) plus real drug–cell pairs from the Experiment-1 test set selected to differ in one parameter at a time. Model/probe as Experiment 1, seeds 0–4; read-outs are the potency and cooperativity probes. Systems compared: movement of each internal signal under each edit. Decisive metrics (first): Reshape Ratio = |Δcooperativity signal| / |Δpotency signal| under the reshape edit; Relocate Ratio = |Δpotency signal| / |Δcooperativity signal| under the relocate edit. Convincing: both ratios ≥ 3 (each edit moves its own axis — a double dissociation). Indecision band: either ratio in [0.7, 2.0] — the two axes are not cleanly separable; clause (b) fails or is inconclusive here. Negative result: ratios ≈ 1 or shape moving whenever location moves — shape is collapsed onto location.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Hill-shape fidelity / ultrasensitivity): Tests the quantitative content of clause (b): the model's predicted curve follows a Hill sigmoid with the correct steepness. Data: the same 9,000 test curves; sweep dose finely and fit the model's predicted response to a Hill equation. Model/probe as above, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: model-implied nH vs true nH; shuffled-nH labels as null; a check that nH>1 curves come out sharper than nH=1. Decisive metric (first): Spearman rho and slope between model-implied nH and true nH. Convincing: rho ≥ 0.6, correct sign, slope within ±30% of 1.0, and ultrasensitive (nH>1) curves reproduced as sharper. Indecision band: rho in [0.2, 0.4] — weak steepness tracking; inconclusive on quantitative fidelity. Negative result: rho < 0.2 or a single canonical steepness for all drugs — no cooperativity mechanism represented.

Experiment 4 (H3 — causal cooperativity steering): Tests clause (c): steering a recovered 'cooperativity' direction reshapes predicted steepness without shifting its location. Data: 9,000 test curves; direction recovered as a supervised nH-probe direction, an SAE feature separating steep from shallow curves, and a delta-representation between high-nH and low-nH cases at matched IC50. Model/probe as above; add matched-norm perturbations along the cooperativity direction at the best layer and re-read the predicted curve, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: cooperativity direction vs a matched potency direction vs matched-norm random directions. Decisive metrics (first): Steering Selectivity = |steepness change from cooperativity steering| / |steepness change from random steering|; Cross-talk = |IC50 shift from cooperativity steering| in log-dose units. Convincing: selectivity ≥ 3 with cross-talk ≤ 0.1 log-dose units (steepness changes, midpoint essentially fixed), while the potency direction shifts IC50 without changing steepness. Indecision band: selectivity in [0.7, 2.0] or cross-talk in (0.1, 0.3] log-dose — steering is non-selective or entangled; clause (c) fails or is inconclusive here. Negative result: selectivity ≈ 1 — no dedicated causal cooperativity direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: nH and IC50 are entangled in screening data (both correlate with overall efficacy and with drug/target class), making the cooperativity-beyond-potency separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with potency-residualization, the shape-vs-potency double-dissociation counterfactual (which holds one parameter fixed while varying the other), and synthetic Hill curves giving exact independent control.

Fitted Hill coefficients from screening data are noisy, especially for curves with few doses or shallow responses, adding label noise to nH; we restrict primary analyses to well-sampled, high-confidence fits, use synthetic curves for the decisive counterfactual, and report sensitivity to fit-quality thresholds; multiphasic curves are analyzed separately.

Some drug-response FMs take only drug and cell-line identity (not a curve) as input and output a single scalar (e.g., IC50), so 'representing curve shape' may be architecturally out of scope for them; we prioritize models that predict full dose-response curves or ingest dose, clearly report per-model scope, and treat scalar-only models as an informative lower bracket that by construction cannot represent nH.

Operationalizing the shape/potency edits depends on the model's input format (curve-in vs identity-in); for identity-in models we test whether the internal representation nonetheless encodes nH as a distinct axis and use synthetic-curve models where a curve can be manipulated directly, reporting the caveat.

Linear probes recovering a cooperativity direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering, cross-talk controls, and random-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions - we use both probe directions and SAE features.

A negative result (models encode a scalar potency proxy and collapse curve shape onto location, failing the shape-vs-potency counterfactual) is scientifically decisive and directly safety-relevant - it would warn that deployed drug-response models miss the cooperativity/steepness information that determines therapeutic window and toxicity margin, especially for ultrasensitive or multiphasic drugs; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether drug-response foundation models represent the Hill cooperative dose-response mechanism.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes/SAEs and public dose-response datasets (GDSC, PRISM, NCI-60), keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: amoc_density_buoyancy_probe
Title: Density, Not Just Temperature: Testing Whether Ocean Foundation Models Represent the Buoyancy-Driven AMOC Mechanism via a Temperature-Salinity Compensation Counterfactual
Short Hypothesis: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is driven by an exactly-known relational mechanism: overturning strength scales (via thermal wind) with the meridional DENSITY gradient set at high latitudes by surface buoyancy loss, where density depends nonlinearly on BOTH temperature and salinity through the equation of state — warming and freshening both REDUCE density and both weaken overturning. This means the same sea-surface temperature (SST) field can imply strengthening or weakening AMOC depending on salinity. We hypothesize that if ocean/climate foundation models represent the buoyancy mechanism rather than SST statistics, then (a) the AMOC-relevant density gradient is decodable from internal representations beyond what temperature alone predicts, (b) a temperature-salinity compensation counterfactual that changes T and S together so surface DENSITY is unchanged shifts the internal overturning signal little, whereas a matched edit that changes density (equal T change, no compensating S change) shifts it strongly, and (c) steering a recovered density-gradient direction causally shifts predicted overturning. The density-compensated-vs-uncompensated counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that SST-based correlation cannot pass.
Related Work: Interpretability of Earth-system foundation models has surged: SAE studies on GraphCast (2025) recover interpretable features (tropical cyclones, atmospheric rivers, sea-ice) and steer them; GraphDOP work (2025) shows unified observation-driven world-model representations and applies data-assimilation diagnostics (FSOI); an ocean-atmosphere emulator-error study (2026) correlates GraphCast forecast errors with SST to infer implicit ocean information. All of these recover single features or global input-output error correlations — none tests whether a model's internal representation encodes the RELATIONAL, density-driven buoyancy mechanism that governs the AMOC, nor uses a temperature-salinity compensation counterfactual to separate density from temperature. Physical oceanography establishes the mechanism precisely: AMOC strength scales with the meridional density gradient via near-geostrophic/thermal-wind balance and is controlled by high-latitude surface buoyancy loss and the nonlinear equation of state (AMOC reviews 2015/2019; 'What Causes the AMOC to Weaken in CMIP5?' 2019 uses thermal wind to attribute weakening to density changes; 'Controls on AMOC strength' 2024 links buoyancy forcing and stratification to overturning). Because SST and density are correlated in ordinary ocean data, correlation-based benchmarks and SST-error diagnostics cannot arbitrate whether a model uses temperature statistics or the density mechanism. Our density-beyond-temperature probe, TS-compensation counterfactual, and causal density-gradient steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, transferred into the safety-critical setting of AMOC tipping-point prediction.
Abstract: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a climate tipping element, and machine-learning ocean/Earth-system foundation models are increasingly used to emulate and forecast ocean state. AMOC dynamics are governed by an exactly-known relational mechanism: overturning strength scales with the meridional density gradient, which is set at high latitudes by surface buoyancy loss, and density depends nonlinearly on both temperature and salinity through the equation of state. Crucially, warming and freshening both reduce density and both weaken overturning, so the same sea-surface-temperature field can accompany strengthening or weakening AMOC depending on salinity. This makes the AMOC an ideal, mechanism-defining testbed for whether ocean foundation models learn the buoyancy mechanism or merely temperature statistics. We probe pretrained ocean/climate foundation models (and observation-driven Earth-system emulators exposing internal states) on reanalysis data (ORAS5/GLORYS, plus CMIP output) where temperature, salinity, density, and the AMOC streamfunction are known. First, a density-beyond-temperature probe: is the AMOC-relevant meridional density gradient decodable from internal representations beyond what temperature alone predicts, along an axis distinct from SST? Second, and most decisively, a temperature-salinity compensation counterfactual: we perturb surface T and S together so that density is unchanged (density-compensated) versus perturbing T without compensating S (density-changing) with matched temperature magnitude; a mechanistic representation must move its overturning signal for the density-changing edit but not the compensated one, while a temperature-statistics model responds to both equally. Third, causal density-gradient steering. Metrics quantify a density-beyond-temperature index, a compensated-vs-uncompensated causal asymmetry, and a buoyancy dose-response test. Either outcome sharpens whether deployed ocean models represent the mechanism behind a major climate tipping point.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — density gradient decodable beyond temperature): Tests clause (a): the AMOC-relevant meridional density gradient (and AMOC index) is decodable from internal representations beyond what temperature alone predicts. Data: ORAS5 and GLORYS12 ocean reanalyses (3D temperature, salinity, potential density; monthly fields ~1958–present) and a set of CMIP6 members spanning AMOC strengths; use 480 monthly North Atlantic snapshots per product (split by decade into train/val/test so no year crosses splits) with ground-truth density from the equation of state, the meridional density gradient, and an AMOC index (streamfunction max at 26N) — fewer than the full archive because we focus on the subpolar/deep-water-formation region where salinity modulates density. Model: a public ocean emulator with accessible internal states where available; as the primary testbed, a modest academic-scale multi-variable ocean surrogate (~10M-parameter transformer) pretrained on reanalysis, frozen, with ridge probes on the best layer, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: probe R^2 for density gradient (and AMOC index) from the representation vs a temperature-only baseline, representation residualized against temperature; plus the angle between recovered temperature and density directions. Decisive metric (first): Density-Beyond-Temperature Index = R^2(density gradient | representation) − R^2(density gradient | temperature). Convincing: Index ≥ 0.15 (95% CI lower bound above 0.05) and temperature–density axis angle ≥ 60 degrees. Indecision band: Index in [−0.03, 0.05] or angle in [30, 45] degrees — density barely separable from temperature; clause (a) fails or is inconclusive here. Negative result: Index ≤ −0.03 or angle < 30 degrees — the model encodes temperature statistics and ignores the salinity contribution to density.

Experiment 2 (H2 — temperature–salinity compensation counterfactual): Tests clause (b): a T–S edit that leaves surface density unchanged shifts the internal overturning signal little, whereas an equal T change with no compensating S change shifts it strongly. Data: 500 subpolar North Atlantic test snapshots; for each build (compensated) change surface T by delta_T and S by the delta_S that leaves potential density unchanged via the equation-of-state expansion coefficients; (uncompensated) the same delta_T with no S change (density changes). Density (un)changed is verified by the equation of state before feeding the model. Model/probe as Experiment 1, seeds 0–4; read-out is the density-gradient/AMOC probe (and forecast AMOC-relevant fields where the emulator rolls out). Systems compared: |overturning-signal change| under uncompensated vs compensated edits, as a function of delta_T. Decisive metric (first): Compensated-vs-Uncompensated Causal Asymmetry = median(|Δsignal uncompensated|) / median(|Δsignal compensated|). Convincing: asymmetry ≥ 3. Indecision band: asymmetry in [0.7, 2.0] — the model responds to temperature regardless of density compensation; clause (b) fails here. Negative result: asymmetry ≈ 1, i.e., a temperature-statistics reading blind to whether salinity compensates the buoyancy change.

Experiment 3 (H2 — buoyancy dose-response with correct sign): Tests the quantitative content of clause (b): the internal AMOC signal responds monotonically and with the physically correct sign to density-changing buoyancy forcing. Data: the same 500 snapshots; sweep density-changing perturbations across a range — both freshwater-hosing-like (salinity) and warming-like (temperature) — that alter high-latitude density. Model/probe as above, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: induced AMOC-signal change vs the thermal-wind prediction (increasing high-latitude density strengthens overturning; decreasing it weakens overturning); shuffled-perturbation labels as null. Decisive metric (first): Spearman rho and sign agreement between induced AMOC change and predicted change, computed separately for salinity- and temperature-driven perturbations. Convincing: rho ≥ 0.6 with correct sign for BOTH perturbation types (the model integrates T and S into density, not just T). Indecision band: rho in [0.2, 0.4], or correct sign for temperature but not salinity — partial, temperature-leaning response; inconclusive on (b). Negative result: rho < 0.2 or wrong sign — no density-driven buoyancy law represented.

Experiment 4 (H3 — causal density-gradient steering): Tests clause (c): steering a recovered density-gradient direction causally shifts predicted overturning. Data: 500 test snapshots; direction recovered as a supervised density-gradient probe direction and a delta-representation between high- and low-gradient states. Model/probe as above; add matched-norm perturbations along the density direction at the best layer and read the AMOC output, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: density-gradient direction vs matched-norm random directions vs a pure SST direction. Decisive metrics (first): Steering Selectivity = |ΔAMOC from density-direction steering| / |ΔAMOC from random-direction steering|; Cross-talk with the SST direction. Convincing: selectivity ≥ 3 with the buoyancy-consistent sign and the SST direction not reproducing it. Indecision band: selectivity in [0.7, 2.0] — no better than random; clause (c) fails here. Negative result: selectivity ≈ 1 — no dedicated causal density-gradient direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Temperature and density are strongly correlated in ocean data (temperature dominates density variance in many regions), making the density-beyond-temperature separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with temperature-residualization, the TS-compensation counterfactual (which holds density fixed while varying temperature), the buoyancy dose-response test that a temperature-only model cannot reproduce with correct sign in salinity-dominated regimes, and by focusing decisive tests on the subpolar North Atlantic where salinity strongly modulates density.

The compensation counterfactual is a synthetic surface edit; unrealistic T-S combinations may push inputs off the model's data distribution, confounding the density-changing response with generic out-of-distribution failure. We mitigate with small physically-plausible perturbations, verify density is (un)changed via the equation of state before feeding to the model, report OOD diagnostics, and compare compensated vs uncompensated edits of matched temperature magnitude so any OOD effect is shared.

Many ocean/Earth-system foundation models are proprietary or lack accessible internal states; we prioritize models with public weights and usable representations and, as a fallback, pretrain a modest multi-variable ocean surrogate on reanalysis (academic-scale) to serve as the primary testbed, reporting this scope clearly.

The AMOC streamfunction is a deep, integrated quantity while foundation models may emphasize surface fields; the internal 'overturning signal' may be weak or only surface-proxied. We probe both the density gradient (a more directly represented quantity) and any AMOC-index readout, and treat the density-gradient result as the primary mechanism evidence.

Reanalysis salinity (especially subpolar/estuarine) has known biases, adding label noise; we use consensus regions, multiple reanalysis products, and CMIP output for controlled T-S variation, reporting sensitivity to product choice.

Linear probes recovering a density direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/SST-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions — we use both probe directions and delta-representations.

A negative result (models encode temperature statistics but not the density-driven buoyancy mechanism, failing the compensation counterfactual) is scientifically decisive and directly safety-relevant — it would warn against trusting ocean foundation models for AMOC weakening/tipping-point prediction, precisely where freshening breaks the temperature-density correlation; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether ocean foundation models represent the buoyancy-driven AMOC mechanism.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models (or one modest academic-scale surrogate) plus small probes and public reanalysis/CMIP data, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: pseudoscalar_chirality_probe
Title: Sign Flips Under a Mirror: Testing Whether Molecular Foundation Models Represent Chirality as a Pseudoscalar Mechanism, Not Just Enantiomer Labels
Short Hypothesis: Chirality is an exactly-known geometric mechanism with a precise mathematical signature: it is a PSEUDOSCALAR quantity - invariant to rotation and translation but flipping SIGN under mirror reflection (parity) - and it is what distinguishes enantiomers, which are identical in every scalar/achiral property yet can differ drastically in binding and toxicity. We hypothesize that if a molecular foundation model represents the chirality MECHANISM rather than a memorized R/S label or surface substructure, then (a) a recoverable internal 'chirality' direction behaves as a pseudoscalar - unchanged under 3D rotation but flipping sign under mirror reflection of the geometry, (b) a mirror-reflection counterfactual that flips ONLY handedness (holding all scalar invariants - distances, angles, connectivity - fixed) flips the internal chirality signal and the model's enantioselective property prediction, whereas an achiral-preserving perturbation of matched magnitude does not, and (c) steering this pseudoscalar direction causally swaps predicted enantiomer-dependent properties. The mirror-flip counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that R/S classification accuracy and substructure correlation cannot provide.
Related Work: Two lines bracket the gap. (1) Chirality-aware architectures - ChiENN (2023), tetrahedral-chirality message passing (2020), MolKGNN (2023), ChIRo (2021), ChiDeK (2026), Chi-Geometry benchmark (2025) - are motivated by the proof that standard/E(3)-invariant GNNs CANNOT represent chirality ('E(3)-equivariant models cannot learn chirality', 2024), and they BUILD handedness in by construction, judged by R/S accuracy or enantioselective-property RMSE. (2) FM-representation work hints chirality is decodable: Rem3Di (2026) constructs explicit pseudoscalar features from atomistic-FM latents to distinguish enantiomers, SMILES-heteroencoder latent arithmetic (2025) builds chirality descriptors by subtracting enantiomer latents, and the reaction-analogy GNN work (2025) shows linear structure in atom embeddings. Crucially, all of these either engineer chirality by construction, or measure downstream enantiomer-discrimination accuracy - none tests whether a general molecular foundation model's INTERNAL representation already encodes chirality with its defining pseudoscalar (parity-odd, rotation-even) symmetry, whether that signal is causally load-bearing for enantioselective predictions, or uses a mirror-reflection counterfactual to separate the mechanism from a memorized R/S label. Because R/S labels, chiral substructure, and true handedness are entangled in training data, classification accuracy cannot arbitrate this. Our pseudoscalar-symmetry probe, mirror-flip counterfactual, and causal chirality steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution.
Abstract: Chirality - molecular handedness - is one of chemistry's most consequential and exactly-known geometric mechanisms: enantiomers are mirror images identical in every achiral property yet can differ dramatically in biological activity and toxicity (the thalidomide tragedy being the canonical example). Its mathematical signature is precise: chirality is a pseudoscalar, invariant under rotation and translation but flipping sign under mirror reflection. This makes it an ideal, unambiguous probe for whether molecular foundation models learn geometric mechanism or surface statistics - especially since a theorem shows standard E(3)-invariant models cannot represent it at all. We probe pretrained 3D atomistic and molecular foundation models (e.g., atomistic MLIP backbones such as MACE, Uni-Mol, and chirality-capable encoders) plus SMILES/graph chemical FMs, asking three mechanism-defining questions. First, a pseudoscalar-symmetry probe: is a recoverable internal chirality direction invariant under 3D rotation yet sign-flipping under mirror reflection, as physics dictates? Second, and most decisively, a mirror-reflection counterfactual: we reflect a molecule's geometry to flip ONLY handedness while exactly preserving all scalar invariants, and test whether the internal chirality signal and the model's enantioselective property prediction flip, whereas an achiral perturbation of matched magnitude does not. Third, causal steering along the pseudoscalar direction should swap enantiomer-dependent predictions. Metrics quantify a pseudoscalar-fidelity index, a mirror-flip-vs-achiral causal asymmetry, and an enantioselective prediction-swap rate. Either outcome sharpens whether molecular foundation models - increasingly used in drug design where the wrong enantiomer can be toxic - represent the handedness mechanism or are blind to it.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — chirality direction behaves as a pseudoscalar): Tests clause (a): a recoverable internal 'chirality' direction is unchanged under 3D rotation but flips sign under mirror reflection. Data: enantiomer pairs with ground-truth handedness — the Chi-Geometry synthetic benchmark (clean isolation of a single stereocenter) plus real drug-like R/S pairs; use 2,000 molecules (1,200 train / 300 val / 500 test, split by scaffold), with paired mirror-image 3D conformers generated for each — fewer than all available because we require a single well-defined chiral element. Model: Uni-Mol (3D graph, ~48M parameters, stereochemistry-aware) and ChemBERTa-2 (~46M parameters, ingests @/@@ stereo tags), frozen; a supervised probe separating R from S (and a delta-representation between a molecule and its mirror image) recovers the candidate direction, seeds 0–4; MACE-MP-0 (E(3)-invariant, provably chirality-blind) is a built-in negative control expected to yield a definitional null. Systems compared: the chirality signal under (i) many random 3D rotations and (ii) mirror reflection. Decisive metric (first): Pseudoscalar-Fidelity Index combining rotation invariance (1 − normalized variance of the signal under rotation) and mirror sign-flip consistency (fraction of test molecules whose signal reverses sign under reflection). Convincing: rotation invariance ≥ 0.9 AND sign-flip consistency ≥ 0.9, with the E(3)-invariant control showing no decodable handedness. Indecision band: sign-flip consistency in [0.4, 0.6] (chance-like) or rotation invariance in [0.5, 0.8] — no consistent parity-odd, rotation-even behavior; clause (a) fails or is inconclusive here. Negative result: sign-flip consistency ≈ 0.5 or rotation invariance < 0.5 — the direction is not a pseudoscalar (a label/statistics reading).

Experiment 2 (H2 — mirror-reflection vs achiral-perturbation counterfactual): Tests clause (b): flipping only handedness (holding all scalar invariants fixed) flips the internal chirality signal and the enantioselective property prediction, whereas an achiral-preserving perturbation of matched magnitude does not. Data: 500 chiral test molecules; each yields a matched pair — (mirror-flip) reflect the 3D geometry (for SMILES/graph models flip the @/@@ tag), holding distances, angles, connectivity, and formula fixed; (achiral control) a matched-RMSD conformational/isometric perturbation that does not change handedness — plus a double-dissociation control on achiral molecules (no stereocenter) expected to show no swap. Model/probe as Experiment 1, seeds 0–4; read-outs are the chirality probe and an enantioselective property head (predicted optical-rotation sign, chiral-column elution order, or enantiosensitive docking score). Systems compared: |signal/prediction change| under mirror-flip vs under achiral perturbation. Decisive metric (first): Mirror-Flip-vs-Achiral Causal Asymmetry = median(|Δ mirror-flip|) / median(|Δ achiral|). Convincing: asymmetry ≥ 3 and ≥ 80% of mirror-flips produce the physically correct sign-reversal/order-swap in the enantioselective read-out, with the achiral-molecule control showing none. Indecision band: asymmetry in [0.7, 2.0] — handedness flip is not privileged over an achiral perturbation; clause (b) fails here. Negative result: asymmetry ≈ 1 — the model responds to geometric change, not to the parity flip that defines enantiomers.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal pseudoscalar steering): Tests clause (c): steering the pseudoscalar direction causally swaps predicted enantiomer-dependent properties. Data: the same 500 chiral test molecules; steer the recovered chirality direction with matched magnitude and both signs. Model/probe as above, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: chirality direction vs matched-norm random directions vs an achiral-feature direction. Decisive metrics (first): Enantioselective Prediction-Swap Rate under chirality steering, and Steering Selectivity = |effect of chirality direction| / |effect of random direction|. Convincing: swap rate ≥ 0.7 and selectivity ≥ 3, with random and achiral directions not producing swaps. Indecision band: selectivity in [0.7, 2.0] or swap rate in [0.4, 0.6] — steering is non-selective; clause (c) fails or is inconclusive here. Negative result: selectivity ≈ 1 or swap rate ≈ 0.5 — no causal handle that swaps enantioselective predictions.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Many 3D atomistic FMs are E(3)-invariant by construction and therefore provably cannot represent chirality; for these the pseudoscalar probe returns a definitional null, so the rich mechanism tests apply mainly to chirality-capable models (Rem3Di-style pseudoscalar-feature backbones, Uni-Mol with stereochemistry, stereo-aware SMILES/graph FMs). We report the invariant-model null as a decisive, separately-stated positive control and prioritize chirality-capable models for the mechanism tests.

SMILES/graph models encode chirality via discrete stereo-tags (@/@@) rather than continuous geometry, so 'mirror reflection' is operationalized as a tag flip; this tests whether the model propagates a handedness label to enantioselective predictions (still mechanism-relevant) but is a slightly different claim than geometric pseudoscalar behavior. We run both the 3D-geometry reflection (for 3D models) and the tag-flip (for SMILES models) and clearly distinguish the two claims.

R/S labels, chiral substructure, and true handedness are entangled, making the mechanism-beyond-label separation demanding; we mitigate with the mirror-flip counterfactual (which holds all scalar invariants and the substructure fixed while flipping only handedness), the achiral-molecule double-dissociation control, and the pseudoscalar-symmetry test that a label-lookup cannot pass under 3D rotations.

Enantioselective ground-truth data (optical rotation, ECD sign, chiral elution order, enantiosensitive docking) is limited and noisy; we use curated benchmarks (chiral-chromatography datasets, ECD/OR sets, Chi-Geometry) and report sensitivity to data confidence, focusing decisive tests on molecules with a single well-defined chiral element.

Reflecting a 3D geometry can push conformers off the model's data distribution; but the enantiomer is itself a valid physical molecule, so the reflected geometry is in-distribution by construction - we nonetheless verify conformer validity and match the achiral control perturbation on RMSD so any residual OOD effect is shared.

Linear probes recovering a chirality direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering, the mirror-flip counterfactual, and random/achiral-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions - we use both probe directions and delta (enantiomer-difference) representations.

A negative result (models encode R/S labels or achiral substructure but do not represent chirality as a pseudoscalar, failing the mirror-flip counterfactual) is scientifically decisive and directly safety-relevant - it would warn against trusting molecular FMs for enantioselective property and toxicity prediction, precisely where the wrong enantiomer can be harmful; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether molecular foundation models represent the pseudoscalar chirality mechanism.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and public chirality/enantioselective datasets, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: sign_epistasis_context_flip_probe
Title: Does the Mutation's Meaning Depend on Its Neighbors? Testing Whether Protein Language Models Internally Represent Context-Dependent Sign Epistasis, Not Just Additive Effects
Short Hypothesis: The mechanism-defining signature of epistasis is context-dependence: a mutation's fitness effect is not fixed but depends on the genetic background, and in sign epistasis the effect fully REVERSES (beneficial<->deleterious) when a partner mutation is present. If a protein language model internally represents this mechanism rather than a context-independent additive effect, then the internal representational effect of applying a fixed mutation must CHANGE (and, for sign-epistatic pairs, flip sign relative to fitness) when the background carries a sign-epistatic partner, while remaining invariant when the background carries an additive (non-interacting) partner. The same-mutation/different-background counterfactual, with combinatorial deep-mutational-scanning ground truth, is an exact mechanism-defining test that output-score correlation and single-mutation interpretability cannot provide.
Related Work: Recent work shows PLM OUTPUT scores reflect epistasis correlationally: 'PLMs Capture Structural and Functional Epistasis in a Zero-Shot Setting' (2025) finds epistasis emerges in ESM scores, with raw scores aligning to contacts and a nonlinear rescaling shifting toward functional couplings. Epistasis theory establishes SIGN epistasis - where a mutation's effect reverses sign with background - as the mechanistically-defining, hardest, and rarest form ('Mechanistic causes of sign epistasis' 2024; 'Simple sign epistasis and evolutionary detours' 2026; 'The simplicity of protein sequence-function relationships' 2023 and its rebuttal 2024, which agree additive+pairwise terms dominate but that specific interactions are the crux). PLM interpretability (InterPLM, ProtoMech cross-layer transcoders, BERTology attention studies, SAE low-N design, CB-pLM) recovers LOCAL, context-independent features (binding sites, contacts, motifs) and validates against marginal annotations. Crucially, no work tests whether a PLM's INTERNAL representation encodes the CONTEXT-DEPENDENCE that defines epistasis - i.e., whether the internal effect of a fixed mutation changes with background - nor uses a same-mutation/sign-epistatic-vs-additive-background counterfactual to separate context-dependent (mechanistic) from additive (context-free) representation. Because output scores can capture epistasis without the representation encoding context-dependence per se, and because prior interpretability probes local features only, this representational, causal, sign-flip counterfactual is the novel, mechanism-defining contribution.
Abstract: Epistasis - the dependence of a mutation's effect on its genetic background - is the phenomenon that makes protein sequence-function landscapes hard, and its sharpest form is sign epistasis, in which a mutation's effect fully reverses from beneficial to deleterious (or vice versa) when a partner mutation is present. Protein language models (PLMs) are known to reflect epistasis in their output scores and to encode local structural features, but whether their internal representations encode the defining property of epistasis - context-dependence itself - has never been tested. We propose a mechanism-defining representational test. For a fixed point mutation, we measure its induced change in ESM-2's internal representations when applied to two matched backgrounds drawn from combinatorial deep-mutational-scanning (DMS) data: a sign-epistatic background (a partner mutation that reverses the fitness sign of our mutation) and an additive background (a partner mutation whose combined effect is the sum of singles, i.e. no interaction), matched on structural/sequence distance. If the PLM represents epistasis mechanistically, the internal mutation-effect vector must change substantially - and align with the fitness sign flip - across the sign-epistatic background, while remaining near-invariant across the additive background; a context-free additive representation shows equal, background-independent effects. We further test whether a recoverable 'context-dependence' direction causally tracks the true sign flip and whether internal context-sensitivity predicts where the model mispredicts combinatorial fitness. Metrics quantify a context-flip asymmetry, a sign-alignment index, and an epistasis failure predictor. Either outcome sharpens whether PLMs, now central to variant-effect prediction and protein design, represent the interactions that dominate real fitness landscapes.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — same-mutation/different-background context-flip asymmetry): Tests the core representational claim: the internal effect of a fixed mutation changes when the background carries a sign-epistatic partner but stays invariant when the background carries an additive (non-interacting) partner. Data: combinatorial deep-mutational-scanning sets with measured single and double mutants so pairwise epistasis and sign are computed exactly — GB1 (~149,000 combinatorial variants across 4 sites), avGFP (Sarkisyan, ~51,000 variants), a PABP/RRM double-mutant set, beta-lactamase, and ProteinGym multi-mutant tracks; from these enumerate mutation pairs, classify each as additive, magnitude-epistatic, or sign-epistatic, and select the sign-epistatic pairs (rare) plus distance-matched additive controls — targeting ≥300 clean sign-epistatic pairs pooled across proteins, fewer being possible because clean sign-epistatic pairs are scarce (this floor is reported and drives the power analysis). Define delta(m|B) = repr(B+m) − repr(B), the pooled per-layer ESM-2 activation change. Model: ESM-2 at 150M and 650M parameters (3B as compute allows), inference-only, frozen; a linear fitness probe trained on single-mutant scores selects the best layer, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: change in delta(m1|.) between a sign-epistatic background and wildtype vs between a distance-matched additive background and wildtype (m2_sign and m2_add matched on sequence separation and 3D distance from m1). Decisive metric (first): Context-Flip Asymmetry = ||delta(m1|sign-epistatic bg) − delta(m1|wt)|| / ||delta(m1|additive bg) − delta(m1|wt)||. Convincing: asymmetry ≥ 3 (95% CI lower bound above 1.5). Indecision band: asymmetry in [0.7, 2.0] — the interacting background is not privileged over a distance-matched non-interacting one; the mechanism claim fails here. Negative result: asymmetry ≈ 1 — the model represents mutation effects context-independently (additively), the decisive negative for the hypothesis.

Experiment 2 (H1 — sign-alignment double dissociation): Tests the second half of the claim: for sign-epistatic pairs the internal effect flips sign consistently with the measured fitness reversal, while for additive controls it does not. Data: the same ≥300 sign-epistatic pairs and their additive controls. Decode a scalar fitness-effect read-out from delta(m1|B) using the Experiment-1 probe. Model/probe as Experiment 1, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: sign-flip rate of the internal read-out across sign-epistatic backgrounds vs across additive backgrounds. Decisive metric (first): Sign-Alignment Index = fraction of sign-epistatic pairs whose internal read-out reverses sign in the direction of the true fitness reversal, minus the additive-control flip rate. Convincing: Index ≥ 0.4, with sign-epistatic flip rate ≥ 0.6 and additive-control flip rate ≤ 0.2 (a double dissociation). Indecision band: Index in [0.1, 0.25] — weak, inconsistent sign tracking; inconclusive on the sign claim. Negative result: Index ≤ 0.1 (sign-epistatic flip rate near the additive-control rate) — no fitness-consistent sign reversal is represented.

Experiment 3 (H1 — dose-response to epistasis magnitude): Tests the quantitative form of the claim: the internal effect-change scales with true pairwise epistasis rather than with mere proximity. Data: ALL enumerated pairs (additive through strong-epistatic) across the pooled proteins. Model/probe as above, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: ||delta(m|bg) − delta(m|wt)|| vs true pairwise epistasis magnitude, controlling for sequence separation and 3D distance. Decisive metric (first): partial Spearman rho between internal effect-change and true epistasis, conditioning on sequence and 3D distance. Convincing: partial rho ≥ 0.4 (95% CI lower bound above 0.15). Indecision band: partial rho in [0.15, 0.3] — weak residual association beyond distance; inconclusive. Negative result: partial rho < 0.15 — the internal effect-change tracks distance, not interaction, so context-dependence is not epistasis-specific.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Epistasis magnitude correlates with 3D contact and sequence proximity, so context-dependence could partly reflect distance rather than genuine interaction encoding; we mitigate with distance-matched additive control backgrounds, partial correlations controlling for distance, and the sign-alignment double dissociation (which distance alone cannot produce).

Combinatorial DMS with true double/higher-order measurements is limited to a modest set of proteins, constraining sample size and the number of clean sign-epistatic pairs (which are rare); we pool across GB1, avGFP, RRM, beta-lactamase and ProteinGym multi-mutant sets and report statistics accounting for small n, emphasizing sign-epistatic pairs as the diagnostic subset.

DMS measurements are noisy and reference-based epistasis estimates can inflate apparent interactions; we use reference-free / global-nonlinearity-corrected epistasis estimates where possible and restrict decisive tests to high-confidence, replicate-supported pairs, reporting sensitivity to the epistasis threshold.

Applying two mutations to build the background may push sequences off the model's training distribution; but double mutants near wildtype are common and mild, and we bound the number and severity of background mutations and report OOD diagnostics, with the additive-background control sharing any generic OOD effect.

Linear probes and delta-representations recovering a context-dependence direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/distance-matched controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions - we report aggregate-direction results.

A negative result (ESM-2 represents mutation effects additively and shows no background-specific sign flip, i.e. context-flip asymmetry ~ 1) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting PLMs for combinatorial variant-effect prediction and multi-mutant protein design, where sign epistasis causes catastrophic failures; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining, representational test of whether PLMs encode the context-dependence that defines epistasis.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained ESM-2 plus small probes and public combinatorial DMS datasets, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: temporal_directionality_ehr_probe
Title: A Then B, Not B Then A: Testing Whether EHR Foundation Models Represent the Temporal Directionality of Disease Progression, Not Just Symmetric Co-occurrence
Short Hypothesis: Disease progression is a directed, temporally asymmetric mechanism: the trajectory diabetes -> nephropathy -> renal failure is causal and irreversible, whereas its reverse is clinically nonsensical, and this directionality (not mere co-occurrence) is what determines prognosis and treatment. We hypothesize that if EHR foundation models represent the progression mechanism rather than symmetric co-occurrence statistics, then (a) the temporal direction of a diagnosis pair (A-before-B vs B-before-A) is decodable from internal representations beyond what unordered co-occurrence predicts, (b) an exact sequence-reversal counterfactual - reversing only the order of two events while holding their identities, times-between, and all else fixed - flips the internal risk/prognosis signal for directed (progression) pairs but not for order-invariant (comorbidity) pairs, and (c) steering a recovered 'progression-direction' axis causally shifts downstream risk predictions. The reversal counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that predictive accuracy and attention-pathway alignment cannot provide.
Related Work: EHR foundation models built on next-event prediction (NEP EHR FM 2025; Sequential Pattern Transformer 2026) report attention patterns that 'align with known disease pathways,' and trajectory-mining work (All of Us ordered-sequence discovery 2025; directed hypergraphs of multimorbidity 2023; THCM-CAL 2025) shows ordered A->B->C sequences carry risk beyond bag-of-codes. Clinical causal-discovery methods (EHR causal structure learning 2021; LLM edge-directionality in NSCLC 2023) and symptom-causality probes (CausaLM/TReATE for chest pain 2025) estimate causal effects at the output level. Crucially, the systematic single-cell FM evaluation (2026) and 'Medical Interpretability and Knowledge Maps' (2025) show these models' internals often capture co-occurrence rather than causal/mechanistic structure, and that disease-progression representations can be circular/non-monotonic. But no work tests whether an EHR foundation model's INTERNAL representation encodes the TEMPORAL DIRECTIONALITY (A-before-B vs B-before-A asymmetry) that defines progression, whether that directionality is causally load-bearing, or uses an exact sequence-reversal counterfactual to separate directed progression from symmetric comorbidity. Because directed pairs and mere comorbid pairs both show high co-occurrence, predictive benchmarks and attention-pathway alignment cannot arbitrate this. Our directionality-beyond-co-occurrence probe, sequence-reversal counterfactual, and causal progression-direction steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, transferred into a safety-critical clinical setting where getting the arrow backwards inverts prognosis.
Abstract: Electronic health record (EHR) foundation models trained by next-event prediction are increasingly used to forecast disease progression and clinical risk, and their attention patterns reportedly align with known disease pathways. But a pathway is not merely a set of co-occurring diagnoses: it is a directed, temporally asymmetric mechanism, where diabetes preceding kidney failure carries a prognosis that its reverse does not. Because predictive accuracy and attention-alignment cannot distinguish encoding this directionality from encoding symmetric co-occurrence, whether these models represent the progression mechanism is untested. We propose the first mechanism-defining test. Using public EHR foundation models trained on MIMIC-III/IV and, where available, larger event-sequence models, we ask three questions. First, a directionality-beyond-co-occurrence probe: is the temporal order of a diagnosis pair (A-before-B vs B-before-A) decodable from internal representations beyond what unordered co-occurrence predicts? Second, and most decisively, a sequence-reversal counterfactual: for matched patient trajectories we reverse only the order of two events - holding their identities, inter-event times, and surrounding context fixed - and test whether the internal risk/prognosis signal flips for directed progression pairs (e.g., nephropathy->renal-failure) but stays stable for order-invariant comorbidity pairs (e.g., hypertension and hyperlipidemia); a co-occurrence-statistics model responds identically to both. Third, causal steering along a recovered progression-direction axis should shift downstream risk. Metrics quantify a directionality-beyond-co-occurrence index, a reversal-vs-comorbidity causal asymmetry, and a mechanism-based failure predictor. Either outcome sharpens whether deployed clinical models understand which way the arrow points.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — temporal direction decodable beyond unordered co-occurrence): Tests clause (a): the temporal direction of a diagnosis pair (A-before-B vs B-before-A) is decodable from internal representations beyond what unordered co-occurrence predicts. Data: timestamped diagnosis/procedure/medication sequences from MIMIC-III (~40k patients) and MIMIC-IV (~300k); curate ~50 DIRECTED progression pairs with clinically established, largely irreversible order (e.g., diabetic nephropathy -> end-stage renal failure; hypertension -> heart failure; adenoma -> colorectal cancer) and ~50 ORDER-INVARIANT comorbidity pairs (e.g., hypertension & hyperlipidemia), then extract patient trajectories containing each pair — targeting ≥1,000 trajectories per pair class (split by patient), restricting directed pairs to large time gaps across separate admissions to reduce coding-order artifacts. Model: an event-sequence next-event-prediction transformer trained on MIMIC (~tens of M parameters, per-event representations) and a bag-of-codes baseline model, frozen; a logistic order-probe on the best layer, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: order-decoding from the representation vs an unordered co-occurrence/prevalence baseline, representation residualized against co-occurrence, reported separately for directed vs comorbidity pairs. Decisive metric (first): Directionality-Beyond-Co-occurrence Index = order-classification accuracy(representation) − accuracy(co-occurrence features). Convincing: Index ≥ 0.10 (95% CI lower bound above 0.03) for directed pairs and ≤ 0.03 for comorbidity pairs (double dissociation). Indecision band: Index in [−0.02, 0.03] for directed pairs — within probe noise; clause (a) fails here. Negative result: Index ≤ −0.02 or in band for directed pairs — the model encodes symmetric co-occurrence, not order.

Experiment 2 (H2 — sequence-reversal counterfactual with prognosis-sign consistency): Tests clause (b): reversing only the order of two events (holding identities, inter-event time, and all else fixed) flips the internal risk/prognosis signal for directed pairs but not for comorbidity pairs. Data: matched patient trajectories from Experiment 1 (≥1,000 per pair class); for each, build (true order A-before-B) and (reversed order B-before-A) by swapping only the two events' positions/timestamps. Model/probe as Experiment 1, seeds 0–4; read-out is a probed risk score and the model's outcome head (e.g., predicted mortality or downstream complication). Systems compared: |signal change under reversal| for directed vs for comorbidity pairs; plus the signed comparison forward-order risk vs reversed-order risk for directed pairs. Decisive metrics (first): Reversal-vs-Comorbidity Causal Asymmetry = median(|Δsignal directed|) / median(|Δsignal comorbidity|); and Prognosis-Sign Consistency = fraction of directed pairs with forward-order risk exceeding reversed-order risk. Convincing: asymmetry ≥ 3 and prognosis-sign consistency ≥ 0.8, while comorbidity pairs show near-zero directed difference. Indecision band: asymmetry in [0.7, 2.0] or prognosis-sign consistency in [0.5, 0.65] — order barely matters; clause (b) fails or is inconclusive here. Negative result: asymmetry ≈ 1 and consistency ≈ 0.5 — forward and reversed progressions read alike, a co-occurrence-statistics representation.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal progression-direction steering): Tests clause (c): steering a recovered 'progression-direction' axis causally shifts downstream risk predictions. Data: the directed-pair trajectories from Experiment 2; the axis is recovered as a supervised order-probe direction and a delta-representation between forward-order and reversed-order versions. Model/probe as above; add matched-norm perturbations along the axis at the best layer and read the risk head, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: progression-direction axis vs matched-norm random directions vs a co-occurrence-magnitude direction. Decisive metric (first): Steering Selectivity = |Δrisk from progression-direction steering| / |Δrisk from random-direction steering|. Convincing: selectivity ≥ 3 with the progression-consistent sign and the co-occurrence direction not reproducing it. Indecision band: selectivity in [0.7, 2.0] — no better than random; clause (c) fails here. Negative result: selectivity ≈ 1 — no dedicated causal progression-direction axis.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Recorded event order in EHRs is a noisy proxy for true clinical onset order (billing/coding order, batched diagnoses, same-admission codes with identical timestamps); we mitigate by restricting directed pairs to those with large, clinically meaningful time gaps across separate admissions, using validated ordered-trajectory resources, and reporting sensitivity to timestamp-quality thresholds.

Directed progression pairs and order-invariant comorbidity pairs both have high co-occurrence, making the directionality-beyond-co-occurrence separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with co-occurrence residualization, the sequence-reversal counterfactual (which holds identities and timing fixed and varies only order), and the directed-vs-comorbidity double dissociation.

The reversal counterfactual creates clinically implausible trajectories that may fall off the model's training distribution, confounding the reversal response with generic out-of-distribution behavior; we mitigate by comparing directed-pair reversals against comorbidity-pair reversals of matched implausibility/edit-magnitude (both are edited, so any generic OOD effect is shared) and reporting edit-magnitude sensitivity.

Some EHR foundation models tokenize events without fine-grained timestamps or use position-invariant pooling, limiting access to order; we document each model's temporal encoding, prioritize models that ingest ordered/timestamped sequences, and treat pooling-invariant models as an informative lower bracket that by construction cannot represent direction.

Ground-truth causal direction for some pairs is debated or bidirectional; we restrict decisive tests to well-established, largely irreversible progressions and report sensitivity to pair-confidence thresholds.

Linear probes recovering a progression-direction axis do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/co-occurrence-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions - we use both probe directions and delta-representations.

A negative result (models encode symmetric co-occurrence and respond identically to forward vs reversed progression, failing the reversal counterfactual) is scientifically decisive and directly safety-relevant - it would warn that deployed clinical risk models may not distinguish cause from consequence, risking inverted prognoses and inappropriate interventions for atypically-ordered patients; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether EHR foundation models represent the temporal directionality of disease progression.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and public EHR datasets (MIMIC-III/IV) with validated trajectory resources, keeping compute at academic scale.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) probe whether EHR FMs encode temporal directionality of disease progression (A-before-B vs B-before-A), not just co-occurrence; (2) use an exact sequence-reversal counterfactual as the key test; (3) show a causal steerable 'progression-direction' axis; (4) distinguish directed progression pairs from comorbidity pairs via double dissociation. The problem and setting are not new -- order-aware EHR modeling and trajectory mining already exist -- but the mechanistic interpretability claim is a meaningful delta. The closest prior family is order-aware pretraining / trajectory-order objectives (e.g., TOO-BERT, temporal entailment, ordered sequence mining). Name: nernst_overpotential_decomposition_probe
Title: Voltage Is Not Charge: Testing Whether Battery Foundation Models Decompose Terminal Voltage into Thermodynamic Nernst OCV and Kinetic Overpotential, Not Just Raw Voltage Statistics
Short Hypothesis: A battery's terminal voltage is set by an exactly-known decomposition: V = OCV(SOC) - overpotential(current), where the open-circuit voltage is a purely thermodynamic, current-independent function of state-of-charge (Nernst equation) and the overpotential is a kinetic, current-dependent loss (Butler-Volmer / diffusion). These are physically independent contributions: the same terminal voltage can correspond to very different SOCs depending on the load current, which is exactly why SOC estimation fails under high current. We hypothesize that if a battery/time-series foundation model represents this mechanism rather than raw voltage statistics, then (a) SOC (the thermodynamic OCV component) is decodable from internal representations beyond what instantaneous terminal voltage predicts, along an axis distinct from overpotential, (b) a current-holding vs SOC-holding counterfactual moves the two internal signals independently, and (c) steering a recovered 'overpotential' direction reshapes the voltage-current relationship without changing the SOC readout. The load-current counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that terminal-voltage correlation cannot pass.
Related Work: Two lines bracket the gap. (1) Physics-informed and electrochemical battery models - ECINN (2024, embedding Nernst/Butler-Volmer/diffusion equations), single-particle-model + Nernst SOC estimators (2020), and equivalent-circuit models - BUILD the OCV/overpotential decomposition in by construction; they are judged by SOC estimation error, not by what a general model internally represents. (2) Data-driven battery foundation/time-series models (BatteryML, transformer SOC/SOH estimators, general TSFMs like Chronos/TimesFM applied to battery telemetry) predict SOC/state directly from voltage-current-temperature sequences; interpretability of such models is limited to feature-attribution over input channels. Interpretability of scientific foundation models (Physics Steering 2025, showing steerable physical-concept directions; From Neurons to Neutrons 2024) recovers and steers single physical quantities, but none tests whether a battery model internally SEPARATES the thermodynamic Nernst OCV(SOC) from the kinetic overpotential(current), whether that decomposition is causally load-bearing, or uses a load-current counterfactual to arbitrate mechanism vs voltage statistics. Because terminal voltage, SOC, and current are entangled in ordinary discharge data, correlation-based SOC benchmarks cannot separate the two contributions. Our OCV-beyond-voltage probe, current-holding counterfactual, and causal overpotential steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, in a safety-critical setting where confusing kinetic voltage sag with true depletion causes dangerous SOC misestimation.
Abstract: Battery management systems increasingly use machine-learning models to estimate state-of-charge (SOC) from voltage, current, and temperature telemetry, and errors are most dangerous precisely under high load, where the terminal voltage sags for kinetic reasons even though the battery is not actually depleted. The physics is exactly known: terminal voltage decomposes into a thermodynamic open-circuit voltage that depends only on SOC (the Nernst equation) and a kinetic overpotential that depends on current (Butler-Volmer and diffusion losses). These are independent contributions - the same voltage can mean very different SOCs at different currents - making batteries an ideal, mechanism-defining testbed for whether foundation models learn the electrochemical mechanism or merely voltage statistics. We probe pretrained battery/time-series foundation models on public cycling datasets (e.g., NASA, Oxford, CALCE, and BatteryML benchmarks) where SOC, current, and OCV are known or computable. First, an OCV-beyond-voltage probe: is SOC (the thermodynamic component) decodable from internal representations beyond what instantaneous terminal voltage predicts, along an axis distinct from overpotential? Second, and most decisively, a current-holding counterfactual: we change the load current at fixed SOC (which changes overpotential, not OCV) versus change SOC at fixed current (which changes OCV, not overpotential), and test whether the two internal signals move independently - a mechanistic representation separates them, a voltage-statistics representation collapses them. Third, causal steering of a recovered overpotential direction should reshape the voltage-current response without shifting the SOC readout. Metrics quantify an OCV-beyond-voltage index, a thermodynamic-kinetic disentanglement ratio, and a SOC-error failure predictor. Either outcome sharpens whether deployed battery models estimate charge for the right physical reason.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — SOC decodable beyond terminal voltage, distinct from overpotential): Tests clause (a): SOC (the thermodynamic OCV component) is decodable from internal representations beyond what instantaneous terminal voltage predicts, along an axis distinct from overpotential. Data: public cycling datasets — NASA PCoE, Oxford Battery Degradation (8 cells), CALCE, and BatteryML benchmark cells — providing time series of terminal voltage, load current, temperature, and coulomb-counted SOC; compute ground-truth OCV(SOC) from low-rate/pseudo-OCV data and per-timestep overpotential = terminal voltage − OCV(SOC). Use ~200,000 timesteps from cells with reliable SOC labels (split by cell so no cell crosses splits) — fewer than all telemetry because decisive tests require cells with trustworthy pseudo-OCV/relaxation labels. Model: a BatteryML transformer SOC/SOH estimator (~few-M parameters, per-timestep representations) and a general time-series FM (Chronos, ~200M parameters, or TimesFM ~200M) applied to the telemetry, frozen; ridge probes on the best layer, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: probe R^2 for SOC from the representation vs an instantaneous-terminal-voltage baseline, representation residualized against voltage; plus the angle between recovered SOC/OCV and overpotential directions. Decisive metric (first): OCV-Beyond-Voltage Index = R^2(SOC | representation) − R^2(SOC | terminal voltage). Convincing: Index ≥ 0.15 (95% CI lower bound above 0.05) and SOC–overpotential axis angle ≥ 60 degrees. Indecision band: Index in [−0.03, 0.05] or angle in [30, 45] degrees — SOC barely separable from voltage; clause (a) fails or is inconclusive here. Negative result: Index ≤ −0.03 or angle < 30 degrees — SOC collapses onto terminal voltage, the dangerous voltage-statistics reading.

Experiment 2 (H2 — current-holding vs SOC-holding double-dissociation counterfactual): Tests clause (b): a current-holding vs SOC-holding counterfactual moves the two internal signals independently. Data: matched edits — (overpotential edit) change load current at fixed SOC (changes overpotential/terminal voltage, not OCV); (OCV edit) change SOC at fixed current (changes OCV, not overpotential) — built from controlled real telemetry segments plus synthetic sequences from a calibrated equivalent-circuit/single-particle model for exact independent manipulation (≥5,000 matched pairs; results reported separately for real vs synthetic and cross-validated). Model/probe as Experiment 1, seeds 0–4; read-outs are the SOC and overpotential probes. Systems compared: movement of each internal signal under each edit. Decisive metrics (first): Overpotential-Edit Ratio = |Δoverpotential signal| / |ΔSOC signal| under the current edit; OCV-Edit Ratio = |ΔSOC signal| / |Δoverpotential signal| under the SOC edit. Convincing: both ratios ≥ 3 (each edit moves its own physical axis — a double dissociation). Indecision band: either ratio in [0.7, 2.0] — the axes are not cleanly separable; clause (b) fails or is inconclusive here. Negative result: ratios ≈ 1, or SOC moving whenever voltage moves — the model reads current-induced voltage sag as depletion, the mechanism failure of interest.

Experiment 3 (H2 — overpotential dose-response to current): Tests the quantitative content of clause (b): the internal overpotential signal grows with current in the physically correct direction while SOC stays constant. Data: the same test cells; sweep load current across a range at fixed SOC. Model/probe as above, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: induced overpotential-signal change vs the Butler–Volmer/ohmic prediction; SOC-readout stability across the sweep; shuffled-current labels as null. Decisive metrics (first): Spearman rho and sign agreement between induced overpotential change and predicted overpotential; and SOC drift (max |ΔSOC readout| across the sweep, in SOC %). Convincing: rho ≥ 0.6 with correct sign and SOC drift ≤ 3 SOC %. Indecision band: rho in [0.2, 0.4] or SOC drift in (3, 8] SOC % — weak or leaky decomposition; inconclusive on (b). Negative result: rho < 0.2 or SOC drift > 8 SOC % — no current-dependent overpotential law, or SOC contaminated by current.

Experiment 4 (H3 — causal overpotential-direction steering): Tests clause (c): steering a recovered 'overpotential' direction reshapes the voltage-current relationship without changing the SOC readout. Data: the same test cells; direction recovered as a supervised overpotential-probe direction and a delta-representation between high-current and low-current states at matched SOC. Model/probe as above; add matched-norm perturbations along the overpotential direction at the best layer and re-read the predicted voltage-current response and SOC, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: overpotential direction vs a matched SOC/OCV direction vs matched-norm random directions. Decisive metrics (first): Steering Selectivity = |voltage-sag change from overpotential steering| / |change from random steering|; Cross-talk = |SOC shift from overpotential steering| in SOC %. Convincing: selectivity ≥ 3 with cross-talk ≤ 3 SOC % (voltage response reshapes, SOC essentially fixed), while the SOC/OCV direction shifts SOC without changing overpotential. Indecision band: selectivity in [0.7, 2.0] or cross-talk in (3, 8] SOC % — non-selective or entangled steering; clause (c) fails or is inconclusive here. Negative result: selectivity ≈ 1 — no dedicated causal overpotential direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: SOC, terminal voltage, and current are entangled in ordinary discharge data, making the OCV-beyond-voltage separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with voltage-residualization, the current-holding double-dissociation counterfactual (which holds one physical quantity fixed while varying the other), synthetic equivalent-circuit sequences giving exact independent control, and physics dose-response tests a voltage-only model cannot reproduce.

Ground-truth OCV(SOC) and overpotential require accurate coulomb-counted SOC and low-rate OCV curves, which drift with aging and temperature and are noisy; we use well-characterized benchmark cells with pseudo-OCV/relaxation data, restrict decisive tests to cells with reliable SOC labels, and report sensitivity to OCV-curve and aging assumptions.

The current-holding counterfactual on real telemetry is constrained by what operating points exist in the data; we supplement with synthetic sequences from a calibrated equivalent-circuit/single-particle model for exact independent manipulation, clearly reporting which results are synthetic vs real and treating cross-validation between them as key.

Some battery/time-series foundation models take fixed input windows, normalize channels, or output only a scalar SOC, limiting fine-grained decomposition analysis; we document each model's preprocessing, prioritize models exposing per-timestep representations, probe pre-normalization activations where feasible, and treat scalar-only models as an informative lower bracket.

Linear probes recovering OCV/overpotential directions do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering, cross-talk controls, and random-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions - we use both probe directions and delta-representations.

A negative result (models encode voltage statistics and collapse the thermodynamic-kinetic decomposition, failing the current-holding counterfactual) is scientifically decisive and directly safety-relevant - it would warn that deployed battery models may misread kinetic voltage sag as true depletion, causing dangerous SOC misestimation under high load and low temperature; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether battery foundation models decompose terminal voltage into Nernst OCV and kinetic overpotential.

All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and public battery cycling datasets (NASA, Oxford, CALCE, BatteryML) with standard equivalent-circuit simulation, keeping compute at academic scale.
