Name: teleconnection_remote_forcing_probe
Title: Weather Here Because of the Ocean There: Testing Whether Weather/Climate Foundation Models Represent the Non-Local ENSO Teleconnection Mechanism, Not Just Local Persistence
Short Hypothesis: A defining, causally-directional, non-local mechanism of climate is the teleconnection: a remote tropical Pacific SST anomaly (ENSO) forces a Rossby-wave train that reorganizes distant mid-latitude weather (e.g., the Pacific-North American pattern) with a characteristic lag and phase, whereas local persistence carries no such distant, directional signal. We hypothesize that if data-driven weather/climate foundation models represent this teleconnection mechanism rather than local autocorrelation, then (a) the remote-forcing state (ENSO phase) is decodable from internal representations and linked to distant mid-latitude circulation beyond what local antecedents predict, (b) a remote-forcing counterfactual that perturbs ONLY the tropical Pacific state propagates the physically-correct downstream teleconnection pattern (correct sign, region, and lag), while a distance-matched control perturbation elsewhere does not, and (c) steering a recovered 'ENSO-forcing' direction causally shifts distant weather in the teleconnection-consistent direction. The tropical-Pacific-vs-elsewhere perturbation is an exact, mechanism-defining test that local-statistics correlation cannot pass.
Related Work: Interpretability of weather foundation models recovers single physical OBJECTS/features: SAE studies on GraphCast (2025) find tropical cyclones, atmospheric rivers, and sea-ice and steer them; GraphDOP work (2025) shows a unified observation-driven world model that infers non-local structures (jet streams) and applies FSOI/DA diagnostics; Physics Steering (2025) steers vorticity/diffusion directions. Separately, an ocean-role study (2026) correlates GraphCast OUTPUT errors with SST (an input-output diagnostic, not an internal test), and a coupled DL emulator study (2025) finds AMPLIFIED ENSO teleconnections at the OUTPUT level. Climate science establishes the mechanism precisely: ENSO remotely forces mid-latitude circulation via Rossby-wave teleconnections, distinct from local air-sea coupling (QTCM 2006; tropical-Atlantic remote-vs-local studies 2001-2021). Crucially, no work tests whether a weather/climate foundation model's INTERNAL representation encodes the non-local, causally-directional teleconnection mechanism (remote cause -> distant effect with correct lag/phase), whether it is causally load-bearing, or uses a remote-forcing counterfactual to separate teleconnection from local persistence. Because ENSO state and local antecedents are correlated, output-level benchmarks and error-SST correlations cannot arbitrate this. Our teleconnection-beyond-local probe, tropical-Pacific-vs-elsewhere counterfactual, and causal ENSO-forcing steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution.
Abstract: Data-driven weather and climate foundation models now rival physical models and have been shown to encode recognizable physical objects such as cyclones and atmospheric rivers. But one of the deepest organizing mechanisms of the climate system is non-local and causally directional: teleconnections, in which a remote tropical Pacific sea-surface-temperature anomaly (El Nino/La Nina) forces a Rossby-wave train that reorganizes weather thousands of kilometers away, with a characteristic lag and phase. A model can forecast well by exploiting local persistence without ever internalizing that distant weather is caused by the ocean elsewhere, making teleconnections an ideal, mechanism-defining probe. We test whether pretrained weather/climate foundation models (GraphCast, Pangu-Weather, and a coupled ocean-atmosphere emulator such as DLESyM where available) internally represent the ENSO teleconnection, using ERA5 and coupled-emulator states. First, a teleconnection-beyond-local probe: is the remote-forcing state (ENSO phase) decodable from internal representations and predictive of distant mid-latitude circulation beyond what local antecedents allow? Second, and most decisively, a remote-forcing counterfactual: we perturb ONLY the tropical Pacific state (imposing an ENSO anomaly) and measure whether the model's internal representation and rollout produce the physically-correct downstream teleconnection (e.g., the Pacific-North American pattern) with the right sign, region, and lag, compared to a distance-matched control perturbation elsewhere that should not trigger it. Third, causal steering along a recovered ENSO-forcing direction. Metrics quantify a teleconnection-beyond-local index, a remote-vs-control propagation asymmetry, and a lag/phase fidelity score. Either outcome sharpens whether these operationally-deployed models represent the non-local causality behind seasonal climate.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 -- ENSO-forcing is decodable and carries distant circulation beyond local persistence): Tests hypothesis clause (a): that the remote-forcing state (ENSO phase) is decodable from internal representations and predicts distant mid-latitude circulation beyond what local antecedents predict. Data: ERA5 reanalysis (Copernicus CDS; hourly 1940-present, ~83 years). We use monthly-mean SST, 500 hPa geopotential (Z500), 850/250 hPa winds, and 2 m temperature on a 1.5-degree grid for 1940-2022 (996 monthly fields, an existing set used as is); ground-truth Nino3.4 index and the Pacific-North American (PNA) index come from NOAA CPC. We composite over the ~40 El Nino/La Nina events since 1950 (NOAA ONI list) for event-level statistics. Model: GraphCast (~37M parameters) and Pangu-Weather (~256M parameters), both public pretrained weights, entirely frozen; only linear probes are trained. We extract per-grid activations at every block and pool to the North-Pacific/North-American PNA region. Probes: ridge regression (continuous targets: Nino3.4, Z500) and logistic regression (El Nino vs La Nina), L2 strength chosen by 5-fold CV on the train split, features standardized; 5 seeds for year-blocked train/val/test splits (leave-whole-years-out to bar temporal leakage); report mean +/- SD. Systems compared: (i) decoding of Nino3.4 from representations; (ii) a local-persistence baseline predicting the PNA-region Z500 from its own and neighboring recent antecedents; (iii) the Teleconnection-Beyond-Local Index = distant-Z500 decoding R^2 from the model representation minus the R^2 of the local-persistence baseline, after regressing the local-antecedent-predictable component out of the representation. Decisive metric first: Teleconnection-Beyond-Local Index. Convincing: Index >= 0.10 R^2 with a 95% bootstrap CI (1000 resamples over held-out years) excluding 0, in >=4 of 5 seeds, and the residual distant signal correlating |r|>=0.4 with the ENSO-forcing direction rather than local features. Refute: Index <= 0.02 with CI including 0 (the representation adds nothing beyond local persistence). Indeterminate band 0.02-0.10 R^2 (stated before the data): treated as unresolved -- some non-local signal is present but too weak to claim the teleconnection is robustly encoded, and we do not advance to the causal tests as if H1 held. A negative result means the model's distant-circulation information is explained by local autocorrelation, contradicting clause (a).

Experiment 2 (H2 -- a tropical-Pacific-only perturbation propagates the correct downstream teleconnection while a matched control does not): Tests clause (b): a remote-forcing counterfactual perturbing ONLY the tropical Pacific produces the physically-correct downstream teleconnection (correct sign, region, lag), whereas a distance-matched control perturbation elsewhere does not. Data: 30 initialization dates drawn from ERA5 neutral-ENSO winters (1979-2022, existing set used as is) so the injected anomaly is the dominant remote forcing; canonical PNA response pattern and its 2-6 week onset lag from NOAA CPC composites as ground truth. Model: for the decisive coupled test we prioritize an SST-aware/coupled DL emulator (DLESyM-class, public weights) that ingests evolving SST, frozen; for atmosphere-only GraphCast/Pangu (which do not ingest SST) we instead impose the ENSO-associated atmospheric anomaly and report per-model exactly what is manipulable. No training; inference-only rollouts. Systems compared: (i) tropical-Pacific El-Nino-like warm anomaly (and La-Nina-like cold) imposed on the initial state, rest held fixed, rolled forward to the model's horizon; (ii) a distance-matched, equal-magnitude control anomaly placed in a basin with no relevant remote link; (iii) the true canonical PNA pattern. Decisive metric first: Remote-vs-Control Propagation Asymmetry = |projection of the distant response onto the canonical PNA pattern under the tropical-Pacific perturbation| / |same projection under the matched control|, with 30 initializations per condition. Convincing: median asymmetry >= 3 with the correct PNA sign in >=70% of cases and a bootstrap-CI lower bound > 1.5. Refute: asymmetry in [0.7, 1.5] (both perturbations act only locally; no non-local propagation). Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (stated up front): weak/partial support -- the model shows some preferential propagation but not the clean mechanism-defining asymmetry; reported as such, not as confirmation. Because both perturbations are equal-magnitude, any generic off-distribution effect is shared and cancels. A negative result means the model treats the tropical-Pacific forcing like any local perturbation, contradicting clause (b).

Experiment 3 (H2 -- sign reversal and lag fidelity of the teleconnection response): Further tests clause (b) by checking that the propagated response has the physically-correct sign and lag, the parts of (b) a location-only asymmetry does not by itself establish. Data: the same 30 neutral-winter initializations as Experiment 2 (reused), each run under an El-Nino-like and an opposite La-Nina-like tropical-Pacific anomaly; canonical PNA sign and 2-6 week onset lag from NOAA CPC. Model: the coupled/SST-aware emulator (primary) and atmosphere-only models (reported separately), all frozen, inference-only. Systems compared: warm vs cold tropical-Pacific perturbation, plus a shuffled-region control that scrambles where the anomaly is placed. Decisive metric first: sign-reversal consistency = fraction of cases whose distant PNA-pattern response flips sign when the perturbation sign flips. Secondary: correlation between the model's response-onset lag and the canonical lag. Convincing: sign-reversal consistency >= 0.80 AND lag correlation >= 0.5 across cases, with the shuffled-region control near 0.5 consistency. Refute: sign-reversal consistency <= 0.6 (no reliable anti-symmetry) OR lag correlation <= 0.1. Indeterminate band: sign-reversal 0.6-0.8 or lag correlation 0.1-0.5 (stated in advance) -- partial fidelity, logged as a qualified positive that does not on its own settle clause (b). A negative result means the response lacks the sign/lag structure the teleconnection mechanism dictates.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- steering a recovered ENSO-forcing direction causally shifts distant weather in the teleconnection-consistent sense): Tests clause (c). Data: representation pairs from El-Nino vs La-Nina composites (ERA5, existing) used to recover the forcing direction; the same 30 neutral-winter states as steering targets. Model: frozen GraphCast/Pangu and the coupled emulator; the only fitted object is the probe/delta direction. We recover an 'ENSO-forcing' direction two ways -- a supervised logistic-probe direction and an El-Nino-minus-La-Nina delta-representation -- and add it at matched L2 norm to the chosen block's activations during rollout. Systems compared: (i) ENSO-forcing direction; (ii) 20 matched-norm random directions; (iii) a local-feature direction. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |shift of the distant PNA-region readout along the teleconnection-consistent axis under ENSO-forcing steering| / |mean shift under random directions|. Convincing: selectivity >= 3, correct PNA sign, and the local-feature direction producing no teleconnection-consistent shift, consistent across the two direction-recovery methods. Refute: selectivity <= 1.5 (indistinguishable from random). Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared before the data): the direction has some causal traction but not the clean selectivity needed to claim causal use; superposed/distributed encoding is the leading alternative, so we report both recovery methods and withhold a strong causal claim. A negative result means the recovered direction is not causally wired to distant circulation, contradicting clause (c).

Experiment 5 (H1-H3 -- layer emergence, cross-model convergence, and mechanism brackets): Tests whether the clause-(a)-(c) findings are robust properties rather than single-model artifacts, and locates them on an interpretable spectrum. Data: all ERA5 fields and ENSO events above (reused). Model: GraphCast, Pangu, and the coupled emulator, all frozen; probes/directions as in Experiments 1 and 4. Systems compared: (i) per-block Teleconnection-Beyond-Local Index (H1) and steering selectivity (H3) across depth; (ii) linear CKA between recovered ENSO-forcing subspaces across the models; (iii) an upper-bound bracket = a linear-baroclinic-model / AGCM pacemaker teleconnection response that encodes the mechanism by construction, and a lower-bound bracket = a local-persistence forecaster with no remote access. Decisive metric first: where on the persistence-to-mechanism bracket each model's Index and selectivity fall (fraction of the gap between lower and upper bracket closed). Convincing: at least one model closes >=50% of the bracket gap AND cross-model CKA >= 0.5, indicating a convergent internal mechanism. Refute: all models sit within measurement noise of the lower (persistence) bracket. Indeterminate band: bracket-gap closure 20-50% or CKA 0.3-0.5 (declared in advance) -- partial/idiosyncratic representation, reported without a universality claim. A negative result means no model materially exceeds local persistence, consistent with the mechanism being absent. All runs are inference-only on public weights plus small probes and public ERA5 data, feasible on a single 40-80GB GPU.
Risk Factors and Limitations: ENSO state and local antecedents are correlated, making the teleconnection-beyond-local separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with local-antecedent residualization, the tropical-Pacific-vs-matched-control counterfactual (which holds perturbation magnitude fixed and varies only location), and the sign/lag fidelity tests that a local-statistics model cannot reproduce.

Many atmosphere-only weather foundation models (GraphCast, Pangu) do not ingest evolving SST as an input variable, so imposing an ENSO SST anomaly may be limited to perturbing the atmospheric state consistent with ENSO or requires an SST-aware/coupled emulator; we prioritize the coupled emulator (DLESyM) and SST-inclusive models for the decisive counterfactual, and for atmosphere-only models perturb the ENSO-associated atmospheric pattern, clearly reporting per-model what is manipulable.

Medium-range weather models have short rollout horizons (days), while teleconnections develop over weeks to a season; the downstream response may be truncated. We use models/emulators with extended or subseasonal-to-seasonal rollout where possible, focus on the fast component of the wave-train response, and report horizon caveats.

Imposing a tropical-Pacific anomaly may push the state off the model's training distribution, confounding the response with generic OOD failure; we mitigate with physically-plausible anomaly magnitudes, compare against a matched-magnitude control perturbation (so any generic OOD effect is shared), and report sensitivity to anomaly strength.
Teleconnection ground truth (PNA response, lags) has internal-variability noise; we composite over many ENSO events and use canonical patterns, reporting statistical uncertainty.

Linear probes recovering an ENSO-forcing direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/local-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions - we use both probe directions and delta-representations.

A negative result (models exploit local persistence and fail to propagate the correct non-local teleconnection) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting these operationally-deployed models for subseasonal-to-seasonal and ENSO-year forecasts, though it may be perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether weather/climate foundation models represent the non-local teleconnection mechanism.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and public ERA5 / coupled-emulator data, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: selection_rule_forbidden_transition_probe
Title: Bright or Dark? Testing Whether Molecular/Materials Foundation Models Represent Symmetry-Based Optical Selection Rules, Not Just the Energy Gap
Short Hypothesis: Whether an electronic transition absorbs light is set by an exactly-known symmetry mechanism—optical selection rules (Laporte/parity, spin, and orbital-symmetry rules)—that determines the oscillator strength (bright vs dark) largely independently of the energy-gap size: two molecules can have nearly identical HOMO-LUMO gaps yet one is intensely absorbing and the other symmetry-forbidden (dark). We hypothesize that if a molecular/materials foundation model represents this selection-rule mechanism rather than treating optical activity as a monotone function of the energy gap, then (a) transition brightness (oscillator strength) is decodable from internal representations along an axis distinct from the gap, (b) a symmetry-breaking counterfactual—a small distortion that lowers molecular symmetry and turns a forbidden (dark) transition allowed (bright) at nearly-fixed gap—shifts the internal brightness signal accordingly, whereas a symmetry-preserving perturbation of matched magnitude does not, and (c) steering a recovered 'allowedness' direction causally reshapes predicted absorption without changing the gap. The forbidden-vs-allowed symmetry counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that gap correlation cannot pass.
Related Work: Two lines bracket the gap. (1) ML for optical/excited-state properties—TD-DFT surrogate models, oscillator-strength and UV-Vis spectrum predictors (e.g., message-passing and transformer models on QM8/QM9-spectra, Oled/optical datasets), and excited-state foundation models—are trained to predict excitation energies and intensities but are judged by regression error, not by whether they internalize the selection-rule mechanism. (2) Interpretability of chemistry/atomistic foundation models—SAE studies on chemistry FMs, 'Circuits, Features, and Heuristics in Molecular Transformers' (2025), MoleX (2024), and periodic-law/spin-state probes—recover substructure/element/valence features validated against ground/scalar annotations, none of which concern excited-state symmetry. Physics/interpretability work recovers and steers single scalar quantities (energy, vorticity) but never the parity/spin symmetry that decides whether a transition is bright or dark. Crucially, no work tests whether a foundation model internally represents optical selection rules—the symmetry mechanism separating oscillator strength from the energy gap—whether that representation is causally load-bearing, or uses a symmetry-breaking counterfactual to arbitrate mechanism vs gap correlation. Because bright transitions also tend to have accessible gaps in typical data, correlation-based benchmarks cannot separate the two. Our brightness-beyond-gap probe, forbidden-vs-allowed symmetry counterfactual, and causal allowedness steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, distinct from the chirality (pseudoscalar) and spin-state probes in also targeting the parity/orbital-symmetry selection mechanism of excited states.
Abstract: Whether a molecule absorbs light at a given color is governed not by the size of its energy gap alone but by an exactly-known symmetry mechanism: optical selection rules. Parity (Laporte), spin, and orbital-symmetry rules decide whether an electronic transition is allowed (bright, large oscillator strength) or forbidden (dark, vanishing intensity), and this can flip a transition from dark to bright with a tiny symmetry-lowering distortion that barely changes the gap. This makes selection rules an ideal, mechanism-defining probe for whether molecular/materials foundation models learn excited-state symmetry or merely a gap-to-intensity correlate. We probe pretrained molecular foundation models and optical-property predictors on datasets with computed oscillator strengths and excitation energies (e.g., QM8, QM9-spectra, and curated symmetric/near-symmetric molecule sets). First, a brightness-beyond-gap probe: is transition oscillator strength decodable from internal representations beyond what the energy gap predicts, along a distinct axis? Second, and most decisively, a symmetry-breaking counterfactual: we apply a small distortion that lowers molecular symmetry and turns a forbidden transition allowed at nearly-fixed gap, versus a matched symmetry-preserving distortion that keeps it dark, and test whether the internal brightness signal responds to the symmetry change, not the gap; a gap-correlate model responds identically. Third, causal allowedness steering reshapes predicted absorption without shifting the gap. Metrics quantify a brightness-beyond-gap index, a symmetry-break-vs-preserve causal asymmetry, and an intensity-error failure predictor. Either outcome sharpens whether deployed optical-property models represent selection rules or are blind to them—critical for photochemistry and materials discovery.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 -- transition brightness is decodable along an axis distinct from the energy gap): Tests clause (a): oscillator strength (brightness) is decodable from internal representations on an axis distinct from the HOMO-LUMO gap. Data: QM8 (an existing set used as is; 21,786 molecules with TD-DFT excitation energies and oscillator strengths for the lowest transitions) plus QM9-spectra; from these we curate a diagnostic subset of ~500 high-symmetry / near-symmetric molecules (centrosymmetric species, symmetric aromatics) that host Laporte/parity-forbidden transitions, chosen because forbidden-vs-allowed pairs at matched gap are the decisive cases. For each low-lying transition we record excitation energy (gap), oscillator strength f, spin/symmetry-forbidden class, and point group. Model: a 3D atomistic FM (Uni-Mol or MACE latents, ~few-x10M parameters) and a SMILES/graph FM (ChemBERTa-2, ~46-125M parameters), public weights, frozen; only linear probes trained. Probes: ridge (f, gap) and logistic (forbidden vs allowed), L2 via 5-fold CV, standardized features, 5 seeds with scaffold-grouped splits (no molecular scaffold shared across splits); report mean +/- SD. Systems compared: (i) a gap-only baseline predicting f from excitation energy; (ii) Brightness-Beyond-Gap Index = probe R^2 for f from the representation minus the gap-only R^2, after residualizing the gap-predictable component; (iii) the angle between the recovered gap direction and the recovered brightness direction. Decisive metric first: Brightness-Beyond-Gap Index. Convincing: Index >= 0.10 R^2 (95% bootstrap CI over held-out scaffolds excluding 0, >=4/5 seeds) AND gap-vs-brightness axis angle >= 60 degrees (distinct axes), holding on the matched-gap forbidden/allowed subset. Refute: Index <= 0.02 and angle <= 20 degrees (brightness collapses onto the gap). Indeterminate band 0.02-0.10 R^2 or angle 20-60 degrees (stated before the data): unresolved -- some gap-independent brightness signal but not a cleanly separate axis; we report it and do not treat clause (a) as established. A negative result means the model encodes intensity as a gap correlate, contradicting clause (a).

Experiment 2 (H2 -- a symmetry-breaking edit brightens a forbidden transition while a matched symmetry-preserving edit does not): Tests clause (b), the decisive counterfactual. Data: ~150 centrosymmetric/high-symmetry molecules from the Experiment-1 diagnostic subset each hosting a parity-forbidden dark transition; for every molecule we construct one symmetry-breaking distortion (lowers the point group; by selection rules turns the transition allowed at nearly-fixed gap) and one symmetry-preserving control distortion at matched RMSD (transition stays dark). Both edits are constructed and verified by recomputing TD-DFT oscillator strengths and confirming the gap moves <5%. Model: the same frozen FMs, plus (where available) an excited-state/optical head for a direct brightness readout; inference-only, probe from Experiment 1 reused. Systems compared: symmetry-breaking edit vs matched symmetry-preserving edit, per molecule. Decisive metric first: Symmetry-Break-vs-Preserve Causal Asymmetry = |change in the internal brightness signal under the symmetry-breaking edit| / |change under the matched symmetry-preserving edit|. Convincing: median asymmetry >= 3 across the ~150 molecules with the brightness signal rising under symmetry breaking in >=70% of cases and bootstrap-CI lower bound > 1.5. Refute: asymmetry in [0.7, 1.5] (both edits move the signal similarly -- a gap correlate). Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared up front): partial support, reported as a qualified positive. Matched RMSD and verified near-fixed gap make any generic off-distribution effect shared. A negative result means brightness does not respond to the symmetry change that the selection rule requires, contradicting clause (b).

Experiment 3 (H2 -- parity/spin double dissociation): Strengthens clause (b) by checking the model reproduces the correct qualitative selection-rule structure, distinguishing two mechanisms an intensity-from-gap model cannot. Data: from the diagnostic subset, ~150 parity-forbidden (Laporte) transitions in centrosymmetric molecules and ~100 spin-forbidden (singlet-triplet) transitions, each with the symmetry-breaking edit from Experiment 2 (reused); reference TD-DFT confirms parity-forbidden transitions brighten under symmetry lowering while spin-forbidden ones stay dark. Model: frozen FMs with the brightness probe/head. Systems compared: parity-forbidden vs spin-forbidden classes under identical geometric symmetry breaking; shuffled-symmetry-label control. Decisive metric first: double-dissociation score = fraction of parity-forbidden transitions correctly predicted to brighten minus the fraction of spin-forbidden transitions incorrectly predicted to brighten. Convincing: score >= 0.5 (parity brightens, spin does not) with the shuffled-label control near 0. Refute: score <= 0.1 (the model cannot separate the two rules). Indeterminate band 0.1-0.5 (declared in advance): partial dissociation, reported without claiming a mechanistic separation. A negative result means the model does not distinguish parity from spin selection rules, weakening clause (b).

Experiment 4 (H3 -- steering an allowedness direction changes predicted absorption without moving the gap): Tests clause (c). Data: bright-vs-dark transition pairs and symmetric/symmetry-broken molecule pairs (from the sets above) used to recover the direction. Model: frozen FMs with excited-state/optical head; only the direction is fitted. We recover an 'allowedness/brightness' direction three ways -- supervised probe, SAE feature separating bright from dark, and a symmetry-broken-minus-symmetric delta -- and steer at matched L2 norm. Systems compared: (i) allowedness direction; (ii) 20 matched-norm random directions; (iii) a matched gap direction. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |predicted-absorption change under allowedness steering| / |mean change under random steering|; cross-talk = |gap shift under allowedness steering| / |gap shift under the gap direction|. Convincing: selectivity >= 3, cross-talk <= 0.2 (brightness moves, gap barely does), and the gap direction moving the gap but not brightness -- a disentangled double dissociation replicated across the three recovery methods. Refute: selectivity <= 1.5 or cross-talk >= 0.6. Indeterminate band: selectivity 1.5-3 or cross-talk 0.2-0.6 (declared before the data): entangled/partial control, reported without a clean causal claim. A negative result means allowedness is not an independently steerable axis, contradicting clause (c).

Experiment 5 (H1-H3 -- layer emergence, cross-model convergence, and selection-rule brackets): Tests robustness of clauses (a)-(c) across depth and models and places them on a spectrum. Data: QM8/QM9-spectra and the diagnostic subset (reused). Model: Uni-Mol/MACE and ChemBERTa-2, frozen; probes/directions as above. Systems compared: (i) per-layer Brightness-Beyond-Gap Index and steering selectivity; (ii) CKA between recovered allowedness subspaces across models; (iii) upper bracket = a symmetry-aware transition-dipole model computing f from symmetry by construction, lower bracket = a gap-to-intensity regressor with no symmetry access. Decisive metric first: fraction of the gap-to-mechanism bracket each model closes. Convincing: >=50% bracket closure for at least one model AND cross-model CKA >= 0.5. Refute: all models within noise of the gap-regressor lower bracket. Indeterminate band: 20-50% closure or CKA 0.3-0.5 (declared up front) -- partial/model-specific, reported without a universality claim. A negative result means no model exceeds a gap shortcut. All runs are inference-only on public FMs plus small probes/SAEs and public excited-state data, with reference TD-DFT only for the counterfactual geometries, feasible on a single GPU.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Oscillator strength and energy gap are correlated in typical datasets (accessible bright transitions dominate), making the brightness-beyond-gap separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with gap-residualization, the symmetry-breaking double-dissociation counterfactual (which holds the gap nearly fixed while varying symmetry), and the parity-vs-spin dissociation that a gap-correlate model cannot reproduce.

Constructing symmetry-breaking vs symmetry-preserving distortions with matched magnitude but different selection-rule consequences requires care with point-group assignment and verifying the intended brightness flip via reference TD-DFT; we compute reference oscillator strengths for the distorted geometries and report sensitivity to distortion magnitude and to point-group-assignment confidence.

Small geometric distortions may push conformers off the model's training distribution, confounding the symmetry-breaking response with generic out-of-distribution failure; we bound distortion RMSD, verify the gap stays nearly fixed, and compare against the matched symmetry-preserving distortion so any generic OOD effect is shared.

Many molecular FMs predict ground-state/scalar properties and may not natively output excited-state brightness; for these we probe whether the representation encodes brightness/selection-rule structure at all and prioritize models with excited-state or optical heads for the causal-steering readout, reporting per-model scope and treating scalar-only models as an informative lower bracket.

Excited-state reference data (TD-DFT oscillator strengths) is functional- and basis-set-dependent and noisy for weak transitions; we use curated consensus datasets (QM8, QM9-spectra), restrict decisive tests to well-characterized symmetric molecules, and emphasize the qualitative bright/dark flip over exact intensity magnitude.

Linear probes recovering an allowedness direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering, cross-talk controls, and random-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions—we use both probe directions and SAE features.

A negative result (models predict intensity as a gap correlate and fail the symmetry-breaking counterfactual) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting molecular/materials FMs for photochemistry, OLED/dye, and optical-materials discovery, where symmetry-forbidden dark states are a central design consideration; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether foundation models represent optical selection rules.

All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes/SAEs and public excited-state datasets (QM8, QM9-spectra), with reference TD-DFT for counterfactual geometries, keeping compute at academic scale.

Closest prior work is excited-state/oscillator-strength prediction and chemistry-FM interpretability probes, but those mostly do regression or recover ground-state features. The delta is a mechanism-defining causal test of selection rules, not just better prediction. This looks genuinely new if executed as described, and not an obvious next step from baseline property prediction.

Name: developmental_arrow_directionality_probe
Title: Which Way Is Forward? Testing Whether Single-Cell Foundation Models Represent the Irreversible Arrow of Differentiation, Not Just Cell-State Identity
Short Hypothesis: Differentiation has a defining, directional, quasi-irreversible mechanism: cells flow along lineages from high-potency progenitors to low-potency differentiated states, with transcriptional potency (entropy) decreasing monotonically and the reverse transition physically disfavored. Crucially, a static expression snapshot is directionless - RNA-velocity and trajectory tools must inject direction from splicing/metabolic-labeling signals the model never sees. We hypothesize that if a single-cell foundation model (scFM) represents the developmental-arrow mechanism rather than merely cell-state identity, then (a) the signed developmental direction between two adjacent states along a known lineage is decodable from internal representations beyond what marginal cell-state similarity predicts, (b) its internal 'developmental progression' axis reproduces the monotonic, irreversible decrease of transcriptional potency/entropy (a dose-response), and (c) an in-silico transition that moves a cell in the forward (differentiation) direction is treated differently from the equal-magnitude reverse (dedifferentiation) transition. The forward-vs-reverse asymmetry is a mechanism-defining test that identity-clustering and pseudotime-correlation cannot pass.
Related Work: RNA-velocity and trajectory-inference tools (Velocyto, scVelo, CellRank, dynamo, LatentVelo, VelvetVAE) all establish that snapshot expression is directionless: they must obtain the arrow of differentiation from EXTERNAL spliced/unspliced ratios or metabolic labeling, and Hodge-decomposition/dynamical-systems treatments formalize the directional (curl-free/gradient) structure of the velocity field. scFM interpretability instead recovers static concepts: SAE/transcoder studies (scFeatureLens 2024, Concept-SAE 2025, transcoder circuits 2025) find features matching cell types, tissues, and cell-cycle phase, and a systematic evaluation (2026) shows scGPT/Geneformer attention captures co-expression, not causal regulation. Causal single-cell VAEs (sVAE+, SAMS-VAE) learn intervention structure but are bespoke, not tests of pretrained scFMs. Crucially, no work tests whether a pretrained scFM's INTERNAL representation encodes the temporal DIRECTIONALITY and quasi-irreversibility of differentiation (the developmental arrow) from snapshot input alone, whether that direction is causally load-bearing, or uses a forward-vs-reverse transition asymmetry to separate the arrow mechanism from static cell-state identity. Because adjacent developmental states are also the most similar in expression, identity-based clustering and raw pseudotime correlation cannot arbitrate this; the signed-direction-beyond-identity probe, potency dose-response, and forward-vs-reverse counterfactual are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution.
Abstract: Single-cell foundation models (scFMs) are increasingly used to annotate cell states and infer developmental trajectories, and their internal features are known to encode cell-type identity. But differentiation is defined not by identity alone but by a directional, quasi-irreversible mechanism: cells flow from high-potency progenitors to low-potency differentiated fates, transcriptional potency decreases along the way, and the reverse transition is physically disfavored. A static expression snapshot is directionless - this is precisely why RNA-velocity tools must inject the arrow from splicing signals the model never receives - making developmental directionality an ideal, mechanism-defining probe for whether scFMs internalize developmental priors or merely cluster cell states. We probe pretrained scFMs (scGPT, Geneformer, cell2sentence) on well-characterized developmental atlases with ground-truth lineage order and pseudotime/velocity (pancreatic endocrinogenesis, hematopoiesis, dentate gyrus neurogenesis). First, a direction-beyond-identity probe: is the signed developmental direction between two adjacent lineage states decodable from internal representations beyond what marginal cell-state similarity predicts? Second, a potency dose-response: does a recovered 'developmental progression' axis reproduce the monotonic decrease of transcriptional entropy/potency, rather than tracking arbitrary cell-type labels? Third, and most decisively, a forward-vs-reverse counterfactual: an in-silico gene-program shift that moves a cell in the differentiation direction versus the equal-magnitude dedifferentiation direction should be treated asymmetrically by a mechanism-representing model. We validate causally by steering a recovered direction axis. Metrics quantify a direction-beyond-identity index, a potency-monotonicity score, and a forward-vs-reverse asymmetry. Either outcome sharpens whether deployed scFMs understand which way development runs - critical for reprogramming, regeneration, and cancer.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 -- signed developmental direction is decodable beyond cell-state similarity): Tests clause (a): the signed direction between two adjacent states along a known lineage is decodable from internal representations beyond what marginal cell-state similarity predicts. Data: three developmental atlases with established lineage order and RNA-velocity/metabolic-labeling ground truth, used as is: pancreatic endocrinogenesis (Bastidas-Ponce 2019, ~36,000 cells), mouse hematopoiesis, and dentate-gyrus neurogenesis (Hochgerner 2018, ~18,000 cells), all scVelo/CellRank-processed; per cell we record branch, ground-truth pseudotime, velocity-derived direction, and potency (CytoTRACE / expression entropy). We form ~5,000 adjacent-cell pairs per atlas along lineages plus a matched control set of unrelated-cell-type pairs. Model: scGPT (~51M parameters), Geneformer (~10-40M), cell2sentence (GPT-2-based, ~124M), public weights, frozen; only linear probes trained. Probes: logistic (signed earlier-vs-later order), L2 via 5-fold CV, 5 seeds with donor/batch-grouped splits; report mean +/- SD. Systems compared: (i) a static identity/similarity baseline predicting order from raw-expression cell-state similarity; (ii) Direction-Beyond-Identity Index = signed-order accuracy from the representation minus the similarity-baseline accuracy, after residualizing the identity-predictable component; reported separately along-lineage vs across-unrelated-types. Decisive metric first: Direction-Beyond-Identity Index (percentage points of accuracy). Convincing: Index >= 10 points along-lineage (95% bootstrap CI over held-out donors excluding 0, >=4/5 seeds) with the across-unrelated control near 0. Refute: Index <= 2 points (no directional information beyond similarity). Indeterminate band 2-10 points (stated before the data): unresolved -- weak directional signal, reported without treating clause (a) as established. A negative result means order is explained by cell-state similarity, contradicting clause (a).

Experiment 2 (H1 -- potency dose-response along the lineage): Further tests clause (a) by checking the recovered progression axis reproduces the monotonic, signed decrease of transcriptional potency, the specific directional structure similarity cannot supply. Data: the same three atlases (reused) with per-cell CytoTRACE/entropy potency. Model: frozen scFMs; we recover a 'developmental progression' direction as a supervised probe direction and as a progenitor-minus-differentiated delta. Systems compared: internal progression signal vs ground-truth potency along the lineage; shuffled-order-label control. Decisive metric first: Spearman correlation between the internal progression signal and ground-truth potency, plus a monotonicity fraction (share of consecutive lineage steps with the correct sign). Convincing: |Spearman| >= 0.5 AND monotonicity >= 0.75, with the shuffled control near 0. Refute: |Spearman| <= 0.2 or monotonicity <= 0.55 (non-monotonic / identity-tracking). Indeterminate band: Spearman 0.2-0.5 or monotonicity 0.55-0.75 (declared up front) -- partial gradient, reported as qualified. A negative result means the axis does not reproduce the potency gradient, weakening clause (a).

Experiment 3 (H2 -- forward vs reverse in-silico transition asymmetry): Tests clause (b), the decisive counterfactual: a forward (differentiation) edit is treated differently from an equal-magnitude reverse (dedifferentiation) edit. Data: along each lineage we build ~2,000 forward edits (shift expression toward the next, more-differentiated real neighbor by up/down-regulating lineage-driver genes) and matched-magnitude reverse edits (toward the previous progenitor neighbor), using real neighboring-state profiles as targets; plus a non-developmental cell-cycle axis (cyclic, reversible) as a double-dissociation control. Model: frozen scFMs, including a generative/masked head where available (scGPT) for plausibility. Systems compared: forward vs reverse edit (matched magnitude), and developmental vs cell-cycle axis. Decisive metric first: Forward-vs-Reverse Asymmetry = |model response to the forward edit| / |model response to the reverse edit| (response = change in internal progression signal and in masked-gene/next-state prediction). Convincing: median asymmetry >= 3 along developmental lineages with the reverse edit flagged as more anomalous/implausible in >=70% of cases, AND the cell-cycle control asymmetry within [0.7, 1.5] (vanishes) -- a double dissociation. Refute: developmental asymmetry in [0.7, 1.5] (forward and reverse treated symmetrically). Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared before the data): partial arrow, reported as qualified. Matched magnitude makes any generic off-distribution effect shared. A negative result means the model treats differentiation and dedifferentiation symmetrically, contradicting clause (b).

Experiment 4 (H2 -- branch-point directional specificity): Strengthens clause (b) at lineage bifurcations. Data: known branch points in the three atlases (reused; e.g., endocrine alpha/beta split), each with a pre-commitment progenitor and two fates. Model: frozen scFMs with the progression axis from Experiment 2. Systems compared: internal ordering of progenitor vs both fates, against a similarity-collapse baseline. Decisive metric first: fraction of branch points where the internal direction orders the progenitor before BOTH fates without collapsing them. Convincing: >= 0.8 of branch points ordered correctly, exceeding the similarity baseline by >= 0.2. Refute: <= 0.55 (chance-like / collapsed). Indeterminate band 0.55-0.8 (declared up front): partial, reported as qualified. A negative result means the model collapses divergent fates by similarity, weakening clause (b).

Experiment 5 (H3 -- steering the progression axis produces a signed, asymmetric downstream shift): Tests clause (c). Data: progenitor-vs-differentiated pairs (reused) to recover the axis; cells along lineages as steering targets. Model: frozen scFMs; only the direction is fitted. We steer the recovered developmental-progression axis at matched L2 norm in the forward vs reverse sense. Systems compared: (i) progression axis; (ii) 20 matched-norm random directions; (iii) a static identity-difference direction. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |downstream cell-state/potency readout shift under progression steering| / |mean shift under random directions|, together with sign consistency (forward steering lowers potency, reverse raises it). Convincing: selectivity >= 3 with correct signed, asymmetric effect, and the identity-difference direction failing to reproduce it, across probe and delta recovery. Refute: selectivity <= 1.5 or no sign asymmetry. Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared before the data): partial causal traction, reported without a strong claim; superposed encoding is the leading alternative. A negative result means the axis is not causally wired to differentiation, contradicting clause (c).

Experiment 6 (H1-H3 -- layer emergence, cross-model convergence, and arrow brackets): Tests robustness of clauses (a)-(c) across depth and models. Data: the three atlases (reused). Model: scGPT, Geneformer, cell2sentence, frozen; probes/directions as above. Systems compared: (i) per-layer Direction-Beyond-Identity Index and steering selectivity; (ii) CKA between recovered progression subspaces across models; (iii) upper bracket = an RNA-velocity/CellRank directional model that encodes the arrow by construction, lower bracket = a static-identity classifier with no directional access. Decisive metric first: fraction of the identity-to-arrow bracket each model closes. Convincing: >=50% closure for at least one model AND cross-model CKA >= 0.5. Refute: all models within noise of the static-identity lower bracket. Indeterminate band: 20-50% closure or CKA 0.3-0.5 (declared up front) -- partial/model-specific, no universality claim. A negative result means no scFM exceeds identity clustering. All runs are inference-only on public models plus small probes and public velocity-annotated atlases, feasible on a single GPU.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Adjacent developmental states are the most similar in expression, so directional signal is entangled with cell-state identity, making the direction-beyond-identity separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with identity/similarity residualization, the forward-vs-reverse counterfactual (which holds edit magnitude fixed and varies only direction), and the cell-cycle (reversible) double-dissociation control.

Ground-truth developmental direction itself comes from RNA velocity/metabolic labeling, which is noisy and can be unreliable in some regions; we use datasets where velocity/pseudotime is well-validated (pancreas, hematopoiesis, dentate gyrus), cross-check with independent potency (CytoTRACE) and known lineage biology, and report sensitivity to ground-truth confidence.

The forward/reverse in-silico edits are synthetic and may push profiles off the model's data distribution, confounding the asymmetry with generic out-of-distribution behavior; we mitigate by matching forward and reverse edit magnitudes (so any generic OOD effect is shared), using real neighboring-state profiles as edit targets where possible, and reporting edit-magnitude sensitivity.

scFMs use different tokenizations (rank-based for Geneformer, value-binned for scGPT, sentence for cell2sentence) and may pool to a single cell embedding, limiting fine-grained edits; we document each model's input scheme, prioritize models exposing usable per-cell representations, and report per-model caveats.

Linear probes recovering a progression direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/identity-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions - we use both probe directions and delta-representations.

A negative result (scFMs cluster cell states but do not represent the directional, irreversible arrow of differentiation, treating forward and reverse transitions symmetrically) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting scFMs for trajectory inference, reprogramming, regeneration, and cancer dedifferentiation - precisely the settings where getting the arrow backwards is catastrophic; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether single-cell foundation models represent the developmental arrow.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and public developmental atlases with velocity/pseudotime ground truth, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: le_chatelier_shift_probe
Title: Does the Model Shift the Right Way? Testing Whether Reaction Foundation Models Represent Le Chatelier Equilibrium Shifts, Not Just Static Reaction Identity
Short Hypothesis: Chemical equilibrium has an exactly-known, directional, relational mechanism: Le Chatelier's principle plus the law of mass action say that when an equilibrium is stressed (add/remove a species, change pressure/volume, change temperature for an exo/endothermic reaction), the equilibrium shifts in a specific, sign-determined direction to counteract the stress, with a magnitude set by the reaction quotient relative to K. We hypothesize that if a reaction/thermodynamics foundation model represents this mechanism rather than static reaction identity, then (a) the SIGNED shift direction under a given stress is decodable from internal representations beyond what the reaction's identity/stoichiometry alone predicts, (b) a stress-direction counterfactual - adding versus removing the same species, or the same temperature change for an exothermic versus endothermic reaction - flips the internal shift signal as thermodynamics dictates, whereas a stress that leaves the equilibrium unchanged (e.g., adding an inert species at constant volume, or a pressure change for a reaction with equal moles on both sides) does not, and (c) steering a recovered 'shift-direction' axis causally moves predicted product/reactant balance in the Le-Chatelier-consistent direction. The add-vs-remove and exo-vs-endo counterfactuals are exact, mechanism-defining tests that static reaction-identity correlation cannot pass.
Related Work: Two lines bracket the gap. (1) Reaction/thermodynamics ML - equilibrium-constant predictors, reaction-thermodynamics models, and chemistry foundation models (SMI-TED/FM4M, ChemBERTa, reaction transformers) - predict K, dG, or products but are judged by regression/accuracy, not by whether they internalize the directional Le Chatelier response to a stress. (2) Chemistry-model interpretability - SAEs on chemistry LMs ('Unveiling Latent Knowledge', 2025) recovering static substructure/physicochemical/pharmacological features, attribution for solubility (2024), design-choice/latent-space studies (2025), and the SchNet reaction-analogy work (2025) showing constant static 'reaction vectors' (alcohol->carbonyl = '-H2') - all recover static, non-relational structure. Physics-model steering (Physics Steering 2025; emergent energy features 2025) recovers and steers single scalar quantities, not a directional equilibrium-shift response. Crucially, no work tests whether a model internally represents the RELATIONAL, directional Le Chatelier mechanism - that stressing an equilibrium produces a sign-determined shift - whether that shift representation is causally load-bearing, or uses an add-vs-remove / exo-vs-endo counterfactual to separate the mechanism from static reaction identity. The reaction-analogy work is the closest, but it encodes a fixed transformation, not the response of an equilibrium to a perturbation. Our shift-direction-beyond-identity probe, stress-direction counterfactual, and causal shift-axis steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution.
Abstract: Chemical equilibrium is governed by one of chemistry's most fundamental and exactly-known relational mechanisms: Le Chatelier's principle and the law of mass action, which dictate that stressing an equilibrium - by adding or removing a species, changing pressure/volume, or changing temperature - shifts it in a specific, sign-determined direction to counteract the stress. The direction is not a property of the reaction alone but of the reaction-and-stress together: the same reaction shifts toward products when a reactant is added and toward reactants when it is removed. This makes Le Chatelier an ideal, mechanism-defining probe for whether reaction foundation models learn equilibrium mechanism or merely static reaction identity. We probe pretrained reaction/thermodynamics and chemistry foundation models on curated and synthetic equilibrium systems where the equilibrium constant and the true shift direction under each stress are exactly known. First, a shift-direction-beyond-identity probe: is the signed equilibrium-shift direction under a given stress decodable from internal representations beyond what the reaction's identity and stoichiometry predict? Second, and most decisively, a stress-direction counterfactual: adding versus removing the same species (opposite shifts) and the same temperature change applied to an exothermic versus endothermic reaction (opposite shifts) should flip the internal shift signal, while an equilibrium-neutral stress (inert-species addition, or pressure change for equal-mole reactions) should not. Third, causal steering of a recovered shift-direction axis. Metrics quantify a shift-beyond-identity index, a stress-direction causal asymmetry, and a mass-action dose-response test. Either outcome sharpens whether reaction models represent the equilibrium mechanism that underlies reaction design and process chemistry.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 -- signed shift direction is decodable beyond static reaction identity): Tests clause (a): the SIGNED shift direction under a given stress is decodable from internal representations beyond what reaction identity/stoichiometry alone predicts. Data: (i) a constructed set of 2,000 synthetic gas/solution equilibria with specified stoichiometry, K, and reaction-enthalpy sign, so the shift direction under each add/remove/pressure/temperature stress is analytically known; and (ii) ~200 curated real equilibria (acid-base, esterification/hydrolysis, Haber-type, solubility) with literature K and dH signs. We encode each (reaction, current-composition, stress) case in each model's native input format. Synthetic data is generated because no public dataset pairs reactions with signed shift labels across matched stresses; real cases provide a transfer check. Model: a masked chemistry FM (SMI-TED / FM4M, ~10-100M parameters), a reaction transformer, and (where available) a reaction-thermodynamics/equilibrium-constant predictor, public weights, frozen; only linear probes trained. Probes: logistic (signed shift direction), L2 via 5-fold CV, 5 seeds with reaction-family-grouped splits; report mean +/- SD. Systems compared: (i) a static-identity baseline predicting shift direction from reaction identity/stoichiometry alone (which cannot resolve add-vs-remove); (ii) Shift-Beyond-Identity Index = signed-shift accuracy from the representation minus the static-identity accuracy, after residualizing the identity-predictable component. Decisive metric first: Shift-Beyond-Identity Index (accuracy points). Convincing: Index >= 10 points (95% bootstrap CI over held-out families excluding 0, >=4/5 seeds). Refute: Index <= 2 points. Indeterminate band 2-10 points (stated before the data): unresolved -- some stress-conditioned signal but not enough to claim the mechanism; reported as such. A negative result means the model carries only static reaction identity, contradicting clause (a). Note: models that ingest no stress/composition are, by construction, an informative lower bracket that cannot exceed the baseline; we report per model how stress is supplied.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- add-vs-remove and exo-vs-endo stress-direction counterfactual): Tests clause (b), the decisive counterfactual. Data: from the synthetic set (reused) we form matched stress pairs holding the reaction fixed -- add a reactant vs remove the same reactant (opposite shift), and the same temperature increase applied to an exothermic vs an endothermic reaction (opposite shift); ~1,000 pairs per stress type. Model: the frozen chemistry/reaction-thermodynamics FMs that ingest reaction conditions/composition (prioritized); condition-agnostic models reported as the lower bracket. Systems compared: one stress direction vs its opposite; shuffled-stress control. Decisive metric first: fraction of pairs whose internal shift signal flips sign correctly across add/remove and across exo/endo. Convincing: correct sign-flip fraction >= 0.8 across both counterfactuals with the shuffled-stress control near 0.5. Refute: sign-flip fraction <= 0.6 (stress-agnostic signal). Indeterminate band 0.6-0.8 (declared up front): partial, reported as qualified. Matched stress magnitude makes any generic off-distribution effect shared. A negative result means the internal signal does not respond to stress direction as thermodynamics dictates, contradicting clause (b).

Experiment 3 (H2 -- equilibrium-neutral double dissociation and mass-action dose-response): Strengthens clause (b) with the neutral-stress control and the magnitude law, both of which a static or stress-agnostic model fails. Data: from the synthetic set (reused), equilibrium-neutral stresses that do NOT shift equilibrium (inert species added at constant volume; pressure change for equal-moles-of-gas reactions) paired with genuine stresses; plus a dose ladder varying stress magnitude with the mass-action-predicted shift (reaction quotient vs K) as ground truth. Model: frozen FMs with the shift probe. Systems compared: genuine vs equilibrium-neutral stress; increasing stress magnitude. Decisive metric first: (i) genuine-vs-neutral shift-signal magnitude ratio, and (ii) Spearman correlation between internal shift-signal magnitude and the mass-action-predicted shift. Convincing: ratio >= 3 (neutral stresses near-zero signal) AND dose-response Spearman >= 0.5 with correct saturation, shuffled-magnitude control near 0. Refute: ratio in [0.7, 1.5] OR Spearman <= 0.2. Indeterminate band: ratio 1.5-3 or Spearman 0.2-0.5 (declared before the data) -- partial, reported as qualified. A negative result means the model cannot separate real from neutral stresses or track magnitude, weakening clause (b).

Experiment 4 (H3 -- steering a shift-direction axis moves predicted balance the Le-Chatelier way): Tests clause (c). Data: add-stress-vs-remove-stress case pairs (reused) to recover the axis. Model: frozen FMs; only the direction is fitted, recovered as a supervised probe direction and as an add-minus-remove delta, steered at matched L2 norm. Systems compared: (i) shift-direction axis; (ii) 20 matched-norm random directions; (iii) a static-reaction-identity direction. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |predicted product-reactant balance shift under shift-axis steering| / |mean shift under random directions|, with correct Le-Chatelier sign. Convincing: selectivity >= 3, correct sign, and the identity direction producing no consistent shift, across probe and delta recovery. Refute: selectivity <= 1.5. Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared up front): partial causal traction, reported without a strong claim. A negative result means the axis is not causally wired to the predicted balance, contradicting clause (c).

Experiment 5 (H1-H3 -- layer emergence, cross-model convergence, and mechanism brackets): Tests robustness of clauses (a)-(c). Data: synthetic and curated real equilibria (reused). Model: the chemistry and reaction-thermodynamics FMs, frozen; probes/directions as above. Systems compared: (i) per-layer Shift-Beyond-Identity Index and steering selectivity; (ii) CKA between recovered shift-direction subspaces; (iii) upper bracket = an explicit mass-action/equilibrium solver that computes shifts by construction, lower bracket = a static reaction-identity classifier with no stress access; plus synthetic-vs-real agreement. Decisive metric first: fraction of the identity-to-mechanism bracket each model closes. Convincing: >=50% closure for at least one model AND CKA >= 0.5 AND synthetic-real sign agreement >= 0.8. Refute: all models within noise of the static-identity lower bracket. Indeterminate band: 20-50% closure or CKA 0.3-0.5 (declared up front) -- partial/model-specific. A negative result means no model exceeds static identity. All runs are inference-only on public FMs plus small probes and synthetic/public equilibrium data, feasible on a single GPU.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Reaction identity and shift behavior are entangled in real data, making the shift-beyond-identity separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with identity-residualization, the add-vs-remove and exo-vs-endo counterfactuals (which hold the reaction fixed and vary only the stress), the equilibrium-neutral double-dissociation control, and mass-action dose-response tests a static model cannot pass.

Most chemistry FMs take a single molecule or reaction as input and no explicit stress/composition, so 'applying a stress' must be operationalized via the model's input format (e.g., altered composition tokens, temperature/pressure conditioning where available, or reaction-condition inputs for reaction-thermodynamics models); we prioritize models that ingest reaction conditions or composition, clearly report per-model how stress is supplied, and treat condition-agnostic models as an informative lower bracket that by construction cannot represent shifts.

Synthetic equilibria give exact control but may differ from what models saw in training, risking off-distribution behavior; we cross-validate with curated real equilibria (acid-base, esterification, Haber) and report sensitivity to synthetic-vs-real agreement.

Real equilibrium constants and enthalpy signs are condition-dependent and noisy; we use well-characterized reactions, restrict decisive tests to cases with confident K and dH signs, and report sensitivity to thermodynamic-data confidence.

Linear probes recovering a shift-direction axis do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/identity-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions - we use both probe directions and delta-representations.

A negative result (models encode static reaction identity but not the directional Le Chatelier shift, failing the stress-direction counterfactual) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting reaction models for reaction design, yield optimization, and process chemistry - where predicting how conditions shift equilibrium is central; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether reaction foundation models represent Le Chatelier equilibrium shifts.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and public/synthetic equilibrium datasets, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: orphan_feature_triage
Title: Signal or Artifact? A Prospective, Externally-Grounded Protocol for Triaging Unannotated Discovery Features in Scientific Foundation Models
Short Hypothesis: Sparse-autoencoder features of scientific foundation models that do NOT map onto any existing annotation ('orphan features') fall into two separable classes: (a) genuine latent scientific signals that predict independent, held-out external measurements the model never saw, and (b) technical/dataset artifacts. We hypothesize these two classes are distinguishable in advance by a small set of cheap, model-internal and cross-modal criteria - external-modality predictivity, cross-dataset stability, and causal ablation specificity - yielding a reusable triage protocol that turns interpretability from post-hoc confirmation into prospective, validated discovery.
Related Work: A wave of dictionary-learning work extracts SAE features from scientific FMs and validates them against KNOWN annotations: InterPLM (2024) and Adams et al. (2025) on protein LMs, Discovering Interpretable Biological Concepts in scRNA-seq FMs (2025), SAEs Reveal Interpretable Features in Single-Cell FMs (2025), ICFL on microscopy FMs (2024), and Open-Ended Visual Scientific Discovery with SAEs (2025). All of these note that MANY features do NOT map to existing annotations, and InterPLM/ICFL propose auto-interpretation to label them - but auto-interpretation still hallucinates and cannot distinguish a real undiscovered signal from an artifact. The Pleiades Alzheimer's biomarker study (2026) shows interpretability CAN surface a genuinely novel biomarker class (fragmentomics), but it is a single bespoke success validated by heavy downstream work, not a general triage rule. 'On the definition and importance of interpretability in SciML' (2025) argues that without prior knowledge one cannot tell whether a discovered structure is meaningful. The critical, unaddressed gap is a GENERAL, PROSPECTIVE decision procedure that, for an arbitrary orphan (unannotated) feature, predicts whether it is a real latent signal or an artifact BEFORE expensive follow-up. Our protocol - using cross-modal external ground truth the model never ingested plus cross-dataset stability and causal ablation as a triage classifier - is that missing piece, and is distinct from all prior annotation-matching and single-case discovery work.
Abstract: Sparse autoencoders now routinely extract thousands of interpretable features from scientific foundation models of proteins, cells, and images, and the field has begun to celebrate features that align with known biological concepts. But every such study reports a large fraction of 'orphan' features that map onto no existing annotation, and interpretability's promise for discovery hinges precisely on these: some are undiscovered scientific signals, others are dataset artifacts (batch effects, sequencing depth, staining, plate position), and current practice - auto-interpretation by a stronger LLM - cannot reliably tell them apart. We propose the first general, prospective triage protocol that decides, for an arbitrary unannotated feature, whether it is a genuine latent signal or an artifact, and validates the decision against independent evidence the model never saw. Working with public single-cell RNA-seq foundation models (scGPT, Geneformer) and protein language models (ESM-2), we train SAEs, remove features matching known annotations, and score the remaining orphans on three cheap criteria: (1) external-modality predictivity - does the feature predict a held-out measurement from a DIFFERENT modality/assay the model was never trained on (e.g., a scRNA feature predicting matched CITE-seq surface-protein levels, or an ESM-2 feature predicting an experimental deep-mutational-scanning quantity)? (2) cross-dataset stability - does an equivalent feature reappear across independent datasets/labs? (3) causal ablation specificity - does ablating it selectively change model outputs for a coherent biological subset, not diffusely? We test whether these three criteria jointly separate a curated set of known-signal orphans from planted-artifact orphans, calibrate a triage classifier, and then apply it prospectively to surface and externally confirm candidate novel signals. The result is a reusable instrument that converts interpretability from confirmation into validated discovery.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 -- feature extraction, orphan set, and a two-class development set of known-signal vs planted-artifact orphans): Establishes the substrate and the ground-truth labels that clauses (a)/(b) and the triage claim are tested on -- namely that orphan SAE features split into genuine latent scientific signals and technical/dataset artifacts. Data: two scRNA-seq FMs (scGPT ~51M and Geneformer ~10-40M or scFoundation) and a protein LM (ESM-2 650M), public weights, frozen (inference-only); SAEs are the only trainable objects. We train TopK SAEs (dictionary width 16x hidden dim, k=32, Adam lr 1e-4, up to ~1e8 token-activations, 3 SAE seeds) on one hidden layer of each model, following InterPLM/single-cell SAE recipes. Each feature is matched to known annotations (cell type, tissue, cell-cycle phase, GO terms, secondary structure, binding sites) by activation-vs-label alignment; features with F1 or AUROC >= 0.7 are 'annotated', the remainder are ORPHANS. From the orphans we build a labeled development set: KNOWN-SIGNAL orphans = features correlating (Spearman >= 0.5) with an independently-validated signature deliberately held out of the annotation set; PLANTED-ARTIFACT orphans = features aligning (AUROC >= 0.8) with technical covariates (sequencing depth, batch/lab ID, plate/well position, staining intensity, mitochondrial fraction). Target >= 100 orphans per class per model. Decisive metric first: development-set class balance and label-confidence (fraction with covariate/signature alignment above threshold). Convincing: >= 100 orphans per class per model with confident labels. If fewer than ~40 per class are recoverable for a given model, that model is reported as underpowered and excluded from the decisive triage test rather than analyzed at low power. A negative finding here (orphans do not resolve into the two labeled classes at all) would itself contradict the premise that the classes exist and are identifiable.

Experiment 2 (H1 -- Criterion 1, external-modality predictivity separates the two classes): Tests whether external-modality predictivity distinguishes genuine-signal from artifact orphans. Data: the development-set orphans from Experiment 1 (reused). scRNA case: paired CITE-seq (matched cells with ~130-200 surface-protein readouts) and multiome ATAC (existing public sets used as is); protein case: an experimental deep-mutational-scanning fitness set and a mega-scale stability ddG set (existing, used as is). Model: frozen FMs and fixed SAE features; only a ridge/logistic read-out from a feature's activation to the held-out external measurement is fitted (5 seeds, cell/protein-grouped splits). Systems compared: each orphan's cross-modal predictive R^2/AUROC residualized against the matched ANNOTATED features, known-signal vs planted-artifact. Decisive metric first: AUROC of Criterion-1 score for separating known-signal from planted-artifact orphans. Convincing: separation AUROC >= 0.75 with 95% bootstrap CI (over features) excluding 0.5. Refute: AUROC <= 0.6. Indeterminate band 0.6-0.75 (stated before the data): Criterion 1 is a weak-but-usable signal, retained only as one of three inputs, not a sole arbiter. A negative result means external-modality predictivity does not separate the classes, weakening the triage protocol.

Experiment 3 (H1 -- Criterion 2, cross-dataset stability separates the two classes): Tests whether cross-dataset stability distinguishes the classes. Data: independent datasets from different labs/protocols for each modality (existing public sets); we train independent SAEs (same recipe) on each and match features across dictionaries by activation-correlation and matched top-activating examples. Model: frozen FMs; SAEs trainable. Systems compared: cross-dataset stability score of known-signal vs planted-artifact orphans (genuine signals expected stable; artifacts dataset-specific, or, if stable, covariate-aligned and caught by Criterion 3). Decisive metric first: AUROC of Criterion-2 score for class separation. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.75 (bootstrap CI over features excluding 0.5). Refute: AUROC <= 0.6. Indeterminate band 0.6-0.75 (declared up front): weak-but-usable, kept as one of three inputs. We report robustness to SAE width/k because feature splitting/merging can blur matching. A negative result means stability does not separate the classes, weakening the protocol.

Experiment 4 (H1 -- Criterion 3, causal ablation specificity separates the two classes): Tests whether ablation specificity distinguishes the classes. Data: development-set orphans (reused). Model: frozen FMs; we ablate each orphan feature in the SAE reconstruction and measure the induced change in downstream outputs, bounding edits and comparing to matched random-feature ablations. Systems compared: specificity index = concentration of the ablation effect on a coherent biological subset (cell type / protein family) vs diffuse or technical-covariate-aligned change, known-signal vs planted-artifact. Decisive metric first: AUROC of Criterion-3 score for class separation. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.75 (bootstrap CI over features excluding 0.5). Refute: AUROC <= 0.6. Indeterminate band 0.6-0.75 (declared before the data): weak-but-usable, one of three inputs. A negative result means ablation specificity does not separate the classes, weakening the protocol.

Experiment 5 (H1 -- triage classifier calibrates and beats the LLM auto-interpretation default): Tests the core claim that the three cheap criteria JOINTLY yield a reusable triage instrument, and that it beats the current default. Data: development-set orphans with the three criterion scores (reused). Model: a logistic-regression triage classifier on the three scores (the only fitted model), with leave-one-model-family-out and leave-one-modality-out cross-validation to test generality; per-criterion ablations to see which carries the signal. Baseline system: LLM auto-interpretation (labeling top-activating examples) confidence used as a predictor of genuine-vs-artifact status. Decisive metric first: cross-validated AUROC of the triage classifier separating known-signal from planted-artifact orphans. Convincing: triage AUROC >= 0.8 that generalizes across held-out model families/modalities (drop <= 0.1) AND exceeds the LLM-auto-interpretation baseline AUROC by >= 0.15. Refute: triage AUROC <= 0.6 or no improvement over the LLM baseline. Indeterminate band 0.6-0.8 (declared up front): a partial instrument -- reported with its precision/recall and error analysis, not advanced as a validated triage rule. A negative result means the cheap criteria do not jointly separate the classes better than the current default, contradicting the central hypothesis.

Experiment 6 (H2 -- prospective, externally-confirmed discovery): Tests the claim that the calibrated triage turns interpretability into prospective, validated discovery -- that top-ranked unlabeled orphans confirm against external evidence not used in triage. Data: the remaining UNLABELED orphans (held out of Experiments 2-5); external confirmation sources not used in triage -- a newer/independent database for enrichment, a matched-cell external assay, and a held-out DMS set. Model: the frozen triage classifier from Experiment 5 applied to unlabeled orphans; no further fitting. Systems compared: confirmation rate of the top-ranked predicted 'genuine signals' vs a random-orphan baseline. Decisive metric first: discovery precision = fraction of top-K predicted-genuine orphans that externally confirm, relative to the random-orphan baseline rate. Convincing: top-K confirmation rate >= 2x the random-orphan baseline with a 95% CI excluding parity, plus 2-3 externally-confirmed novel-signal case studies. Refute: confirmation rate within noise of the random baseline. Indeterminate band: 1.2x-2x baseline (declared before the data) -- suggestive prospective value that does not yet establish the triage as a discovery instrument; reported as such. A negative result means the triage does not prospectively surface genuine signals, contradicting the discovery claim. All work is inference-only on public FMs plus academic-scale SAE training and public paired datasets, feasible on a single GPU.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The 'known-signal vs planted-artifact' development labels may be imperfect; some presumed artifacts could carry biology and vice versa. We mitigate by using clearly technical covariates (depth, batch, plate) for artifacts and independently-validated signatures for signals, and report sensitivity to label noise.

Paired cross-modal data (CITE-seq/multi-omic matched cells, DMS with sequence) is limited in quantity and coverage, which constrains Criterion 1; we use the best available public paired datasets and treat cross-modal predictivity as one of three criteria rather than the sole arbiter.

Some genuine signals may be dataset-specific (cross-dataset stability fails) and some artifacts may be stable across labs; the three criteria are designed to be complementary so no single failure is decisive, but the triage classifier may still misclassify edge cases - we report calibration and error analysis rather than claim perfect separation.

SAE features can be split/merged across dictionaries, complicating cross-dataset matching; we use matched-top-example and activation-correlation matching and report robustness to SAE hyperparameters and width.
Ablation in SAE reconstruction may push activations off-manifold; we bound edits and report specificity relative to matched random-feature ablations.

External confirmation of prospectively-surfaced novel signals is inherently harder to guarantee within one paper; we frame the contribution primarily as a validated TRIAGE INSTRUMENT (evaluated on the development set with ground truth) plus a small number of externally-confirmed case studies, so the paper stands even if only a few novel signals confirm.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus academic-scale SAE training and public paired datasets, keeping compute feasible for an academic lab.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims: (1) a new problem framing for unannotated SAE “orphan” features in scientific foundation models; (2) a prospective triage protocol to predict signal vs artifact before follow-up; (3) the mechanism uses cheap criteria—external-modality predictivity, cross-dataset stability, and causal ablation specificity; (4) novelty is mainly in the decision procedure and prospective validation, not in SAE extraction itself. Relative to prior work, this is a non-trivial step beyond post-hoc annotation matching and one-off discovery cases. Closest prior family is SAE-based interpretability in protein/single-cell/scientific FMs plus LLM auto-labeling of features; the actual delta is a reusable, externally grounded classifier for orphan-feature triage and prospective confirmation.
