Name: space_group_absence_probe
Title: Forbidden Reflections: Testing Whether Crystal Foundation Models Represent Space-Group Symmetry Operations and Their Systematic-Absence Selection Rules, Not Just Atomic Coordinate Statistics
Short Hypothesis: Crystal structure is governed by an exactly-known discrete-group mechanism: the crystallographic space group, whose symmetry operations (screw axes, glide planes, centering) impose exact selection rules on diffraction — systematic absences (certain reflections have identically zero intensity) — and fix atomic multiplicities/degeneracies via Wyckoff positions. These are relational consequences of the group operations, not readable from any single atom's coordinates. We hypothesize that if a crystal foundation model fed only raw atomic positions (no symmetry labels) represents the space-group mechanism rather than coordinate statistics, then (a) space-group symmetry class and systematic-absence structure are decodable from internal representations beyond what local coordinate/composition features predict, (b) a symmetry-breaking counterfactual — a tiny displacement that lifts a systematic absence (turns a forbidden reflection allowed) at nearly-fixed geometry — shifts the internal symmetry signal, whereas a symmetry-preserving displacement of matched magnitude does not, and (c) steering a recovered symmetry-operation direction causally reshapes symmetry-dependent predictions. The absence-lifting vs symmetry-preserving counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that coordinate-magnitude correlation cannot pass.
Related Work: Two lines bracket the gap. (1) Symmetry is BUILT IN by construction: space-group-equivariant generative models (SGEquiDiff 2025, Space Group Conditional Flow Matching 2025, DiffCSP++ 2024) and equivariant property predictors constrain outputs to obey the group by design; they never ask whether a symmetry-agnostic model internally discovers it. (2) Space group is PREDICTED as a supervised label from XRD patterns (Suzuki 2020; MSDN 2020; contrastive powder-XRD 2025) or from composition (Cosy 2024) — these are classifiers, not tests of what a coordinate-based foundation model internally encodes. Interpretability of crystal models (CGCNN interpretability 2018 extracting site energies; Site-Net attention 2022; 'Comparing latent features of uMLIPs' 2025; my own periodic-law and convex-hull probes) recovers pointwise/energetic or generic latent structure. 'On the Symmetries of Deep Learning Models and their Internal Representations' (2022) and 'Interpreting Equivariant Representations' (2024) analyze architectural (weight-space) symmetry, not whether a model represents the DATA's crystallographic space group. Crucially, no work tests whether a general crystal FM's internal representation encodes the space-group OPERATIONS and their exact systematic-absence selection rules, whether that representation is causally load-bearing, or uses an absence-lifting counterfactual to separate the symmetry mechanism from coordinate statistics. That relational, causal, selection-rule-grounded test is our novel contribution.
Abstract: The atomic arrangement of every crystal is organized by an exactly-known discrete-group mechanism: its crystallographic space group. The group's symmetry operations — screw axes, glide planes, and lattice centering — have precise, testable consequences: they force systematic absences (specific diffraction reflections are identically zero) and fix atomic multiplicities through Wyckoff positions. These are relational properties of the whole structure, invisible in any single atom's coordinates, making space-group symmetry an ideal mechanism-defining probe for whether crystal foundation models learn crystallographic mechanism or merely coordinate statistics — especially models fed only raw positions with no symmetry labels. We probe pretrained crystal foundation models (universal MLIP backbones such as MACE-MP-0 and a crystal representation FM such as CLOUD/CGCNN) on Materials Project structures with known space groups and computable structure factors. First, a symmetry-beyond-coordinates probe: are the space-group class and systematic-absence pattern decodable from internal representations beyond what local coordinate and composition features predict? Second, and most decisively, an absence-lifting counterfactual: we apply a tiny atomic displacement that breaks a symmetry operation and turns a systematically-absent (forbidden) reflection allowed, holding geometry nearly fixed, versus a symmetry-preserving displacement of matched magnitude; a mechanism-representing model must shift its internal symmetry signal for the absence-lifting edit but not the preserving one, while a coordinate-statistics model responds to displacement magnitude regardless. Third, causal steering of a recovered symmetry-operation direction. Metrics quantify a symmetry-beyond-coordinates index, an absence-lifting causal asymmetry, and a Wyckoff-multiplicity fidelity test. Either outcome sharpens whether deployed crystal models represent the symmetry that governs materials properties.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 -- space-group class and systematic-absence structure are decodable beyond local coordinate/composition features): Tests clause (a). Data: Materials Project (existing, used as is; ~150,000 relaxed inorganic structures). We draw a subset of ~30,000 structures balanced across crystal systems / the 230 space groups where possible, each with its space group, Wyckoff assignments, and computed structure factors / systematic-absence pattern (from space-group extinction rules via spglib/pymatgen). Model: a universal MLIP (MACE-MP-0 or SevenNet, foundation-scale, ~1-10M parameters) and a crystal representation FM (CGCNN / CLOUD), all ingesting raw atomic coordinates and species with NO explicit space-group input, public weights, frozen; only linear probes trained. Probes: logistic (crystal system, point group, space group; absence-pattern multi-label F1), L2 via 5-fold CV, 5 seeds with composition-grouped splits (no shared composition prototype across splits); report mean +/- SD. We probe invariant scalar channels first for equivariant MLIPs and report per-channel. Systems compared: (i) a local-coordinate/composition baseline (nearest-neighbor distances, angles, element counts) predicting the same labels; (ii) Symmetry-Beyond-Coordinates Index = model-representation decoding score (absence-pattern F1 / space-group accuracy) minus the local-feature baseline, after residualizing the coordinate-predictable component. Decisive metric first: Symmetry-Beyond-Coordinates Index. Convincing: Index >= 0.10 (F1 or accuracy) with 95% bootstrap CI over held-out compositions excluding 0, in >=4/5 seeds. Refute: Index <= 0.02. Indeterminate band 0.02-0.10 (stated before the data): unresolved -- some relational symmetry signal beyond coordinates but not enough to claim the mechanism; reported as such. A negative result means the representation carries only coordinate statistics, contradicting clause (a).

Experiment 2 (H2 -- absence-lifting vs symmetry-preserving counterfactual): Tests clause (b), the decisive counterfactual. Data: from the Experiment-1 subset (reused) we select ~500 structures with a symmetry operation producing a systematic absence (e.g., a 2_1 screw axis forcing 0k0, odd k, absent). For each we construct two equal-RMSD atomic-displacement edits: an absence-lifting edit that breaks the operation so a forbidden reflection acquires nonzero structure factor (verified by recomputing structure factors; space group lowered), and a symmetry-preserving control edit of matched RMSD that keeps the operation and the reflection absent. Model: the frozen crystal FMs; the Experiment-1 probe reused as the internal symmetry readout (plus a symmetry-dependent property head where available). Systems compared: absence-lifting vs matched symmetry-preserving edit, per structure. Decisive metric first: Absence-Lifting Causal Asymmetry = |symmetry-signal change under the absence-lifting edit| / |change under the matched symmetry-preserving edit|. Convincing: median asymmetry >= 3 over the ~500 structures with the signal moving toward lower symmetry under absence lifting in >=70% of cases and bootstrap-CI lower bound > 1.5. Refute: asymmetry in [0.7, 1.5] (responds to raw displacement, not the symmetry change). Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared up front): partial support, reported as qualified. Matched RMSD makes any generic off-distribution effect shared. A negative result means the model does not track the symmetry operation behind the absence, contradicting clause (b).

Experiment 3 (H2 -- Wyckoff-multiplicity fidelity): Strengthens clause (b) by testing whether the representation encodes symmetry-equivalent (same-Wyckoff-orbit) atoms as a coupled, degenerate set. Data: structures with high-multiplicity special positions and general positions (reused subset). Model: frozen crystal FMs exposing per-atom representations (prioritized; pooled-only models use a coarser whole-structure fallback with the caveat reported). Systems compared: perturbing one atom of a symmetry-equivalent orbit vs a general-position atom, and the induced response pattern against the Wyckoff-predicted equivalence structure; shuffled-orbit control. Decisive metric first: correlation between the model's induced response pattern and the Wyckoff-predicted equivalence structure. Convincing: correlation >= 0.5 with the shuffled-orbit control near 0. Refute: correlation <= 0.15. Indeterminate band 0.15-0.5 (declared before the data): partial multiplicity encoding, reported as qualified. A negative result means the model does not respect Wyckoff degeneracy, weakening clause (b).

Experiment 4 (H3 -- steering a symmetry-operation direction reshapes symmetry-dependent predictions): Tests clause (c). Data: high-symmetry structures and their symmetry-broken counterparts (reused) to recover the direction. Model: frozen crystal FMs; only the direction is fitted, recovered as a supervised symmetry-class probe direction and as a high-symmetry-minus-broken delta, steered at matched L2 norm on invariant channels. Systems compared: (i) symmetry direction; (ii) 20 matched-norm random directions; (iii) a coordinate-magnitude direction. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |symmetry-dependent readout change under symmetry steering| / |mean change under random directions|. A decisive sub-test: steer toward/away from centrosymmetry and check whether centrosymmetry-gated property predictions (piezoelectric/optical activity, which require non-centrosymmetry) turn on/off accordingly. Convincing: selectivity >= 3, correct sign, centrosymmetry gate flips as predicted, and the coordinate direction failing to reproduce it, across probe and delta recovery. Refute: selectivity <= 1.5 or no centrosymmetry-gate response. Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared up front): partial causal traction, reported without a strong claim. A negative result means the direction is not causally wired to symmetry-dependent predictions, contradicting clause (c).

Experiment 5 (H1-H3 -- layer emergence, cross-model convergence, and symmetry brackets): Tests robustness of clauses (a)-(c). Data: the Materials Project subset (reused). Model: MACE-MP-0/SevenNet and CGCNN/CLOUD, frozen; probes/directions as above. Systems compared: (i) per-layer Symmetry-Beyond-Coordinates Index and steering selectivity; (ii) CKA between recovered symmetry subspaces across models; (iii) upper bracket = a space-group-equivariant model (SGEquiDiff/DiffCSP++ representations) that encodes the group by construction, lower bracket = a coordinate-only classifier with no relational access. Decisive metric first: fraction of the coordinate-to-symmetry bracket each model closes. Convincing: >=50% closure for at least one model AND CKA >= 0.5. Refute: all models within noise of the coordinate-only lower bracket. Indeterminate band: 20-50% closure or CKA 0.3-0.5 (declared up front) -- partial/model-specific, no universality claim. A negative result means coordinate-based crystal FMs do not exceed coordinate statistics. All runs are inference-only on public FMs plus small probes and public Materials Project data with standard structure-factor/symmetry tools, feasible on a single GPU.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Space-group class correlates with local coordinate statistics (high-symmetry structures have characteristic bond geometries), making the symmetry-beyond-coordinates separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with coordinate-residualization, the absence-lifting counterfactual (which holds RMSD fixed and varies only the symmetry operation), the symmetry-preserving control edit, and the Wyckoff-multiplicity double dissociation.

The absence-lifting and symmetry-preserving edits are synthetic distortions; unrealistic displacements may push structures off the model's training distribution, confounding the symmetry response with generic out-of-distribution failure. We mitigate with small displacements, verify the intended absence change via recomputed structure factors, and compare edits of matched RMSD so any generic OOD effect is shared, reporting sensitivity to displacement magnitude.

Equivariant MLIP features are tensorial; probing must respect invariant vs equivariant channels. We focus probes on invariant scalar channels first and report per-channel results, and note that a strongly equivariant model may encode symmetry implicitly in a way that requires careful readout.

Some crystal FMs pool to a single structure embedding, limiting per-atom Wyckoff analysis; we prioritize models exposing per-atom representations for the multiplicity test and report pooling caveats, using whole-structure probes as a coarser fallback.

Ground-truth space-group and Wyckoff assignments from Materials Project can have tolerance-dependent ambiguity for near-symmetric structures; we use standard symmetry-finder tolerances, restrict decisive tests to unambiguous cases, and report sensitivity to the symmetry tolerance.

Linear probes recovering a symmetry direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/coordinate-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions — we use both probe directions and delta-representations.

A negative result (models encode coordinate statistics but not the space-group symmetry mechanism, failing the absence-lifting counterfactual) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting crystal foundation models for symmetry-dependent properties (ferroelectricity, piezoelectricity, optical activity, all gated by point-group/centrosymmetry) and for symmetry-aware materials discovery; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether coordinate-based crystal FMs represent crystallographic space-group operations and their systematic-absence selection rules.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and public Materials Project data with standard structure-factor/symmetry tools, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: lagrangian_pv_conservation_probe
Title: Conserved Along the Flow? Testing Whether Weather Foundation Models Represent Potential Vorticity as a Lagrangian Material Invariant, Not Just a Snapshot Field
Short Hypothesis: Potential vorticity (PV) is defined by an exactly-known relational mechanism: it is a material Lagrangian invariant, exactly conserved FOLLOWING an air parcel in adiabatic/frictionless flow, and modified only by diabatic/frictional processes in a specific, quantifiable way. A single snapshot of PV is directionless about conservation; the invariant only exists along trajectories. We hypothesize that if a weather foundation model represents this mechanism rather than storing PV as an instantaneous field, then (a) the model's internal PV signal is conserved along its OWN predicted parcel trajectories in adiabatic regions, (b) a diabatic-vs-adiabatic counterfactual makes the internal PV drift specifically where latent heating/friction act (and stay conserved elsewhere), and (c) steering a recovered 'diabatic-PV-source' direction causally injects PV anomalies in the physically-correct sense. The along-trajectory conservation and diabatic-source counterfactual are exact, mechanism-defining tests that snapshot-field decodability cannot pass.
Related Work: Weather-model interpretability recovers single instantaneous features and steers them: SAEs on GraphCast (2025) find tropical cyclones, atmospheric rivers, sea-ice; GraphDOP work (2025) shows a unified world model inferring non-local fields (jet streams) and applies FSOI data-assimilation diagnostics; Physics Steering (2025) steers vorticity/diffusion directions; 'Uncovering Emergent Physics Representations' (2025) finds steerable energy features. All recover a quantity at a point/instant. Separately, atmospheric dynamics establishes PV as a MATERIAL Lagrangian invariant (Haynes-McIntyre 1990 impermeability/conservation theorems; Lagrangian PV-tracer conservation tests 1994; PV-tracer diabatic-attribution technique 2015/2019; Wernli-Gray 2024 review of diabatic PV modification), exactly conserved along trajectories except for quantifiable diabatic/frictional sources. Crucially, no interpretability work tests whether a weather foundation model's INTERNAL representation encodes PV as a trajectory-conserved invariant with its diabatic-source structure, whether that is causally load-bearing, or uses a diabatic-vs-adiabatic counterfactual to separate the Lagrangian-conservation mechanism from a mere snapshot field. Prior work answers 'is a quantity encoded'; the material-invariant question asks 'is it conserved following the flow, and modified only by the right processes'. Our along-trajectory conservation probe, diabatic-source counterfactual, and causal PV-source steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, distinct from spatial-balance or total-integral conservation tests.
Abstract: Data-driven weather foundation models now rival physical solvers, and interpretability studies show they encode recognizable instantaneous fields such as cyclones, vorticity, and energy. But atmospheric dynamics is defined by relational invariants, chief among them potential vorticity (PV): a material Lagrangian quantity that is exactly conserved following an air parcel in adiabatic, frictionless flow, and altered only by diabatic heating and friction in a precise, attributable way. A single snapshot cannot express this conservation mechanism, which lives along trajectories, making PV an ideal mechanism-defining probe. We ask whether pretrained weather foundation models (GraphCast and Pangu-Weather) internally represent PV as a trajectory-conserved invariant rather than an instantaneous field. Using ERA5 and the model's own rollouts, we first probe whether PV is decodable from internal representations. Then, most decisively, we test along-trajectory conservation: following the model's predicted parcel trajectories, does the internal PV signal remain constant in adiabatic regions and drift only where diabatic processes act? A diabatic-vs-adiabatic counterfactual perturbs latent heating in a target region and tests whether the internal PV drift appears specifically there, with the physically-correct sign, while remote adiabatic parcels stay conserved; a spatially-scrambled control of matched magnitude should not. Finally, causal steering of a recovered diabatic-PV-source direction should inject PV anomalies in the correct sense. Metrics quantify along-trajectory conservation, a diabatic-vs-adiabatic drift asymmetry, and steering selectivity. Either outcome sharpens whether operational weather models represent the material invariant behind extratropical dynamics.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 -- the internal PV signal is conserved along the model's own predicted parcel trajectories in adiabatic regions): Tests clause (a). Data: ERA5 (existing, used as is; hourly 1940-present). We use 6-hourly winds, temperature, geopotential, and humidity for ~200 extratropical rollout cases sampled across seasons and regions (2000-2020), computing ground-truth Ertel PV on isentropic surfaces at each step, parcel trajectories integrated from the wind field, and diabatic tendencies (latent heating from moisture/precipitation, boundary-layer friction) so adiabatic vs diabatic parcels are labeled. Model: GraphCast (~37M parameters) and Pangu-Weather (~256M parameters), public weights, frozen; only linear probes trained. Probes: ridge regression to decode PV (and its constituents, absolute vorticity and static stability) from per-grid activations, L2 via 5-fold CV, 5 seeds with case-grouped splits; report mean +/- SD. Systems compared: (i) a snapshot-field baseline (PV predictable from the instantaneous field); (ii) along the model's own rollout, the drift of probed PV FOLLOWING a parcel (Lagrangian) vs the Eulerian fixed-point variance; (iii) the true Lagrangian PV (approximately constant). Decisive metric first: Lagrangian-to-Eulerian drift ratio = along-trajectory coefficient-of-variation of probed PV in adiabatic parcels divided by the Eulerian PV variability over the same segment. Convincing: ratio <= 0.5 with a 95% bootstrap CI (over cases) upper bound < 0.7, i.e. probed PV is substantially more conserved following the flow than a fixed-point view would predict, and above the reanalysis numerical-conservation floor reported as reference. Refute: ratio >= 0.9 (no better than Eulerian; PV stored as a snapshot). Indeterminate band 0.5-0.9 (stated before the data): unresolved -- partial Lagrangian conservation, reported without claiming the mechanism. A negative result means the internal PV does not conserve following the flow, contradicting clause (a).

Experiment 2 (H2 -- diabatic lawful drift along trajectories): Tests part of clause (b): where diabatic processes act, the probed PV changes along trajectories with the physically-correct sign and magnitude. Data: the same ~200 rollout cases (reused), restricted to diabatic parcels (latent-heating cores, boundary-layer friction), with the true diabatic PV source from the PV-tracer diabatic-attribution framework (PV generated below, destroyed above a heating maximum). Model: frozen GraphCast/Pangu with the Experiment-1 PV probe. Systems compared: along-trajectory probed-PV change vs the true diabatic PV source; shuffled-region control. Decisive metric first: Spearman correlation between along-trajectory probed-PV change and the true diabatic PV source, with sign-agreement fraction. Convincing: Spearman >= 0.5 AND sign agreement >= 0.7, shuffled control near 0. Refute: Spearman <= 0.2 or sign agreement <= 0.55. Indeterminate band: Spearman 0.2-0.5 or sign agreement 0.55-0.7 (declared up front) -- partial lawful drift, reported as qualified. A negative result means the model does not track diabatic PV modification, weakening clause (b).

Experiment 3 (H2 -- diabatic-vs-adiabatic counterfactual): Tests the decisive part of clause (b): a diabatic perturbation makes internal PV drift specifically where latent heating acts while remote adiabatic parcels stay conserved. Data: ~30 moist warm-conveyor-belt cyclone cases (subset of the rollout cases, reused). For each we perturb the initial state to enhance/remove latent heating in a target region, holding remote adiabatic regions fixed, and compare to a spatially-scrambled control perturbation of matched magnitude placed where it should not generate PV. Model: frozen GraphCast/Pangu, inference-only rollouts, PV probe reused. Systems compared: diabatic-region perturbation vs matched scrambled control. Decisive metric first: Diabatic-vs-Adiabatic Drift Asymmetry = |probed-PV drift in the perturbed diabatic region| / |drift under the matched control|. Convincing: median asymmetry >= 3 over the 30 cases with the correct PV dipole sign in >=70% and bootstrap-CI lower bound > 1.5, while remote adiabatic parcels retain along-trajectory conservation (Experiment-1 ratio unchanged). Refute: asymmetry in [0.7, 1.5]. Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared before the data): partial support, reported as qualified. Matched magnitude makes any generic off-distribution effect shared. A negative result means the internal PV drift is not diabatically localized, contradicting clause (b).

Experiment 4 (H3 -- steering a diabatic-PV-source direction injects the physically-correct PV dipole): Tests clause (c). Data: diabatic-vs-adiabatic parcel-state pairs (reused) to recover the direction. Model: frozen GraphCast/Pangu; only the direction is fitted, recovered as a supervised probe direction and as a diabatic-minus-adiabatic delta, steered at matched L2 norm at a target region during rollout. Systems compared: (i) diabatic-source direction; (ii) 20 matched-norm random directions; (iii) an adiabatic-advection direction. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |PV-readout/rollout dipole response under diabatic-source steering| / |mean response under random directions|, with correct dipole sign. Convincing: selectivity >= 3, correct sign, and the advection direction failing to reproduce the dipole, across probe and delta recovery. Refute: selectivity <= 1.5. Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared up front): partial causal traction, reported without a strong claim. A negative result means the direction is not causally wired to PV generation, contradicting clause (c).

Experiment 5 (H1-H3 -- layer emergence, cross-model convergence, and PV brackets): Tests robustness of clauses (a)-(c). Data: the ERA5 rollout cases (reused). Model: GraphCast and Pangu, frozen; probes/directions as above. Systems compared: (i) per-block Lagrangian-to-Eulerian drift ratio and steering selectivity; (ii) CKA between recovered PV-conservation subspaces across the two models; (iii) upper bracket = a PV-tracer diagnostic that conserves PV by construction, lower bracket = a snapshot-PV regressor with no trajectory information. Decisive metric first: fraction of the snapshot-to-Lagrangian bracket each model closes. Convincing: >=50% closure for at least one model AND CKA >= 0.5. Refute: all models within noise of the snapshot lower bracket. Indeterminate band: 20-50% closure or CKA 0.3-0.5 (declared up front) -- partial/model-specific, no convergence claim. A negative result means weather FMs store PV as a snapshot rather than a Lagrangian invariant. All runs are inference-only on public FMs plus small probes and public ERA5 data with standard PV/trajectory diagnostics, feasible on a single GPU.
Risk Factors and Limitations: PV along trajectories correlates with instantaneous field structure, making the along-trajectory-conservation-beyond-snapshot separation demanding; we mitigate by comparing Lagrangian (following-flow) drift against Eulerian variance, using the diabatic-vs-adiabatic counterfactual (which holds magnitude fixed and varies only whether diabatic processes act), and the spatially-scrambled control.

Parcel trajectories must be computed from the model's own wind field and are subject to integration error, especially at long lead times; we use short trajectory segments, standard trajectory-integration schemes, and report sensitivity to integration accuracy.

Perturbing latent heating in the initial state may push inputs off the model's training distribution, confounding the diabatic drift with generic OOD failure; we mitigate with physically-plausible perturbation magnitudes, compare against a matched-magnitude scrambled control (so any generic OOD effect is shared), and report sensitivity to perturbation strength.
GraphCast operates on an icosahedral mesh with grid-locked features; we control for grid position, aggregate along isentropic-surface parcels, and prioritize invariant scalar channels for probing.

PV is only approximately conserved numerically even in reanalysis (dynamical-core non-conservation is comparable to physical processes, per the PV-tracer literature); we restrict adiabatic conservation tests to regions and lead times where numerical PV conservation is well-controlled and report the reanalysis conservation floor as a reference.

Linear probes recovering a PV/diabatic-source direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/advection-direction controls, though distributed encodings may blur single-direction interventions.

A negative result (models store PV as a snapshot field but do not conserve it following the flow, failing the along-trajectory and diabatic-source tests) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting weather foundation models for extratropical cyclone and Rossby-wave dynamics where PV thinking is central, and for long rollouts; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether weather foundation models represent PV as a Lagrangian material invariant.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and public ERA5 data with standard PV/trajectory diagnostics, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: foldon_pathway_ordering_probe
Title: Does the Model Know the Order of Folding? Testing Whether Protein Language Models Represent the Kinetic Foldon Pathway, Not Just the Thermodynamic Native Structure
Short Hypothesis: Protein folding has two distinct mechanisms: the thermodynamic native structure (which contacts exist at equilibrium) and the kinetic folding PATHWAY (the ordered, time-sequenced assembly of cooperative foldon units, early vs late). These are separable: two residues equally important to the native fold can form at very different folding stages, and foldon ORDER is a relational, temporal property invisible to native-contact statistics. We hypothesize that if a protein language model (PLM) represents the kinetic pathway rather than only the native structure, then (a) a residue's folding stage / foldon-order (early-to-late) is decodable from internal representations beyond what native-structure importance predicts, (b) representational coupling between residues is stronger for those that co-fold in the same foldon (kinetic co-assembly) than for distance-matched residues that are native-contacting but fold at different stages, and (c) steering a recovered folding-order axis causally shifts predictions in a stage-consistent way. The same-native-contact/different-fold-stage counterfactual is a mechanism-defining test that native-structure correlation cannot pass.
Related Work: Existing PLM interpretability recovers features aligned with the THERMODYNAMIC native structure: BERTology-Meets-Biology (2020) shows attention captures contact maps and binding sites; InterPLM (2024) and 'Interpreting and Steering PLMs' (2025) recover SAE features for binding sites, motifs, and structural domains; 'Insights Into the Inner Workings' (2023) finds heads correlating with active sites. All validate against static, equilibrium annotations. Separately, decades of biochemistry establish the KINETIC folding pathway as a distinct mechanism: proteins fold via ordered, cooperative foldon units in a defined stepwise pathway (Englander & Mayne 'The nature of protein folding pathways' 2014; 'The case for defined protein folding pathways' 2017), and folding kinetics/order are encoded in sequence and can evolve independently of thermodynamic stability (RNases H ancestral-folding study 2016 shows kinetics and thermodynamics tuned independently; philosophy-of-folding review 2023 stresses thermodynamic vs kinetic explanations are separable). Native-state hydrogen-exchange gives residue-resolved folding-stage/foldon ground truth. Crucially, no interpretability work tests whether a PLM internally represents the kinetic folding ORDER (foldon pathway) as opposed to the native structure, whether that representation is causally load-bearing, or uses a same-native-contact/different-fold-stage counterfactual to separate the two mechanisms. Because native importance and folding stage are correlated (both track structural centrality), native-annotation matching cannot arbitrate this. Our folding-stage-beyond-native probe, foldon-co-assembly coupling test, and folding-order counterfactual are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution.
Abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) are known to encode the thermodynamic native structure of proteins — which residues contact, where binding sites and secondary-structure elements sit. But how a protein reaches that structure is governed by a distinct kinetic mechanism: the folding pathway, in which cooperative units called foldons assemble in a defined temporal order, early foldons forming before late ones. These two mechanisms are separable — folding order can evolve independently of native stability, and a residue's folding stage is a relational, temporal property that native-contact statistics do not reveal — making the kinetic pathway an ideal mechanism-defining probe for whether PLMs learn folding mechanism or merely equilibrium structure. We probe ESM-2 using proteins with residue-resolved folding-stage ground truth from native-state hydrogen-exchange and defined foldon pathways. First, a folding-stage-beyond-native probe: is a residue's foldon-order (early-to-late folding stage) decodable from internal representations beyond what native-structure importance (contacts, solvent accessibility, conservation) predicts? Second, a foldon-co-assembly coupling test: is representational coupling stronger between residues that fold together in the same foldon than between distance-matched native-contacting residues that fold at different stages? Third, and most decisively, a folding-order counterfactual: comparing mutations/perturbations that alter the kinetic pathway (change foldon order or stability) versus native-preserving controls, we test whether the internal folding-order signal responds to kinetic changes specifically. We validate causally by steering a recovered folding-order axis. Metrics quantify a stage-beyond-native index, a co-assembly coupling ratio, and a kinetic-vs-native causal asymmetry. Either outcome sharpens whether PLMs, used for stability and design, represent how proteins fold or only what they fold into.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 -- a residue's folding stage/foldon-order is decodable beyond native-structure importance): Tests clause (a). Data: proteins with residue-resolved kinetic ground truth (existing, used as is): native-state hydrogen-exchange (HX) datasets giving per-residue protection/opening free energies and foldon assignments (cytochrome c, RNase H, and other proteins with published foldon pathways), plus Phi-value datasets giving per-residue transition-state involvement. Because such residue-resolved kinetic data exists for only a modest set of well-studied proteins, we pool ALL available foldon-mapped proteins (~15-20 proteins, ~2,000-4,000 residues total) and report statistics accounting for small protein-level n. Per residue we record foldon/folding-stage order and native-structure features (native contacts, relative solvent accessibility, secondary structure, conservation). Model: ESM-2 150M and 650M (3B as compute allows), public weights, frozen; only linear probes trained. Probes: ridge (continuous stage) and logistic (early-vs-late), L2 via 5-fold CV, 5 seeds with leave-whole-protein-out splits (no residues from a protein shared across splits) to bar leakage; report mean +/- SD. Systems compared: (i) a native-structure baseline predicting folding stage from native-structure features alone; (ii) Stage-Beyond-Native Index = probe R^2 (and early-vs-late accuracy) from the representation minus the native-structure baseline, after residualizing the native-structure-predictable component. Decisive metric first: Stage-Beyond-Native Index. Convincing: Index >= 0.10 R^2 with a 95% bootstrap CI (over held-out proteins) excluding 0, in >=4/5 seeds. Refute: Index <= 0.02 (CI includes 0). Indeterminate band 0.02-0.10 R^2 (stated before the data; especially likely given small protein-level n): unresolved -- reported as underpowered rather than as support or refutation. A negative result means folding stage is explained by native-structure centrality, contradicting clause (a).

Experiment 2 (H2 -- foldon co-assembly coupling): Tests clause (b), the decisive test: co-folding (same-foldon) residues are internally coupled beyond spatial proximity. Data: residue pairs from the foldon-mapped proteins (reused); same-foldon pairs vs distance-matched, native-contacting control pairs from DIFFERENT foldons, matched on 3D distance and native-contact status so the only difference is kinetic co-assembly. Pairs (thousands) give more statistical power than the protein count. Model: frozen ESM-2; coupling measured by how a masked/mutated perturbation at residue i propagates to residue j (and conditional representational dependence). Systems compared: same-foldon pairs vs distance-matched different-foldon native-contacting pairs. Decisive metric first: Co-Assembly Coupling Ratio = coupling(same-foldon) / coupling(distance-matched different-foldon). Convincing: median ratio >= 3 with a 95% bootstrap CI (over pairs, clustered by protein) lower bound > 1.5. Refute: ratio in [0.7, 1.5] (coupling tracks only distance/contact). Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared up front): partial support, reported as qualified. A negative result means coupling tracks native contact rather than co-assembly, contradicting clause (b).

Experiment 3 (H2 -- folding-order mutation counterfactual): Strengthens clause (b) with input-space causal-adjacent evidence. Data: mutations with known kinetic effects (existing, from HX/Phi-analysis): pathway-altering mutations shown to shift foldon order/stability with minimal native-structure change, vs native-preserving/kinetics-neutral control mutations matched on native-structure and conservation change; tens of such mutation pairs across the foldon-mapped proteins. Model: frozen ESM-2, folding-order probe from Experiment 1 reused. Systems compared: pathway-altering vs kinetics-neutral mutation at the affected foldon. Decisive metric first: Kinetic-vs-Native Causal Asymmetry = |folding-order-signal change under the pathway-altering mutation| / |change under the kinetics-neutral control|. Convincing: median asymmetry >= 3 with bootstrap-CI lower bound > 1.5. Refute: asymmetry in [0.7, 1.5]. Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared before the data): partial, reported as qualified. Matched native/conservation change makes generic off-manifold effects shared. A negative result means the model does not respond specifically to kinetic changes, weakening clause (b).

Experiment 4 (H2 -- kinetics-vs-thermodynamics double dissociation): Strengthens clause (b) by showing the folding-order signal tracks the kinetic axis, not stability. Data: proteins/series where folding kinetics and thermodynamic stability vary independently (e.g., the RNase H ancestral series; existing). Model: frozen ESM-2 with the folding-order signal. Systems compared: partial correlation of the internal folding-order signal with folding order controlling for stability, and with stability controlling for order. Decisive metric first: the difference (partial-correlation with kinetics) minus (partial-correlation with stability). Convincing: kinetics partial-correlation >= 0.4 AND exceeds the stability partial-correlation by >= 0.3 (a double dissociation). Refute: the two partial correlations within 0.1 of each other (no dissociation). Indeterminate band: gap 0.1-0.3 (declared up front) -- partial dissociation, reported as qualified. A negative result means the signal is not distinctly kinetic, weakening clause (b).

Experiment 5 (H3 -- steering a folding-order axis shifts predictions stage-consistently): Tests clause (c). Data: early-folding vs late-folding residue sets (reused) to recover the axis. Model: frozen ESM-2; only the direction is fitted, recovered as a supervised probe direction and as an early-minus-late delta, steered at matched L2 norm at target residues. Systems compared: (i) folding-order direction; (ii) 20 matched-norm random directions; (iii) a native-structure-importance direction. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |masked-prediction/variant-effect readout shift under folding-order steering| / |mean shift under random directions|, with stage-consistent sign. Convincing: selectivity >= 3, correct sign, and the native-structure direction failing to reproduce it, across probe and delta recovery. Refute: selectivity <= 1.5. Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared up front): partial causal traction, reported without a strong claim. A negative result means the axis is not causally wired to stage-consistent predictions, contradicting clause (c).

Experiment 6 (H1-H3 -- layer/scale, cross-model analysis, and pathway brackets): Tests robustness of clauses (a)-(c) across depth and model scale. Data: the foldon/Phi-value datasets (reused). Model: ESM-2 150M/650M/3B and (as a comparison) AF2 single-sequence Evoformer representations, frozen; probes/directions as above. Systems compared: (i) Stage-Beyond-Native Index and steering selectivity across layers and from 150M to 3B; (ii) CKA between recovered folding-order subspaces (ESM-2 vs AF2); (iii) upper bracket = an explicit foldon-pathway/HX-derived folding-order model, lower bracket = a native-structure-only predictor with no temporal information. Decisive metric first: fraction of the native-to-kinetic bracket each model closes, and its trend with scale. Convincing: >=50% closure for at least one model AND CKA >= 0.5 between models carrying the signal. Refute: all models within noise of the native-structure lower bracket at all scales. Indeterminate band: 20-50% closure or CKA 0.3-0.5 (declared up front) -- partial/model-specific. A negative result means PLMs represent native structure but not the kinetic pathway. All runs are inference-only on public models plus small probes and public HX/Phi-value/structure datasets, feasible on a single GPU.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Folding stage correlates with native-structure centrality (buried, highly-connected residues often fold early), making the stage-beyond-native separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with native-structure residualization, the distance-matched different-foldon control pairs, the folding-order counterfactual, and the kinetics-vs-thermodynamics double dissociation.

Residue-resolved kinetic ground truth (native-state HX foldon assignments, Φ-values) exists for only a modest set of well-studied proteins, limiting sample size; we pool across all available foldon-mapped proteins (cytochrome c, RNase H, and others) and report statistics accounting for small n, treating the co-assembly and counterfactual tests as the diagnostic core.

Foldon assignments and HX-derived folding order are themselves experimental inferences with uncertainty and some debate (defined-pathway vs energy-landscape views); we restrict decisive tests to well-established foldon pathways, report sensitivity to foldon-assignment confidence, and frame results relative to the specific ground-truth used.

PLMs are trained on evolutionary sequences that reflect native structure, and it is genuinely plausible they encode no kinetic-pathway information; a null result is expected under skepticism. We treat this as scientifically decisive (PLMs represent thermodynamic structure but not the kinetic folding pathway) and include AF2 and an explicit foldon model as brackets.

Linear probes recovering a folding-order axis do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering, the counterfactual, and random/native-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions — we use both probe directions and delta-representations.

In-silico perturbations may push representations off-manifold; we bound perturbation magnitude, use single mild mutations and masking, and report sensitivity, relying on the input-space mutation counterfactual as primary causal-adjacent evidence.

A negative result is directly relevant to trusting PLMs for folding-kinetics-dependent tasks (misfolding, aggregation, folding-rate and pathway design), where the native structure alone is insufficient; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether PLMs represent the kinetic foldon folding pathway distinct from the thermodynamic native structure.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models (ESM-2, optionally AF2 single-sequence) plus small probes and public HX/Φ-value/structure datasets, keeping compute at academic scale.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims requiring novelty are: (1) sequence PLMs encode biochemical kinetic foldon order, not just native thermodynamic structure; (2) residue folding stage is decodable beyond native-structure importance/centrality; (3) same-foldon co-folding residues are more representationally coupled than matched native-contacting residues from different stages; (4) steering a recovered folding-order axis causes stage-consistent prediction shifts; (5) a same-native-contact/different-fold-stage counterfactual plus kinetics-vs-thermodynamics double dissociation can separate pathway information from static structure. From the proposal and search summary, the closest prior family is PLM interpretability for static structure/function features, plus nearby work on computational stages inside ESMFold/AF-style folding trunks. The actual delta is testing biochemical kinetic pathway representations in sequence PLMs against residue-resolved HX foldon annotations, with explicit controls to distinguish kinetics from native structure. That is meaningfully different and non-trivial relative to cited work. The main novelty weakness is that the setting is small and the methods are mostly standard probing/counterfactual tools, so novelty lives more in the finding/test/problem framing than in a new ML mechanism.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is whether PLMs capture kinetic folding pathway information rather than only static native structure. Stakeholders include protein ML researchers, interpretability researchers, folding biophysicists, and protein design/engineering groups interested in folding rate, misfolding, aggregation, and pathway-aware design. This is an important scientific question, and either outcome is informative: a positive result would broaden what PLMs are thought to know; a negative result would sharpen the limits of sequence-only representations. Name: radiative_feedback_pattern_probe
Title: Where the Warming Is, Not Just How Warm: Testing Whether Weather Foundation Models Represent the Pattern-Dependent Radiative Feedback Mechanism, Not Just Global-Mean Temperature
Short Hypothesis: Earth's radiative response to warming is governed by an exactly-known relational mechanism: the top-of-atmosphere (TOA) radiation anomaly is not a function of global-mean surface temperature alone but of the SPATIAL PATTERN of warming (the 'pattern effect'), because local feedbacks (Planck, lapse-rate, cloud, water-vapor) differ by region - e.g., warming concentrated in tropical stratocumulus decks produces a far more negative radiative feedback than the same global-mean warming spread elsewhere. A single scalar mean temperature is degenerate about feedback strength. We hypothesize that if a machine-learning weather/climate emulator represents the radiative-feedback mechanism rather than a mean-temperature-to-radiation shortcut, then (a) the TOA radiation anomaly is decodable from internal representations beyond what global-mean surface temperature predicts, along an axis carrying warming-pattern information, (b) a pattern-holding counterfactual - rearranging the spatial pattern of a surface-temperature anomaly while holding its global mean fixed - shifts the internal radiation/feedback signal as physics dictates, whereas a pattern-preserving amplitude change moves it along the Planck line, and (c) steering a recovered 'pattern-effect' direction causally shifts predicted TOA radiation in the feedback-consistent direction. The same-mean/different-pattern counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that mean-temperature correlation cannot pass.
Related Work: Two lines bracket the gap. (1) ML for radiative feedbacks: 'CNNs Trained on Internal Variability Predict Forced Response of TOA Radiation by Learning the Pattern Effect' (2025) shows a CNN can predict TOA radiation from surface-temperature MAPS and, via XAI saliency, draws skill from physically-meaningful regions; 'Examining Fast Radiative Feedbacks Using ML Weather Emulators' (2026) shows historically-trained emulators reproduce fast CO2 radiative responses at the OUTPUT level; causal-emulation work (Bayesian filtering 2025; forced-response limitations 2025) studies forced responses externally. (2) Weather-model interpretability: SAE studies on GraphCast (2025) recover single instantaneous features (cyclones, atmospheric rivers, sea-ice) and steer them; GraphDOP work (2025) shows a unified world-model representation; the ocean-role study (2026) correlates OUTPUT errors with SST. Crucially, all of these operate at the input-output / saliency level or recover single instantaneous fields - none tests whether a foundation model's INTERNAL representation encodes the RELATIONAL pattern-effect mechanism (that radiative feedback depends on WHERE warming occurs, not just the global mean), whether that representation is causally load-bearing, or uses a same-mean/different-pattern counterfactual to separate the radiative-feedback mechanism from a mean-temperature shortcut. The CNN pattern-effect paper uses saliency to show WHICH regions matter for a prediction; it does not test whether the internal representation encodes feedback as a pattern-dependent quantity distinct from the mean, nor perform causal pattern-holding interventions. Our pattern-effect-beyond-mean probe, same-mean/different-pattern counterfactual, and causal pattern-effect steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, in a safety-critical climate-sensitivity setting.
Abstract: Machine-learning weather and climate emulators are increasingly used to study Earth's response to greenhouse-gas forcing, and interpretability studies have shown they encode recognizable physical fields. But the quantity that ultimately sets climate sensitivity - the top-of-atmosphere (TOA) radiative feedback - is governed by a relational mechanism that a single number cannot express: the 'pattern effect'. The TOA radiation anomaly depends not on global-mean surface temperature alone but on the spatial PATTERN of warming, because local Planck, lapse-rate, cloud, and water-vapor feedbacks differ sharply by region; the same global-mean warming can imply strongly or weakly stabilizing feedback depending on where it is concentrated. This makes the pattern effect an ideal, mechanism-defining probe for whether emulators learn the feedback mechanism or a mean-temperature shortcut. We probe pretrained weather/climate foundation models (GraphCast, Pangu-Weather, and a fast-feedback-capable emulator) on reanalysis and climate-model data where surface-temperature fields, TOA radiation, and diagnosed feedbacks are known. First, a feedback-beyond-mean probe: is the TOA radiation anomaly decodable from internal representations beyond what global-mean surface temperature predicts, along an axis carrying warming-pattern information? Second, and most decisively, a same-mean/different-pattern counterfactual: we rearrange the spatial pattern of a surface-temperature anomaly holding its global mean fixed (which physics says changes the radiative feedback), versus a pattern-preserving amplitude change (which moves along the Planck line), and test whether the internal radiation/feedback signal responds to the pattern - a mean-shortcut model responds only to amplitude. Third, causal steering of a recovered pattern-effect direction. Metrics quantify a feedback-beyond-mean index, a pattern-vs-amplitude causal asymmetry, and a regional-feedback fidelity test. Either outcome sharpens whether emulators represent the mechanism behind climate sensitivity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 -- TOA radiation is decodable beyond global-mean surface temperature, along a pattern-carrying axis): Tests clause (a). Data (existing, used as is): ERA5 surface-temperature fields paired with CERES top-of-atmosphere (TOA) radiation (2000-2022), plus CMIP6 amip-piForcing and abrupt-4xCO2 members and the Green's-function / patterned-SST experiments that provide regional radiative-feedback kernels; per state we record the global-mean surface-temperature anomaly, the warming-pattern field, the TOA radiation anomaly, and the pattern-implied feedback. We use ~10,000 monthly states across reanalysis and CMIP members. Model: GraphCast (~37M) and Pangu-Weather (~256M), plus a fast-feedback-capable emulator (ACE-class), public weights, frozen; only linear probes trained. Because the pattern effect appears in the FAST radiative feedback on weekly timescales, we probe fast-feedback-relevant fields and prioritize the emulator that exposes/can be probed for TOA-relevant output, reporting per-model what is measurable; we probe pre-normalization activations where preprocessing would remove absolute-anomaly information. Probes: ridge, L2 via 5-fold CV, 5 seeds with time-blocked splits; report mean +/- SD. Systems compared: (i) a mean-temperature baseline predicting TOA radiation from global-mean surface temperature (the Planck/shortcut predictor); (ii) Feedback-Beyond-Mean Index = probe R^2 for TOA radiation from the representation minus the global-mean R^2, after residualizing the global-mean-predictable component; (iii) alignment of the recovered radiation direction with a pattern probe vs a mean probe. Decisive metric first: Feedback-Beyond-Mean Index. Convincing: Index >= 0.10 R^2 (95% bootstrap CI over held-out time blocks excluding 0, >=4/5 seeds) with the recovered direction correlating more strongly with the pattern probe than the mean probe. Refute: Index <= 0.02. Indeterminate band 0.02-0.10 R^2 (stated before the data): unresolved -- some pattern-dependent signal but not enough to claim the mechanism; reported as such. A negative result means TOA radiation is explained by global-mean temperature alone, contradicting clause (a).

Experiment 2 (H2 -- same-mean/different-pattern vs pattern-preserving-amplitude counterfactual): Tests clause (b), the decisive counterfactual. Data: ~40 base states from which we build two matched surface-temperature-anomaly edits each: a pattern edit that rearranges the spatial anomaly (e.g., moving warming out of tropical stratocumulus/east-Pacific low-cloud decks) while holding the GLOBAL MEAN exactly fixed (changing feedback by the pattern effect), and an amplitude control edit that scales the anomaly (changing the mean) with the PATTERN fixed (moving radiation along the Planck line). Patterns are drawn from CMIP pattern-effect experiments to stay physically plausible; the global mean is verified fixed. Model: the frozen emulators, inference-only; probe from Experiment 1 as the internal radiation readout. Systems compared: same-mean pattern edit vs pattern-preserving amplitude edit. Decisive metric first: Pattern-vs-Amplitude Causal Asymmetry = |radiation-signal change under the same-mean pattern edit| / |radiation-signal change per unit anomaly magnitude under the amplitude edit, matched on total anomaly magnitude|. Convincing: median asymmetry >= 3 over the 40 states with the pattern edit moving radiation in the feedback-consistent sign in >=70% and bootstrap-CI lower bound > 1.5. Refute: asymmetry in [0.7, 1.5] (negligible response to pattern at fixed mean -- a shortcut). Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared up front): partial support, reported as qualified. Matched magnitude makes any generic off-distribution effect shared. A negative result means feedback does not depend on where warming is, contradicting clause (b).

Experiment 3 (H2 -- regional-feedback fidelity against Green's-function ground truth): Strengthens clause (b) by testing that localized warming produces region-specific feedback, not a uniform response. Data: localized warming patches placed in different regions at fixed global mean (constructed from the base states, reused), with region-specific Green's-function/kernel feedbacks as ground truth (strongly negative for tropical low-cloud regions, weaker elsewhere). Model: frozen emulators with the radiation probe. Systems compared: model-induced regional radiation change vs ground-truth regional feedback; shuffled-region control. Decisive metric first: Spearman correlation between the model's regional radiation response and the ground-truth regional feedback, with sign agreement. Convincing: Spearman >= 0.5 AND sign agreement >= 0.7, shuffled control near 0. Refute: Spearman <= 0.2 or sign agreement <= 0.55 (pattern-agnostic uniform response). Indeterminate band: Spearman 0.2-0.5 or sign agreement 0.55-0.7 (declared before the data) -- partial regional fidelity, reported as qualified. A negative result means the model does not resolve regional feedback differences, weakening clause (b).

Experiment 4 (H3 -- steering a pattern-effect direction shifts predicted TOA radiation the feedback-consistent way, without moving the mean): Tests clause (c). Data: high-feedback vs low-feedback patterns at matched global mean (reused) to recover the direction. Model: frozen emulators; only the direction is fitted, recovered as a supervised probe direction and as a high-minus-low-feedback delta, steered at matched L2 norm. Systems compared: (i) pattern-effect direction; (ii) 20 matched-norm random directions; (iii) a global-mean-temperature direction. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |TOA-radiation readout change under pattern-effect steering| / |mean change under random directions|; cross-talk = |global-mean shift under pattern-effect steering| / |mean shift under the mean direction|. Convincing: selectivity >= 3, correct feedback sign, cross-talk <= 0.2 (radiation moves, global mean barely does), across probe and delta recovery. Refute: selectivity <= 1.5 or cross-talk >= 0.6. Indeterminate band: selectivity 1.5-3 or cross-talk 0.2-0.6 (declared up front) -- entangled/partial control, reported without a clean causal claim. A negative result means the pattern-effect axis is not independently steerable, contradicting clause (c).

Experiment 5 (H1-H3 -- layer emergence, cross-model convergence, and feedback brackets): Tests robustness of clauses (a)-(c). Data: the reanalysis/CMIP states (reused). Model: GraphCast, Pangu, and the fast-feedback emulator, frozen; probes/directions as above. Systems compared: (i) per-layer Feedback-Beyond-Mean Index and steering selectivity; (ii) CKA between recovered pattern-effect subspaces across emulators; (iii) upper bracket = a Green's-function/radiative-kernel model that computes feedback from the pattern by construction, lower bracket = a global-mean-temperature-to-radiation regressor with no pattern access. Decisive metric first: fraction of the mean-shortcut-to-pattern-effect bracket each model closes. Convincing: >=50% closure for at least one model AND CKA >= 0.5. Refute: all models within noise of the mean-only lower bracket. Indeterminate band: 20-50% closure or CKA 0.3-0.5 (declared up front) -- partial/model-specific, no convergence claim. A negative result means emulators predict radiation from global-mean temperature. All runs are inference-only on public FMs plus small probes and public reanalysis (ERA5/CERES) and CMIP pattern-effect data, feasible on a single GPU.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Global-mean surface temperature and warming pattern are correlated in ordinary data, making the feedback-beyond-mean separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with mean-residualization, the same-mean/different-pattern counterfactual (which holds the global mean fixed and varies only the pattern), the regional-feedback fidelity test using Green's-function ground truth, and the amplitude-control edit.

The pattern-rearrangement counterfactual is a synthetic edit; physically-implausible warming patterns may push inputs off the model's training distribution, confounding the pattern response with generic out-of-distribution failure. We mitigate with physically-plausible patterns (drawn from CMIP pattern-effect experiments), verify the global mean is held fixed, compare against amplitude edits of matched magnitude (so any generic OOD effect is shared), and report sensitivity to pattern-edit magnitude.

Many medium-range weather emulators (GraphCast, Pangu) may not directly output TOA radiation and have short rollout horizons, while the pattern effect is usually a decadal/forced concept; we focus on the FAST radiative feedback that is present on weekly timescales (per the 2026 fast-feedback study, historically-trained emulators reproduce it), prioritize emulators that expose or can be probed for radiation-relevant fields, and report per-model what is measurable, treating the fast-feedback-capable emulator as the primary testbed.

Ground-truth regional feedbacks (Green's functions/kernels) are themselves model-derived and uncertain; we use consensus Green's-function experiments and radiative kernels, restrict decisive tests to regions with robust feedback estimates, and report sensitivity to the feedback reference.

Emulators normalize/tokenize inputs, which may remove absolute-anomaly information relevant to radiation; we document each model's preprocessing, probe pre-normalization activations where feasible, and prioritize models retaining the surface-temperature field.

Linear probes recovering a pattern-effect direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering, cross-talk controls, and random/mean-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions - we use both probe directions and delta-representations.

A negative result (models predict radiation from global-mean temperature and fail the same-mean/different-pattern counterfactual) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting ML emulators for climate-sensitivity and pattern-effect studies - precisely where the mean-temperature shortcut breaks for novel warming patterns; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether weather/climate foundation models represent the pattern-dependent radiative feedback mechanism.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and public reanalysis (ERA5/CERES) and CMIP pattern-effect data, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: backdoor_confounder_flip_probe
Title: Does the Model Adjust for Confounders? Testing Whether Tabular/Scientific Foundation Models Represent the Backdoor Simpson's-Flip Mechanism, Not Just Observational Association
Short Hypothesis: The mechanism-defining feature that separates causation from correlation is confounder adjustment: the backdoor criterion says the interventional effect P(Y|do(X)) can differ in sign from the observational association P(Y|X) once a common cause (confounder) is adjusted for - the Simpson's-paradox sign flip. We hypothesize that if a tabular/scientific foundation model (e.g., TabPFN, pretrained over structural causal models) internally represents this adjustment mechanism rather than raw observational association, then (a) the adjusted (interventional) effect direction is decodable from internal representations beyond what the observational association predicts, (b) a confounder-presence counterfactual - supplying versus withholding the confounding variable, holding all else fixed - flips the model's internal effect signal in the Simpson's-flip cases but not in confounder-free cases, and (c) steering a recovered 'adjustment' direction causally moves predictions toward the do-calculus answer. The confounder-in-vs-out sign-flip is an exact, mechanism-defining test that predictive accuracy and observational correlation cannot pass.
Related Work: TabPFN, pretrained on synthetic structural-causal-model datasets, is the natural testbed: 'Does TabPFN Understand Causal Structures?' (2025) shows its mid-layer embeddings contain decodable causal-graph information and beat statistical causal-discovery baselines, but it decodes the STATIC adjacency graph - it never tests whether the model represents the ADJUSTMENT mechanism (backdoor/Simpson's-flip) that distinguishes observational from interventional effects, nor uses a confounder-presence counterfactual. 'How Transformers Learn Causal Structure' (2024) and 'Causal Interpretation of Self-Attention' (2023) show transformers encode latent causal graphs in attention, again structural not adjustment-focused. Benchmark studies (CLadder 2023, CausalPitfalls 2025, 'Ice Cream Doesn't Cause Drowning' 2025, contingency-judgment 2025) show LLMs FAIL at confounding and Simpson's paradox at the OUTPUT/prompt level, but none probes internal representations or performs a causal confounder-in/out counterfactual. My own single-cell d-separation probe tested conditional-independence structure but not the sign-flipping backdoor-adjustment mechanism or a confounder-presence intervention. Because observational association and adjusted effect coincide in confounder-free data, correlation-based benchmarks cannot arbitrate this; the adjusted-effect-beyond-observational probe, confounder-in-vs-out sign-flip counterfactual, and causal adjustment-direction steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution.
Abstract: The single most important distinction in causal inference - and the dominant failure mode of data-driven science - is confounder adjustment: an observed association between a variable X and outcome Y can vanish or even reverse sign once a common cause (confounder) is accounted for, the phenomenon known as Simpson's paradox, formalized by the backdoor criterion. Because a model can predict Y well while relying entirely on the confounded observational association, whether foundation models internally represent the adjustment mechanism is untested and safety-critical: confounding by indication, batch, or population dominates errors in drug-response, clinical, and materials data. We propose the first mechanism-defining, representational test. Using TabPFN - a tabular foundation model pretrained over structural causal models - and a general tabular baseline, we generate datasets with known causal graphs where the observational X-Y association and the true interventional (backdoor-adjusted) effect are controllably concordant or sign-discordant (Simpson's-flip). First, an adjusted-effect-beyond-observational probe: is the true interventional effect direction decodable from internal representations beyond what the observational association predicts, along a distinct axis? Second, and most decisively, a confounder-presence counterfactual: we supply versus withhold the confounding variable, holding all else fixed, and test whether the model's internal effect signal flips toward the adjusted answer specifically in Simpson's-flip cases, while confounder-free cases stay stable; an association-only model responds identically. Third, causal steering of a recovered adjustment direction. Metrics quantify an adjustment-beyond-observational index, a confounder-in-vs-out flip asymmetry, and an interventional-fidelity dose-response. Either outcome sharpens whether these models distinguish do(X) from X.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 -- the backdoor-adjusted interventional effect direction is decodable beyond observational association): Tests clause (a). Data (constructed, because no public dataset pairs tables with exact do-calculus ground truth across matched confounding regimes): 3,000 synthetic datasets from known structural causal models, 1,000 per regime -- (i) confounder-free (observational X-Y association equals the true interventional effect), (ii) magnitude-confounded (adjustment shrinks but preserves the sign), and (iii) Simpson's-flip (a common cause Z makes the observational X-Y association OPPOSITE in sign to the true backdoor-adjusted P(Y|do(X))). For each we record the causal graph, the observational association, and the exact do-calculus effect. Model: TabPFN (~25M parameters, pretrained over structural causal models, per-layer embeddings accessible) and a general tabular baseline (a supervised MLP/gradient-boosting embedding or tabular transformer), public/standard, frozen; only linear probes trained. Probes: logistic (adjusted-effect direction), L2 via 5-fold CV, 5 seeds with dataset-grouped splits; report mean +/- SD. Systems compared: (i) an observational baseline predicting the interventional effect direction from the observational association alone (wrong in Simpson's-flip cases); (ii) Adjustment-Beyond-Observational Index = adjusted-effect accuracy from the representation minus the observational-baseline accuracy, after residualizing the observational-predictable component, reported separately on the Simpson's-flip subset; (iii) angle between the recovered observational-association and adjusted-effect directions. Decisive metric first: Adjustment-Beyond-Observational Index on the flip subset (accuracy points). Convincing: Index >= 10 points (95% bootstrap CI over held-out datasets excluding 0, >=4/5 seeds) AND axis angle >= 60 degrees (distinct axes). Refute: Index <= 2 points and angle <= 20 degrees. Indeterminate band: 2-10 points or angle 20-60 degrees (stated before the data): unresolved -- some adjustment signal but not a cleanly separate axis; reported as such. A negative result means the model encodes only observational association, contradicting clause (a).

Experiment 2 (H2 -- confounder-in-vs-out counterfactual, with a confounder-free control and semi-realistic transfer): Tests clause (b), the decisive counterfactual. Data: from the synthetic sets (reused) each dataset is presented two ways holding the data-generating process fixed -- confounder-in (Z included as an observed column) and confounder-out (Z withheld, so backdoor adjustment is impossible). As a matched control against generic schema change, in confounder-FREE datasets we instead withhold an equally-informative NON-confounding column (which should not flip the effect). We add a semi-realistic transfer check on tables where the adjusted effect is known/estimable (confounding-by-indication in a drug-outcome table; batch confounding in an omics table). Model: frozen TabPFN and the tabular baseline; effect-direction probe from Experiment 1 reused. Systems compared: internal effect signal confounder-in vs confounder-out, in Simpson's-flip vs confounder-free cases. Decisive metric first: Confounder-In-vs-Out Flip Asymmetry = fraction of Simpson's-flip cases whose internal effect signal moves toward the correct sign-flipped adjusted answer when Z is supplied, contrasted with the near-zero change in confounder-free/control cases. Convincing: flip-toward-correct fraction >= 0.8 in flip cases with the confounder-free control change near 0 (< 0.2), and the semi-realistic tables trending the same way. Refute: flip-toward-correct fraction <= 0.4, or equal movement in the control (a schema-change artifact). Indeterminate band 0.4-0.8 (declared up front): partial support, reported as qualified. A negative result means the model does not adjust when the confounder is present, contradicting clause (b).

Experiment 3 (H2 -- interventional-fidelity dose-response sign-crossing): Strengthens clause (b) by testing that the internal signal tracks the do-calculus effect across the sign change rather than the observational association. Data: synthetic datasets (reused) with confounding strength (Z-to-X and Z-to-Y coupling) varied continuously from zero through the sign-flip threshold, with the true do-calculus effect as ground truth. Model: frozen TabPFN/baseline with the adjusted-effect signal. Systems compared: internal adjusted-effect signal vs true interventional effect across the dose ladder; shuffled-confounder control; the observational association as a foil. Decisive metric first: Spearman correlation between the internal signal and the true interventional effect, plus sign-crossing-location agreement (does the internal signal cross zero at the correct confounding strength). Convincing: Spearman >= 0.5 AND the internal sign-crossing within a small tolerance of the true crossing (|delta confounding-strength| <= 0.1 of the swept range), shuffled control near 0. Refute: Spearman <= 0.2 or the signal follows the observational association (no crossing). Indeterminate band: Spearman 0.2-0.5 or crossing offset 0.1-0.25 of the range (declared before the data) -- partial fidelity, reported as qualified. A negative result means the internal signal does not track the do-calculus effect through the flip, weakening clause (b).

Experiment 4 (H3 -- steering an adjustment direction moves predictions toward the do-calculus answer): Tests clause (c). Data: confounder-in vs confounder-out states in flip cases (reused) to recover the direction. Model: frozen TabPFN/baseline; only the direction is fitted, recovered as a supervised probe direction and as a confounder-in-minus-out delta, steered at matched L2 norm. Systems compared: (i) adjustment direction; (ii) 20 matched-norm random directions; (iii) an observational-association direction. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |predicted X->Y effect shift toward the do-calculus answer under adjustment steering| / |mean shift under random directions|. Convincing: selectivity >= 3, movement toward the correct adjusted sign, and the observational-association direction failing to reproduce it, across probe and delta recovery. Refute: selectivity <= 1.5. Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared up front): partial causal traction, reported without a strong claim. A negative result means the adjustment axis is not causally wired to the predicted effect, contradicting clause (c).

Experiment 5 (H1-H3 -- layer emergence, cross-model convergence, and adjustment brackets): Tests robustness of clauses (a)-(c) and whether adjustment structure is specific to SCM-pretrained models. Data: synthetic and semi-realistic tables (reused). Model: TabPFN and the general tabular baseline, frozen; probes/directions as above. Systems compared: (i) per-layer Adjustment-Beyond-Observational Index and steering selectivity (testing the prior expectation that TabPFN's mid layers carry it); (ii) CKA between recovered adjustment subspaces across TabPFN and the baseline; (iii) upper bracket = an explicit backdoor-adjustment estimator computing P(Y|do(X)) by construction, lower bracket = an observational-association regressor with no confounder access. Decisive metric first: fraction of the observational-to-adjustment bracket each model closes. Convincing: >=50% closure for TabPFN AND either cross-model CKA >= 0.5 (convergent) or a clear TabPFN-vs-baseline gap (SCM-pretraining-specific) -- both are informative. Refute: all models within noise of the observational lower bracket. Indeterminate band: 20-50% closure or CKA 0.3-0.5 (declared up front) -- partial/model-specific. A negative result means no model exceeds observational association. All runs are inference-only on public models plus small probes and synthetic/semi-realistic tabular data, feasible on a single GPU.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Observational association and adjusted effect coincide except in confounded cases, making the adjustment-beyond-observational separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with observational-residualization, the confounder-in-vs-out counterfactual (which holds the data-generating process fixed and varies only confounder availability), the Simpson's-flip diagnostic subset, and the dose-response sign-crossing test that an association-only model cannot reproduce.

Withholding the confounder column changes the input dimensionality/schema, which for some tabular models is a structural edit that could confound the comparison with generic distribution shift; we mitigate by using confounder-free datasets (where withholding an equally-informative non-confounding column should NOT flip the effect) as a matched control, so any generic schema-change effect is shared, and report sensitivity.

TabPFN and tabular transformers may implicitly perform some adjustment when all variables are supplied simply by conditioning, blurring 'representing the mechanism' from 'conditioning gives the right answer'; we distinguish these by requiring the correct SIGN FLIP specifically in Simpson's-flip cases, the distinct-axis probe, and the dose-response sign-crossing, none of which a naive conditioner passes without representing adjustment.

Synthetic SCM data gives exact ground truth but may not reflect real confounding structure; we cross-validate on semi-realistic tables (confounding-by-indication, batch confounding) where the true adjusted effect is known or estimable, and report synthetic-vs-real agreement, treating synthetic as the decisive-counterfactual testbed and real as the transfer check.

Linear probes recovering an adjustment direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/observational-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions - we use both probe directions and delta-representations.

A negative result (models encode observational association and fail to flip under confounder presence in Simpson's-flip cases) is scientifically decisive and directly safety-relevant - it would warn against trusting tabular/scientific foundation models for causal-effect estimation in confounded domains (drug outcomes, clinical, omics) where confounding by indication or batch dominates; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining, representational test of whether foundation models represent the backdoor confounder-adjustment mechanism.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models (TabPFN, a tabular baseline) plus small probes and synthetic/semi-realistic tabular datasets, keeping compute at academic scale.

novelty.reasoning: Core claims that would need to be novel are: (1) testing whether a tabular/scientific FM internally represents backdoor confounder adjustment rather than mere observational association; (2) using Simpson's-paradox sign-flip regimes as a mechanism-defining setting where observational and interventional effects diverge; (3) proposing a confounder-present vs withheld counterfactual probe, with matched non-confounder withholding controls, to test whether internal effect signals flip only in confounded cases; (4) steering a recovered 'adjustment direction' to move predictions toward the do-calculus answer; and (5) localizing this mechanism across layers and relative to non-pretrained baselines. The novelty is mainly in the finding/mechanism/test design, not in causal theory itself. Relative to prior work, the closest family is TabPFN causal-structure interpretability and transformer causal-graph decoding; those study static graph information, not whether the model internally computes backdoor adjustment. The proposal's actual delta is therefore meaningful and non-trivial. That said, it is still an extension of existing probing/steering methodology into a new causal-mechanism setting, rather than a brand-new theory or task, so novelty is solid but not exceptional.

If possible, include one genuinely new dataset artifact or benchmark release centered on sign-flip/backdoor cases to strengthen novelty beyond a single-model interpretability study.

impact.reasoning: The phenomenon under study is whether foundation models for tabular/scientific data distinguish causal effect from confounded observational association in the specific, safety-relevant backdoor setting. The stakeholders are causal ML researchers, interpretability researchers, tabular-FM developers, and users deploying such models in confounded scientific domains like clinical prediction, drug response, and omics. The strongest one-line case is: if these models do not internally perform confounder adjustment, they may appear competent while systematically encoding the wrong sign of effect under confounding. This is an important problem, not a niche curiosity, because correlation-versus-causation failures are central in high-stakes scientific use. Even a negative result would be useful, since it would temper claims about causal competence of pretrained tabular models. Follow-up work could build on the probes, benchmark, and failure mode. It is somewhat less likely to shift the entire field than to sharpen evaluation standards within causal/tabular interpretability, so impact is high but not maximal.

review.reasoning: The proposal is technically promising and fairly well scoped, but there are important reviewer-facing gaps. The central hypothesis is interesting and mostly falsifiable, yet the leap from decodable/steerable signal to 'represents the adjustment mechanism' remains the key conceptual vulnerability. The related work is decent but still too broad and slogan-like in places; it needs tighter positioning against exact baselines and exact claims. The experiments are reasonably specific and likely feasible, but several controls are crucial: withholding a confounder changes input schema; sign flips could arise from superficial conditional-statistics heuristics rather than genuine adjustment; and probing/steering can overstate causal use. Synthetic SCM evaluation is appropriate for ground truth but may limit external validity if not carefully parameterized. If executed well, this could be a respectable workshop or niche conference paper, and possibly stronger for a serious ML venue if the controls are rigorous and the claims are narrowed. As written, the narrative slightly overclaims mechanism-level understanding relative to what linear probes and steering can establish.
